---

### Tax Implications on Replacement of FSRU  

**Customs Duty**  
SRO 678(I)/2004 caps customs duty on an FSRU at 5% ad valorem and provides targeted relief for replacement situations. Where an *initial* FSRU is first imported on a stop-gap basis and later substituted with a *primary* FSRU, the SRO allows duty only on the differential value between the two. The rationale is that the initial unit is transitional and not intended as the permanent operating vessel, so the law prevents double taxation of the same base value.  

In contrast, Engro’s plan to permanently replace Exquisite with a new, higher-capacity FSRU represents a **primary-to-primary substitution**. Exquisite was imported as the primary unit and full 5% duty was discharged on its value; the incoming vessel, though leased, will also function as a primary unit for the remaining term. This does not fall within the scope of the proviso, which is confined to initial-to-primary transitions. Extending it to primary replacements would effectively allow indefinite duty-free upgrades, a result inconsistent with both the wording of the SRO and the strict construction of exemptions. Accordingly, the new FSRU will be treated as a fresh import subject to 5% duty on its **entire CIF value**. By contrast, as explained under Scenario 1, temporary replacements for ≤180 days remain fully exempt if re-exported within the prescribed period.  

**Sales Tax**  
The position mirrors Scenario 1. Despite imports generally being taxable at 18% under the Sales Tax Act, 1990, SRO 678 provides a full exemption for FSRUs, whether imported temporarily or as a permanent replacement.  

**Income Tax (Advance Tax at Import Stage)**

- To address the issue of **double taxation** when replacing an already duty-paid FSRU (like *Exquisite*), the 2019 amendment introduced a **differential duty rule**.

# Balochistan Sales Tax 2025 – Key Amendments Explained (Infographic Guide)

【37†embed_image】 *Figure: Visual representation of the Balochistan Sales Tax on Services changes in 2025 (conceptual infographic).* 

## Introduction – From Positive List to **“Tax-All”** Regime  
In 2025, the **Balochistan Finance Act** brought sweeping changes to the Balochistan Sales Tax on Services Act, 2015 (BSTS Act 2015). These amendments fundamentally shift how sales tax on services works in Balochistan. The biggest change: **all services are now taxable by default** unless specifically exempted【31†L4565-L4573】. Previously, only services listed in the law were taxed; now the law adopts a **“negative list”** approach where every service is subject to Balochistan Sales Tax (BST) unless it’s on an exemption list. This update aligns Balochistan with a broader tax base, aiming to improve revenue and reduce ambiguities. 

This blog post breaks down **all the major 2025 amendments** in a clear, non-technical way. We’ll use bullet points, highlights, and simple examples (with infographics placeholders) to help business owners and the general public understand what’s new. Key topics include changes in **definitions**, the expanded **scope** of tax, new **tax rate schedules**, **reverse charge** mechanisms, updated **exemptions**, **special procedures**, and new **compliance obligations**. 

> **Important:** Effective July 1, 2025, **every service** provided in Balochistan is considered a taxable service **unless** it’s specifically listed as exempt【10†L1774-L1782】. Business owners should review the new exemption schedule to see if their service is exempt; if not, BST at the standard rate applies.

## Definitions and Scope – *What’s Taxable and Who’s Covered*  
**Broader Definition of “Service”:** The law now defines *“service”* very broadly. Essentially any activity, facility, or advantage provided for consideration counts as a service【5†L1537-L1545】. Even if some goods are involved incidentally (e.g. providing equipment along with a service), it’s still treated as a service【5†L1539-L1547】. This closes loopholes where mixing goods with services might avoid tax. 

**“Economic Activity” Clarified:** A new comprehensive definition of **economic activity** is inserted (Section 6 substituted). It covers **any activity (profit-oriented or not)** that involves providing or consuming a service for consideration【9†L1624-L1632】【9†L1642-L1650】. This explicitly includes: 

- **Digital and online services:** Providing services through digital platforms or software, even if the provider has no physical presence in Balochistan【9†L1642-L1650】. *(For example, a non-resident company offering online streaming to Balochistan customers is engaged in “economic activity” in the province.)*  
- **Inter-provincial or international services:** Services used or enjoyed in Balochistan are considered provided in Balochistan【9†L1648-L1656】【9†L1659-L1667】. This means if a business in Quetta avails an out-of-province consultant’s service, it’s taxable in Balochistan.  
- **Clubs and nonprofits:** Services by clubs, societies, or trusts to their members are considered economic activities even if not for profit【9†L1640-L1648】【9†L1649-L1657】. 

The law also spells out what *doesn’t* count as economic activity. Notably, an individual’s services as an **employee to their employer** are not taxable services【9†L1672-L1680】. Normal employer-employee contracts remain outside BST. However, if workers are provided by a third-party manpower supplier or contractor, those **are** taxable services despite being “in-house” work【9†L1678-L1687】. The distinction is clarified to prevent hiding a taxable service under the guise of salaried employment. 

**All Services Taxable (Scope Expansion):** Section 3 was amended to state unequivocally that **“Every service is a taxable service”** if provided by a person from a business/place in Balochistan, as part of an economic activity【5†L1557-L1564】. It no longer matters whether the service is provided to a local or a foreign customer – if the provider is in Balochistan, it’s taxable【5†L1559-L1566】. Likewise, services provided by **non-residents to customers in Balochistan** are now taxable in Balochistan (this implies the local recipient may have to pay the tax – more on that in reverse charge below)【5†L1576-L1584】. 

**Omitted Definitions:** With such a broad scope, the Act **removed dozens of specific service definitions** that previously existed in Section 2. Terms like *“Accountant”, “beautician”, “banker”, “advertisement”*, and many others were **deleted**【5†L1515-L1523】【5†L1524-L1532】. Why? Because when all services are taxable by default, you no longer need to individually define each service category in the law. This streamlines the act – making it shorter and focused on general principles. It also introduced a definition for **“CPC” (Central Product Classification) codes** to standardize service classification【5†L1530-L1538】. The Balochistan Revenue Authority (BRA) can now adopt internationally recognized CPC codes to categorize services【31†L4603-L4607】【18†L2383-L2391】, which helps in consistent reporting and aligning with global service categories.

**Transitional Provision:** A new Section 10A was added to ensure a smooth shift to the new regime. It basically says any service not listed in the exemption schedule (*First Schedule*) **“shall be deemed to be taxable” from July 1, 2025**【10†L1774-L1782】. If any service was previously enjoying an exemption through a notification, that stays in place until BRA amends or withdraws it【10†L1775-L1782】. In simple terms, **businesses should assume their service is taxable unless they find it on the new exemption list or have a valid official exemption**. BRA has grandfathered existing notified exemptions for now, to be reviewed later.

## Tax Rates and New Schedules – *Standard Rate, Higher Rate, Reduced Rate*  
**Standard Rate 15%:** The general sales tax rate on services in Balochistan remains **15% of the service value**【9†L1739-L1747】. This is the amount a service provider must charge and remit for taxable services. The Finance Act 2025 reaffirmed this in the revised Section 10(1)【9†L1739-L1746】. 

**Multiple Schedules Introduced:** The amendment replaced the old system of schedules. Previously, Balochistan had a Second Schedule listing taxable services. That’s gone. Now we have: 

- **First Schedule – Exempt Services:** Services listed here are **not taxable** (often with conditions). Section 10(2) now directly links to this schedule【31†L4577-L4585】. If your service is in the First Schedule, you don’t charge BST (subject to any conditions specified). This schedule was overhauled in Finance Act 2025【31†L4565-L4573】. For example, **small businesses** in certain sectors are exempt – one entry exempts *“Accommodation, food and beverage services”* by small caterers with annual turnover under Rs. 2.5 million【18†L2427-L2435】【18†L2437-L2445】. (Infographic idea: A chart of key exempt service categories and thresholds). BRA can also impose conditions on exemptions via notification【10†L1797-L1804】. 

- **Second Schedule – Higher Tax Rates:** Some services may attract a rate above 15%. The new Section 10(3) points to a Second Schedule for any services with **“such higher rate”**【10†L1745-L1753】. For instance, **telecommunications** is one sector often taxed at higher rates (e.g. 19.5% in some provinces). In Balochistan, telecommunication services continue at **19.5%**; the Act even adjusted input tax rules to accommodate this (telecom providers charging ≥19.5% can claim inputs taxed up to 18%)【11†L1920-L1928】【11†L1921-L1927】. The Second Schedule lists all such exceptions where the rate is above 15%. *(Business tip: If you operate in a sector like telecom, check Second Schedule for your specific rate.)*

- **Third Schedule – Reduced (Concessional) Rates:** The new Section 10(4) introduces a Third Schedule for services taxed at a **“lower rate… without input tax adjustment”**【10†L1749-L1757】. That means certain services have a discounted GST rate but cannot claim purchase tax credits. Commonly, this is used for incentivizing sectors or simplifying tax for small service providers (charging a low fixed rate but no input credit facility). For example, professional services like **lawyers’ fees** might be taxed at a fixed nominal amount per case instead of 15% ad valorem in Balochistan – indeed, the updated schedules set a **fixed tax of Rs. 500 per case** for legal practitioners (instead of a percentage)【28†L4194-L4202】【28†L4213-L4217】. Some other professional services (accountants, consultants, etc.) have reduced rates (e.g. 5% without input adjustment) to encourage compliance in previously hard-to-tax sectors【28†L4188-L4196】【28†L4209-L4217】. 

**Choice to Pay Standard Rate:** An important facility – if your service is listed for a **reduced rate without input tax**, you have the **option to pay 15% with input tax instead**. The existing Section 16D allows a service provider to opt out of the concession and go with the full 15% so they can claim input tax credits【31†L4583-L4588】. This flexibility is useful if your business has significant taxable purchases (inputs); you might prefer to charge full tax and recover input tax rather than forego credits.

**Government’s Power to Modify Rates:** The Finance Act empowered the provincial government (with BRA’s recommendation) to change tax rates for any service via official notification【31†L4589-L4597】. They can declare specific services or providers to be charged at **higher, lower, fixed, or specific rates** as needed【31†L4589-L4593】. This means going forward, rate changes for certain industries might not require a new Act – the government can adjust by notifying in the Gazette (e.g. a temporary reduction for an industry or a new fixed tax scheme). For businesses, it’s important to stay alert to BRA notifications for any rate changes. 

**Annual Turnover Thresholds:** The BRA now has explicit authority to **set turnover thresholds for exemption**【31†L4593-L4598】. With government approval, BRA can say, for example, that service providers with turnover below (say) Rs. 5 million need not register or pay tax. This was added as Section 10(6)【10†L1759-L1767】. It’s a pro-small-business measure to **exempt very small service providers**. Currently, BRA has set certain thresholds in the First Schedule (like the 2.5 million for caterers as noted), and more general thresholds could come via notification. If you’re a small business, watch out for such threshold announcements – it could mean you fall out of the tax net entirely. 

> **Note:** The Second Schedule that used to list taxable services was **omitted** entirely【31†L4565-L4569】. This symbolizes the shift to the new regime. Now, **First Schedule = Exempt list** (everything else is taxable). Businesses should obtain the updated First, Second, and Third Schedules (2025) from BRA to know where their services stand in terms of tax rate or exemption.

## Reverse Charge and Withholding – *Who Pays the Tax?*  
Normally, the **service provider** is responsible for charging and paying sales tax on services. The 2025 amendments reinforce and expand cases where the **service recipient** must pay (known as **reverse charge** or withholding). This is crucial for services imported into Balochistan or certain sectors.

**Non-Resident Services – Reverse Charge:** As mentioned, if a foreign or out-of-province provider renders a service consumed in Balochistan, that service is taxable here【5†L1576-L1584】. Practically, since the provider is not registered in Balochistan, the **recipient in Balochistan is made liable** for the tax. The law now clearly treats that service as taxable and allows BRA to enforce tax on the local recipient (reverse charge mechanism). For example, if a company in Balochistan hires a consulting firm from abroad, the local company must self-assess 15% BST on the fee and deposit it to BRA, since the foreign firm won’t. 

**Specific Reverse Charge Case – International Calls:** A new proviso was added in Section 4(5) targeting **incoming international telephone calls**. Now, Pakistan telecommunication companies terminating international calls in Balochistan must pay BST **on a reverse charge basis** for the portion of revenue they receive from abroad【5†L1589-L1597】. In simpler terms, if an overseas call is made to a phone in Balochistan, the local telecom operator is deemed the recipient of an international service and must pay sales tax on the charges they get from the foreign carrier【5†L1593-L1600】. This plug ensures tax is paid on international telecom traffic – previously a gray area.

**Withholding Agents:** The Act inserted the phrase **“as a withholding agent”** in Section 4(2)【5†L1585-L1592】. This means certain recipients of services (usually large buyers or government bodies) are designated to **withhold the sales tax** out of the payment and directly remit it to the government. For instance, if a provincial department is paying a contractor for services, it might deduct the 15% BST from the payment and send that to BRA, instead of the contractor doing it. The law now explicitly includes this mechanism. Moreover, **any person specified by government** can be made to pay the tax on certain services on behalf of the provider【9†L1617-L1625】. Section 4(9) added in 2025 says the government may notify **additional categories of services subject to reverse charge**, where the recipient will be liable for the tax【9†L1617-L1622】. This gives flexibility to extend reverse charge to, say, sectors where providers are unorganized or outside Balochistan’s jurisdiction. 

**Examples of Reverse Charge:** BRA has the power now to declare via notification that *“Service X will be taxed from the buyer instead of seller.”* Potential examples: services acquired from unregistered persons, or services like rentals or royalties where the payer can be asked to withhold. The amendment’s wording is broad【9†L1617-L1625】, so businesses might see new reverse charge notifications in 2025 onward (e.g. requiring companies to withhold tax on payments to freelancers or unregistered small service providers). 

**Liability of Unregistered Persons:** A new Section 25(3A) was inserted to ensure **no one can escape tax by staying unregistered if they have tax obligations**【13†L2049-L2057】. It states that if a person is *“required to withhold and pay”* tax under the Act or rules (even if they don’t provide taxable services themselves), they **“shall be deemed as a registered person for all legal purposes”**【13†L2051-L2059】. In other words, an unregistered client who must deduct tax is treated like a registered taxpayer – if they fail to comply, they face penalties just like a registered person would. BRA can require such persons to **enroll** or fulfill formalities for withholding【13†L2053-L2060】. For businesses, this means if you’re on the hook to withhold tax (e.g. a large company paying unregistered service providers), you must follow through, even if you’re not otherwise registered for BST. Failing to do so can invite penalties.

**Special Procedure for Collection (Section 14A):** A brand-new Section 14A empowers BRA to make **any person or class of persons** (whether or not they are the service provider or recipient) to **collect tax on its behalf**【10†L1852-L1860】. This is essentially a legal basis for withholding tax arrangements. For example, BRA could require **banking companies** to collect sales tax on credit card service fees, or require **online platforms** to collect tax on services sold through them. The person tasked with collecting must then deposit that tax to the government. If they fail to collect or deposit, **they become personally liable for the tax, plus default surcharge and penalties**【10†L1869-L1876】. This is a potent tool to enforce tax at source. From a business perspective, if you are in a position where you handle payments for others’ services (like an aggregator or marketplace), BRA could rope you in to collect the tax. Always check BRA’s special procedure notifications to see if your industry has such obligations.

In summary, the amendments significantly tighten the **reverse charge and withholding regime**: more scenarios where the **service receiver** or even a third party must pay the BST. This ensures services coming into Balochistan or hard-to-tax transactions don’t slip through the cracks.

## Exemptions and Special Procedures – *What’s Not Taxed and Special Cases*  
**Updated Exemption List:** As noted, the **First Schedule** now lists exempt services (replacing the old concept where the law only listed taxable ones). The Finance Act 2025 substituted Section 12 entirely to outline the exemption framework【10†L1796-L1804】. Key points: services **specified in the First Schedule are exempt** from tax, **subject to any conditions** set by the government【10†L1797-L1804】. This means the exemption may depend on meeting certain criteria (e.g. turnover limits, location, nature of service). For instance, certain educational, health, or public services might be exempt to relieve consumers, or small-scale providers enjoy exemption thresholds as mentioned. It’s crucial to read the fine print of the First Schedule entries.

The Government (on BRA’s advice) can **add or remove exemptions** by notification, even with retrospective effect【10†L1811-L1819】. So, exemptions aren’t set in stone annually; they can evolve mid-year if needed. The First Schedule introduced in 2025 includes many conditional exemptions. **Example:** Small caterers (turnover <2.5m) are exempt, *but* if they operate within a hotel premises, the exemption won’t apply【18†L2427-L2435】【18†L2437-L2445】. Another example: certain non-profit services or government services might be listed as exempt. Business owners should carefully check if any exemption covers their activity and ensure they meet any conditions attached (like registration with an authority, or a cap on annual revenue).

**Reverse Exemptions:** Interestingly, Section 25(3AA) now allows BRA to **force even exempt service providers to register and file returns** in special cases【13†L2062-L2069】. If BRA notifies a class of exempt services for registration, those providers must comply (even though they don’t pay tax) and submit returns. This could be used to monitor sectors that are exempt to prevent abuse or gather data.

**Special Procedures (Section 14):** The Finance Act replaced Section 14(1) to broaden BRA’s power to devise **special procedures**【10†L1821-L1829】. BRA can, by notification, prescribe special rules for **payment of tax, valuation, registration, record-keeping, invoicing, returns, and “other related matters”** for any service or class of service【10†L1821-L1829】. This gives flexibility to tailor rules for different industries. For example, BRA could introduce a **simplified scheme for small service providers** (like a fixed quarterly tax), or a special **telecom sector regime** for billing, or special invoicing requirements for restaurants, etc. These procedures override the normal rules, to the extent specified. The idea is to make compliance easier or administration more effective in specific cases. If you’re in an industry that might benefit from tailored rules (say, **ride-hailing services** or **digital platforms**), keep an eye on BRA notifications – a special procedure might apply to you, altering how you calculate or pay tax.

**Example:** BRA had already introduced in 2022 an **online business integration** service fee (as per Special Procedure Rules 2022). The 2025 amendment adds a penalty (Serial 2C in the penalty schedule) for failing to deposit that *“service fee”*【17†L2177-L2185】【17†L2193-L2201】, showing BRA’s intent to enforce special schemes. So if a special procedure requires you to pay a fixed fee or additional levy, non-compliance can now trigger fines and even imprisonment【17†L2179-L2187】【17†L2193-L2201】. 

**No Double Taxation or Classification Issues:** A new Section 78B was added to handle **classification of services**【18†L2374-L2382】. BRA can prescribe a classification system (likely using CPC codes) for uniform categorization【18†L2385-L2393】. Importantly, it says using a code system doesn’t by itself change the taxability of a service【18†L2391-L2399】 – it’s just for organizing information. And if any confusion arises in classification during transition, BRA can issue clarifications or transitional rules【18†L2399-L2407】. For businesses, this means the description of your service in the law or schedules might now include a **CPC code**, but if a code reclassifies your service, BRA assures it won’t invalidate prior taxes or suddenly tax something previously exempt just by recoding it【18†L2391-L2399】. It’s an administrative improvement for clarity.

Finally, Section 14(3) was tweaked to clarify that in any special procedure or otherwise, if you default, the recovery can include **penalty** as well as tax and surcharge【1†L1839-L1847】【1†L1849-L1856】. They simply made sure **penalties** are explicitly collectible, closing a small gap in wording.

## Compliance and Administrative Changes – *Tightening the Rules*  
The 2025 amendments place a strong emphasis on **compliance**. Many changes aim to ensure more people register, file returns, and pay on time, and that BRA has the tools to enforce the law. Here are the key compliance-related changes:

- **Mandatory Registration & No Escape:** Section 25(1) now adds that if you are a **withholding agent**, you must register under the Act【13†L2043-L2051】. Combined with Section 25(3A) (deeming unregistered withholders as registered【13†L2051-L2059】), this means **no one with tax liability can legally stay unregistered**. Moreover, a new subsection in Section 1(!) was inserted (perhaps meant to be Section 11 or a general provision) stating **“No person shall be absolved of any tax liability for want of registration”**【10†L1784-L1792】. In plain terms, *not registering is not an excuse to avoid tax.* BRA can come after you for the tax due even if you failed to register. So, businesses should register as required; flying under the radar is no longer an option—if it ever was.

- **Temporary Suspension of Registration:** BRA can now **temporarily inactivate or suspend** a registration (Section 28(1) amended)【13†L2070-L2078】. This might be used if a business is non-compliant or has ceased operations. Suspension can prevent a taxpayer from issuing tax invoices, etc., until issues are resolved. It’s a tool to enforce compliance (e.g. if you don’t file returns for months, BRA might suspend your registration).

- **E-Invoicing and Digital Recordkeeping:** A major modernization is the push toward **electronic invoicing**. Section 30(3) was substituted to explicitly allow that a registered service provider **“may… issue invoices electronically”** and transmit copies to the BRA’s system as specified【11†L1978-L1986】. This legal cover paves the way for BRA’s e-invoicing system (integrating sales data in real-time). In fact, the penalty schedule now includes a hefty penalty (Serial 2B) for not complying with the **e-invoicing system requirements**【17†L2157-L2165】【17†L2166-L2174】. If a person *“voids, defies, fails to comply with the e-invoicing system or issues invoices outside the e-invoicing system”*, BRA can impose up to Rs. **100,000** penalty (minimum Rs. 10,000) and even seal the business premises for repeat offense【17†L2157-L2165】. Plus, criminal prosecution is possible (up to one year jail) for willful non-compliance with e-invoicing【17†L2166-L2174】. This is a strong signal that BRA is implementing electronic invoicing (perhaps via POS integrations or software reporting). Business owners should prepare to adopt whatever e-invoice solution BRA mandates to avoid these penalties.

- **Invoice Contents:** Section 30(1) got some cosmetic changes – essentially to properly punctuate a list of required invoice details and **add one new requirement**. Now invoices must also show the **“applicable rate of tax”** on the invoice【13†L2083-L2091】. That’s the new clause (g) added. So a sales tax invoice in Balochistan should include: name, address, etc., and now the tax rate (e.g. 15% or 5% etc.) in addition to the amount of tax. This helps transparency for the buyer and auditor to know what rate was applied.

- **Returns and Filing:** Section 35(1) explicitly added that **“Every registered person shall e-file** or file a return…”【11†L2003-L2006】. E-filing was already the norm, but now the law uses the term “e-file” to keep up with the times (manual filing is virtually phased out). More notably, a new subsection 35(7) was added requiring even **persons who deal only in exempt or non-taxable services** to **file periodic declarations** if BRA asks【11†L2007-L2016】. BRA can notify such persons or class (e.g. perhaps large organizations providing exempt services) to submit a return/declaration with information, even if no tax is due【15†L2010-L2018】. Failing to file these nil returns is treated as failure to file a tax return (penalties can apply)【15†L2015-L2023】. The rationale is BRA wants data on economic activities even if exempt – to curb misuse and maintain records. So, if you get notified by BRA to file a “null return” periodically, don’t ignore it thinking “I don’t owe tax” – it’s legally obligatory. 

- **Audit and Enforcement Powers:** Several adjustments strengthen BRA’s hand in audits and recovery:
  - Section 39(1) added new categories of officers – **“Inspector of the Balochistan Revenue Authority”** and **“any officer… with any other designation”** as authorized persons【15†L2021-L2027】. This means BRA can appoint inspectors and variously titled officers to enforce the Act, expanding the team that can visit and check businesses.
  - Section 39(3) was replaced (text not fully shown in source) to likely update how officers are authorized【15†L2021-L2029】. Possibly to streamline appointments or powers.
  - Section 40(1) now clarifies that an officer’s powers include specified **pecuniary (value) and territorial jurisdiction** as assigned【13†L2103-L2112】. This just formalizes that BRA can limit an officer’s authority to certain areas or cases.
  - Section 41 (Delegation of powers) was updated: changing designations (Additional Commissioner replaced by Deputy Commissioner as appellate authority)【13†L2107-L2114】, removing one clause (perhaps redundant layer)【13†L2110-L2115】, and adding a new subsection 41(4) to avoid conflict of interest in appeals【13†L2115-L2123】. The new 41(4) says a Commissioner (Appeals) shall **not hear an appeal against an order he himself passed** in original capacity【13†L2115-L2123】 – obviously to ensure fairness, and BRA must arrange an alternative in such cases (i.e., a different officer will handle that appeal).
  - Section 44(2) now has a proviso that if a case is already under trial by the Special Judge (i.e. in criminal court for tax fraud), BRA’s officers are **not barred from completing departmental adjudication for tax recovery simultaneously**【13†L2123-L2131】. In other words, just because you’re being prosecuted in court doesn’t halt BRA from finalizing the tax due and issuing an order. This closes a loophole where some might argue sub-judice (under trial) matters should pause tax assessment – BRA can now proceed in parallel【13†L2123-L2130】.
  - A big change in appeals: **Section 47A – Appeal to High Court** is introduced【13†L2132-L2140】. This allows any person or even the government to appeal to the High Court against the decision of the Special Judge (who handles BST offenses) within 60 days【13†L2134-L2142】. It basically mirrors the federal law by providing a second tier of appeal in criminal tax cases, and applies the High Court’s usual procedures. For most business owners, this may not be directly relevant (it’s for serious tax evasion cases), but it’s good to know the legal hierarchy: Special Judge’s order isn’t necessarily final if there’s an error of law – one can go to the High Court.

- **Penalties Overhaul:** The Finance Act 2025 made numerous additions and revisions in the penalty provisions (Section 48 and 49):
  - As mentioned, a new penalty (Serial 1) now penalizes not just providing taxable services without registration, but also **receiving taxable services without registration when required**【17†L2146-L2154】. This correlates to the idea that if you needed to register as a **service recipient (withholding agent)** and didn’t, you face penalties. They also removed the word “taxable” in that context【17†L2146-L2154】, implying even if you are dealing in what you *think* are exempt services but were required to register (due to a BRA notification, for example), you could be penalized. 
  - We covered Serial 2B (e-invoicing penalty) and 2C (failure to deposit **service fee** under integration rules) which are new【17†L2157-L2165】【17†L2175-L2183】. 
  - Serial 5 (failure to furnish information or allow access to records) was replaced and toughened. Now, not providing documents or data when asked incurs **Rs. 100,000 penalty for each default**【17†L2209-L2217】【17†L2224-L2232】. If you ignore three notices over three months to produce records, it’s deemed you **failed to maintain records** (another offense)【17†L2219-L2227】【17†L2241-L2243】. Criminal charges (up to one year jail) can also follow【17†L2229-L2237】. This is a wake-up call to maintain proper records and respond to BRA’s notices. 
  - Serial 7A is new: it penalizes any person who **denies or obstructs the entry of a BRA officer** posted to monitor their business premises【17†L2248-L2256】. The penalty is **Rs. 100,000 or two times the minimum tax amount** (as assessed) whichever is higher【17†L2251-L2258】, plus potential prosecution up to one year jail【17†L2259-L2266】. BRA sometimes posts inspectors at big businesses to monitor real-time sales – now if someone tries to stop them or not cooperate, there’s a direct penalty clause. 
  - Serial 10 was tweaked: if a person **refuses to receive a notice or order** from the tax officer, that itself is an offense now【17†L2270-L2278】. Also, previously Serial 10’s further penalty reference to non-compliance cited wrong sections; they corrected it to refer to Section 40 (which deals with powers of officers)【17†L2273-L2276】. This basically means dodging service of an order (e.g. not signing or accepting a delivered notice) won’t help – it’s punishable. 
  - Serial 14 (likely about tax fraud or causing revenue loss) was amended so that the penalty can be **up to the amount of tax loss or Rs. 25,000, whichever is higher**【17†L2277-L2281】. Before, there might have been a lower fixed penalty; now it’s scaled to the damage caused – 100% of the tax evaded at minimum. This deters willful evasion by making the penalty equal to the evaded amount (doubling the cost when you pay the due tax plus penalty).
  - Section 49(2) minor edit: removed the word “sixteenth”【17†L2283-L2290】, which probably aligned with the omission of the Second Schedule (perhaps it was referencing an outdated schedule entry for late payment surcharge date which is on 16th of a month in some laws – but in any case, a tiny cleanup not affecting taxpayers directly).

- **Recovery without Notice:** A significant addition is the new Section **52A: Un-paid and Short Paid Amounts Recoverable Without Notice**【18†L2297-L2305】【18†L2319-L2327】. If BRA’s audit or computerized systems show that a registered person **charged sales tax from customers but didn’t deposit it** (or deposited short), BRA can **directly recover that amount by attaching the person’s bank accounts, without issuing a show-cause notice**【18†L2299-L2307】【18†L2319-L2327】. This is a strong measure to catch those who collect tax and pocket it. It bypasses the usual lengthy adjudication – since the fact that tax was charged and not paid is evidence enough. However, BRA must get approval from the Commissioner or Authority before freezing accounts【18†L2321-L2328】, and importantly, **no penalty** under Section 48 will be imposed without giving a notice【18†L2323-L2331】【18†L2327-L2329】. So you won’t get penalized or jailed without due process, but the core tax and default surcharge can be yanked from your bank pretty much immediately. The lesson: **Don’t ever collect BST and fail to remit it** – BRA now has power to swoop in and take it. Businesses should ensure the amount of sales tax charged to clients is safely kept and paid to the government, not used as working capital.

- **Audit Inventory:** Section 56(4) is added to make audit proceedings more transparent. When BRA seizes documents or records during an audit or raid, they must make an **inventory list** of all items taken, and have it jointly signed by the officer and the taxpayer (or their representative)【18†L2330-L2338】. If the taxpayer refuses to sign, it won’t invalidate the inventory【18†L2333-L2337】, but at least BRA will document what was seized. This protects both sides – you have a list of what papers/USBs were taken, and BRA can’t later add something that wasn’t there. For business owners, whenever records are impounded, insist on an inventory and try to have a representative present to sign it. This amendment shows a commitment to procedural fairness during enforcement.

- **Time Limits Extended:** The amendment to Section 52(1) changed “five” to “eight” years【17†L2283-L2291】, likely extending the period for BRA to issue certain assessment orders (commonly, tax statutes allow assessments within so many years from the relevant date). If this aligns with other provinces, it means BRA can go back **8 years** to assess unpaid tax, up from the previous 5-year limit. This gives BRA a longer window to audit past periods. Businesses should thus keep records for at least 8 years (as record-keeping requirements likely align with this; federal law is also 6 years and moving to 8). Similarly, Section 67(3) changed “Two” to “Twenty”【18†L2361-L2364】 – this might refer to an increase in a monetary limit or a time period in recovery or appeal (possibly it’s about 2% default surcharge to 20% in some context, but likely a typo fix or aligning with federal law on automatic stay of recovery on 10% payment, etc.). Regardless, it suggests more stringent or longer allowances for BRA in appeals or recovery.

- **Administrative Titles:** Various changes simply replace *“Additional Commissioner”* with *“Deputy Commissioner”* and *“Deputy”* with *“Assistant Commissioner”* in sections 60, 67, 71 etc【18†L2339-L2347】【18†L2359-L2367】. This is an administrative reorganization to presumably flatten the hierarchy (perhaps BRA’s structure now uses Deputy Commissioners where previously Additional Commissioners were mentioned). It doesn’t directly affect taxpayers except knowing who might sign your orders – e.g. appeals that earlier may be handled by an Additional Commissioner (Appeals) now a Deputy Commissioner (Appeals) could do.

- **Worker Welfare Cess Exemption for Mega Projects:** (This was a brief item in our sources around Section 19). Although not the main BST Act, the Finance Act also mentioned that **foreign investments ≥ $1.5 Billion** in Balochistan shall be exempt from the Balochistan Workers Welfare Act, 2022【5†L1495-L1503】【5†L1497-L1504】. This is a side note but of interest to large investors – a kind of incentive for mega projects (though not directly related to sales tax, it appeared in the same amendment section possibly).

**Bottom line:** The compliance environment is now stricter – **register, e-invoice, file your returns, pay your collected tax, cooperate with audits** – or face substantial penalties. BRA has more power to enforce and you have fewer loopholes to hide behind. On the flip side, honest taxpayers benefit from clearer rules (e.g. clarity in definitions, ability to e-invoice, appeals structure) which makes it a more level playing field in the long run.

## Conclusion – What Should Businesses Do?  
The Balochistan Finance Act 2025 has thoroughly amended the sales tax framework on services. It marks a shift to a **“tax everything, exempt a few”** model, bringing Balochistan in line with Sindh and other provinces’ approach of broad taxation. Business owners and service providers in Balochistan need to **adapt quickly** to these changes: 

- **Review the new schedules:** Find out if your service is now taxable or exempt, and at what rate. Don’t assume old exemptions or exclusions still apply – check the **First, Second, Third Schedules (2025)**【31†L4577-L4585】. (For example, many previously untaxed services are now taxable because they’re not on the exemption list.)  

- **Ensure registration and compliance:** If you’re providing or even just *receiving* taxable services, make sure you’re properly **registered with BRA** (or enrolled as withholding agent). The new mantra is “no escape from liability through non-registration”【10†L1784-L1792】. It’s far better to come forward voluntarily than to be caught unregistered – penalties are harsh for non-filers now, and BRA can back-tax you for up to 8 years. 

- **Implement e-invoicing and record systems:** Embrace technology for tax compliance. BRA is heading towards e-invoicing and real-time reporting【11†L1978-L1986】, with heavy penalties for those who resist【17†L2157-L2165】. Invest in compliant invoicing software or systems that can integrate with BRA’s requirements (e.g. generate the required **BST invoice with all details** including tax rate, and perhaps QR codes or whatever BRA mandates). Keep your accounting records tidy and readily available for inspection – and *do not* think about suppressing sales, because e-invoicing will make that near-impossible.

- **Train your staff or consult advisors:** The changes in legal language can be confusing. It’s wise to train your accounting and sales staff on issues like **withholding tax on services, reverse charge scenarios, new invoicing rules, filing nil returns**, etc. For instance, your purchase department should know that if they buy a service from an unregistered vendor or a foreign supplier, **you may have to pay the tax** (reverse charge). Your billing staff should know to charge 15% by default unless an exemption or reduced rate clearly applies. Engaging a tax consultant or attending a BRA seminar on the Finance Act 2025 changes (if available) could save you from costly mistakes.

- **Monitor BRA Notifications:** Many of these amendments empower BRA to make further rules via notifications (e.g. specifying **withholding categories【9†L1617-L1625】, turnover thresholds【31†L4593-L4598】, special procedures【10†L1821-L1829】, etc.). Stay updated by regularly checking the BRA website or subscribing to a tax news service. New **BRA amendments 2025** updates could come at any time altering practical implementation.

From a broader perspective, these reforms aim to **increase the tax net** (by covering all services and plugging loopholes) and **modernize tax administration** (through e-invoicing and data sharing). If compliant, many businesses may find the process more straightforward than before – you charge standard tax and file, without worrying if your service “falls under taxable category” or not. Meanwhile, the government gains flexibility to adjust rates and monitor compliance in real-time. 

In conclusion, **Balochistan Sales Tax 2025** (as amended) is a new landscape. It’s crucial for businesses to align with it. The cost of non-compliance has risen, but so have the tools to comply (electronic systems, clearer rules). By understanding the changes – from definitions and scope to rates, reverse charges, exemptions, and penalties – you can steer your enterprise safely and avoid any unpleasant surprises from the Balochistan Revenue Authority. Always remember: when in doubt, consult the law (and the references we’ve cited) or reach out to BRA’s **Taxpayer Facilitation**. It’s better to ask a question now than to pay a penalty later. Stay informed, stay compliant, and your business will navigate the new BST regime just fine.

**SEO Keywords:** *Balochistan Sales Tax 2025, BRA amendments 2025, Balochistan Finance Act 2025, sales tax on services in Balochistan*【31†L4565-L4573】【9†L1739-L1747】

content_references.snippet: Change of regime In order to give effect to the change of regime of sales tax that all services shall be taxable except specifically exempted, the Balochistan Finance Act has omitted Second Schedule meant for taxable services. Balochistan Sales Tax 2025 – Key Amendments Explained
Introduction – From Positive List to “Tax-All” Regime
The Balochistan Finance Act 2025, brought sweeping changes to the Balochistan Sales Tax on Services Act, 2015 (BSTS Act 2015). These amendments basically shift how sales tax on services works in Balochistan. The principal transformation: all services are now taxable by default unless explicitly exempted. Earlier, only services listed in the schedule were taxed; now the law implements a ‘negative list’ approach where every service is subject to Balochistan Sales Tax (BST) unless it’s on an exemption schedule. 
Broader Definition of ‘Service’ 
The law now defines ‘service’ very broadly. Essentially any activity, facility, or advantage provided for consideration counts as a service. Even if some goods are involved incidentally (e.g. providing equipment along with a service), it’s still treated as a service. This closes loopholes where mixing goods with services might avoid tax.
‘Economic Activity’ Explained: A new all-inclusive definition of economic activity is inserted (Section 6 substituted). It covers any activity (profit-oriented or not) that involves providing or consuming a service for consideration. This explicitly includes:
•	Digital and online services: Providing services through digital platforms or software, even if the provider has no physical presence in Balochistan. (For example, a non-resident company offering online streaming to Balochistan customers is engaged in ‘economic activity’ in the province.)

•	Inter-provincial or international services: Services used or enjoyed in Balochistan are considered provided in Balochistan. This means if a business in Quetta avails an out-of-province consultant’s service, it’s taxable in Balochistan.

•	Clubs and nonprofits: Services by clubs, societies, or trusts to their members are considered economic activities even if not for profit.
All Services Taxable (Scope Expansion) 
Section 3 was amended to state unequivocally that ‘Every service is a taxable service’ if provided by a person from a business/place in Balochistan, as part of an economic activity. It no longer matters whether the service is provided to a local or a foreign customer, if the provider is in Balochistan, it’s taxable. Likewise, services provided by non-residents to customers in Balochistan are now taxable in Balochistan (this implies the local recipient may have to pay the tax, more on that in reverse charge below).
Omitted Definitions
With such a broad scope, the Act removed dozens of specific service definitions that previously existed in Section 2. Terms like ‘Accountant’, ‘beautician’, ‘banker’, ‘advertisement’, and many others were deleted. Why? Because when all services are taxable by default, you no longer need to individually define each service category in the law. This streamlines the act, making it shorter and focused on general principles. It also introduced a definition for ‘CPC’ (Central Product Classification) codes to standardize service classification. The Balochistan Revenue Authority (BRA) can now adopt internationally recognized CPC codes to categorize services, which helps in consistent reporting and aligning with global service categories.
Transitional Provision 
A new Section 10A was added to ensure a smooth shift to the new regime. It basically says any service not listed in the exemption schedule (First Schedule) ‘shall be deemed to be taxable’ from July 1, 2025. If any service was previously enjoying an exemption through a notification, that stays in place until BRA amends or withdraws it. In simple terms, businesses should assume their service is taxable unless they find it on the new exemption list or have a valid official exemption. BRA has grandfathered existing notified exemptions for now, to be reviewed later.
Multiple Schedules Introduced
The amendment replaced the old system of schedules. Previously, Balochistan had a Second Schedule listing taxable services. That’s gone. Now we have:
•	First Schedule – Exempt Services: Services listed here are not taxable (often with conditions). Section 10(2) now directly links to this schedule. If your service is in the First Schedule, you don’t charge BST (subject to any conditions specified). This schedule was overhauled in Finance Act 2025. For example, small businesses in certain sectors are exempt, one entry exempts ‘Accommodation, food and beverage services’ by small caterers with annual turnover under Rs 2.5 million. BRA can also impose conditions on exemptions via notification.

•	Second Schedule – Higher Tax Rates: Some services may attract a rate above 15%. The new Section 10(3) points to a Second Schedule for any services with ‘such higher rate’. For instance, telecommunications is one sector often taxed at higher rates (e.g. 19.5% in some provinces). In Balochistan, telecommunication services continue at 19.5%; the Act even adjusted input tax rules to accommodate this (telecom providers charging ≥19.5% can claim inputs taxed up to 18%). The Second Schedule lists all such exceptions where the rate is above 15%. 

•	Third Schedule – Reduced (Concessional) Rates: The new Section 10(4) introduces a Third Schedule for services taxed at a ‘lower rate… without input tax adjustment’. That means certain services have a discounted GST rate but cannot claim purchase tax credits. Commonly, this is used for incentivizing sectors or simplifying tax for small service providers (charging a low fixed rate but no input credit facility). For example, professional services like lawyers’ fees might be taxed at a fixed nominal amount per case instead of 15% ad valorem in Balochistan, indeed, the updated schedules set a fixed tax of Rs. 500 per case for legal practitioners (instead of a percentage). Some other professional services (accountants, consultants, etc.) have reduced rates (e.g. 5% without input adjustment) to encourage compliance in previously hard-to-tax sectors.
Choice to Pay Standard Rate
An important facility, if your service is listed for a reduced rate without input tax, you have the option to pay 15% with input tax instead. The existing Section 16D allows a service provider to opt out of the concession and go with the full 15% so they can claim input tax credits. This flexibility is useful if your business has significant taxable purchases (inputs); you might prefer to charge full tax and recover input tax rather than forego credits.
Annual Turnover Thresholds
The BRA now has explicit authority to set turnover thresholds for exemption. With government approval, BRA can say, for example, that service providers with turnover below (say) 
Rs 5 million need not register or pay tax. This was added as Section 10(6). It’s a pro-small-business measure to exempt very small service providers. 
Currently, BRA has set certain thresholds in the First Schedule (like the 2.5 million for caterers as noted), and more general thresholds could come via notification. If you’re a small business, watch out for such threshold announcements, it could mean you fall out of the tax net entirely.

# Federal Finance Act 2025 – Amendments to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001

The **Federal Finance Act 2025** brought a host of changes to Pakistan’s Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. These changes aim to provide relief to middle-class taxpayers, tighten compliance, and modernize tax collection in light of a digitalizing economy. Below, we break down the key amendments in simple terms for the general public.

## Relief for Salaried Individuals 📉

One of the most impactful changes is the **reduction in income tax rates for salaried people, especially those in lower and middle income brackets**. The government revised the tax slabs to ease the burden on employees who have long borne heavy taxes. For annual incomes between **Rs. 600,000 and Rs. 1,200,000**, the tax rate has been slashed significantly – by up to **80%** – providing substantial relief【33†L69-L77】. For instance, previously an income of Rs. 1,200,000 might incur a 2.5% tax; under the new slabs this bracket is taxed at only **1%**【33†L118-L122】. Middle-income earners (e.g. those earning up to ~Rs. 4 million) also see progressive tax cuts, boosting their take-home pay【33†L110-L118】. Higher earners (above Rs. 4.1 million annually) get a much smaller cut (around 3% reduction), as the government aimed to maintain revenue from top incomes【33†L69-L77】. Overall, these adjustments mean **more money in the pockets of most salary-earners** and are intended to spur spending and ease financial pressure.

## Taxation of High Pensions 🏦

The Finance Act 2025 has **changed how large pension incomes are taxed**, targeting especially pensions from former employers. **Previously, pensions from a past employer were fully tax-exempt**, but now **if you receive an annual pension over Rs. 10 million and you’re under 70 years old, that pension will be taxed at 5% (final tax) starting July 2025**【18†L269-L277】【18†L273-L281】. In simple terms, very high pension payouts are no longer completely tax-free. However, **pensioners above 70 years** or those with smaller pensions (below Rs. 10 million a year) **remain exempt** from this tax【18†L275-L283】. Importantly, any pension someone continues to receive **while still working for the same employer** (or an associated organization) will **not** fall under the 5% final tax; instead it will be taxed at normal income tax rates【18†L279-L287】. Also, the **commutation of pension (lump-sum withdrawal), gratuity, and certain portions of pension accounts remain exempt** as before, so retirees’ basic entitlements aren’t affected【18†L293-L301】. In summary, the change targets only very large, ongoing pensions to ensure high earners contribute some tax, while protecting seniors and typical retirees.

## Encouraging Digital Payments & E-Commerce 💳

To modernize the economy and document the digital marketplace, a **new tax mechanism for online commerce** has been introduced. **Online and e-commerce transactions will now face a small withholding tax collected at source**: **1%** on payments made through digital channels (e.g. credit cards, online bank transfers) and **2%** on **Cash-on-Delivery (COD)** payments【18†L173-L181】. These taxes are collected by **“payment intermediaries” like banks or digital wallets for online payments, and by courier services for COD payments**【18†L173-L181】【18†L229-L237】. The idea is to **encourage cashless transactions** by making digital payments slightly cheaper tax-wise than cash. For sellers, this withholding is treated as **final tax** on their income from those sales【18†L181-L188】 – meaning if you sell goods/services online, this 1% or 2% is the tax on that income, simplifying tax filing for many small e-businesses. **Online marketplaces** (like e-commerce platforms) and couriers are now **required to ensure their sellers are tax-registered**; they can face penalties if they facilitate unregistered sellers【18†L207-L215】【18†L213-L221】. In fact, every person selling online **must register with the tax authorities** under the new rules【18†L207-L215】. The government’s goal is to **bring the booming digital economy into the tax net** in a business-friendly way – a low tax rate but broad compliance. For the public, this means you might notice online sellers asking for tax registration or slightly different pricing for COD vs online payment, as the system adjusts to these new rules.

## Discouraging Cash and Informal Transactions 💵

Hand-in-hand with promoting digital payments, the Act also **penalizes heavy cash transactions and the informal economy** to improve tax compliance:

- **Higher Tax on Cash Withdrawals:** If you are not on the Active Taxpayers List (i.e. a non-filer) and withdraw cash from a bank beyond a certain amount, the **withholding tax on that withdrawal has increased from 0.6% to 0.8%**【18†L311-L318】【18†L312-L320】. This is an advance tax aimed at non-taxpayers. In practical terms, large cash withdrawals by unregistered individuals now incur a bit more tax – an incentive to either limit cash dealings or, better yet, **file your tax returns and get on the active taxpayer list** to avoid this tax altogether.

- **Business Expenses Require Documentation:** To crack down on the informal sector, businesses will face **limits on claiming certain expenses if those expenses involve unregistered parties or cash sales**. For example, any business purchase from an **unregistered seller (no NTN)** could lead to **10% of that expense being disallowed** (not tax-deductible)【20†L419-L427】. This rule exempts purchases of raw agricultural produce directly from farmers – recognizing the informal nature of farming – **unless a middleman is involved**, in which case the disallowance applies【20†L421-L429】. Similarly, if a business makes a large sale (over Rs. 200,000 on one invoice) and **doesn’t receive payment through a bank or digital channel**, then **50% of the related expense deduction can be denied**【20†L433-L441】. In plain language, if you insist on cash dealings for big transactions, you lose some tax benefit. However, a **smart workaround** exists: if the buyer deposits the cash directly into the seller’s bank account, it **counts as a bank-channel payment** and avoids the penalty【20†L439-L446】. These measures are meant to **nudge businesses to transact through banks or digital means** and to source from tax-registered suppliers, thereby **shrinking the undocumented, cash-based economy**.

## Support for Education and Retirees 🎓👵

The Finance Act 2025 brings a bit of good news for educators and certain retirees:

- **Teachers’ and Researchers’ Tax Rebate Restored:** Full-time teachers and researchers had enjoyed a 25% tax rebate on their income for many years, but that benefit had lapsed after Tax Year 2022. The new Act **reintroduces a 25% tax rebate for full-time teachers and researchers** on their tax payable【18†L316-L324】【18†L328-L336】. This rebate is *temporary*, covering Tax Years 2023, 2024, and 2025 only【18†L328-L336】. In effect, professors, lecturers, and researchers get some tax relief again (for a limited time), acknowledging their role in society.

- **Senior Citizens’ Pension Exemption:** As noted earlier, if you’re over 70, your pension remains exempt from the new pension tax. This ensures **senior retirees are not burdened** by the changes to pension taxation【18†L275-L283】. Furthermore, **commuted pension and gratuity remain tax-free**, which is crucial for those cashing out retirement benefits.

These measures indicate the government’s attempt to strike a balance – easing taxes for educators and seniors, while raising revenue from other areas.

## Broadening the Tax Net & Compliance Measures 🕵️‍♂️

Several amendments aim to broaden the tax net and improve compliance, making it harder to remain outside the system:

- **“Ineligible Persons” for Economic Activities:** A new concept of **“ineligible persons”** has been adopted whereby individuals who are **not tax-compliant (e.g. not filing returns)** may be **barred from certain key economic activities**【14†L42-L49】. For instance, such persons could be restricted from registering property, purchasing high-value assets, or other transactions until they **get into the tax net**. (A very harsh proposal to bar non-filers from even maintaining bank accounts was considered but ultimately **dropped** in the final Act【14†L42-L49】.) This move effectively says: “If you don’t pay your taxes, you can’t play” – a strong incentive for people to file their returns to avoid being locked out of routine business or financial dealings. A new **Fifteenth Schedule** in the law specifies the thresholds and types of transactions that ineligible persons would be restricted from【14†L44-L52】, though the government will notify the exact enforcement date separately. **Bottom line:** being an active taxpayer is now more important than ever for hassle-free economic life.

- **Faster Audit & Appeal Process:** The Act attempts to make tax administration more efficient. It has **extended the time for tax officials to finalize an audit assessment from 180 days to 1 year** (if you’ve been issued a notice)【14†L53-L57】. This provides more reasonable time for thorough audits. On the appeals side, some 2024 changes had forced high-value disputes straight to the tribunal or High Court; now the **taxpayer can choose to go either to the Commissioner (Appeals) or directly to the Appellate Tribunal** regardless of amount, restoring flexibility【20†L370-L378】. Additionally, only legal questions from tribunal decisions can be taken up to the High Court, which should reduce frivolous litigation【20†L381-L388】. These tweaks aim to **reduce unnecessary delays and backlog** in tax litigation, making it a bit easier for genuine disputes to be resolved.

- **Other Notable Changes:** A few other technical changes were made to close loopholes and update rules. For example, **intangible assets with an indefinite life (like goodwill, patents)** must now be amortized over 15 years for tax purposes, instead of the previous 25 years【20†L463-L471】. This means businesses can deduct the cost of such assets faster (over 15 years), which could be seen as a relief measure for companies investing in IP or other intangibles. Also, **business losses from one source can no longer be used to offset income from property rentals**【20†L474-L481】, preventing some aggressive tax planning. For the corporate sector, **if a company’s income isn’t taxable under the normal corporate tax regime (e.g. certain exempt incomes), that company can’t join a group for group-tax relief**【20†L482-L490】 – a step to prevent tax avoidance through group loss-sharing mechanisms. Lastly, the **withholding tax on sale of immovable property**: if you sell your personal house after 15 years of ownership, the Commissioner can now exempt the buyer from deducting withholding tax on that purchase, *and* that sale won’t be hit by the “super tax” on gains【14†L58-L66】. This is a nice relief for folks selling a long-held family home – you effectively get that gain tax-free once in a 15-year period.

In summary, the Federal Finance Act 2025 made significant changes to income tax law – **major tax cuts for salaried citizens, new taxes and rules for the digital economy, measures to clamp down on cash economy and non-filers, and various tweaks to ensure fairness and efficiency**. The aim is to stimulate the economy and increase the tax base, all while providing relief where it’s needed and ensuring the wealthy and the digital sector contribute their share.

# Punjab Finance Act 2025 – Changes to Sales Tax on Services

The **Punjab Finance Act 2025** introduced sweeping reforms to how services are taxed in Punjab. If you live or do business in Punjab, these changes will affect what services are taxable and at what rate. The emphasis is on broadening the tax base – meaning **more services will now come under the tax net** – but also on making the system clearer by explicitly listing what’s not taxed. Here’s an accessible breakdown of the changes to Punjab’s sales tax on services:

## From Positive List to Negative List: **All Services Taxable by Default** 📜

Punjab has shifted its sales tax regime **from a “positive list” to a “negative list” system**. What does that mean? Under the old method, Punjab only taxed those services that were specifically listed in the law (a positive list). Now, **the default is flipped** – **all services are considered taxable unless they are explicitly mentioned as exempt (tax-free)**【6†L77-L85】. In legal terms, **Section 3 of the Punjab Sales Tax on Services Act 2012 was amended** to introduce this negative list framework【6†L77-L85】. 

For the average person, this means many services that previously weren’t charged Punjab Sales Tax (PST) because they weren’t on the list **will now be subject to tax**. It’s a big broadening of the tax net in Punjab’s service sector. **Only those services that appear in an exemption schedule or are otherwise exempt by law will not be taxed; everything else is fair game.** This reform was done to increase revenue and align Punjab with the approach other provinces are taking in taxing services.

## Tax-Free Services: **New First Schedule of Exemptions** ✅

Don’t let the term “all services taxable” scare you – the government isn’t taxing basic essential services indiscriminately. Along with the negative list approach, Punjab introduced the concept of **“tax-free services”** by inserting a new Section 3A in the law【6†L88-L96】. They **created a First Schedule that lists services which are **exempt** (i.e. not subject to sales tax) in Punjab**【6†L88-L96】. 

This **First Schedule** essentially is the “Negative List” – services on this list are not taxed. For example, it likely includes critical services like certain healthcare, educational services, or other public interest services (the detailed list would be in the law). If a service is listed as tax-free (and meets any conditions mentioned), **providers of that service will not charge Punjab sales tax to customers**. The idea is to protect certain sectors or public services from taxation, even as the overall base expands. 

**Important:** If a service isn’t on the tax-free list, it’s taxable. So the onus is now on the law to specify exemptions, rather than specifying taxable items. This makes the tax system more encompassing but also clearer – **“if in doubt, it’s taxable unless exempted.”**

## Standard Rate and Special Rates 💰

Punjab’s standard sales tax rate on services remains **16%** (unchanged) for most taxable services. However, the Act gives the Punjab government power to modify tax rates for specific services via the schedules. In fact, the law now explicitly **empowers the provincial government to amend the First or Second Schedule by notification**【6†L95-L102】, which means they can add or remove exemptions or change rates for certain services more flexibly over time.

Alongside the reform, Punjab has also introduced or updated **special reduced rates for certain services** to promote industry or provide relief:

- **Ride-Hailing Services (Ride-Share Apps):** These are now taxed at a reduced rate of **5% (with no input tax credit)**【25†L1003-L1011】. This includes services by cab aggregators (e.g., Uber, Careem). A 5% final tax means rides might get slightly cheaper compared to the standard 16% rate, but the operators can’t claim input tax credits in return.

- **Entertainment Services (Cinemas, Theatres, etc.):** In a surprising and public-friendly move, **cinema tickets and similar entertainment events have been taxed at 0%** – effectively **no sales tax** on these services【25†L1008-L1014】. The condition is without input adjustment, meaning cinemas can’t reclaim input tax, but patrons benefit from tax-free tickets. This measure likely aims to **revive and support the entertainment industry** (like cinemas and stage theaters) by making it cheaper for the public to attend movies and shows, especially after the slowdown in the entertainment sector.

Other specific services may also have new entries in the Second Schedule with different rates (either higher or lower than 16%) as the government sees fit. For instance, telecommunication services are often taxed at a higher rate (like 19.5% in some jurisdictions) – such details would be in the Second Schedule if Punjab chose to set them. The key takeaway is, while the blanket rate is 16%, **Punjab can now fine-tune rates for particular services to encourage or discourage them**.

## Input Tax Credit Restrictions 📝

With the expansion of what’s taxable, Punjab also tweaked some rules about **input tax credits** (the tax businesses pay on their inputs that they normally can deduct). There are **new restrictions on claiming input tax in certain scenarios**:

- **No Input Credit on Exempt Services:** If a business is dealing in any **tax-free (exempt) services**, the Punjab Finance Act 2025 explicitly disallows them from claiming input tax related to those services【6†L102-L110】. In simple terms, if your output service isn’t taxed, you can’t claim back sales tax you paid on inputs to provide that service. This is logical and prevents abuse of the system (no refunds or adjustments for tax-exempt sectors).

- **Cap on Input Credit for High-Tax Services:** Punjab has set caps on the input tax one can claim for certain sectors with federal or inter-provincial tax components. For example, **telecommunication services** often carry a higher federal tax rate of 19.5%; **Punjab won’t allow input claims beyond 19.5% for telecom** (since that’s the max output tax applicable)【6†L103-L110】. Likewise, for services like **rail or road transportation of goods**, which might have a 15% rate cap, input tax beyond 15% won’t be claimable【6†L103-L110】. For other standard services, the cap is 16%【6†L105-L110】. The practical effect is to prevent companies from claiming excessive input tax adjustments (for example, due to tax rate mismatches or errors) – you can only adjust up to the relevant output tax rate. Most regular businesses charging the standard 16% PST won’t feel any difference, but those in specialized sectors with different rates must watch their bookkeeping.

## Record-Keeping and Administrative Changes 📂

The law now requires some additional diligence from registered service providers in Punjab:

- **Include Exempt Services in Records:** Previously, businesses had to maintain records of taxable services provided (and any exempt services separately). Now, since “tax-free services” are a category, **if you’re providing any exempt (tax-free) services, you must keep records of those as well** just like taxable services【6†L111-L118】. This ensures that if you’re claiming an activity is exempt, you have documentation to back it up, and the tax authority (Punjab Revenue Authority – PRA) can audit it.

- **Government Flexibility to Amend Schedules:** As mentioned, Section 5 was amended to let Punjab’s government modify the exemption or taxation schedules via notifications【6†L95-L102】. This means the list of exempt services (First Schedule) or any special rate list (Second Schedule) could change without needing a whole new Act each time – a flexible approach to tax policy. Businesses and consumers will need to stay alert through official notifications for any new service becoming taxable or exempt.

- **Harsher Penalties for E-invoicing Non-Compliance:** While not explicitly detailed in our snippet, Punjab likely aligned penalties with federal sales tax for things like not integrating with electronic invoice systems. If a large retailer (Tier-1) doesn’t install the prescribed point-of-sale integration, they can face heavy fines (this was a federal concept extended to provinces). The PwC memo notes that penalties for not integrating were extended to all sales tax laws【31†L25-L29】. So in Punjab, expect strict enforcement if you’re required to issue e-invoices or connect your cash register to PRA’s system.

In summary, **Punjab’s Finance Act 2025 radically overhauled the sales tax on services**: instead of enumerating every taxable service, it now taxes everything except what’s on a special exempt list. It also introduced targeted tax relief or rates for select services (like ride-sharing and cinemas) and tightened rules to ensure the new system is watertight (through input tax and record rules). For consumers, services that were never taxed before may now carry a 16% PST charge – for example, if a certain type of consultancy or digital service wasn’t listed before, it could now be taxable unless exempted. For businesses, it’s crucial to check if what you provide is now taxable and to comply with the new frameworks. This change is a **“big bang” reform to broaden the provincial tax base** while giving the government tools to adjust policy quickly via schedules.

# Sindh Finance Act 2025 – Changes to Sales Tax on Services

Sindh, through its Finance Act 2025, has introduced significant changes to the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act 2011. The changes are quite similar in spirit to Punjab’s reforms – aiming to tax a broader array of services with a clearer framework. For residents and businesses in Sindh, here’s what changed regarding sales tax on services:

## Broadening the Tax Base: **All Services Taxable Unless Exempt** 📋

Sindh has confirmed and clarified its **“negative list” approach** to taxing services. Essentially, **Sindh will tax **all services** provided in the province **by default, except those specifically listed as exempt**【23†L1-L9】【23†L19-L27】. This is achieved by **omitting the Second Schedule which previously listed taxable services** – meaning they no longer maintain a finite list of taxable services【23†L1-L9】. Now, if a service isn’t explicitly exempted (in the First Schedule or via notification), it’s considered taxable under Sindh Sales Tax. 

This isn’t entirely new – Sindh was already moving in this direction – but the 2025 Act cements it. **Practically, it aligns with the idea that anything you pay for – from traditional services to digital or novel services – could be subject to Sindh Sales Tax at the standard rate, unless it falls in the exemption list.** So the tax net is cast wide to include modern and emerging services that maybe weren’t thought of when the law first came out.

## Exemption Schedule and Standard Rate 💡

The **First Schedule** to the Sindh sales tax law now serves as the list of **exempt services** (services not charged sales tax), whereas the **Second Schedule is repurposed** to list any services that have **higher or reduced tax rates** than the norm【23†L13-L21】. Under the updated Section 8 of the Act, **the standard rate of Sindh Sales Tax on Services is 15%** of the value of the service【23†L7-L15】. This has been the case since Sindh raised the rate from 13% to 15% in 2024, and 15% continues to be the general rate in 2025.

The Act added a proviso that **allows certain services to have different rates as specified in the Second Schedule**【23†L13-L21】. For example, **telecommunications services might be listed with a higher rate (e.g. 19.5%)** or **specific sectors like restaurants or beauty parlors might have a reduced rate**, if the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) decides so. These specifics are in the Second Schedule, subject to conditions. So while **15% is the rule**, there are exceptions where Sindh gives a break or charges extra – the law explicitly caters to that.

As for the **First Schedule (Exemptions)**: The Act **introduced a new Section 10** to outline a First Schedule of exempt services【23†L19-L27】. Services in this schedule are **tax-free in Sindh**, possibly subject to certain conditions. For instance, services like healthcare, educational institutions, or maybe exports of services could be listed here. The Act states those listed services are exempt as long as any conditions in the schedule are met【23†L19-L27】. In everyday terms, if you’re consuming or providing a service and you want to know if it’s taxed, you’d check this First Schedule – if it’s listed, it’s not taxed; if not, assume 15% applies.

## Revised Definitions & Removal of Specific Categories 🔄

To accommodate taxing all services, **Sindh broadened the definition of “service”** in the law. Now “Service” means **any activity, facility, utility or advantage provided for consideration**【23†L25-L33】. This wide definition ensures even things that don’t neatly fall into a traditional category are still services if someone is paying for some benefit. It includes granting or surrendering a right as a service, etc. Essentially, **if you’re doing something for someone for money (that isn’t an outright sale of goods), it’s a service** in the eyes of the law【23†L25-L33】.

Conversely, the Act **cleaned up a lot of specific service definitions** that used to be listed. Since everything is taxable unless exempt, there’s no need to define each service in detail. The Finance Act **deleted definitions of specific services like “Accountant”, “Advertisement”, and others from the law**【23†L43-L47】. Those were originally included to clarify the scope of taxable categories, but now they’re redundant. For example, whether you call someone an “accountant” or a “consultant”, if they’re providing a service, it’s taxable either way – so such fine definitions aren’t needed in the law text anymore.

## Jurisdictional Clarity: Avoiding Double Taxation ⚖️

An important clarification was added to avoid any clash with federal taxes: **Certain services that fall under the federal government’s domain cannot be taxed by Sindh.** The Act inserted an Explanation (likely Explanation-II to the definition of “services”) that **excludes any services on which a tax can be imposed by the federal government under the Constitution (Federal Legislative List, Entry 53)**【23†L29-L36】. In plain terms, if the Constitution reserves a certain kind of tax for the federation (for instance, taxes on **“services by corporations”** could arguably be federal domain), then Sindh will not tax those under its sales tax law. This is to ensure **no overlapping or unconstitutional taxing happens**. For the general public, this is behind-the-scenes legal hygiene – it doesn’t change what you pay as much as it protects against legal confusion (so you won’t be double-taxed provincially and federally on the same service).

## Classification Codes (CPC) Adoption 🗂️

Sindh has modernized how services are categorized by adopting **CPC (Central Product Classification) codes**. The Finance Act 2025 added a definition for “CPC Code” which refers to the international classification system by the United Nations【23†L37-L45】. The **Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) is now empowered to assign CPC codes to services** via notification【23†L61-L69】. 

What does this mean in practice? **Each service can be tagged with a specific code for identification**, which aligns with global standards. It helps in consistency, especially if comparing data or integrating with federal systems or other provinces. However, the law clearly states that this coding **will not determine whether a service is taxable or not**【23†L61-L69】. It’s purely for classification. So even if a service doesn’t have a code yet, it can still be taxable; the code is just a label. Conversely, if a service has a code but is listed as exempt in First Schedule, it remains exempt. This move is largely administrative, making the tax system more systematic and ready for the digital age where things are often tracked by standardized codes.

## Transitional and Administrative Provisions 🔧

The Finance Act introduced some sections to ensure a smooth transition to the new scheme:

- **Continuity of Previously Taxed Services:** A new section (likely Section 72C) was added to clarify that even though the law’s structure changed, **any service that was being charged sales tax as of 30 June 2025 will continue to be taxed after the Finance Act**【23†L67-L75】. In other words, there’s no loophole where something falls through the cracks due to the list change. This protects against any disruption in revenue – services taxable before remain taxable now (most at 15% unless adjusted).

- **SRB’s Powers for Implementation:** The Act empowers **SRB (with Sindh Government approval)** to issue orders making modifications in how the law is applied【23†L71-L76】. This essentially gives SRB a bit of flexibility to iron out any wrinkles during implementation of these big changes. For example, if certain procedural issues arise or if something needs phasing, SRB can, with approval, temporarily adjust application via an order rather than waiting for another act. This ensures **practical adaptability**.

- **Economic Activity Definition Exclusions:** They’ve fine-tuned what counts as an “economic activity” (which generally defines the scope of taxable activities). **Services by courts, tribunals, or similar statutory bodies are explicitly excluded from the definition of economic activity**【23†L49-L57】, meaning **no sales tax on services rendered by a court or tribunal**. That’s logical (a court fee isn’t a “service” in the taxable sense). Likewise, services provided by employees to their employers in the course of employment aren’t taxed as services (salary is covered by income tax, not sales tax). These clarifications help prevent misinterpretation of the new broad definitions.

In summary, the Sindh Finance Act 2025 has **streamlined and broadened the sales tax regime for services** in Sindh. **If you’re a consumer**, you might not notice immediate differences in your bills except that **more services are likely to have Sindh Sales Tax added** now than before. **If you’re a service provider**, you should check the new First Schedule (exemptions) – if your service isn’t listed there, you’re required to charge 15% SST on it (or whatever special rate applies to your service). The changes aim to make the tax system fairer (everyone pays a share) and simpler (clear lists of what’s not taxed, rather than chasing an ever-growing list of what is taxed). Sindh’s approach closely mirrors what Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Balochistan are also doing, as provinces unify their tax structures on services.
