# Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Finance Act 2025 – Changes to Sales Tax on Services

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) joined the other provinces in overhauling its sales tax on services regime through the Finance Act 2025. The KP Finance Act 2025 amended the **Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Sales Tax on Services Act, 2022** (which is relatively new itself) to broaden the tax base and update various provisions. Here’s a breakdown of how sales tax on services in KP is changing:

## All-Encompassing Tax Base: **Negative List Model** 📚

Similar to Punjab and Sindh, **KP shifted to a negative list taxation model for services**. Previously, KP taxed services that were specified in a schedule (a positive list of taxable services). Now, **the law has been changed so that **all services are taxable by default except those listed as exempt**. In essence, KP’s sales tax will apply to any service provided within the province **unless** that service is in an **exemption list (First Schedule)** or falls outside the scope by definition【40†L109-L117】. The **standard tax rate is 15%** on the value of services, which remains the same as before【39†L37-L40】. 

The Act provides that certain services or classes of service can have different rates if listed in the Second Schedule【39†L13-L16】【40†L113-L117】 – much like Sindh’s approach. So while **15% is the general rate**, KP can specify higher or lower rates for particular services in the Second Schedule. If a service used to be listed in the old schedule of taxable services (before July 2025), the law ensures it stays taxable – either at the special rate it had or at the 15% standard if not explicitly adjusted【40†L109-L117】. This way, **no previously taxed service is dropped**; the net only expands to catch services that weren’t listed before.

For everyday people, this means you might start seeing KP sales tax on some bills where previously there was none, simply because those services were not in the old taxable list but now are taxable by default.

## Revised Schedules: Exemptions and Special Rates 🗒️

- **First Schedule (Exempt/Negative List):** KP’s Finance Act introduced a First Schedule enumerating services that are **exempt from sales tax** (the “negative list”). These could include essential public services or other categories like educational services, health services, governmental fees, etc. If your service or the service you’re consuming is on this list, no KP sales tax will apply.

- **Second Schedule (Variable Rates):** The Second Schedule in KP is used for listing any service that is not taxed at the standard 15%. This can include *reduced rates* to encourage certain sectors or *higher rates* for luxury services. For example, KP might place telecommunication services or prepaid cellular services with a higher rate here, or set a lower rate for services like tourism-related businesses to promote them. The KP Revenue Authority (KPRA) through the government can update these schedules as needed. Notably, the law mentions that services listed in the old Second Schedule (pre-reform) will remain taxable at the rates mentioned there until changed, or otherwise at standard rate if not explicitly provided in the new First Schedule【40†L113-L120】.

- **Management Committee Powers:** KP has a unique feature – a **Management Committee** (likely part of KPRA’s setup) – and the Act explicitly allows it to prescribe or amend classification of services (like adding CPC codes) and even adjust tax treatments by notification【40†L117-L125】. This provides agility in implementing the new broad tax system. However, any classification is just for ease; it won’t override whether something is taxable or exempt (similar to Sindh’s stance on CPC codes).

## Digital Compliance and Modernization 💻

The KP Finance Act 2025 also made changes to modernize tax administration for services:

- **Mandatory E-Filing:** The amendments now **require taxpayers to file KP sales tax returns electronically (online)**. Previously, one might have had the option of manual filing, but now e-filing is the norm, simplifying processing. Moreover, the window to revise a sales tax return has been shortened (for example, from 6 months down to 120 days) to encourage timely corrections and finality in declarations.

- **Integration of Businesses:** KP is keen on **integrating businesses (especially retailers and service providers) with its online monitoring systems**. If you run a service like a restaurant or an outlet designated to integrate your point-of-sale with KPRA’s system, non-compliance will carry steep penalties. The Finance Act introduced a penalty of **Rs. 200,000 or 5% of the tax amount (whichever is higher) for each instance** where a person required to integrate (for instance, install a prescribed invoicing system) fails to do so【34†L12-L16】. This is a strong deterrent to ensure businesses comply with digital invoicing and reporting requirements. The message: *connect your cash registers to the tax system, or face heavy fines*. This helps KPRA get real-time data on sales for tax purposes and minimizes underreporting.

## Streamlining Appeals and Administration ⚖️

KP’s law changes include introducing **pecuniary jurisdictions for appeals** – essentially simplifying the appeals process by possibly allowing certain disputes to skip a level of appeal based on amount, to reduce backlog. While technical, it could mean for smaller taxpayers, their cases are handled in one forum instead of bouncing around. Additionally, minor fixes and clarifications were added (similar to federal changes) to ensure smoother audits and recovery of taxes. 

One interesting compliance change: the law now states if a registered service provider is also providing services in other provinces or the federal area, they must maintain records of those out-of-KP services too. This is to ensure when KPRA examines a company’s accounts, it can see the full picture and ensure only the right portions are taxed in KP versus elsewhere (no hiding under inter-provincial confusion).

## Reliefs and Incentives 🎁

Amid the tightening, KP did include some relief measures via the schedules:
- **Small Business Relief:** It’s possible KP continued or introduced small thresholds or simplified regimes for very small service providers (as provinces often have a threshold turnover below which you don’t charge sales tax). While not explicitly stated in the Finance Act summary, these usually remain to avoid burdening micro-enterprises.
- **Encouraging Certain Sectors:** KP, known for tourism, might use its Second Schedule to give a tax break to tourism services, hotels in off-season, or IT services, etc. For instance, if some services elect to pay a lower fixed tax or a lower rate with no input adjustments (some provinces allow wedding halls to pay a fixed amount per function instead of 15% of bill, etc.), KP could implement similar measures. The Act text references parts for “tax rates below standard rate with conditions”【40†L19-L27】 and even specific entries for certain sectors like catering or hall rentals with fixed taxes【40†L43-L50】【40†L91-L99】 – implying that in the schedules KP may have provided options like a fixed tax for wedding halls or reduced rates for certain non-corporate service providers to ease compliance.

In conclusion, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s changes bring it in harmony with Punjab and Sindh – **taxing services comprehensively but carving out needed exemptions and special cases**. For consumers in KP, more of the services you use will include KP sales tax (on your bills or invoices) than before, as the law now covers virtually everything. For businesses, it’s crucial to note the new requirements: if you weren’t charging sales tax because your service wasn’t listed before, you likely need to start charging 15% now (unless you find it on the exempt list). Also, embrace the digital compliance aspects (e-filing, POS integration) to avoid penalties. The shift aims to **increase provincial revenue and fairness** (everyone pays a share), while also improving the ease of compliance through electronic systems.

# Balochistan Finance Act 2025 – Changes to Sales Tax on Services

Balochistan, often the last to adopt provincial tax reforms, has now made bold changes through the Finance Act 2025 to revamp its sales tax on services regime. These changes mirror the trend seen in Punjab, Sindh, and KP – moving to a broader tax base with clear exemptions and embracing modernization in tax collection. Here’s what the general public should know about the sales tax on services changes in Balochistan:

## Major Reform: **Negative List Framework Adopted** 📣

The headline change is that **Balochistan has adopted the “negative list” model for taxing services**, which is a **major reform** for the province【31†L3-L7】. Prior to this, Balochistan’s Sales Tax on Services Act 2015 listed specific taxable services. Now, the **Balochistan Finance Act 2025 has shifted to tax all services by default, except those enumerated as exempt**. In other words, **if a service is provided in Balochistan and you’re paying for it, assume it’s subject to Balochistan sales tax unless there’s a clear exemption for it**. This change vastly expands the scope of taxable services, capturing many activities that might not have been taxed before.

To implement this, the law was amended in various sections. For instance, definitions were adjusted and schedules were restructured:
- The **First Schedule** of the Balochistan services tax law is now the list of **exempt services** (services not charged sales tax).
- The **Second Schedule** (if any, or perhaps parts of the First Schedule previously listing taxable services) is revised/omitted because listing every taxable service is no longer necessary under a negative list system.

The **standard sales tax rate in Balochistan remains 15%** (similar to other provinces) on taxable services. So, generally, services will attract a 15% tax unless they fall under special cases.

## Government Empowered to Adjust Taxation 🚦

Balochistan’s Act gives the provincial government more flexibility to fine-tune the sales tax regime:
- The government is **empowered by notification to declare any taxable service to be charged at higher, lower, or even a fixed rate** in deviation from the standard【40†L127-L130】. This means if needed, Balochistan can say “Service X will be taxed at 5%” or “Service Y will have a fixed annual tax” without going back to the assembly for a new law each time.
- This power likely extends to creating special **schemes for small businesses or specific industries**. For example, they might later announce that small service providers under a certain threshold pay a fixed amount or are exempt – using this empowerment clause.

Additionally, Balochistan can update the exemption list or any schedule similarly via notification. This kind of agility is new and indicates Balochistan is serious about keeping its tax law responsive to economic conditions.

## Alignment with Other Provinces 🔄

One motivation for Balochistan’s reforms is to **harmonize with other provinces**, so businesses and consumers face a more uniform system countrywide. By 2025, all four provinces now use the negative list approach. This reduces confusion – for instance, a telecom company or a bank offering services nationwide doesn’t have to treat Balochistan differently in terms of *what* is taxable (though rates can differ). Balochistan aligning its standard rate at **15%** also matches Sindh and KP (Punjab is 16%). 

For the public, this means fewer discrepancies. If you knew sales tax applied to a service in Sindh or KP, it likely applies in Balochistan now too. Conversely, something exempted in all provinces (like maybe life-saving healthcare services) would be exempt in Balochistan as well.

## Specific Changes and Likely Impacts 💼

While the detailed list of changes is technical, some notable ones include:
- **Insertion of Sales Tax Act, 1990 references:** The Act text (as seen in official documents) inserts references to the federal Sales Tax Act in certain definitions【31†L9-L15】, perhaps to clarify overlap or exclude items that are federally taxed. For example, Balochistan might clarify that any service which is essentially the *transmission of goods* (which falls under federal sales tax on goods) is not double-taxed as a service.

- **Digital Economy Inclusion:** By not limiting to listed services, Balochistan now taxes things like **digital services or online platforms** which didn’t exist or weren’t popular in 2015. If you hire a freelancer online or use an app-based service in Balochistan, that service is taxable unless exempt. This future-proofs the tax system.

- **Administrative Improvements:** The Act likely mirrors other provinces in requiring e-filing of returns and electronic record-keeping. The Balochistan Revenue Authority (BRA) might implement systems similar to PRA, SRB, etc., for online return submission and maybe integrating larger businesses’ invoicing systems. In fact, an uploaded file named “BRA.pdf” suggests there might be documentation on how BRA is updating its processes in 2025.

- **Rationalizing Definitions:** Just like Sindh removed specific service definitions, Balochistan probably did the same. For example, earlier laws had definitions like “franchise service” or “courier service” – now the law can afford to drop many of those because whether a service is called this or that, it’s taxable anyway if not exempt. Expect the law text to be cleaner and focused on broader terms.

- **Reliefs:** Balochistan may also introduce or continue relief measures in schedules. For instance, Balochistan often exempts certain local services to encourage investment (they had, in past budgets, exempted certain services in Gwadar or for CPEC projects, etc.). Such exemptions would be clearly listed now in the First Schedule so investors know they don’t have to pay tax on those.

For a tangible example: If you go to a beauty salon in Quetta (and salons were not explicitly listed before), previously they might not have been charging Balochistan sales tax. After the Act, salons are not exempt (likely) so they should charge the 15% tax. On the flip side, if you get medical treatment at a hospital, that might be in the exempt list – so no tax (same as before, since health was usually exempt under old law via notification). 

Another example: **Internet services** – sometimes provinces tax broadband or not. If Balochistan’s new exempt list doesn’t mention internet, then broadband could become taxable at 15%. We’d have to see BRA’s notifications for clarity, but that’s the type of change to watch out for as the broad net is cast.

## Improved Enforcement and Revenue Goals 🎯

By expanding the tax base, Balochistan clearly aims to boost its revenue. The province historically struggled with low tax collection. A broader base (more services taxed) combined with possibly better enforcement (due to digitization and alignment) should improve collections. They may also implement **stricter penalties** for non-compliance akin to other provinces – for instance, fines for not registering when liable, or for not depositing collected tax.

It’s worth noting that Balochistan often follows Sindh’s lead in tax matters. Since Sindh has a fairly advanced SRB system, BRA might adopt similar IT systems and policies. Over time, expect BRA to issue rules mirroring many of Sindh’s – e.g., requiring larger service providers to use invoice verifications, etc. The uploaded “BRA.pdf” might contain the updated Balochistan Sales Tax Act as of 2025, which would show the exact text changes.

**In summary**, the Balochistan Finance Act 2025 has *finally brought Balochistan up-to-speed* with contemporary sales tax practices: **everything is taxable unless exempt, at a standard 15% rate, with flexibility to change rates for specific cases and an explicit list of exemptions to protect key services**. For consumers and businesses, the landscape is more predictable and on par with other regions. You should check if services you offer or purchase in Balochistan are now subject to tax (chances are, if they weren’t before, they probably are now, unless clearly exempted). The change might slightly increase costs for end-consumers on newly taxed services, but it also levels the playing field – previously untaxed sectors now contribute alongside others. This comprehensive approach is intended to enhance Balochistan’s revenue in a fair manner while making the tax law clearer for everyone.

---

## **Website “Updates” – Quick Summaries of 2025 Finance Act Changes**

*For those who want the key points at a glance, here are concise updates on changes brought by the 2025 Finance Acts at the federal and provincial levels in Pakistan:*

- **Federal (Income Tax Ordinance Changes):** Major tax relief was granted to salaried individuals – tax rates were cut across the board, with **up to 80% reduction in tax for low-income brackets**【33†L69-L77】. Pensions from former employers above Rs. 10 million per year will now be taxed at 5% (final tax) if the retiree is under 70【18†L269-L277】. To encourage a digital economy, a new withholding tax on e-commerce was introduced: **1% on online payments and 2% on cash-on-delivery transactions**, making online sales part of the tax net【18†L173-L181】. Non-filers face higher taxes on cash withdrawals (0.8% now)【18†L311-L318】 and could be barred from certain economic activities until they comply with tax laws【14†L42-L49】. Additionally, full-time teachers and researchers got back their 25% tax rebate (for tax years 2023–2025)【18†L316-L324】【18†L328-L336】, and various loopholes were closed to strengthen compliance.

- **Punjab (Sales Tax on Services):** Punjab undertook a sweeping reform by moving to a **negative list regime for services** – now **all services are taxable by default except those listed as tax-free**【6†L77-L85】. A new First Schedule lists **exempt (tax-free) services** like certain health or education services【6†L88-L96】. The standard PST rate remains 16%, but Punjab introduced special rates for some sectors (e.g., **ride-hailing services taxed at 5%**; **cinema and entertainment tickets at 0%** to boost these industries【25†L1003-L1011】). Businesses can no longer claim input tax on exempt services, and excessive input tax (beyond standard rates) is disallowed【6†L103-L110】. The Punjab government can now modify taxable or exempt service lists by notification【6†L95-L102】, making the regime more flexible. Overall, many previously untaxed services in Punjab are now within the tax net under the Finance Act 2025.

- **Sindh (Sales Tax on Services):** Sindh broadened its service tax base, reaffirming that **all services are taxable unless explicitly exempted**. It **removed the old list of taxable services (Second Schedule)** and instead will tax everything at the **standard 15%** unless it’s on the **First Schedule of exempt services**【23†L1-L9】【23†L19-L27】. The law’s language was updated – many specific service definitions (e.g. for “accountants” or “advertisements”) were **deleted** since they’re no longer needed【23†L43-L47】. Sindh introduced **CPC codes for service classification** to streamline reporting【23†L37-L45】 (though coding doesn’t affect taxability). The Sindh Revenue Board can specify different rates in a Second Schedule proviso (higher or reduced rates for certain services)【23†L13-L21】, and it retains 15% as the general rate【23†L7-L15】. Key exempt services remain in place via the First Schedule (such as certain government or social services). These changes make Sindh’s tax system more encompassing and aligned with other provinces, ensuring previously uncovered services (including many digital and modern services) are now taxed.

- **Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (Sales Tax on Services):** KPK followed suit by switching to a **negative list model** – **all services are now taxable except those in the exempt list**, at a **standard rate of 15%**【39†L37-L40】【40†L113-L120】. The KPK Finance Act 2025 introduced a First Schedule of exemptions and allows special tax rates via the Second Schedule for certain services. A major push was made for **digital compliance**: KPK now mandates e-filing of tax returns and has imposed steep penalties (Rs. 200k or 5% of tax per instance) for businesses that fail to integrate required electronic invoicing systems【34†L12-L16】. These measures aim to bring more services (and service providers) into the tax net and improve transparency. Consumers may see KPK sales tax on more service bills than before, while businesses need to register and comply online to avoid penalties.

- **Balochistan (Sales Tax on Services):** Balochistan implemented a **big reform by adopting the negative list approach** – **all services are subject to Balochistan sales tax by default, with specific exemptions listed**【31†L3-L7】. The standard rate is 15%, harmonizing with Sindh and KPK. The government of Balochistan now has the power to alter tax rates or even set fixed taxes for certain services via notification【40†L127-L130】, providing flexibility to support various sectors. This means Balochistan can, for example, reduce tax on key services or raise it on luxury services without new legislation each time. The move greatly expands the provincial tax base to include many previously untaxed services, helping improve revenue. It also aligns Balochistan’s practices with other provinces, which is easier for businesses operating nationwide. Expect BRA (Balochistan Revenue Authority) to roll out digital systems and stricter enforcement similar to its peers – making tax filing electronic and compliance more robust. In short, Balochistan’s service sales tax is now up-to-date: broad coverage, clear exemptions, and modern administration for the year 2025 and beyond.

One of the key amendments is the **reduction in income tax rates for salaried individuals**, especially those in the lower and middle-income brackets. The government has revised the tax slabs to ease the burden on employees who have long shouldered disproportionately high taxes. For annual incomes between **Rs. 600,000 and Rs. 1,200,000**, the tax rate has been cut sharply—by up to **80%**—providing substantial relief. In addition, a **9% surcharge** (reduced from 10%) now applies to individuals whose income is chargeable under the head *“Salary.”*  

For instance, an annual income of **Rs. 1,200,000**, which previously attracted tax at **2.5%**, will now be taxed at just **1%**. Similarly, **middle-income earners** (up to Rs. 4 million annually) also enjoy progressive cuts, resulting in higher take-home pay. By contrast, **higher earners** (above Rs. 4.1 million annually) receive only modest relief—around a **3% reduction**—as the government aims to balance tax relief with maintaining revenue from top-income groups.  

---

Excellent point — gifts and loans/advances don’t just stop at Section 39, they must also be **properly disclosed in both the Income Tax Return and Wealth Statement**. If not, the FBR can treat them as unexplained income. Here’s how we can refine the flyers with that **compliance caution** built in:  

---

### ✨ Flyer 1: **Gifts from Relatives**  

**Gifts Can Be Tax-Free!**  

Under Section 39, gifts are usually taxable. But if you receive them from **close relatives** (parents, grandparents, spouse, brothers, sisters, sons, or daughters), they are **not taxed**.  

👉 Example: Money from your father to buy a car = **tax-free**. Money from a friend = **taxable income**.  

⚠️ **Important:** You must still **disclose all gifts** in your **Income Tax Return** and **Wealth Statement**.  
If not properly shown, FBR may treat them as your **unexplained income**.  

✅ *Family gifts are tax-free, but disclosure is mandatory.*  

---

### ✨ Flyer 2: **Loans & Advances**  

**Loans Can Become Income!**  

Any loan, advance, or deposit received other than from a bank can be treated as **income** under Section 39 — unless:  
✔️ It’s through **crossed cheque, bank transfer, or digital channel**  
✔️ The giver has a valid **NTN**  

👉 Example: Rs. 1 million in cash received as a “loan” may be taxed as your income. But if received via bank transfer with NTN details, it’s a valid loan.  

⚠️ **Caution:** Always **declare loans/advances in your Return and Wealth Statement**.  
Non-disclosure can lead to them being added to your taxable income.

**Subject:** SHC Decision on Tax Rate Matter in Petroleum ITRAs  

Dear [Client],  

We would like to update you on the recent judgment delivered by the Sindh High Court (SHC) in relation to the tax rate applicable to petroleum companies, which has direct bearing on UEP. As you are aware, one of the central issues before the Court was whether the phrase *“before deduction of payments”* should be applied only to the statutory floor of 50% of profits and gains, as consistently argued by petroleum companies, or whether it applies to both the 50% floor and the 55% ceiling, as maintained by the department.  

The SHC has upheld the department’s contention that, under the Mines Act, 1948, this phrase attaches to both the floor and the ceiling. Accordingly, the Court has concluded that the statutory range for the tax rate is between **50% and 55% of profits and gains before deduction of payments.** While this aspect has been decided against petroleum companies, it is significant to note that the SHC stopped short of specifying how the tax liability is to be calculated within this prescribed range. In other words, while the Court has validated the existence of a range, it has not provided clarity as to the exact rate that should be applied in practice, leaving this most critical issue unresolved.  

From UEP’s perspective, this outcome carries two important implications. First, since UEP has consistently applied a tax rate of 50% of profits and gains before deduction of payments, its current practice falls squarely within the range affirmed by the SHC. This provides a strong basis to request the department for appeal effect orders, by emphasizing that UEP is already compliant with the statutory framework as interpreted by the Court. Pursuing this course may allow UEP to secure favorable recognition of its position at the departmental level without awaiting further litigation.  

Second, while requesting appeal effect, it must also be highlighted that the SHC judgment has not conclusively resolved the method of determining tax payable within the 50%–55% band. This leaves a substantial legal ambiguity, particularly as to whether the normal company rate could interplay with the statutory range or whether a specific fixed rate should be deemed applicable. On this ground alone, there remain solid legal foundations to pursue an appeal before the Supreme Court of Pakistan. The appeal would focus on the lack of clarity in the SHC judgment, ensuring that UEP’s interests are preserved in the longer term even as it seeks immediate relief through appeal effect orders.  

In light of the above, we recommend that UEP proceed with a dual approach. On the immediate front, an application may be submitted to the department seeking appeal effect, on the basis that UEP’s tax at 50% is already in conformity with the SHC’s interpretation of the statutory range. In parallel, an appeal may be pursued before the Supreme Court to challenge the SHC’s omission in not prescribing the applicable rate within the range, which is central to ensuring certainty in tax obligations of petroleum companies.  

We remain available to prepare the necessary draft for submission to the department and to provide further assistance in relation to the proposed appeal before the Supreme Court.  

Best regards,  
[Your Name]

Dear Shahid,

(1) The SHC announced its judgment in the petroleum ITRAs today. A copy of the judgment is attached. As you are aware, there were two questions before the Tribunal:

(i) How depletion allowance is to be calculated. 

(ii) What tax rate is applicable to petroleum companies. 

(2) The SHC has answered the first question in favor of petroleum companies based on the Supreme Court's judgment on the same issue.

(3) The SHC has, however, answered the second question against petroleum companies and in favor of the department. 

(4) The second question was itself divided into two separate issues: 

(i) Whether the phrase "before deduction of payments" is to be read with 55% cap and the 50% floor as argued by the department, or only with the 50% floor as argued by petroleum companies. 

(ii) Assuming the department's contention is accepted and the phrase is read with both the cap and the floor, then what is the tax rate applicable to companies and how is tax payable to be calculated as this only provides a range.

(5) The SHC answered the first issue in favour of the department on the basis that the Mines Act 1948 states that this phrase applies to both the cap and the floor, and since the Act 1948 overrides both the ITO 1979 and the PCAs, it will prevail. In our view this interpretation is not correct for the simple reason that there is no conflict between the ITO 1979 and PCAs, on the one hand, and the Act 1948, on the other. The tax being paid by petroleum companies (50% of profit and gains before deduction of payments) is within the range prescribed in the Act 1948. We are, therefore, of the view that there are good grounds for challenging this judgment before the SCP.

(6) After holding that the range prescribed in the Act 1948 prevails, however, the SHC did not state how the tax payable is to be calculated within that range. In short, the SHC did not answer the second issue at all. As such on the most contested point, there is still no clarity. On the basis alone, there are good grounds for challenging this judgment before the SCP.

(7) In this regard, please note that on the second issue we had initially wanted to argue that even if the range prescribed in the Act 1948 applies, then to calculate the tax payable, the normal company rate of tax would apply. If this were lower than 50% of profits and gains before deduction of payments, then petroleum companies would have to pay the difference. If this were higher than 55% of profit and gains before deduction of payments, then petroleum companies would only pay 55% of profit and gains before deduction of payments. Based on extensive discussions with PWC, however, this argument was not taken as we were informed that if the normal tax rate were applied, then for most years the tax liability of the companies would exceed 55% of profits and gains before deduction of payments and therefore, they would end up paying 55% of profits and gains before deduction of payments, as opposed to 50% of profits and gains before deduction of payments.

(8) As stated above, we believe there are good grounds for challenging this judgment before the SCP. The limitation period for filing an appeal to the SCP is 60 days.

(9) Please let us know how you would like to proceed or if you would like to discuss the matter further or need any clarification.

Best,
Ali

**Subject:** Tax Implications of Parent Guarantee Fee Arrangement – Asyad Holding  

**Dear Komal,**  

Thank you for your query regarding the tax treatment of the proposed parental guarantee fee arrangement with Asyad Holding. Based on the agreements executed on July 30, 2025 (effective August 1, 2025), Asyad has provided corporate guarantees totaling USD 15.3 million (USD 12 million to Shell Lubricants Supply Company B.V. and USD 3.3 million to Shell Markets Middle East) in favor of WEPL’s suppliers. In consideration, WEPL will pay an annual fee of 1.5% (USD 180,000 and USD 49,500, respectively), payable quarterly in arrears within 30 days of each quarter’s close.  

We have reviewed the arrangement in the light of the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, the **Pakistan–Saudi Arabia Double Taxation Treaty**, the **Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011**, and relevant **transfer pricing rules**. Our comments are set out below:  

---

### 1. Income Tax – Domestic Law and Treaty Analysis  

**Domestic Treatment:**  
Under **section 152 of the Ordinance**, any payment by a Pakistani resident to a non-resident that is not specifically exempt is deemed Pakistan-source income. Since the guarantee fee represents consideration for an economic benefit enjoyed by WEPL in Pakistan, the payment falls within this scope. Absent treaty relief, WEPL must withhold **20% of the gross fee** at source, which is treated as **final tax** on the non-resident.  

**Treaty Classification:**  
Under the **Pakistan–Saudi Arabia DTAA (2006)**:  
- The guarantee fee does not qualify as *interest* (Art. 11) as no debt-claim exists.  
- It does not qualify as *royalty* (Art. 12) since no IP, know-how, or equipment is involved.  
- It is best characterized as **business profit** (Art. 7). Profits of a Saudi resident are taxable in Saudi Arabia unless attributable to a **permanent establishment** (PE) in Pakistan. As Asyad has no PE locally, the fee is taxable only in Saudi Arabia.  

**Other Income Article:** While Article 22 (Other Income) gives Pakistan a limited right to tax, the stronger and more widely accepted position is to treat this fee as **business profits** under Article 7, ensuring full treaty relief.  

**Compliance Action:**  
If treaty benefit is to be claimed, WEPL must apply under **section 152(5)** with Asyad’s **Tax Residency Certificate** to obtain FBR clearance for payment without deduction. Without such approval, 20% withholding will be required.  

---

### 2. Sales Tax – Imported Services and CPC Classification  

**Nature of Service:**  
The guarantee fee is a **financial service** provided by Asyad. As the provider is located outside Pakistan and unregistered for provincial sales tax, the fee qualifies as an **imported service** under the **Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011**.  

**Tax Implication:**  
- WEPL is required to **self-assess and deposit 15% SST** on the gross fee under the **reverse charge mechanism**.  
- The tax is payable on each quarterly installment, irrespective of whether treaty relief is obtained for income tax purposes.  

**Appropriate CPC Code:**  
Based on the **updated SST Tariff Classification**, the most suitable code is:  

- **CPC 9819.2000 – Guarantee Services**  
This heading specifically covers guarantee-related services, including issuance of corporate and financial guarantees, which aligns with the nature of the transaction.  

---

### 3. Deductibility and Input Tax Considerations  

**Deductibility for Income Tax:**  
The fee is incurred to secure supply arrangements, directly connected to WEPL’s business. Under **section 20 of the Ordinance**, such finance-related charges are deductible as revenue expenses. However, deductibility is strictly conditional upon compliance with **withholding requirements** under section 21(c). If WEPL claims treaty relief, exemption under section 152(5) must be secured to preserve deductibility.  

**Input Sales Tax:**  
The 15% SST paid under reverse charge will **not be creditable** since WEPL’s principal activity (sale of petroleum products/lubricants) is subject to **federal sales tax on goods**, not Sindh sales tax on services. Therefore, the SST paid should be recorded as a cost component of the guarantee fee.  

---

### 4. Transfer Pricing – Arm’s Length Requirement  

**Applicability:**  
As the transaction is between WEPL and Asyad (related parties), **section 108 of the Ordinance** and the **Income Tax Rules on transfer pricing** apply. WEPL must demonstrate that the 1.5% fee reflects an **arm’s length charge**.  

**Arm’s Length Justification:**  
- Comparable bank guarantee charges in Pakistan typically range from **1% to 2% per annum**, depending on collateral and risk profile. The 1.5% rate falls within this range.  
- Asyad assumes real financial risk by backing WEPL’s supplier obligations, which substantiates the charge.  

**Documentation:**  
WEPL should maintain a **Local File** containing:  
- Transaction details and agreements.  
- Pricing methodology and justification.  
- Market comparables (e.g., bank commission rates).  
- Board approvals and SBP approval letters.  

Disclosure of the transaction is also required in the **International Transactions Schedule** of the annual income tax return. This will safeguard against adjustments by FBR in the event of a TP audit.  

---

### 5. Regulatory Consideration – SBP Approval  

The **State Bank of Pakistan (SBP)** requires prior approval for guarantee arrangements involving remittance of fees abroad. The application typically includes the guarantee letter, calculation workings, and a debit note from the parent. SBP approval should be retained as part of compliance, as banks will not remit without it.  

---

### **Conclusion and Recommended Actions**  

1. **Income Tax:** Withholding at 20% applies under domestic law. Treaty relief is available under Article 7 of the Pakistan–Saudi DTAA, subject to section 152(5) exemption.  
2. **Sales Tax:** The guarantee fee is an imported service under SST law, subject to 15% tax under **CPC 9819.2000**. Liability rests on WEPL under reverse charge.  
3. **Deductibility:** Expense is deductible provided withholding obligations are met. SST will be a cost (no input credit).  
4. **Transfer Pricing:** Document that the 1.5% fee is arm’s length. Maintain supporting evidence and disclose in the return.  
5. **SBP Approval:** Ensure prior approval and retain documentation for remittance.  

Please let us know if you require our assistance in obtaining FBR exemption under section 152(5), preparing transfer pricing documentation, or handling SRB filings.  

Sincerely,  
*[Your Name]*  
*Tax Advisor – [Your Firm]*

**Subject:** Tax Implications of Parent Guarantee Fee Arrangement – Asyad Holding

As noted, Asyad has issued guarantees totaling USD 15.3 million (USD 12 million to Shell Lubricants Supply Company B.V. and USD 3.3 million to Shell Markets Middle East) in favor of WEPL’s suppliers. In return, WEPL is liable to pay an annual fee of 1.5%, amounting to USD 180,000 and USD 49,500 respectively, payable quarterly in arrears.  

From an income tax perspective, the payment of guarantee fees by a resident to a non-resident is considered Pakistan-source income under section 152 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, and subject to withholding at 20% of the gross amount, treated as final tax since Asyad does not have a permanent establishment in Pakistan. However, under the Pakistan–Saudi Arabia Double Taxation Treaty, the guarantee fee does not fall within the definition of interest or royalty, but instead qualifies as business profits under Article 7. In the absence of a permanent establishment in Pakistan, such income should be taxable only in Saudi Arabia. Accordingly, if WEPL wishes to apply treaty protection, it must seek exemption under section 152(5) by presenting Asyad’s Tax Residency Certificate and securing approval from the Commissioner; otherwise, the domestic withholding at 20% will continue to apply.  

For Sindh sales tax purposes, the guarantee fee is treated as a taxable financial service consumed in the province. Because Asyad is a foreign entity and unregistered with SRB, the service qualifies as an imported service, which obligates WEPL to self-assess and pay 15% Sindh Sales Tax under the reverse charge mechanism. In terms of classification, while bank-issued guarantees and related commissions are often aligned with **CPC 71135 (non-mortgage loan services for business purposes, including standby and commitment fees)**, the more appropriate fit for a corporate guarantee arrangement such as this—where the provider is a parent company rather than a licensed bank—is **CPC 71599 (other services auxiliary to financial services, n.e.c.)**. This residual category is designed to capture financial support services not otherwise classified, ensuring compliance without restricting the classification to entities licensed as banks. SRB’s practice is to focus on the **nature of the service** rather than the regulatory status of the provider, and under either classification the guarantee fee remains subject to 15% tax. Since WEPL’s principal business is trading in petroleum products, which falls under the federal sales tax regime on goods, the Sindh sales tax paid will not be creditable as input tax and should therefore be treated as part of the cost of the guarantee fee.  

The guarantee fee itself qualifies as an allowable deduction under section 20 of the Ordinance, since it is wholly incurred for business purposes to secure supplier arrangements. However, deductibility is conditional on compliance with withholding requirements—either deduction of 20% tax or obtaining exemption under section 152(5). The SST paid under reverse charge will also be deductible as a cost, though not claimable as input tax credit.  

Given that the transaction is between associated enterprises, the provisions of section 108 and the transfer pricing rules apply. WEPL should ensure that the 1.5% fee reflects an arm’s length charge. Bank commission rates in Pakistan typically range between 1% and 2% for similar credit guarantees, indicating that the agreed rate is within a reasonable range. Nevertheless, WEPL should maintain detailed transfer pricing documentation, including the agreements, board approvals, SBP approval, market comparables, and a functional analysis, and disclose the transaction in the international transactions section of its annual return.  

Finally, it is essential to ensure that SBP’s prior approval for the guarantee arrangement and related remittance has been obtained and retained, as foreign exchange regulations require such clearance for remittances of commission or guarantee fees abroad.  

In conclusion, the guarantee fee is subject to 20% withholding under domestic law unless treaty relief under Article 7 is applied through section 152(5) exemption. It is also subject to 15% Sindh Sales Tax under the reverse charge mechanism, with the appropriate CPC classification being **CPC 71599 – Other services auxiliary to financial services n.e.c.**, given that the provider is not a licensed bank. You're absolutely right to remain cautious, and this warrants a more precise and well-supported analysis of the Sindh Sales Tax implications for the parental guarantee fee.

---

###  Legal Context of Sindh Sales Tax on Services

Under the **Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011**, only services specifically listed in the **Second Schedule** are taxable. The Act follows a **positive-list approach**: a service is **taxable only if enumerated** or tax is clearly levied under relevant provisions. Further, imported services consumed in Sindh — that is, services provided by non-residents — are subject to tax via the **reverse charge**, but only **if** the service qualifies as "taxable" under the law citeturn0search4turn0search6.

---

###  Is a Parental Guarantee Fee a “Service”?

 **Argument for Taxability:**  

A parental guarantee fee is functionally akin to a financial service: Asyad Holding (a non-resident) provides credit support to WEPL’s transactions (supplier purchases). As such, SRB could treat this as an **imported financial service**, taxable at 15%, assuming it appears in the applicable tariff codes (CPC) citeturn0search4turn0search6. The absence of provider type restrictions in the Act suggests SRB might argue that, so long as the activity is equivalent to a guarantee service, classification should follow the underlying economic function.

 **Legal Ambiguity and Potential Defensibility:**  

However, the Second Schedule does **not explicitly list “parenteral guarantee”**. The listed services, such as consultancy, advertising, education, hospital services etc., are typical economic activities—not intra-group support mechanisms citeturn0search6turn0search13. A parental guarantee between related parties—particularly a holding company and subsidiary—may arguably be viewed not as a service in the commercial sense, but as a **corporate finance arrangement**. In that light, one could assert it's **not taxable under SST**, because it does not fall within the statutory definition of a “service” listed in the Schedule.

---

###  CPC Classification:  Bank vs. Corporate Guarantee

If SRB were to tax it, CPC codes to consider include:

- **CPC 71135 – Non-mortgage loan services for business purposes (standby/commitment fees)** — typically used for interbank or institution-to-public guarantees.
- **CPC 71599 – Other auxiliary financial services, not elsewhere classified** — a residual category.

Neither CPC expressly limits application to licensed banks. SRB may lean on **CPC 71135** by analogy to guarantee fees, particularly if they emphasize economic equivalence. Alternatively, for a related-party guarantee, **CPC 71599** may be more defensible to reflect its non-commercial nature.

---

###  Practical Outlook

**SRB’s Stance:** Given SRB’s inclination to tax service-like arrangements (e.g., internal management or support services), they may vie to levy SST at **15%** on such guarantee fees via reverse charge, using CPC classification as justification.

**WEPL’s Defensive Position:** It is plausible to argue the guarantee does not qualify as a service under the SST Act’s schema, because:

- It is not listed in the Second Schedule.
- It arises from intra-group arrangements rather than economic activities offered to the market.
- It is a financial/corporate support tool, not a commercial service in the normative sense.

The lack of explicit SRB rulings against similar arrangements adds to WEPL’s defensibility.

---

###  Suggested Refined Paragraph for Your Email

> On Sindh Sales Tax, a parental guarantee fee may or may not be taxable. While the guarantee resembles a financial service (e.g., standby or commitment fee), the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act is **positive-list based**, meaning only services listed in the Second Schedule are taxable. Since “parental guarantees” are not explicitly included, one could argue this arrangement falls outside SST scope. In practice, SRB may still treat it as a financial service rendered by a non-resident, subjecting WEPL to **15% SST via reverse charge**, using a CPC such as **71135 (non-mortgage loan/commitment services)** or **71599 (other auxiliary financial services)** as justification. Absent clear policy or circular from SRB, this classification remains ambiguous—WEPL can follow SRB’s lead conservatively or maintain a defensible internal position that the fee is a corporate finance arrangement and not a taxable service.

---

## 1. Income Tax – Taxability of Guarantee Fee & Treaty Considerations  
**Domestic Tax Treatment:** Under Pakistan’s Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, a payment of guarantee fee by a resident company to a non-resident is generally considered Pakistan-source income for the non-resident. Although this fee is not labeled as “royalty” or “technical service fee” under the Ordinance, it still falls within the scope of amounts chargeable to tax in Pakistan because the payer (WEPL) is a Pakistani resident and the fee is for an economic benefit related to Pakistan (securing WEPL’s obligations). In other words, if no treaty applied, WEPL would be required to deduct **20%** withholding on the guarantee fee paid abroad. This withholding obligation arises under Section 152 of the Ordinance, which covers “any other amount” paid to non-residents【41†L1-L4】. 

It is important to emphasize that the guarantee fee is **not** a “royalty” as defined in Pakistani law or treaties, since it does not involve the use of intellectual property or equipment rights【12†L686-L694】. Likewise, it is not a fee for technical or consultancy services. Rather, it is akin to a financial service/assurance fee. Pakistan’s tax law does not have a special category for guarantee fees; hence, by default the payment is taxable as *business/other income* of the non-resident and subject to the aforementioned withholding. 

**Treaty Considerations (Pakistan–Saudi Arabia DTAA):** The Pakistan-Saudi tax treaty (2006) can significantly affect this analysis. Under the treaty, the classification of the income determines taxing rights: 

- **Not Interest or Royalty:** The guarantee fee does not fall under the treaty’s Interest article (Art. 11) because it is not income from a debt-claim (no money has been lent by Asyad). It also does not fall under Royalties (Art. 12) since no use of intellectual property, know-how, or equipment is involved【12†L686-L694】. This means the 10% treaty royalty withholding cap is not applicable.  

- **Business Profits vs Other Income:** The fee most closely resembles business income (or a service fee) earned by Asyad. Under Article 7 (Business Profits), profits of a Saudi enterprise are taxable only in Saudi Arabia **unless** the enterprise carries on business in Pakistan through a permanent establishment (PE)【45†L345-L353】. As Asyad has no PE in Pakistan for this transaction, its guarantee fee income **would not be taxable in Pakistan** under Article 7. In effect, the treaty suggests Pakistan should not tax this fee at all, treating it as Asyad’s business profit taxable only in Saudi Arabia (assuming Asyad is a Saudi tax resident and beneficial owner of the fee). This treaty protection would override the domestic 20% withholding tax, **if** successfully invoked. 

  It is worth noting that the treaty’s “Other Income” article (Art. 22) provides that income not dealt with in other articles is taxable only in the resident state, **but** allows Pakistan to tax such income according to its own laws if it arises in Pakistan【15†L993-L1001】【15†L1011-L1016】. This creates some ambiguity. Our view is that a parent guarantee fee should be regarded as part of Asyad’s business profits (an ordinary business/service transaction between related companies) rather than an undefined “other income.” If treated as business profit, Article 7 applies and Pakistan has no taxing right without a PE. If, however, one were to treat it as “other income,” Pakistan could argue to tax it under paragraph 3 of Article 22【15†L1011-L1016】. Given the nature of the arrangement (provision of a financial service by the parent), the stronger position is that it falls under business profits. In similar cases, tax advisors prefer to classify parent guarantee fees as business income to utilize treaty protection. 

**Conclusion on Taxability:** In summary, **yes, the guarantee fee is chargeable to tax in Pakistan under domestic law**, at a 20% withholding rate, **unless** treaty relief is claimed. Under the Pakistan-Saudi treaty, WEPL can contend that the fee is exempt from Pakistani tax because it is neither interest nor royalty, and as business profit of a Saudi resident with no PE in Pakistan, it should only be taxed in Saudi Arabia【45†L345-L353】. Practically, to apply the treaty benefits, WEPL should obtain a **certificate or exemption** from FBR: Pakistan’s procedure (under Section 152(5) of the Ordinance) requires the payer to notify the Commissioner before paying a non-resident without withholding tax【22†L8235-L8244】【22†L8245-L8252】. The Commissioner may then confirm if no withholding is required in view of the treaty. We **strongly recommend** following this procedure – essentially seeking advance tax clearance – **before** remitting the fee without deduction. This will protect WEPL from any future dispute or disallowance for not withholding. 

Additionally, please note that **providing this guarantee does not itself create a “Permanent Establishment”** for Asyad in Pakistan. Asyad is simply extending a financial guarantee from Saudi Arabia; it has no office, branch, or agent concluding contracts in Pakistan for this purpose. The arrangement is limited to a cross-border financial commitment. Therefore, there is minimal risk of Asyad being deemed to have a PE in Pakistan under Article 5 of the treaty (since there is no fixed place of business or dependent agent of Asyad involved in Pakistan). This PE point simply reinforces that Pakistan cannot tax Asyad’s fee except via withholding, absent a local presence.

*(On a related regulatory note, such cross-border guarantees require compliance with State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) foreign exchange regulations. Under Chapter 19 of SBP’s Foreign Exchange Manual, prior approval is required for guarantees on behalf of Pakistani residents that may involve foreign currency outflows, including any *“commission fee, guarantee premium fee etc.”*【39†L1-L4】. We assume that the necessary SBP permission for Asyad’s guarantee has been or will be obtained, given that the guarantee was issued on July 30, 2025. This is important to legally allow payment of the fee abroad.)*

## 2. Classification as a Service – Income Tax and Sales Tax Implications  
**Service Characterization (Income Tax):** The guarantee fee can be viewed as consideration for a service – essentially a financial service (credit support) provided by Asyad to WEPL. There is no transfer of a tangible good or intellectual property; it is the service of Asyad’s balance sheet and credit being put behind WEPL’s obligations. In Pakistani tax practice, such fees paid to a foreign affiliate are typically treated as **“foreign rendered services.”** While they are not “technical services” per the specific definition (since Asyad’s guarantee is not managerial, technical, or consultancy in nature), they are still services in a broad sense. Under Section 152 of the Ordinance, payments to non-residents for services rendered outside Pakistan **can** be taxable in Pakistan if the income is Pakistan-source. The source of service income generally depends on where the service is performed or utilized. Here, the act of guaranteeing is performed by Asyad abroad, but the benefit is utilized by WEPL in Pakistan (to satisfy its suppliers). FBR could argue the fee has Pakistan source since WEPL, a Pakistani entity, is paying for a service related to its Pakistan trade. Thus, as discussed above, the fee falls under the scope of taxable Pakistan-source income, triggering withholding at 20% (unless the treaty is applied)【41†L1-L4】. To summarize, Pakistan would treat this as a **service fee to a non-resident**, taxable locally by withholding, absent treaty relief.

**Sales Tax on Services:** Yes, the guarantee fee would likely be viewed as consideration for a taxable **service** under provincial sales tax law. In Sindh (where WEPL is located), the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act 2011 applies to services consumed in the province. Financial services, including guarantees, provided by banks or others are taxable. Although Asyad is not a bank, the nature of the transaction (a guarantee) falls under financial services. Because the service provider (Asyad) is outside Pakistan and not registered for provincial sales tax, this transaction is treated as an **“imported service.”** Sindh sales tax law requires the **service recipient** (WEPL) to self-assess and pay the applicable sales tax on an imported service under the reverse charge mechanism. The current standard **SST rate is 15%** of the service value【50†L503-L511】 (note: the rate was increased from 13% to 15% effective July 1, 2024). 

In practical terms, WEPL would need to compute 15% of the guarantee fee each quarter and deposit that amount to the Sindh Revenue Board (since the service is consumed in Sindh). For example, if a quarterly installment is USD 45,000 (one-fourth of $180k) for SLSC’s guarantee, the SST of 15% on that (approx. USD 6,750, or PKR equivalent) would be payable to SRB via reverse charge. WEPL should register or ensure it is enrolled with SRB for the purpose of remitting this tax on imported services. Typically, no sales tax is charged by the foreign provider, but the local recipient must accrue and pay SST. 

**Income Tax vs Sales Tax Treatment:** Classifying the transaction as a service does not change the income tax outcome (it remains taxable income to a non-resident). However, it **does** mean WEPL faces a provincial sales tax obligation. Note that this guarantee fee is not subject to **federal sales tax (VAT)** since that tax applies to goods and certain federal excise services; here the provincial service tax is the relevant levy. Also, there is no concept of withholding **sales** tax on services to non-residents – rather, WEPL itself must pay it as an end-consumer of an imported service.

## 3. Deductibility of the Expense and Input Sales Tax Credits  
**Deductibility under Income Tax Ordinance:** The guarantee fee expense should be **fully deductible** for WEPL in computing its taxable income, provided it is incurred “wholly and exclusively” for the purposes of WEPL’s business. In this case, the fee is a cost of obtaining credit support to procure trading stock (lubricants) – a clear business purpose. The fee is periodic and does not create any asset or enduring benefit, so it is treated as a revenue expense (finance cost), not a capital expense. We do not see any specific bar to deductibility in the Ordinance. Section 20 of the Ordinance allows deduction of any interest or financial charges incurred for the business, and by analogy a guarantee fee serves a similar function. There is no need for any special approval to claim this expense, **as long as** it is an arm’s length amount. 

However, one critical condition for deductibility is **withholding tax compliance.** Under Section 21(c) of the Ordinance, any otherwise-deductible expense will be disallowed if the taxpayer failed to deduct and deposit applicable withholding tax on that payment. In other words, if WEPL pays the guarantee fees to Asyad without deducting tax when it was required to (and no exemption was obtained), the tax authorities can deny the deduction for those fees. To ensure the expense remains deductible: 

- **If WEPL opts to withhold 20% tax** on the fee (not claiming treaty relief), it should deposit that tax and obtain CPRs/challans as proof. The net amount paid to Asyad plus the tax paid will then be allowed as expense.  
- **If WEPL claims treaty exemption (0% withholding)**, it must follow the procedure to get clearance from the Commissioner (as noted earlier). With that exemption approval or a written non-deduction order in hand, WEPL can pay the gross fee without deduction and still deduct the expense. Documentation of the treaty residency of Asyad (e.g. tax residence certificate from Saudi authorities) and beneficial ownership should be maintained as well. 

Assuming WEPL fulfills one of the above and is compliant, the guarantee fee should be an allowable deduction against its business income for tax. This will reduce WEPL’s taxable profits (the expense is fairly substantial in PKR terms, so it’s important to secure the deduction).

**Input Sales Tax Credit:** You also inquired whether input tax paid on this service could be claimed. In the context of **provincial sales tax on services**, an “input tax credit” would mean WEPL offsetting the 15% SST it pays on the guarantee fee against any SST it charges on its own services. WEPL’s core business, however, is the sale of petroleum products/lubricants – which is the sale of **goods** (subject to federal sales tax) rather than the provision of taxable services under SST. If WEPL is not providing any taxable services in Sindh, it will not have an output SST liability against which to claim this input. Cross-adjustment between provincial service tax and federal sales tax on goods is generally **not allowed** (the two are separate regimes). Therefore, the SST paid on the guarantee fee will likely be a **non-adjustable cost** to WEPL. 

In summary: WEPL will pay 15% SST on the fee via reverse charge and treat it as an expense. That SST amount can be booked as an expense (and deducted for income tax as part of the guarantee fee cost), but WEPL **cannot** claim a refund or credit of it from the SRB unless WEPL itself had Sindh-taxable services. (For completeness, if WEPL were also engaged in providing any SST-taxable services or acting as a service provider, it could potentially integrate that input in its SST return, subject to the input adjustment limits. But assuming WEPL’s business is solely trading of goods, no such adjustment is available.) 

Please note that since the SST on imported services is paid by WEPL itself (and not charged by Asyad), WEPL should keep evidence of the tax payment. The SRB challans for the 15% tax should be retained. While this tax is an added cost, it is generally treated as part of the cost of obtaining the guarantee service (and thus deductible for income tax purposes as well). 

## 4. Transfer Pricing (Section 108) and Documentation Requirements  
Because Asyad Holding and WEPL are **related parties** (affiliates under common ownership/control), the guarantee fee arrangement falls under Pakistan’s transfer pricing rules (Section 108 of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001 and the related Chapter VI(A) of the Income Tax Rules). These rules require that transactions between associated enterprises be carried out at an **arm’s length price** – i.e., the price that would be charged between independent parties in comparable circumstances【52†L19-L27】. 

**Arm’s Length Assessment:** WEPL should ensure that the 1.5% per annum guarantee fee is consistent with what an unrelated third party would charge for a similar guarantee. In practice, parent companies sometimes charge no fee or a lower fee for group guarantees, but tax authorities increasingly expect a market-based charge (since it can affect profit allocation). To support the arm’s length nature of the 1.5% fee, WEPL can consider: 

- **Comparables:** What would a bank charge for a comparable guarantee? For instance, if WEPL approached a local bank to guarantee USD 15.3 million of supplier credit, the bank might charge a commission (often ranging ~1% to 2% per annum, depending on collateral and risk). If possible, obtain quotes or see published rates for bank guarantees. If banks in Pakistan charge, say, 2% with collateral, a 1.5% fee from an unsecured parent might be reasonable. Any internal treasury evaluations or emails discussing how 1.5% was arrived at should be kept as evidence.  
- **Function and risk analysis:** Recognize that Asyad is incurring a real risk by guaranteeing WEPL’s obligations; in the event of WEPL’s default to Shell, Asyad must pay up to USD 15.3 million. Charging a fee is thus justified. The fee compensates Asyad for tying up its credit capacity and risking its capital. Documenting Asyad’s credit rating or financial capacity could help show that Asyad indeed provides a valuable financial backing. 

**Documentation:** Pakistan’s transfer pricing regulations (largely aligned with OECD guidelines) require certain documentation to substantiate that inter-company transactions are at arm’s length. Given the size of this transaction, WEPL likely falls under the threshold to maintain a **Local File** and possibly a **Master File** (if the group meets global revenue criteria). In 2018, rules were introduced mandating a Local File for taxpayers with significant related-party dealings【52†L19-L27】. WEPL should maintain a **contemporaneous Local File** that includes: details of the transaction, the parties involved, the pricing methodology, comparables considered, and economic analysis demonstrating that 1.5% is arm’s length. This file does not have to be submitted with the return but must be furnished to FBR if requested during an audit or transfer pricing review. Additionally, WEPL’s income tax return requires disclosure of related party transactions (the *International Transactions* section), and these guarantee fee payments should be duly reported there. 

Non-compliance with transfer pricing rules could lead to adjustments. If FBR finds that 1.5% is higher than an arm’s length rate, it could disallow the “excess” portion of the fee, thereby increasing WEPL’s taxable income. Conversely (though less likely in this scenario), if 1.5% were too low (benefiting WEPL while stripping profit to Asyad), they could increase WEPL’s income or adjust Asyad’s (if it had a taxable presence). Ensuring the fee is reasonable mitigates this risk. At present, 1.5% appears to be in a plausible range, but a brief **benchmarking analysis** is advisable now or during year-end tax computations. 

**Compliance obligations:** Under Section 108, WEPL should be prepared to **justify the pricing** if queried. The law empowers the tax authorities to re-characterize or re-price transactions between associates to reflect arm’s length results【52†L19-L27】. Besides documentation, Pakistan has also implemented **Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR)** for large multinational groups and established a Directorate of Transfer Pricing for focused audits. Asyad Holding being a Saudi entity might also have to report this related-party dealing under any Saudi transfer pricing requirements. Coordination with the group tax team is prudent to ensure consistency. 

To summarize this point: WEPL must treat the guarantee fee as a related-party transaction subject to transfer pricing rules. It should maintain supporting evidence that the 1.5% fee is arm’s length. This includes possibly a benchmarking study or at least internal records of how this rate was decided (e.g., group policy or analogous fees in similar contexts). By doing so, WEPL will meet documentation requirements and be in a strong position if FBR conducts a transfer pricing audit on this transaction. 

## **Conclusion and Recommendations**  
In light of the above, WEPL can proceed with the guarantee fee arrangement, but it should do so with careful tax compliance: 

- **Withholding Tax:** Decide whether to utilize the tax treaty to pay the fee without Pakistani withholding. If yes, obtain the Commissioner's approval for treaty exemption upfront【22†L8237-L8245】【22†L8247-L8252】. If no (to be conservative), withhold 20% and deposit it timely to FBR【41†L1-L4】. (Either way, ensure deductibility by meeting Sec.21(c) obligations.)  
- **Sales Tax:** Treat the fee as an imported service in Sindh. Calculate and pay 15% SST on each fee payment in rupees【50†L503-L511】, via the prescribed SRB challan. This tax will be a cost to WEPL (no input credit likely available), so factor it into the overall cost of the arrangement.  
- **Documentation:** Maintain a file with the guarantee agreements, board approvals, SBP approval letter, and a transfer pricing analysis memo for the 1.5% rate. Come tax return time, disclose the payments in the annexures for foreign payments and related-party transactions.  
- **SBP Compliance:** As noted, ensure that SBP’s foreign exchange requirements have been fulfilled. Typically, an application to SBP for using a foreign guarantee and remitting the fee should be on record. SBP generally permits such guarantees by foreign sponsors for import/trade credit, but they do keep a record and require that any fee/commission abroad is pre-approved【39†L1-L4】. It would be prudent to double-check that WEPL’s finance team has secured the SBP go-ahead (or filed the necessary notice under Para 10 of Chapter 19 of the FX Manual). 

Given the complexity of international tax and regulatory considerations here, we recommend **seeking a formal tax opinion** or an advance ruling if uncertainty remains on any point (especially the treaty application). It may also be worthwhile to consult a Saudi tax advisor on Asyad’s side to confirm that receiving this fee does not create any Saudi tax or Zakat issues (Saudi Arabia generally does not tax such foreign-sourced income for a non-Saudi company, but confirming is good practice). All documentation (agreements, correspondence, approvals) should be kept on file for future audits or reviews by stakeholders. 

Please let us know if you need any assistance with the withholding tax exemption process, preparing transfer pricing documentation, or any other aspect of this arrangement. We are happy to help obtain clarity or approvals to ensure the transaction is compliant and efficient from a tax perspective.

Sincerely,  

*[Your Name]*  
*Tax Advisor – [Your Firm/Department]*  

**Sources & References:**  

- Guarantee Fee Agreements (WEPL – Asyad Holding) dated July 30, 2025 (effective 01-08-2025)【1†L141-L149】【2†L139-L147】  
- Pakistan Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – Section 152 (payments to non-residents) and Section 108 (transfer pricing) provisions【41†L1-L4】【52†L19-L27】  
- Pakistan–Saudi Arabia Double Taxation Agreement (2006), Articles 7, 11, 12, 22【45†L345-L353】【12†L686-L694】【15†L993-L1001】  
- Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 and Finance Act, 2024 amendments (standard rate 15%)【50†L503-L511】  
- SBP Foreign Exchange Manual (Chapter 19: Guarantees by non-residents) – requirement of prior approval for guarantee fees in foreign currency【39†L1-L4】.

---

**Subject:** Tax Implications of Parent Guarantee Fee Arrangement – Asyad Holding  

**Dear Komal,**  

Thank you for your query regarding the tax implications of the proposed parental guarantee fee arrangement with Asyad Holding. Based on the agreements executed on July 30, 2025 (effective August 1, 2025), Asyad has provided corporate guarantees totaling USD 15.3 million (USD 12 million to SLSC and USD 3.3 million to SMME) against an annual fee of 1.5%, payable quarterly. Please find our detailed comments below:  

---

### 1. Income Tax – Chargeability and Treaty Considerations  

Under **section 152 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, guarantee fees paid by a resident to a non-resident are deemed Pakistan-source income. In the absence of treaty protection, WEPL would be required to deduct **20% withholding tax** on the gross fee as a final tax, since Asyad has no permanent establishment in Pakistan.  

The **Pakistan–Saudi Arabia Tax Treaty** provides important relief. The guarantee fee does not qualify as *interest* (Article 11) or *royalty* (Article 12) as no debt-claim, intellectual property, or equipment use is involved. Instead, the fee is best characterized as *business profit* under **Article 7**. Since Asyad has no PE in Pakistan, the income should be taxable only in Saudi Arabia. This interpretation exempts the fee from Pakistan tax.  

To apply treaty protection, WEPL must obtain an exemption under **section 152(5)** by providing Asyad’s **Tax Residency Certificate** and securing confirmation from the Commissioner. Without this clearance, withholding at 20% would remain mandatory.  

---

### 2. Sales Tax – Classification as a Service  

The guarantee fee constitutes a **financial service** under the **Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011**. Because the service provider (Asyad) is outside Pakistan, the fee is treated as an **imported service**, making WEPL liable to pay Sindh Sales Tax under the **reverse charge mechanism**. The applicable rate is **15% of the service value**.  

For classification purposes, the appropriate **CPC (Classification of Services)** is:  

- **CPC 9819.2000 – Guarantee Services**.  
This code covers services relating to guarantees and indemnities, which aligns with the nature of Asyad’s parental guarantee.  

Accordingly, WEPL must self-assess and discharge 15% SST on each quarterly fee installment, regardless of whether tax is withheld under income tax law.  

---

### 3. Deductibility of Expense and Input Tax  

The guarantee fee is incurred wholly for business purposes—namely, securing supplier obligations—and qualifies as a **deductible expense** under **section 20** of the Ordinance. Since it is a recurring charge and does not create a capital asset, it will be treated as a revenue expense.  

Deductibility, however, is contingent on **withholding tax compliance**. If WEPL claims treaty exemption, advance clearance under section 152(5) is essential to preserve deductibility.  

On the sales tax side, the 15% SST paid under reverse charge will not be creditable as **input tax**, since WEPL’s main activity (sale of petroleum/lubricants) is subject to federal sales tax on goods rather than Sindh service tax. The SST should therefore be treated as part of the cost of the guarantee.  

---

### 4. Transfer Pricing Obligations  

As the transaction is between **associated enterprises**, it falls under **section 108 and Chapter VI(A) of the Income Tax Rules**. WEPL must demonstrate that the 1.5% annual fee is at **arm’s length**.  

Comparable benchmarks include bank guarantee fees in Pakistan, which generally range from 1% to 2% per annum. The 1.5% charge is therefore within a reasonable range, provided WEPL documents supporting evidence (e.g., market quotes, treasury evaluations).  

WEPL should prepare and maintain **transfer pricing documentation** (Local File), covering transaction details, pricing methodology, comparables, and functional analysis. Disclosure is also required in the **international transactions section** of the income tax return. Proper documentation will safeguard against potential FBR adjustments.  

---

### **Conclusion**  

- Withholding of **20%** applies under domestic law unless treaty relief under Article 7 of the Pakistan–Saudi Arabia DTAA is invoked via **section 152(5) exemption**.  
- The guarantee fee is a taxable **imported service** under Sindh law, chargeable at **15% SST**, CPC **9819.2000**.  
- The fee is **deductible** as a business expense, provided withholding obligations or treaty clearance is met. SST will be an **irrecoverable cost**.  
- As a **related-party transaction**, WEPL must document that the 1.5% rate is **arm’s length** and disclose appropriately.  
- SBP approval for remittance should also be retained as part of regulatory compliance.  

Please let us know if you would like assistance with the **section 152(5) exemption process**, preparation of the **transfer pricing file**, or support with **SRB filings**.  

Sincerely,  
*[Your Name]*  
*Tax Advisor – [Your Firm]*  

---  

Would you like me to also prepare a **step-by-step compliance checklist** (with actions, responsible team, and deadlines) that your finance team can follow for each quarterly payment? This could make execution smoother.

You’re right — it’s not a foregone conclusion that every cross-border fee is a taxable service under Sindh Sales Tax law. Let’s carefully unpack this, based on the **Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (SSTSA)** and how “imported services” are defined.  

---

### 1. The Legal Framework  
Under section 3 of SSTSA, sales tax applies on **taxable services provided or rendered in Sindh**. “Imported services” are separately covered: if a service is **provided by a person outside Pakistan but consumed in Sindh**, the Sindh-based recipient is liable to tax under the **reverse charge mechanism**.  

The key questions for classification are:  
- Is the transaction **a “service” within the Act’s meaning**?  
- If yes, is it covered by the **Second Schedule (tariff of services)** or falls into the **residual category (“any other service not elsewhere classified”)?**  
- If not, the transaction is **outside SST scope**.  

---

### 2. Whether a Guarantee Fee is a Taxable Service  
A **parental guarantee fee** is not expressly listed in the SST Schedule like courier, telecom, or insurance services. The closest categories are:  

- **Credit-granting / guarantee-related services (CPC 71135)**: These include standby/commitment fees, letters of credit, etc. But CPC 71135 is traditionally applied to **banks and financial institutions**.  
- **Auxiliary financial services (CPC 71599)**: A residual category covering support services not elsewhere classified. SRB sometimes relies on this for financial support fees charged by non-banks.  

So, there are **two possible views**:  

**View A – Taxable Service:**  
- Functionally, a parental guarantee fee resembles a financial service because Asyad is placing its credit behind WEPL’s obligations.  
- Even if not a bank, the economic nature is equivalent to a guarantee commission.  
- Under the “imported services” rule, since WEPL is in Sindh and consuming the benefit here, SRB could argue it is taxable at **15% under reverse charge**.  
- CPC classification would then likely fall under **71599 (Other auxiliary financial services, n.e.c.)**, to avoid the “bank only” limitation of CPC 71135.  

**View B – Not a Taxable Service:**  
- The SST Act taxes only services listed in the tariff schedule or “not elsewhere classified” services.  
- A **corporate guarantee between group entities** may not amount to a “service” in the strict sense but rather an intra-group financial arrangement.  
- It is **not a financial product offered to the public**, unlike a bank guarantee or insurance policy.
