Please more refined, polished and concise it, whenever possible. Remove unnecessary discussion. Please also that appropriate CPC in the light of the recent amendments in Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011. 

Hi Komal, thank you for your query regarding the tax treatment of the proposed parental guarantee fee. 
We understand that Asyad Holding (Saudi affiliate) is providing corporate guarantees totaling USD 15.3 million (USD 12 million to Shell Lubricants Supply Co. B.V. (SLSC) and USD 3.3 million to Shell Markets Middle East (SMME)) on behalf of Wafi Energy Pakistan Ltd (WEPL). In return, WEPL will pay Asyad a guarantee fee of 1.5% per annum of the guaranteed amounts (USD 180,000 and USD 49,500 per year respectively), as documented in the fee agreements dated July 30, 2025 (effective August 1, 2025). The fee is payable quarterly in arrears, within 30 days of each quarter’s end[3]. Below we address each of your points in turn, in a structured manner:
Income Tax – Taxability of Guarantee Fee & Treaty Considerations
Under Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, a payment of guarantee fee by a resident company to a non-resident is generally considered Pakistan-source income for the non-resident. Although this fee is not labeled as ‘royalty’ or ‘technical service fee’ under the Ordinance, it still falls within the scope of amounts chargeable to tax in Pakistan because the payer (WEPL) is a Pakistani resident and the fee is for an economic benefit related to Pakistan (securing WEPL’s obligations). Such payments to non-residents that are not specifically categorized (e.g. not interest, not royalty/FTS) are subject to a default withholding tax of 20% of the gross amount (final tax, since Asyad has no PE in Pakistan). In other words, if no treaty applied, WEPL would be required to deduct 20% withholding on the guarantee fee paid abroad. This withholding obligation arises under section 152 of the Ordinance, which covers ‘any other amount’ paid to non-residents.
It is important to emphasize that the guarantee fee is not a ‘royalty’ as defined in Pakistani law or treaties, since it does not involve the use of intellectual property or equipment rights. Likewise, it is not a fee for technical or consultancy services. Rather, it is akin to a financial service/assurance fee. Ordinance does not have a special category for guarantee fees; hence, by default the payment is taxable as business/other income of the non-resident and subject to the aforementioned withholding.
The Pakistan-Saudi tax treaty can significantly affect this analysis. Under the treaty, the classification of the income determines taxing rights:
•	The guarantee fee does not fall under the treaty’s Interest article (Art. 11) because it is not income from a debt-claim (no money has been lent by Asyad). It also does not fall under Royalties (Art. 12) since no use of intellectual property, know-how, or equipment is involved. This means the 10% treaty royalty withholding cap is not applicable.

•	The fee most closely resembles business income (or a service fee) earned by Asyad. Under Article 7 (Business Profits), profits of a Saudi enterprise are taxable only in Saudi Arabia unless the enterprise carries on business in Pakistan through a permanent establishment (PE). As Asyad has no PE in Pakistan for this transaction, its guarantee fee income would not be taxable in Pakistan under Article 7. In effect, the treaty suggests Pakistan should not tax this fee at all, treating it as Asyad’s business profit taxable only in Saudi Arabia (assuming Asyad is a Saudi tax resident and beneficial owner of the fee). This treaty protection would override the domestic 20% withholding tax, if successfully invoked.
It is worth noting that the treaty’s ‘Other Income’ article (Art. 22) provides that income not dealt with in other articles is taxable only in the resident state, but allows Pakistan to tax such income according to its own laws if it arises in Pakistan. This creates some ambiguity. Our view is that a parent guarantee fee should be regarded as part of Asyad’s business profits (an ordinary business/service transaction between related companies) rather than an undefined ‘other income.’ If treated as business profit, Article 7 applies and Pakistan has no taxing right without a PE. If, nevertheless, one was to treat it as “other income,” Pakistan could argue to tax it under paragraph 3 of Article 22. Given the nature of the arrangement (provision of a financial service by the parent), the stronger position is that it falls under business profits. In similar cases, tax advisors prefer to classify parent guarantee fees as business income to utilize treaty protection.
In summary, yes, the guarantee fee is chargeable to tax in Pakistan under domestic law, at a 20% withholding rate, unless treaty relief is claimed. Under the Pakistan-Saudi treaty, WEPL can contend that the fee is exempt from Pakistani tax because it is neither interest nor royalty, and as business profit of a Saudi resident with no PE in Pakistan, it should only be taxed in Saudi Arabia. Practically, to apply the treaty benefits, WEPL should obtain an exemption certificate from tax department under section 152(5) of the Ordinance before paying a non-resident without withholding tax. 
Classification as a Service – Sales Tax Implications
The guarantee fee would likely be viewed as consideration for a taxable service under provincial sales tax law. In Sindh (where WEPL is located), the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act 2011 applies to services consumed in the province. Financial services, including guarantees, provided by banks or others are taxable. Although Asyad is not a bank, the nature of the transaction (a guarantee) falls under financial services. Because the service provider (Asyad) is outside Pakistan and not registered for provincial sales tax, this transaction is treated as an “imported service.” Sindh sales tax law requires the service recipient (WEPL) to self-assess and pay the applicable sales tax on an imported service under the reverse charge mechanism. The current standard SST rate is 15% of the service value. 
Deductibility of the Expense and Input Sales Tax Credits
The guarantee fee expense should be fully deductible for WEPL in computing its taxable income, provided it is incurred ‘wholly and exclusively’ for the purposes of WEPL’s business. In this case, the fee is a cost of obtaining credit support to procure trading stock (lubricants), a clear business purpose. The fee is periodic and does not create any asset or enduring benefit, so it is treated as a revenue expense (finance cost), not a capital expense. We do not see any specific bar to deductibility in the Ordinance. section 20 of the Ordinance allows deduction of any interest or financial charges incurred for the business, and by analogy a guarantee fee serves a similar function. There is no need for any special approval to claim this expense, as long as it is an arm’s length amount.
You also inquired whether input tax paid on this service could be claimed. In the context of provincial sales tax on services, an ‘input tax credit’ would mean WEPL offsetting the 15% SST it pays on the guarantee fee against any SST it charges on its own services. WEPL’s core business. 
Transfer Pricing (Section 108) and Documentation Requirements
Because Asyad Holding and WEPL are related parties (affiliates under common ownership/control), the guarantee fee arrangement falls under Pakistan’s transfer pricing rules (Section 108 of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001 and the related Chapter VI(A) of the Income Tax Rules). These rules require that transactions between associated enterprises be carried out at an arm’s length price i.e., the price that would be charged between independent parties in comparable circumstances.
WEPL should ensure that the 1.5% per annum guarantee fee is consistent with what an unrelated third party would charge for a similar guarantee. In practice, parent companies sometimes charge no fee or a lower fee for group guarantees, but tax authorities increasingly expect a market-based charge (since it can affect profit allocation). To support the arm’s length nature of the 1.5% fee, WEPL can consider:
•	What would a bank charge for a comparable guarantee? For instance, if WEPL approached a local bank to guarantee USD 15.3 million of supplier credit, the bank might charge a commission (often ranging 1% to 2% per annum, depending on collateral and risk). If possible, obtain quotes or see published rates for bank guarantees. If banks in Pakistan charge, say, 2% with collateral, a 1.5% fee from an unsecured parent might be reasonable. Any internal treasury evaluations or emails discussing how 1.5% was arrived at should be kept as evidence.

•	Recognize that Asyad is incurring a real risk by guaranteeing WEPL’s obligations; in the event of WEPL’s default to Shell, Asyad must pay up to USD 15.3 million. Charging a fee is thus justified. The fee compensates Asyad for tying up its credit capacity and risking its capital. Documenting Asyad’s credit rating or financial capacity could help show that Asyad indeed provides a valuable financial backing.
Transfer pricing regulations (largely aligned with OECD guidelines) require certain documentation to substantiate that inter-company transactions are at arm’s length. Given the size of this transaction, WEPL likely falls under the threshold to maintain a Local File and possibly a Master File (if the group meets global revenue criteria). In 2018, rules were introduced mandating a Local File for taxpayers with significant related-party dealings. WEPL should maintain a contemporaneous Local File that includes: details of the transaction, the parties involved, the pricing methodology, comparables considered, and economic analysis demonstrating that 1.5% is arm’s length. This file does not have to be submitted with the return but must be furnished to FBR if requested during an audit or transfer pricing review. Additionally, WEPL’s income tax return requires disclosure of related party transactions (the International Transactions section), and these guarantee fee payments should be duly reported there.
Non-compliance with transfer pricing rules could lead to adjustments. If FBR finds that 1.5% is higher than an arm’s length rate, it could disallow the “excess” portion of the fee, thereby increasing WEPL’s taxable income. Conversely (though less likely in this scenario), if 1.5% were too low (benefiting WEPL while stripping profit to Asyad), they could increase WEPL’s income or adjust Asyad’s (if it had a taxable presence). Ensuring the fee is reasonable mitigates this risk. At present, 1.5% appears to be in a plausible range, but a brief benchmarking analysis is advisable now or during year-end tax computations.
Under section 108, WEPL should be prepared to justify the pricing if queried. The law empowers the tax authorities to re-characterize or re-price transactions between associates to reflect arm’s length results. Besides documentation, Pakistan has also implemented Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR) for large multinational groups and established a Directorate of Transfer Pricing for focused audits. Asyad Holding being a Saudi entity might also have to report this related-party dealing under any Saudi transfer pricing requirements. Coordination with the group tax team is prudent to ensure consistency.
To summarize this point: WEPL must treat the guarantee fee as a related-party transaction subject to transfer pricing rules. It should maintain supporting evidence that the 1.5% fee is arm’s length. This includes possibly a benchmarking study or at least internal records of how this rate was decided (e.g., group policy or analogous fees in similar contexts). By doing so, WEPL will meet documentation requirements and be in a strong position if FBR conducts a transfer pricing audit on this transaction.

# **Sindh Sales Tax Implications – Parental Guarantee Fee**  

### 1. Statutory Background  
Effective **1 July 2025**, the **Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011** was amended to move from a **positive list** to a **negative list** system. Under the new regime:  
- **All services are taxable by default**, unless specifically exempted under the **First Schedule**.  
- The statutory definition of “service” has been broadened to include *“any activity, facility, utility, benefit, or advantage (including the granting, assignment, cession or surrender of any right)”*.  
- Imported services consumed in Sindh are taxable under **reverse charge**.  

---

### 2. Application to Guarantee Fee Arrangement  
- **Nature of transaction:** Asyad Holding (Saudi affiliate) has issued parental guarantees to WEPL’s suppliers in return for a 1.5% annual fee.  
- **Benefit to WEPL:** The guarantee provides WEPL with a clear **advantage** by enabling supplier credit and ensuring business continuity. Under the broadened definition, this qualifies as a “service.”  
- **Exemption test:** No exemption applies in the First Schedule for parental or corporate guarantees. Central banking and certain social/sovereign functions are exempt, but not group-level guarantees.  
- **Result:** The parental guarantee fee is a **taxable imported service** under SST, chargeable at **15%**, payable by WEPL on a reverse charge basis.  

---

### 3. CPC Classification for SRB Returns  
To ensure correct reporting in SST returns, the transaction should be mapped to **UN CPC v2.1** headings adopted by SRB:  

- **CPC 71599 – Other services auxiliary to financial services, not elsewhere classified.**  
  - This residual category is most appropriate for **non-bank providers** offering financial support services.  
  - It avoids the bank-specific focus of **CPC 71135** (non-mortgage loan/guarantee services) while still capturing the functional nature of the fee.  
  - SRB guidance clarifies that CPC is for reporting accuracy, not determinative of taxability.  

---

### 4. Compliance Note  
- WEPL must **self-assess and pay 15% SST** on each quarterly fee, treating it as an imported service.  
- SST so paid will be a **non-creditable cost**, since WEPL’s principal activity (sale of petroleum/lubricants) falls under federal sales tax on goods.  
- Payment evidence (SRB challans) should be retained alongside SBP approval and tax documentation.  

---

✅ **Conclusion:** Under the negative-list regime effective 1 July 2025, parental guarantee fees fall within the broadened definition of “service,” are not exempted, and therefore attract 15% SST in Sindh. For reporting, the appropriate classification is **CPC 71599 – Other services auxiliary to financial services, n.e.c.**  

---

**Subject:** Clarification on Initial Contribution to Approved Gratuity Fund and Commissioner’s Approval

Dear Client,

Thank you for your query regarding the **employer’s initial contribution to a recognized (approved) gratuity fund** and whether any further approval from the Commissioner of Inland Revenue is required after the fund itself has been approved. We have reviewed the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (as amended up to July 31, 2025) and the Income Tax Rules, 2002 (as amended up to Nov 24, 2023). Our findings are outlined below for your reference and clarity.

## Background of the Issue  
You informed us that your company’s gratuity fund has already been **approved by the Commissioner** under Part III of the Sixth Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – making it an “approved gratuity fund” under the tax law【25†L890-L898】. Now, the company intends to make an **initial contribution** to this fund (presumably to fund past service gratuity liabilities for employees) and seeks confirmation whether this initial deposit requires any **additional approval by the Commissioner** beyond the original recognition of the fund.

## Relevant Legal Provisions and Analysis  

- **Definition of Approved Gratuity Fund:** Under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, an *“approved gratuity fund”* is defined as *“a gratuity fund approved by the Commissioner in accordance with Part III of the Sixth Schedule”*【25†L890-L898】. By obtaining the Commissioner’s approval, your fund has achieved this status. This approval signifies that the fund meets the statutory conditions laid out in Part III of the Sixth Schedule (such as being a bona fide fund for employees’ benefit, maintained under an irrevocable trust, etc.).

- **Deductibility of Contributions:** Once a fund is approved, contributions to it are generally **tax-deductible** for the employer, whereas contributions to an unapproved fund are not. In fact, Section 21(e) of the Income Tax Ordinance explicitly disallows any deduction for contributions made to a fund that is **not** an approved gratuity fund (or recognized provident fund, approved pension/superannuation fund)【27†L2895-L2903】. This provision implies that **contributions to an approved gratuity fund are permitted expenses**. There is no requirement in Section 21 or elsewhere in the Ordinance for a separate approval for each contribution – the key requirement is that the fund itself must be approved (which in your case has already been accomplished under the Sixth Schedule). 

- **Limits on Employer Contributions (Income Tax Rules, 2002):** While no further *permission* is needed for contributing to an approved fund, the **Income Tax Rules, 2002** impose certain **limits and conditions** on the amount of contributions:
  - **Ordinary Annual Contributions:** Rule 117(1) of the Income Tax Rules, 2002 provides that an employer’s annual contributions to an approved gratuity fund for each employee should be made on a reasonable and defined basis (e.g. following an actuarial formula), as approved as part of the fund’s rules, and **must not exceed the employee’s salary for the last month of each financial year**【5†L3648-L3656】. This generally aligns with common gratuity funding formulas (often capping yearly contributions to one month’s wage per year of service).
  - **Initial Contribution for Past Service:** Importantly for your question, Rule 117(2) addresses the employer’s **initial contribution in respect of an employee’s past services** (i.e. a lump sum to fund gratuity liabilities for service years completed before the fund’s creation or recognition). The Rule states that the amount of initial contribution **allowed as a tax-deductible expense** shall **not exceed one month’s salary for each completed financial year of past service** with the employer【5†L3648-L3656】. In simpler terms, the tax rules permit the initial funding contribution up to a limit of one month’s pay per year of past service for each employee admitted to the fund. As long as the initial contribution is within this prescribed limit (and in line with any conditions the Commissioner specified at the time of approval), it is considered part of the normal funding of the approved gratuity fund and **does not require a separate approval**. The Commissioner’s approval of the fund would typically encompass the contribution formula or funding method, so any initial contribution made according to that approved formula is covered by the existing approval.
  - **Special Contributions to Cover Deficits:** The Rules only require **prior approval for contributions in one specific scenario** – when an employer wishes to make a **special contribution** to meet a deficit in the fund. Rule 117(3) provides that an employer **may, with the prior approval of the Commissioner, make a special contribution** to an approved gratuity fund to make up any deficiency in the fund’s assets【5†L3657-L3662】. This clause envisions extraordinary injections of funds outside the regular contribution schedule (for example, if the fund’s liabilities significantly exceed its assets at some point). In such cases – which are **distinct from the ordinary annual or initial contributions** – the Commissioner’s prior consent is required, likely to ensure the contribution is bona fide and within allowable limits.

- **Part III of the Sixth Schedule (Ordinance Conditions):** The Sixth Schedule, Part III, itself lays down the conditions and procedural requirements for a gratuity fund to be approved. For instance, it covers the application process for approval and conditions that the fund must continue to satisfy. Once a fund is approved, there is **no clause in the Ordinance’s Sixth Schedule requiring further approval for contributions** made in accordance with the fund’s rules. The Commissioner’s role post-approval is generally supervisory (e.g. the Commissioner can call for information or accounts of the fund under Rule 7 of Part III of the Sixth Schedule【5†L3627-L3635】, and can withdraw approval if the fund violates the required conditions【5†L3683-L3690】). There is **no indication in the law that the routine funding contributions (including the initial lump sum within the allowed limit) need to be separately cleared by the tax authorities**. The only exception, as noted, is if a special additional contribution is to be made outside the normal parameters – which then triggers the need for Commissioner’s prior approval per Rule 117(3) of the Rules.

## Conclusion and Advice  

**In summary,** once a gratuity fund has been duly recognized/approved by the Commissioner under Part III of the Sixth Schedule (thus becoming an “approved gratuity fund”), the employer’s contributions to that fund – including the one-time initial contribution to fund past service liabilities – **do not require further approval from the Commissioner**, provided these contributions are within the limits and conditions prescribed by the tax rules. The initial contribution is essentially treated as a permissible funding expense, capped at one month’s last-drawn salary for each year of an employee’s prior service【5†L3648-L3656】, and it is allowable as a deduction for the employer. No additional sanction is needed for this because it falls under the ambit of the fund’s approved structure. 

You should ensure that the initial contribution **complies with the approved scheme’s rules** and does not exceed the maximum deductible limit set by Rule 117(2)【5†L3648-L3656】. As a best practice, document the calculation of the initial contribution for each eligible employee (e.g. number of past service years × last monthly salary) to demonstrate that it adheres to the tax regulation limits. This will safeguard the deductibility of the contribution in the company’s tax computations. 

Only if the company ever finds it necessary to inject a **special contribution over and above normal contributions** (for instance, to rectify an underfunded position of the gratuity fund beyond what regular contributions cover) would you then need to **seek the Commissioner’s prior approval** before making such a payment【5†L3657-L3662】. In ordinary circumstances, no such extra approval step is required after the fund’s initial recognition.

We trust that this addresses your query. The relevant legal references (Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 and Income Tax Rules, 2002) supporting the above conclusions have been cited for your ease of reference. Please feel free to reach out if you need any further clarification or assistance regarding the management of your approved gratuity fund.

Sincerely,  
**[Your Name]**  
Tax Advisor / [Your Firm’s Name]  

**References:** 

- Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (amended up to 31-07-2025), **Section 2(3)** – Definition of “approved gratuity fund”【25†L890-L898】; **Section 21(e)** – disallowance of contributions to unapproved funds (implying contributions to approved funds are allowed)【27†L2895-L2903】.  
- Income Tax Rules, 2002 (amended up to 24-11-2023), **Rule 117** (Part III – Approved Gratuity Funds) – Limits on employer’s annual and initial contributions to approved gratuity funds, and requirement of Commissioner’s prior approval only for special contributions to meet fund deficits【5†L3648-L3656】【5†L3657-L3662】.

---

**Subject:** Key Issues in Draft Computation – Tax Year 2025  

Dear [Client’s Name],  

We have reviewed the draft return computation for Tax Year 2025 in detail. Below are the key issues that require attention and correction before finalization:  

---

**1. Tax Credits on Pension Contribution and Donations – Inclusion of Surcharge under Section 4AB**  
In the draft computation, surcharge under **section 4AB** has been included while computing tax credits on contributions to approved pension funds (**section 63**) and donations (**section 61**). This treatment is legally correct since section 2(29) of the Ordinance defines “income” to include amounts chargeable to tax, and surcharge under section 4AB is expressly imposed as part of tax liability【9†source】.  

However, the **IRIS portal does not presently allow such inclusion** in computing tax credits. The Karachi Tax Bar has already raised this anomaly before the Chairman FBR, but no corrective update has yet been incorporated. Accordingly, while the computation is correct in law, the system restriction continues.  

---

**2. Withholding from K-Electric under Section 153(1)(a)**  
Tax withheld by K-Electric under **section 153(1)(a)** represents **minimum tax** on business income. As per section 153(3) read with section 113, such withholding is not adjustable against other heads of income but is treated as minimum liability on turnover. Therefore, you are required to prepare a Profit and Loss Account and compute tax liability accordingly, charging tax as minimum tax under the relevant provisions【9†source】.  

---

**3. Dividend Income from BP and UEP Shares**  
Dividend income from BP and UEP has been taxed at **25%** in the draft computation. This is not correct. As per **section 5(1)** read with **Division III of Part I of the First Schedule**, dividend income (other than from certain specific entities like REITs or mutual funds where different rates apply) is taxable at **15%**. Therefore, dividends from BP and UEP should be recomputed at the correct rate of 15%【9†source】.  

---

**4. Foreign Rental Income**  
The draft computation currently shows foreign rental income as exempt. We recommend **not declaring foreign rental income at all** instead of disclosing it under “exempt income.” Section 101(1) read with section 11 and section 10 makes it clear that only **Pakistan-source income** is taxable for resident taxpayers, unless specifically brought to charge. Judicial precedents have upheld that foreign rental income of individuals not remitted to Pakistan does not fall within the charge of tax. Although two favorable judgments exist, in our professional view, non-declaration is the more prudent approach to avoid unnecessary queries.  

---

**Summary**  
- Inclusion of surcharge under section 4AB in tax credit computations is correct in law but not currently allowed by IRIS.  
- Withholding under section 153(1)(a) must be treated as minimum tax; proper P&L preparation is required.  
- Dividend from BP and UEP shares should be taxed at 15% instead of 25%.  
- Foreign rental income should not be declared at all rather than shown as exempt.  

We recommend revising the draft computation in light of the above observations. Please confirm if you would like us to prepare and share a revised working.  

Best regards,  
[Your Name]  
[Your Position]  
[Your Firm’s Name]  

---

Dear Mr. Zuhair,

 

Our consignees currently use trucks/dumpers to transport cargo to Punjab and KPK, which results in high logistics costs. To reduce this burden, we plan to facilitate them by offering rail transport as an alternative.

 

For this purpose, we have engaged a Company to handle the loading of cargo onto trains. The said Company issues invoices for their services based on the destination province, as follows:

 

Sindh: Sindh Sales Tax (SST) invoice
Punjab: Punjab Revenue Authority (PRA) invoice
KPK: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Revenue Authority (KPRA) invoice
 

We currently claim input tax on SRB invoices in our Sindh Sales Tax Return. However, we seek clarification on whether input tax from PRA and KPRA invoices can also be claimed in our SRB return, or if any separate treatment is required for those invoices.

Here’s a revised version of the response with an additional paragraph addressing **withholding agent registration**, tailored for both Punjab and KPK:  

---

**Subject:** Clarification on Input Tax Treatment of PRA and KPRA Invoices  

Hi Mazhar,  

We refer to your query regarding the treatment of sales tax charged on rail cargo handling services for consignments transported to Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KPK). As explained, the service provider engaged by you issues sales tax invoices depending on the province of destination, i.e. Sindh Sales Tax under SRB, Punjab Sales Tax under PRA, and KPK Sales Tax under KPRA. Since your company is presently registered only with the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB), you have sought clarification whether invoices bearing PRA and KPRA tax can also be adjusted in the Sindh Sales Tax Return.  

At the outset, it is important to clarify that under the law there is no express statutory prohibition on the adjustment of input tax paid in one province against output tax liability in another. In principle, sales tax on services is designed as a value-added system, and its conceptual foundation would support seamless credit across jurisdictions. However, in practice, the provincial sales tax regime in Pakistan operates in silos. Each province independently administers its sales tax law and return mechanism on the basis of the “place of consumption” rule, i.e. tax is levied by the province where the service is consumed. Because no reciprocal framework or inter-provincial arrangement has been established, the practical implementation does not permit cross-adjustment of input tax.  

In the case of Sindh, the SRB return structure (including Annexure A) is designed to automatically capture only those invoices issued under SRB law. Consequently, while a PRA or KPRA invoice may represent legitimate tax paid on taxable services consumed in Punjab or KPK, the SRB return has no mechanism to reflect or absorb that input tax. The limitation is therefore not one of substantive law but of procedure and framework. This distinction is important: by law, there is no bar to input adjustment, but administratively, the current return format does not allow for recognition of inter-provincial input tax.  

Accordingly, for practical compliance, input tax appearing on PRA or KPRA invoices cannot be claimed in your Sindh Sales Tax Return. Unless your company were to obtain registration in Punjab or KPK and file returns there, the tax charged on such invoices remains unrecoverable and will be treated as an additional cost to your company. Even in the event of registering in other provinces, input tax could only be adjusted against output tax arising in those provinces. Since your activities are registered solely under SRB, registering in other jurisdictions for the limited purpose of claiming refunds may not be commercially viable, as refunds are seldom processed unless directly linked to taxable outputs in that province.  

It is also important to highlight the aspect of **withholding obligations**. Under the Punjab Sales Tax on Services Act, your company does not fall within the definition of a withholding agent and, therefore, is not required to obtain registration or discharge any withholding obligation in Punjab. However, under the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Sales Tax on Services Act, all companies are treated as withholding agents by default. Consequently, where services are procured in KPK, your company would be required to obtain registration with KPRA as a withholding agent and discharge the corresponding obligation of deducting and depositing sales tax. This requirement is separate from the question of input adjustment but is essential from a compliance standpoint.  

In conclusion, while there is no statutory restriction under provincial sales tax laws barring the adjustment of input tax across provinces, the absence of a procedural mechanism in the SRB return effectively prevents you from doing so. For the time being, only SRB invoices can be adjusted in the Sindh return. PRA and KPRA input taxes, though legally not barred, cannot be claimed under the current system and should therefore be treated as non-adjustable costs. At the same time, compliance with withholding obligations in KPK will require separate registration with KPRA as a withholding agent. We recommend that your company continue to restrict input tax claims to SRB invoices in order to ensure compliance and avoid potential disallowances or audit exposures. Should any inter-provincial adjustment framework be introduced in the future, or if registrations in other provinces are contemplated, the matter may be revisited.  

Regards,  
*Your Name*  
*Tax Consultant*  

---

Hi Mazhar, hope you are doing well. 
We refer to your query regarding the treatment of sales tax charged on rail cargo handling services rendered for consignments transported to Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KPK). As outlined, a third-party service provider engaged by you issues sales tax invoices based on the destination province:
•	Sindh Destinations: Sindh Sales Tax (SST) under SRB
•	Punjab Destinations: Punjab Sales Tax under PRA
•	KPK Destinations: KPK Sales Tax under KPRA
Your company is currently registered with the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) and claims input tax on SRB invoices in the Sindh Sales Tax Return. You have sought clarification whether input tax from PRA and KPRA invoices can also be claimed in the SRB return.
Provincial Sales Tax 
Input tax credits (the ability to deduct tax paid on purchases from tax due on sales) are generally restricted to the same jurisdiction where the output tax is payable. In other words, sales tax paid under one province’s law is not automatically creditable against tax liability in another province’s jurisdiction.
This principle curtails from the value-added tax (VAT) concept that tax is levied by the jurisdiction where the service is consumed. Provincial laws follow this ‘place of consumption’ rule: If a taxable service is provided in one territory but consumed in another, the right to levy tax belongs to the province where it is consumed.

# **Clarification on Input Tax from PRA and KPRA Invoices**

## **Background and Context**
Your email outlines a plan to reduce logistics costs by offering rail transport for cargo destined to Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KPK) instead of trucks. A third-party Company has been engaged to load cargo onto trains, and this Company issues sales tax invoices according to the destination province:
- **Sindh Destinations:** Sindh Sales Tax (SST) invoice (issued under Sindh Revenue Board – SRB)  
- **Punjab Destinations:** Punjab Sales Tax invoice (issued under Punjab Revenue Authority – PRA)  
- **KPK Destinations:** KPK Sales Tax invoice (issued under Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Revenue Authority – KPRA)  

Currently, your company is registered with SRB and **claims input tax on SST invoices** in the Sindh sales tax return. The question is whether **input tax from PRA and KPRA invoices** (for services related to Punjab or KPK destinations) can similarly be claimed in the Sindh Sales Tax return, or if those need to be handled separately.

## **Provincial Sales Tax Framework in Pakistan**
Pakistan’s sales tax on services is administered **provincially**. Each province (Sindh, Punjab, KPK, etc.) has its own sales tax law and revenue authority. **Input tax credits** (the ability to deduct tax paid on purchases from tax due on sales) are generally **restricted to the same jurisdiction** where the output tax is payable. In other words, **sales tax paid under one province’s law is not automatically creditable against tax liability in another province’s jurisdiction**.

This principle stems from the value-added tax (VAT) concept that tax is levied by the jurisdiction **where the service is consumed**. Provincial laws follow this “place of consumption” rule:
- If a taxable service is provided in one territory **but consumed in another**, the right to levy tax belongs to the province **where it is consumed**【18†L206-L215】.  
- Unlike international VAT (where exports are zero-rated and imports taxed by the destination country), Pakistan’s provinces **do not have mutual agreements to zero-rate inter-provincial services**【18†L213-L221】. 

As a result, **each province treats the service as taxable in its domain without offering cross-credit to the other**. *For example, Sindh and Punjab have no reciprocal arrangement to adjust sales tax paid in one province against liability in the other【18†L216-L224】*. The same principle applies to KPK and other provinces, since **no inter-provincial tax offset agreements exist** in the current framework.

## **Input Tax Credit Limitations Across Provinces**
Because of the above framework, **input tax paid under PRA or KPRA cannot be claimed in an SRB (Sindh) tax return.** The **Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act** and SRB regulations allow input adjustment only for:
- SST paid on services/procurements **within Sindh**, and 
- in certain cases, federal sales tax on goods (as governed by federal-provincial agreements), but **not** for other provinces’ services tax unless a specific provision is made.

There is currently **no mechanism to credit provincial service tax paid to Punjab or KPK against Sindh output tax**. The PRA’s own published guidance has explicitly noted that **no input tax adjustment is allowed against output tax in Punjab for services taxed in another province, and vice versa** – due to the lack of any cross-border agreement【18†L216-L224】. In practical terms, **the SRB will not recognize a PRA or KPRA invoice for input tax credit** in the Sindh return, since that tax was levied under a different province’s law.

It’s worth noting that historically even **federal vs provincial** sales tax adjustments required special permissions. In 2013, for instance, the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) moved to disallow automatic adjustment of provincial service tax in federal sales tax returns without a notification, emphasizing the need for formal agreements for any cross-jurisdiction credit【11†L53-L62】【11†L63-L72】. Similarly, between provinces themselves, no general provision exists to “import” an input credit from one province into another’s tax return.

## **Proper Treatment of PRA and KPRA Invoices**
Given the above, **PRA and KPRA-taxed service invoices cannot be claimed in your Sindh sales tax return**. Here’s how to handle those invoices:

- **Claim in SRB Return – *Not Permissible*:** You **should not include** the Punjab or KPK sales tax amounts as input tax in the SRB/Sindh return. Any such claim would likely be disallowed upon audit or system check, since SRB only allows input of Sindh sales tax (and eligible federal taxes) in its return.

- **Separate Provincial Treatment:** The input tax paid to PRA or KPRA would generally be **handled within those provinces’ jurisdiction**. This means:
  - **If your company is not registered in Punjab or KPK:** You cannot claim or adjust those taxes at all. The tax paid on the vendor’s PRA/KPRA invoice becomes an **additional cost** to your company. There is currently no refund or credit mechanism from SRB for that.  
  - **If your company decides to register in Punjab/KPK:** In theory, a registered entity in those provinces could file returns there and **claim input credits** against output tax *in the same province*. However, this is only useful if you are **providing taxable services in those provinces or otherwise have output tax liability there**. For example, if you were rendering services **taxable in Punjab**, you could use PRA-paid inputs against Punjab output tax by filing a PRA return. If you have no taxable activities in Punjab/KPK, registering solely to claim refund of input tax on these invoices may not be practical – refunds are not commonly given unless input directly relates to taxable outputs in that province.
  - There is a concept of **withholding** for cross-provincial services: if a Sindh registered service provider renders a service consumed in Punjab, and the service recipient is registered in Punjab, the recipient withholds and deposits Punjab sales tax【18†L232-L238】. In your case, the roles are somewhat reversed (the service provider handling loading appears to be charging the tax for the destination province already). If your company were **registered with PRA/KPRA as a service recipient**, you could have withheld that tax and remitted it yourself, but you would still end up paying it to the respective province (and again, only able to adjust it if you had output there). Since the vendor is already charging provincial tax, it indicates they have taken on that responsibility, and you simply pay the gross amount including that tax.

- **Record-Keeping:** Even though you cannot claim the PRA/KPRA input in Sindh, you should **retain those invoices** for record purposes. They substantiate the expense and tax paid in case of any inquiry from PRA/KPRA (for example, PRA might require proof that tax was charged and paid for services consumed in Punjab).

In summary, for **Sindh sales tax return purposes**, you will **only claim input tax from SRB (Sindh) invoices**, as you currently do. **Invoices bearing PRA or KPRA sales tax must not be claimed in the Sindh return.** There is no separate “section” in the Sindh return to include those – they are simply outside the scope of Sindh’s input tax credit.

## **Conclusion and Recommendation**
**You cannot claim input tax from PRA or KPRA invoices in the SRB/Sindh sales tax return under the current laws.** Each province’s sales tax is administered independently, and **no cross-provincial input adjustment is allowed without a specific reciprocal arrangement**, which does not exist at present【18†L216-L224】. 

For now, the Punjab and KPK sales tax paid on the rail cargo handling services will remain an **additional cost** to your company (since it can’t be offset against Sindh output tax). Ensure that this is factored into your cost calculations for offering the rail transport facility. If the volumes and amounts involved become significant, you may evaluate the option of **registering in Punjab and KPK** to handle those taxes, but that would only be beneficial if you also generate taxable services income in those provinces to utilize the input credit.

It would be prudent to **continue complying** by claiming only SRB-related input tax in Sindh returns. Any attempt to claim PRA/KPRA invoice tax in Sindh would violate the provincial tax regulations. We recommend treating the PRA and KPRA paid amounts as non-adjustable expenses, or alternatively, seek professional tax advice about structuring the arrangement (for instance, having the consignees or another locally-registered entity handle that portion of the tax if feasible).

By adhering to the above, you’ll remain compliant with the provincial tax laws and avoid any disallowances or penalties related to improper input tax claims. If there are any changes in law or if provinces establish cross-adjustment agreements in the future, this position could be revisited. For now, **the safe approach is to keep each province’s sales tax input confined to that province’s output**. This means **PRA and KPRA taxes should not be claimed in the Sindh Sales Tax Return**, and no separate treatment in the Sindh return is available – they are simply **outside SRB’s input tax scope**.

Please let us know if you need further clarification or if you plan any structural changes to accommodate these tax implications. We can also consult with provincial tax authorities or tax advisors for detailed planning, but the core principle remains that **cross-provincial input tax credit is not allowed under current regulations**【18†L216-L224】.

Regards,  

*Your Name/Department*

This position has been reinforced through the Sindh Finance Act, 2025, which has shifted the law from a “positive list” to a “negative list” framework, under which all services are taxable by default unless specifically exempted under the First Schedule. Renting of immovable property therefore now falls squarely within the charge of SST, save where an exemption applies.

It is important to note that such matters cannot be taken directly before the Supreme Court of Pakistan; constitutional jurisdiction must first be invoked before the relevant High Court.

# Response to Notice under Section 111(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (Tax Year 2024)

**To:** Mr. Shahabuddin Bhatti,  
Assistant/Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue (Unit 03, Range A, Zone I)  
Regional Tax Office–II, Karachi.

**Subject:** Explanation in response to Notice u/s 111(1) for Tax Year 2024 – **Moid Khaliq Malik (NTN/Registration No. 4230151634153)**

**Reference:** Your notice **No. 111(1) (Notice to explain Income/Asset)** dated September 9, 2025, for Tax Year 2024.

---

Dear Sir,

I write with reference to the above-mentioned notice issued under Section 111(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, regarding an alleged undisclosed asset/income (property purchase) in Tax Year 2024. I, **Moid Khaliq Malik**, hereby submit a formal explanation and clarification of the issues raised. The observations in the notice appear to be based on incorrect presumptions and incomplete understanding of the facts. I address each point in detail below:

## 1. **No Property Purchase in Tax Year 2024 – Clarification of B-Lease Transaction**

Your notice notes that Rs. 1,518,750 was collected as advance tax under Section 236K on April 1, 2024 against a purported **“purchase of immovable property (Plot No. 107/1/1, 4th Street, Phase VI, DHA, Karachi)”**. This observation is **factually incorrect** – *I did **not** purchase any new property in Tax Year 2024*. The transaction in question was actually the execution of a **“B-Lease”** for a property **I have owned since March 17, 1999** (the same Plot No. 107/1/1, Phase VI, DHA, Karachi). This property was originally acquired in 1999 and has been in my ownership for over two decades; hence **no new acquisition was made in 2024**.

- **B-Lease Explained:** A “B-Lease” in Defence Housing Authority (DHA) terms is a legal formality that converts the property’s lease status once construction is completed. Specifically, Lease “B” is a 99-year lease executed for residential plots **upon completion of the building**【2†L8-L12】. It is *not* a sale or new purchase, but rather a required step to formalize title before a sale can occur. In my case, the house on the plot was constructed and the **B-Lease was executed as a formality in April 2023** (well before the relevant tax year’s end). The **Registrar collected advance tax under Section 236K** (which is an adjustable advance tax on the transfer of immovable property) at the time of this lease execution, amounting to Rs. 1,518,750. This tax was deposited to the government treasury on my behalf, as noted in your records.

- **No Undisclosed Asset:** Since the property was **already owned by me**, it was not required to be declared as a new asset in 2024. The payment under Section 236K was merely related to the *formal lease registration process*, not a purchase. This **adjustable advance tax** will be duly accounted for, and it does not represent any unexplained investment. All property documents can be furnished to evidence that I have held the title since 1999 and that the April 2023 B-Lease was a compliance requirement of DHA (prior to selling or transferring the property). Therefore, the presumption that I purchased a new property in Tax Year 2024 is mistaken, and Section 111(1) should not be invoked on this basis.

## 2. **Non-Resident Status in Tax Year 2024 – No Wealth Statement Required**

I also wish to clarify my **residential status** for Tax Year 2024. I was a **Non-Resident Pakistani** for the relevant tax period (July 1, 2023 to June 30, 2024). This status was clearly declared in my e-filed tax return for 2024. Under Pakistani tax law, an individual is treated as **“resident”** if they stay in Pakistan for **183 days or more** in a tax year【7†L378-L385】. My presence in Pakistan during the year fell short of this threshold, as detailed below:

- **Travel History (FY 2024):**  
  - **Entry into Pakistan:** July 10, 2023 (Pakistani Passport Page 25)  
    **Exit:** July 22, 2023 (Canadian Passport Page 8) – *Stay of 12 days*  
  - **Entry into Pakistan:** November 12, 2023 (Pakistani Passport Page 14)  
    **Exit:** April 19, 2024 (Canadian Passport Page 8) – *Stay of 160 days*  
  - **Total days in Pakistan (July 1, 2023 – June 30, 2024):** **172 days**, which is **below the 183-day residency threshold**.

Because I was a non-resident for the tax year, I was **not obligated to file a Wealth Statement** under Section 116 of the Ordinance. The law expressly requires only **resident taxpayers** to file a wealth statement along with the return【13†L388-L395】. Non-resident persons are **not required** to declare their assets/wealth in Pakistan when filing returns【12†L124-L130】. Therefore, the absence of a wealth statement or the non-declaration of worldwide assets (including the DHA property, which in any case is not a new acquisition) in my filing is **fully in accordance with the law**. I complied with all filing requirements applicable to me as a non-resident. 

To substantiate my non-resident status, I have **attached copies of my entire Pakistani passport** (showing all arrival/departure stamps) and the relevant pages of my Canadian passport indicating exit/entry stamps. These documents confirm the travel dates listed above and corroborate that my stay in Pakistan during Tax Year 2024 was less than 183 days.

## 3. **Procedural Concerns – Notice Issued Without Proper Scrutiny of Facts**

It is respectfully submitted that issuing the subject notice (and the underlying observations) without a proper understanding of the facts and records has caused undue concern. **All relevant information was available in my tax return** or could have been ascertained from record, summarized as follows:

- My **non-resident status** was explicitly declared in the return, which should have signaled that no wealth statement was required and that certain local asset details might not be applicable.
- The **advance tax under Section 236K** was duly paid and reflected against my CNIC/NTN, but before assuming it represented an undisclosed asset, the nature of the transaction warranted verification. A simple scrutiny of property records (e.g., DHA or Registrar’s records) would show that *Plot 107/1/1, Phase VI, DHA* has been under my ownership for many years. The tax was collected due to a procedural formality (B-Lease) rather than a purchase of a new property. 
- I had **nothing to conceal**: the income of Rs. 10,119,408/- I declared for Tax Year 2024 was duly assessed under Section 120 as per law. There was no unexplained wealth or income that year. The property in question was not mentioned as a new asset simply because it was not acquired in that year. 

Initiating proceedings under Section 111(1) in this situation—without first seeking clarification or examining the available facts—appears to be **legally unwarranted**. Section 111 is intended to bring to tax any **unexplained income or asset**. In my case, the asset is very much explained and accounted for (owned since 1999), and the tax payment under Section 236K is accounted for as well. The issuance of the notice **prior to proper fact-checking** has effectively put me in the position of proving something that could have been verified from existing records.

I urge the department to exercise due diligence in such matters. Taxpayers who comply with the law and fully disclose required information should not be subjected to avoidable proceedings. In this instance, the notice seems to stem from a **misunderstanding** that could have been resolved by an internal review of my file (e.g., checking my historical ownership of the property and my residency status).

## 4. **Closing Statement and Request for Withdrawal of Notice**

In light of the above clarifications, I trust it is clear that **no concealment or unexplained income/asset exists** in my case for Tax Year 2024. The **property** referenced in the notice is *an old, already-declared asset*, and the **advance tax (Rs. 1,518,750)** was paid only as part of fulfilling DHA’s procedural requirements – not as a result of any new investment. Additionally, my **non-resident status** meant I was under **no legal obligation to file a wealth statement**, and this has been corroborated by the travel record evidence now provided.

All pertinent documentary evidence is attached herewith for your review, including:  

- **DHA Property Documents:** Showing my long-standing ownership of Plot 107/1/1, Phase VI, DHA Karachi (since 1999).  
- **B-Lease Document (Registered in 2023):** Demonstrating that the lease execution was a formality and not a purchase.  
- **Challan/CPR for Section 236K Tax Payment:** Confirming the advance tax paid on the B-Lease registration.  
- **Passport Copies (Pakistani & Canadian):** Verifying my entry/exit dates and total days in Pakistan, supporting my non-resident status claim.

I respectfully request that, **given the clarifications and evidence provided**, the **notice under Section 111(1) for Tax Year 2024 be withdrawn** forthwith. Proceeding with an amendment under Sections 39(3) and 111(1)(b) would be unjustified under these circumstances, as there is no unexplained income or asset to tax. I have acted in good faith and complied with all tax obligations, and I am ready to cooperate fully with any further queries. However, I believe that upon reviewing the facts, you will agree there is no basis to continue this inquiry.

Thank you for your attention to this matter. I look forward to your confirmation that the notice has been vacated. If any additional information is required, I will be happy to provide it.

Yours sincerely,  

**Moid Khaliq Malik**  
CNIC: XXXXX-XXXXXXX-X (Pakistan) / Passport: XXXXXXXX (Canada)  
Taxpayer NTN: 4230151634153  

*Enclosures:* Copies of Pakistani passport (all pages), Canadian passport (relevant pages), DHA property documents, B-Lease registration, CPR for tax payment under 236K, and any other supporting evidence as mentioned above.

parts:
Here’s a more **polished and expanded draft email** with deeper legal and technical detailing, supported by references to the Grounds of Appeal for TY 2019 and 2023. I’ve structured it to read like a professional advisory response — point-by-point, with strong statutory and appellate support.  

---

**Subject:** Clarifications on Tax Position Summary and Current Tax Computation – FY 2024  

Dear [Auditor’s Name],  

I trust you are doing well.  

With reference to your queries regarding the Tax Position Summary, Current Tax Working, and reconciliation of prior year treatments for the year ended June 30, 2024, we provide our detailed clarifications below. These are supported by positions already taken in our appeals for earlier tax years (2019 and 2023), which remain pending adjudication before the appellate forums.  

---

### **1. Tariff Subsidy – Taxability for FY 2024**  
Through Finance Act, 2024, tariff differential subsidy has been expressly brought into the tax net, effective from **Tax Year 2025**. Accordingly, for the period July 1, 2023 to June 30, 2024 (TY 2024), the exemption under **Clause 102A of Part I of the Second Schedule** continues to apply.  

- In tax orders for TY 2019, 2022, and 2023, the department denied the exemption, contending that tariff differential subsidy falls outside Clause 102A. This denial is under challenge in our pending appeals.  
- In both TY 2019 and TY 2023 appeals, we emphasized that the exemption had historically been accepted in earlier concluded assessments (TY 2016 and TY 2018–2021). The department’s departure from this settled position, without cogent reasoning, has been contested as arbitrary and inconsistent with the principle of consistency【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】【14†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  
- Reliance placed by the department on Sindh High Court orders dated September 30, 2024 is misplaced since the exemption issue was neither raised nor adjudicated therein【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】【14†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  

**Conclusion:** For FY 2024, tariff subsidy remains exempt, and inclusion in taxable income would be premature. The amendment in Finance Act, 2024 operates prospectively only.  

---

### **2. Exchange Losses / Gains**  
It has been a consistent practice that exchange gains were offered to tax when realized or accrued. On the same footing, **exchange losses are deductible under the mercantile system**.  

- The disallowance of exchange loss in TY 2023 on the ground that it was “notional” has been challenged. Our appeal relies upon the binding judgment of the **Sindh High Court in M/s Excell Pakistan (Pvt.) Ltd. (2022 PTD 1535)**, where it was categorically held that exchange losses are allowable on accrual basis【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  
- The Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal in several cases have also recognized that under **Section 32 of the Ordinance**, taxable income must be computed in accordance with the method of accounting regularly employed, which in our case is mercantile.  

**Conclusion:** Exchange losses are deductible in FY 2024, and exclusion from computation would be contrary to binding precedent.  

---

### **3. Amortization of Deferred Revenue**  
Deposits received from customers for new connections represent **deferred liabilities**, not income at the time of receipt. These are recognized as revenue over the useful life of the related assets, consistent with **IFRS-15** and the principle of matching income with expenses.  

- The department in earlier tax years sought to tax such receipts upfront. This was contested in appeals (TY 2019 and 2023), where we emphasized that recognition on amortization basis is consistent with accounting standards and Section 32 of the Ordinance【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】【14†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  
- The Appellate Tribunal in other electricity distribution cases has upheld similar treatment, emphasizing that deferred liabilities cannot be taxed until the income-earning process is complete.  

**Conclusion:** The approach of taxing amortization of deferred revenue only is correct and defensible.  

---

### **4. Add-backs to Taxable Income (per past orders)**  
The following items have been historically added back by the department and are under appeal:  
- **Sales Reversal (Irrecoverable Invoices)** – Disallowed despite recognition as bad debts under **Section 29**.  
- **Unrecognized Late Payment Surcharge (PSC consumers)** – Not accrued under mercantile system; hence, non-taxable.  
- **Recoveries from Customers (Deferred Revenue Note)** – Represent deposits, not income, until amortized.  

Our grounds of appeal for TY 2019 and TY 2023 specifically challenge these additions, highlighting that income must be recognized only when collectability is probable under IFRS-15 and Section 32【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】【14†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  

**Conclusion:** While included under protest in computations for prudence, these items are not taxable in principle.  

---

### **5. Late Payment Surcharge – Finance Cost (Rs. 5.9 billion)**  
The finance cost recorded for delayed payments to NTDC and SSGC represents **contractual obligations**, falling within the ambit of deductible business expenditure under **Section 20 of the Ordinance**.  

- The department’s past disallowances of similar claims were made without statutory basis. Our appeals argue that deduction cannot be denied unless specifically prohibited. Merely being “disputed” does not extinguish the liability【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  
- Established jurisprudence supports deduction of disputed liabilities where the obligation is contractual and accrued under mercantile accounting.  

**Conclusion:** The late payment surcharge expense should remain deductible and need not be added back.  

---

### **6. Minimum Tax under Section 113 – Scope of Turnover**  
The department, in TY 2019, 2022, and 2023, included the following items in turnover for minimum tax:  
- **Statutory Levies** (electricity duty, income tax under sections 235/235A, PHL surcharge, PTV license fee, etc.).  
- **Sales Reversals** (irrecoverable invoices).  
- **Unrecognized LPS on PSC consumers.**  
- **Scrap Sales.**  
- **Collection Charges on PTV License Fee.**  
- **Recoveries from Customers (Deferred Revenue).**  

Our appeals contest these inclusions on the following grounds:  
- **Section 113(3)(a)** defines “turnover” as “gross receipts derived from sale of goods or services.” Statutory collections and fiduciary receipts do not fall within this scope【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】【14†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  
- Scrap sales were conclusively decided in KE’s own favour in **ITA Nos. 169 and 170 (AY 2000–2001 & 2001–2002)**, upheld by the **Supreme Court of Pakistan**, confirming that scrap sales are not part of turnover【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  
- Recoveries from customers for service connections are deferred liabilities, not business receipts.  
- Collection charges for PTV fees are reimbursements, not revenue.  

**Conclusion:** For FY 2024, strong legal grounds exist to exclude these items from turnover. Inclusion would not align with settled appellate jurisprudence.  

---

### **Overall Position**  
- **Tariff Subsidy:** Exempt for FY 2024; taxable prospectively.  
- **Exchange Losses:** Deductible under accrual accounting, supported by case law.  
- **Deferred Revenue:** Taxable only on amortization.  
- **Add-backs:** Contested and included under protest; not taxable in principle.  
- **Late Payment Surcharge:** Deductible as business expenditure.  
- **Turnover under Section 113:** Should exclude statutory levies, deferred liabilities, scrap sales, and fiduciary collections.  

---

**Closing**  
In conclusion, our positions for FY 2024 are consistent with the grounds of appeal already filed for prior tax years (2019 and 2023). These appeals provide a strong legal and factual basis for maintaining the treatments adopted in the current year’s tax computation.  

Please let us know if you require detailed extracts from the appeals or supporting jurisprudence for inclusion in your audit documentation.  

Best regards,  
Zuhair  

---

Would you like me to now prepare a **tabular annexure** mapping: *Auditor Query → Department’s Past Treatment → Our Grounds of Appeal → Recommended FY 2024 Treatment*? That table could serve as a ready reference for your file and strengthen communication with the auditors.

**Subject:** Clarifications on Tax Position Summary – FY 2024  

Dear [Auditor’s Name],  

I trust this finds you well.  

With reference to your queries on the Tax Position Summary, Current Tax Working, and prior year tax treatment for the year ended June 30, 2024, we provide our detailed clarifications below:  

---

### 1. **Taxability of Tariff Subsidy**  
Through Finance Act, 2024, tariff differential subsidy has been specifically made taxable effective from Tax Year 2025. For the year July 1, 2023 to June 30, 2024 (TY 2024), the exemption under Clause 102A of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance continues to apply.

Both in TY 2019 and TY 2023 appeals, we have emphasized that the subsidy qualifies for exemption, consistent with earlier years where the department accepted this position【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】【14†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  
- Therefore, for FY 2024, the correct treatment is to claim exemption under Clause 102A. Taxability will only apply prospectively from TY 2025.  

---

### 2. **Exchange Losses / Gains**  
Historically, exchange gains were offered for tax. By the same principle, exchange losses are deductible. The department disallowed exchange losses in TY 2023 on the assumption that they were notional. This disallowance has been challenged in our appeals with reliance on the Sindh High Court judgment in *Excell Pakistan (Pvt) Ltd* (2022 PTD 1535), which held that exchange losses are allowable on accrual basis under the mercantile system【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  
Accordingly, exchange losses are allowable in FY 2024.  

---

### 3. **Amortization of Deferred Revenue**  
Consumer deposits for service connections are not taxed at the time of receipt since they represent deferred liabilities. The amounts are offered to tax on amortization, consistent with IFRS-15 and the principle of matching income with expenses. This treatment has also been defended in our appeals against additions made by the department in prior years【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】【14†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  
Therefore, offering amortization as taxable income is acceptable and aligned with past practice.

- Sales reversal (irrecoverable invoices).  
- Unrecognized Late Payment Surcharge (PSC consumers).  
- Recoveries from customers (deferred revenue).  

These issues have been specifically challenged in appeals (TY 2019 and 2023), where we argued that these amounts either do not accrue as income (per Section 32 and IFRS-15) or represent deferred liabilities, not taxable income【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】【14†files_uploaded_in_conversation】. Pending appellate adjudication, we have made these add-backs under protest.  

---

During FY 2024, Rs. 5.9 billion has been recorded as finance cost relating to delayed payments to NTDC and SSGC. Since this represents contractual liability, it is a deductible expense under Section 20. The mere fact of dispute does not bar deduction. Similar issues in prior years were disallowed by the tax department, which we have contested in appeals on the ground that expenditure cannot be disallowed unless specifically prohibited【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  
Accordingly, we maintain that the expense is deductible and should not be added back.  

---

### 6. **Minimum Tax under Section 113**

- Other Taxes (income tax, PHL surcharge, electricity duty).  
- Sales reversal.  
- Unrecognized LPS (PSC consumers).  
- Scrap sales.  
- PTV collection charges.  
- Consumer recoveries (deferred revenue).  

Our consistent position in appeals has been that such statutory collections, deferred liabilities, or non-core receipts are not “turnover” under Section 113(3)(a), which only covers gross receipts derived from the sale of goods or services【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】【14†files_uploaded_in_conversation】. In fact, the issue of scrap sales has been conclusively decided in our favour by the Appellate Tribunal and upheld by the Supreme Court【13†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  
Therefore, for FY 2024, strong legal grounds exist to exclude these items from turnover computation.

- Deferred revenue should be taxed on amortization only.

- Items like statutory levies, deferred recoveries, scrap sales, and PTV charges should not form part of turnover under Section 113.
