# Finance Act 2025: Key Income Tax Changes Explained

The Federal Finance Act, 2025 brought **major amendments** to Pakistan’s Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. These changes affect both **individual taxpayers (like salaried persons and pensioners)** and **businesses**, with a special focus on the **digital economy and compliance**. Below, we break down the **key amendments** in simple terms, grouped by category, and explain what they mean for you. We also include a handy **FAQ section** to answer common questions.

## Changes for Salaried Individuals and Pensioners

- **Revised Income Tax Slabs:** Income tax rates for individuals have been adjusted. **No tax** is due on annual taxable income up to **Rs. 600,000**, and the rates then rise progressively【18†L4998-L5006】【18†L5008-L5016】. There are **six tax brackets**, with a **top tax rate of 35%** on income above roughly **Rs. 4.1 million** per year【18†L5038-L5046】【18†L5047-L5054】. This means lower-income earners get relief (zero or minimal tax at the start), while higher earners pay more as their income increases.

- **9% Surcharge on High Salaries:** If you earn a very high salary, an extra **surcharge** now applies. Individuals with **taxable salary income over Rs. 10 million** in a year will pay an additional **9%** of their calculated income tax as a surcharge【3†L3419-L3427】. For example, if your regular tax on salary is Rs. 1,000,000 and you cross the Rs. 10 million threshold, you’ll pay **Rs. 90,000 extra** as a surcharge. This targets Pakistan’s top salaried earners, asking them to contribute a bit more.

- **Taxation of Large Pensions:** Lump-sum or large pension payments from a former employer are now taxable above a limit. If an individual receives **pension exceeding Rs. 10 million** in a tax year, the amount above Rs. 10 million is taxed at a **concessional 5% rate (final tax)【23†L5101-L5109】**. Pension amounts **up to Rs. 10 million remain tax-free【23†L5092-L5100】**. Notably, **senior citizens aged 70 or above** are **fully exempted** – they will **not** be charged tax on their pension income even if it’s above the Rs. 10 million mark【3†L3478-L3486】【3†L3482-L3490】. Also, if someone is drawing a pension **but still working for the same employer (or an associated company)**, their pension will be **treated as normal salary income** and taxed at regular rates instead of the special 5% rate【3†L3498-L3505】【3†L3500-L3504】.

- **Relief for Home Loans (Low-Cost Housing Credit):** To promote home ownership, a **new tax credit** is introduced for individuals on **interest paid for a home loan** (for **low-cost housing**). If you take a loan from a bank or recognized institution to buy or build **one house (up to 2,500 sq. ft. of land) or a flat (up to 2,000 sq. ft.) for personal use**, you can get a **tax credit** for the interest portion of your loan repayments【4†L3631-L3639】【4†L3645-L3653】. In simple terms, this credit will reduce your tax if you have a home loan on a modest house. (Each person can claim this credit for only one house in their lifetime, and not again for 15 years【4†L3683-L3691】.)

- **Higher Withholding on Large Pension Payments:** Companies or institutions paying out pensions need to withhold tax on hefty pensions. If they pay a former employee (under age 70) **more than Rs. 10 million** in pension in a year, they must deduct income tax on the amount above Rs. 10 million at the normal rates【7†L4250-L4258】【7†L4259-L4267】. This ensures the 5% pension tax (explained above) is collected at source for big payouts.

## Changes for Businesses and Corporate Taxpayers

- **Disallowance of Expenses for Unregistered Purchases:** To encourage documentation, businesses will lose some tax deductions if they buy from unregistered persons. Specifically, **10% of any expense on purchases from persons without an NTN (National Tax Number)** cannot be claimed as a deductible business expense【4†L3518-L3526】【4†L3520-L3528】. (Exception: purchases of crops from farmers are excluded – only middlemen in agriculture are targeted【4†L3524-L3531】.) This motivates businesses to buy from tax-registered suppliers or else bear a higher taxable income.

- **Cash Transaction Disallowance:** Similarly, the law discourages large cash dealings. If a business makes sales and receives over **Rs. 200,000 in cash (aggregate per invoice)** instead of through a bank or digital channel, **50% of the related expense** on those sales will **not** be tax-deductible【4†L3545-L3553】【4†L3554-L3562】. In short, accepting big payments in cash could double your taxable profit on those sales. This pushes businesses towards digital or banking channels for transactions, fostering transparency.

- **Depreciation Denied if Withholding Not Done:** A new rule links asset purchases with tax compliance. When a business buys a capital asset (like equipment) and was supposed to deduct withholding tax on the payment (under sections 152 or 153) but didn’t, then **no depreciation deduction is allowed on that asset**【4†L3572-L3580】【4†L3574-L3582】. The firm cannot claim wear-and-tear tax expense on such assets. This incentivizes companies to properly deduct and deposit withholding tax when acquiring assets from others.

- **Faster Depreciation of Intangibles:** On a positive note, if you have intangible assets (goodwill, patents, etc.), the cost can now be amortized over **15 years instead of 25 years**【4†L3589-L3596】. Writing off intangibles faster will give businesses larger tax deductions each year, which is beneficial for companies investing in intellectual property or rights.

- **Business Loss Adjustment Limit:** The Act bars using **business losses to offset property rental income** in a tax year【4†L3611-L3615】. Previously, if your business segment made a loss you could reduce your rental income tax by that loss; now that’s not allowed – each category is taxed on its own.

- **Restricted Group Tax Relief:** In group companies, **group loss relief** is no longer available if any company in the group has income that is taxed under the special **minimum tax regime on turnover**【4†L3621-L3627】. This prevents groups from transferring losses if one of them is paying turnover-based tax (ensuring everyone pays their fair share if using presumptive schemes).

- **Coal Mining Tax Break Focused:** The tax exemption for **coal mining** has been narrowed. Now, only firms mining coal in Sindh **for supplying to power plants** qualify for the income tax exemption【4†L3699-L3703】. This targets the incentive to specific strategic projects (coal for electricity), rather than all mining.

- **Super Tax (Section 4C) Continues:** The **“super tax” on high incomes** (applicable to corporations and wealthy individuals above certain income thresholds) continues with updated rates. For example, income above **Rs. 150 million** faces a small extra tax (1%), scaling up in tiers (up to 10% on income beyond Rs. 500 million)【23†L5178-L5186】【23†L5383-L5392】. Notably, from **2026 onwards**, some super tax rates slightly reduce (e.g. the slab for Rs. 200–250 million drops from 2% to 1.5%) to gradually ease this burden【12†L5231-L5238】【12†L5235-L5242】. This measure, introduced earlier to raise revenue from top companies/earners, remains in force for tax year 2025 with a plan to taper in future years.

- **Reduced Tax on IT Services:** In a business-friendly move for the tech sector, **withholding tax on IT and IT-enabled services** has been **cut to 4%**. Generally, services are subject to higher withholding (15% in many cases after this Act), but payments for qualified IT services will enjoy a **concessional 4% tax rate** at source【14†L5618-L5625】【14†L5626-L5634】. This encourages growth in software development, freelancing, and other IT services by improving cash flow and reducing the effective tax rate for tech firms.

- **Other Withholding Tax Tweaks:** The Act adjusted various withholding tax rates:
  - Payments to **electronic and print media** for advertising now attract only **1.5% withholding tax** (significantly lowered)【14†L5685-L5692】.
  - **Profit on debt (interest)** from banks and financial institutions is now subject to a flat **20% withholding** for most cases (uniform rate introduced)【14†L5556-L5564】【14†L5578-L5586】. Interest from Government securities paid to companies is also 20%, while for individuals it’s 15%【14†L5570-L5578】【14†L5579-L5587】.
  - **Capital gains on debt securities:** A new withholding tax of **15%** will apply on capital gains when debt securities (like government bonds) are sold. Banks or custodians maintaining investor accounts must deduct this tax on the gain amount【14†L5585-L5593】【8†L4298-L4306】. This brings debt investments into the tax net similar to stocks.

## Measures for the Digital Economy and E-Commerce

- **New Definitions – Digital Services and E-commerce:** The law now clearly defines **“digitally delivered services”** and **“e-commerce”** in the tax ordinance. Essentially, any service delivered online with minimal human involvement (like streaming, cloud services, online consulting, telemedicine, e-learning, etc.) is a *digitally delivered service*【3†L3346-L3354】【3†L3355-L3363】. And **e-commerce** is defined as the sale/purchase of goods or services through online platforms or mobile apps, where orders are placed over the internet【3†L3372-L3380】【3†L3386-L3394】. By defining these, the government is bringing internet-based commerce into the formal tax framework.

- **Tax on Online Marketplaces (Section 6A):** A new **tax on digital transactions** has been introduced for sellers using online platforms. If you **sell goods or services online** and the order is placed through a local e-commerce platform (website or marketplace) and delivered within Pakistan, a small tax will be charged on your **gross receipts**【3†L3432-L3440】【3†L3442-L3450】. The **rate is 1%** for payments received through **digital means (e.g. online bank/card payments)** and **2%** if the payment is **Cash on Delivery (CoD)**【14†L5498-L5506】. This tax is generally collected by the payment processor or courier on behalf of the seller. **Export earnings** that are already subject to withholding under other sections (like IT export remittances under section 154A) are exempt from this digital tax【3†L3450-L3458】【3†L3442-L3450】.

- **Platforms Must Withhold/Collect Tax:** The Act makes **payment intermediaries** (such as online payment gateways, banks, mobile wallets) and **courier services** (providing cash-on-delivery) responsible for **collecting the above tax** when they process payments for online sales【8†L4372-L4380】【8†L4398-L4406】. For example, if you sell an item through a marketplace and the buyer pays online, the payment gateway will deduct 1% before forwarding you the money. If the buyer pays cash on delivery, the courier will collect 2% from the payment. The collected amount is then deposited to the government as advance tax on your income.

- **Mandatory Registration for Online Sellers:** If you’re an online seller, note that **e-commerce vendors are now required to register with the tax authorities**. Online marketplaces and couriers **cannot allow unregistered sellers on their platforms**【9†L4679-L4688】【9†L4689-L4696】. This means if you want to continue selling on major Pakistani e-commerce platforms, you must have a taxpayer registration (National Tax Number). To enforce this, a heavy **penalty for non-registration** has been introduced: any online seller who is required to register but fails to do so faces a **Rs. 500,000 fine for the first default, and Rs. 1,000,000 for each repeat offense【18†L4850-L4858】【18†L4859-L4867】**. This steep fine is meant to push all digital sellers into the tax net.

- **Data Reporting by Digital Services:** The law adds new obligations for digital economy facilitators to share information:
  - **Payment intermediaries and couriers** that collect tax on digital transactions must file **quarterly statements** to the tax authority, listing each seller, transaction amount, and tax collected【9†L4546-L4554】【9†L4555-L4563】.
  - **Online marketplaces** must file **monthly reports** of all vendors on their platform, their turnover, and payments made to them【9†L4576-L4584】【9†L4585-L4593】.
  These measures will help the government track e-commerce earnings and ensure compliance.

- **Penalties on Facilitators:** If a **bank, payment gateway, or courier** fails to deduct or deposit the required tax on digital transactions, they can be penalized **100% of the tax amount** that they should have collected【10†L4728-L4736】【10†L4754-L4762】. In short, intermediaries are held strictly accountable for their role in taxing e-commerce.

- **Offshore Digital Services Fee:** The Finance Act also tightened tax on certain payments to foreign digital service providers. It specifies that fees for **“offshore digital services”** will be subjected to withholding tax under the law【14†L5470-L5478】 (generally 15% final tax under section 152). This could include payments for services like foreign streaming subscriptions, online software, etc., ensuring international digital companies pay their share if earning from Pakistan. (For the average consumer, this might mean such services continue to include some tax in their pricing.)

## Compliance and Enforcement Enhancements

- **Restrictions on Non-Filers (Section 114C):** A groundbreaking change is the introduction of **economic restrictions on “ineligible persons”** – basically, people who have **not filed their tax returns**. If you haven’t filed a return for the latest tax year (and don’t meet the alternate criteria of explaining your income sources), you will be barred from certain high-value transactions:
  - **Buying luxury cars:** Non-filers cannot purchase or register a new vehicle worth more than **Rs. 7 million**【21†L6937-L6945】【21†L6951-L6959】.
  - **Buying expensive property:** Non-filers cannot buy, transfer, or register immovable property valued over **Rs. 100 million**【21†L6965-L6973】【21†L6975-L6983】.
  - **Large investments:** Non-filers are not allowed to invest over **Rs. 50 million** in securities, mutual funds or other financial instruments【21†L6997-L7005】【21†L7017-L7023】 (aggregate cost in a year).
  - **Huge cash withdrawals:** Banks will **not allow** an ineligible person to withdraw cash beyond **Rs. 100 million per year** (total from all accounts)【21†L7053-L7061】【21†L7062-L7070】.
  
  These thresholds are quite high, so small transactions aren’t affected. But the message is clear: to buy top-tier cars or property, or make large financial moves, **you must be a tax filer**. This pushes wealthy individuals into the tax net and combats the underground economy. (Non-residents and public companies are exempt from these restrictions, except the cash withdrawal rule applies to everyone【5†L3783-L3789】【5†L3777-L3785】.) The government can adjust these threshold limits over time via notification【6†L3913-L3921】.

- **Higher Advance Tax on Cash Withdrawals (for Non-Filers):** The Finance Act increased the advance tax rate on cash withdrawals from banks by **non-filers** from **0.6% to 0.8%**【18†L4977-L4984】【18†L4978-L4981】. This means if you haven’t filed taxes, 0.8% of any large cash withdrawal (over the minimum threshold of Rs. 50,000 per day) will be taken as advance income tax (refundable only if you become a filer). The higher rate is meant to discourage people from staying outside the tax system and dealing in cash.

- **Streamlining Tax Audits and Appeals:** The Act includes several administrative reforms:
  - Tax authorities now have **a strict timeline to finalize audits** (usually within one year of the notice, extendable by only 90 days)【6†L3947-L3955】【6†L3959-L3967】. This prevents prolonged uncertainty for taxpayers under audit.
  - In an appeal, if the higher court or tribunal confirms some part of tax demand and sets aside the rest, the confirmed part **can be recovered immediately** without waiting for the whole case to resolve【6†L3975-L3983】【6†L3999-L4007】. Similarly, if the department wins at three appellate forums including a High Court, and the amount is over Rs. 200 million, that tax becomes payable even if further appeal is ongoing【7†L4173-L4181】【7†L4182-L4190】. These ensure the government can collect undisputed taxes faster.
  - A taxpayer now has an **option to skip the first appeal stage** (Commissioner Appeals) and go directly to the Tribunal for faster resolution【6†L4025-L4033】【6†L4077-L4083】. This could shorten the dispute process for those who choose it.
  - The time limit to appeal to the High Court is extended from 30 days to **60 days**, giving taxpayers more breathing room to file a case【6†L4037-L4045】【7†L4107-L4115】.

- **Enhanced Data Sharing for Enforcement:** The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) can now **share taxpayers’ data with banks** and receive banking data in return to identify **“high-risk” individuals** whose declared income doesn’t match their bank profiles【9†L4614-L4622】【9†L4626-L4634】. Advanced data analytics will be used to find tax evaders. Strict confidentiality is mandated, but if you’re hiding income, chances are more likely it will be spotted via bank records now.

- **Monitoring and Audits:** FBR is empowered to **deploy Inland Revenue officers onsite** at business premises to monitor production, stock, and sales in real time【9†L4655-L4663】【9†L4664-L4672】. This is expected for industries where suppression of sales is common. Additionally, FBR can hire up to **2,000 contract auditors** from the private sector to strengthen audit capacity【11†L4955-L4963】【11†L4964-L4972】. More auditors and on-ground monitoring mean **greater scrutiny** of businesses for tax compliance.

- **Confidentiality and Information Use:** Changes in Section 216 allow taxpayer information to be shared with:
  - **Contractual third-party auditors** hired by FBR (with NDA)【18†L4919-L4927】,
  - The **Tax Policy office** for research【11†L4939-L4947】,
  - **Universities and international organizations** for research, provided the data is anonymized【11†L4941-L4949】.
  
  This opens doors for policy analysis and technical audits while maintaining privacy safeguards.

- **Miscellaneous:** Many other fine-tuning amendments were made:
  - **Appeals by State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs):** Special provisions now govern disputes involving SOEs to expedite their resolution (e.g., a second ADR committee if the first fails to decide in 60 days)【7†L4139-L4147】【7†L4148-L4156】.
  - **Banks’ profit reporting:** Banks and financial institutions got clarity on certain withholding and tax treatments, especially aligning with the new **Digital Payments Levy Act 2025** (so no double taxation when that levy applies)【7†L4238-L4246】【8†L4332-L4340】.
  - **Higher penalty for not filing withholding statements:** Failing to file required statements (e.g., under sections 165, 165A/B/C) will now cost Rs. 50,000 instead of Rs. 5,000【10†L4708-L4716】 – a tenfold increase to ensure timely compliance.
  - **Alternate Dispute Resolution (ADR):** ADR provisions have been adjusted to make them more effective, including involving ADRC in extension of limitation in exceptional cases of revenue loss【18†L4889-L4897】【18†L4898-L4906】.
  
Overall, these measures signal a strong drive towards a **documented, digital, and fair tax system**. Compliance is being enforced with tighter rules and penalties, while some **reliefs and incentives** are provided to encourage desirable economic activities (like housing and IT services).

## FAQs – Frequently Asked Questions

**Q1. How have income tax slabs changed for salaried people?**  
**A1.** The Finance Act 2025 revised the tax brackets for individuals. Now, annual income up to **Rs. 600,000 is tax-free**【18†L4998-L5006】. Above that, the tax starts at **1%** (for income between Rs. 600k–1.2 million)【18†L5010-L5018】 and gradually increases in steps (11%, 23%, 30% at higher slabs)【18†L5024-L5032】【18†L5038-L5046】. The highest rate is **35%** on income above roughly **Rs. 4.1 million**【18†L5041-L5049】【18†L5066-L5074】. In short, low and middle incomes see minimal changes (some will even pay less tax than before), while higher earners will contribute at a slightly higher rate due to the top slab reaching 35%.

**Q2. I earn Rs. 12 million salary yearly. How will the new surcharge affect me?**  
**A2.** Since your taxable salary is above **Rs. 10 million**, you’ll be subject to the **9% high-income surcharge** on the tax amount【3†L3419-L3427】. This surcharge is **calculated on your income tax**, not your total income. For example, if your normal income tax (based on the slabs) comes to Rs. 2 million, the surcharge would be an extra **9% of 2 million = Rs. 180,000**. So your total tax would be Rs. 2,180,000. If your taxable income was below Rs. 10 million, this surcharge would not apply at all.

**Q3. Do pensioners have to pay tax on their pension now?**  
**A3.** **Regular monthly pensions** are still exempt from tax for most pensioners. The change targets **large one-time pension or retirement commutations**. If you receive a pension payment **over Rs. 10 million** in a year (e.g. a lump sum from a former employer), the amount above Rs. 10 million will be taxed at a low flat rate of **5%**【23†L5101-L5109】. Amounts up to Rs. 10 million remain tax-free【23†L5092-L5100】. Importantly, if you are **70 years or older**, **no tax** will be charged on your pension even if it’s a big amount【3†L3484-L3492】. The idea is to tax very large golden-handshake type pensions for younger retirees, while protecting senior citizens.

**Q4. What is the new “digital tax” on online goods and services?**  
**A4.** If you sell products or services online through Pakistani e-commerce platforms, the government will now take a small **“digital transactions tax”** on your sales revenue. It’s **1%** of the gross amount if the customer paid digitally (credit card, online transfer, etc.), or **2%** if the customer paid cash on delivery【14†L5498-L5506】. You as a seller don’t have to calculate this yourself; the **payment processor or courier will automatically collect it** when handling the payment【8†L4372-L4380】【8†L4384-L4392】. It will then show up as advance tax paid on your behalf. This only applies to sales delivered **within Pakistan** – export sales are excluded from this particular tax【3†L3450-L3458】.

**Q5. I run a small business selling on an online marketplace. What do I need to do?**  
**A5.** First, **make sure you are registered with FBR (have an NTN)**. The new law requires online marketplaces and couriers to **block unregistered sellers【9†L4679-L4688】【9†L4689-L4696】**. If you don’t register and continue to sell, you risk a **heavy penalty – Rs. 500,000** for the first time you’re caught, and **Rs. 1 million** for each repeat offense【18†L4850-L4858】【18†L4859-L4867】. Also, be aware that a small portion (1% or 2%) of your sale amounts will be withheld as tax (as explained in Q4). It’s wise to keep proper records of your sales and taxes withheld. On the plus side, being in the formal system can help your business in the long run (access to loans, confidence of customers, etc.), and the tax rates on small businesses are relatively low or even zero if income is below the taxable threshold.

**Q6. I haven’t filed tax returns before. Can I buy a car or property, or will I be stopped?**  
**A6.** Under the new rules, certain high-value purchases are off-limits to **non-filers**:
  - If the **car** you want to buy has a price tag above **Rs. 7 million**, the manufacturer or registration authority will **refuse to deal with you** unless you’re a filer【21†L6937-L6945】【21†L6951-L6959】. For cars cheaper than that, you can still buy, but you’ll pay higher token taxes as a non-filer.
  - For **property**, if the value of the plot/house is above **Rs. 100 million**, the transfer will not be registered for a non-filer【21†L6965-L6973】【21†L6975-L6983】. That’s a very expensive property (e.g., luxury homes or commercial plots); below that, you can still purchase but will incur advance taxes at higher rates.  
  Essentially, the law is targeting **luxury cars and real estate**. If you plan to make such a big purchase, it’s best to **file your tax return** beforehand. Becoming a filer is now almost a prerequisite for high-end transactions in Pakistan.

**Q7. What is the cash withdrawal limit for non-filers?**  
**A7.** Banks will monitor annual cash withdrawals. If a person is a non-filer, banks shall not allow **cumulative cash withdrawals exceeding Rs. 100 million in a year** from all their accounts【21†L7053-L7061】【21†L7059-L7067】. This is a very large amount (100 million rupees per year), so it won’t affect ordinary individuals withdrawing smaller sums. It’s aimed at those moving huge amounts of cash. Also, remember that every sizable cash withdrawal by a non-filer is subject to **0.8% withholding tax** (up from 0.6% earlier)【18†L4977-L4984】. The easy way to avoid both the limit and the extra tax is to simply **file your tax returns**, after which these restrictions and higher rates don’t apply.

**Q8. I heard something about a tax credit for home loans – how does that work?**  
**A8.** Yes, if you’re an individual who took out a loan to buy or construct a **new home (house or flat)** for yourself, you may get a **tax credit**. The home must be a **“low-cost” housing unit** – roughly meaning up to **2,500 sq. ft. plot or a 2,000 sq. ft. apartment**【4†L3645-L3653】. The credit is basically a portion of the **interest** (profit on debt) you paid on the loan during the year. When you file your tax return, you can claim this credit which will **reduce your tax payable**. There’s a formula in the law, but simply put, the **interest amount (up to 30% of your taxable income) qualifies for the credit【4†L3677-L3685】【4†L3679-L3687】**. The credit is proportional to your tax bracket and income. Also, you can claim this only for **one house/loan in your lifetime** and not again for the next 15 years【4†L3683-L3691】, to keep it targeted. This incentive is meant to make home financing more affordable.

**Q9. Did the corporate super tax go away?**  
**A9.** No, the **super tax (Section 4C)** on high incomes is still in effect for Tax Year 2025. Companies (and individuals) with **income over Rs. 150 million** pay this extra tax at graduated rates. For example, income from Rs. 150–200 million is taxed an extra 1%; Rs. 200–250m at 2%; and so on, up to 10% for income above Rs. 500 million【23†L5178-L5186】【23†L5383-L5392】. What changed is the **rates for future years**: starting Tax Year 2026, some rates will be slightly reduced (e.g., the 2% slab becomes 1.5%, 3% becomes 2.5%, etc.)【12†L5231-L5238】【12†L5235-L5242】. But for the current year, super tax is the same as before. This tax mostly concerns large corporations and ultra-high-net individuals, and it’s used by the government to raise additional revenue from those with the greatest ability to pay.

**Q10. How does the Finance Act 2025 impact the IT and freelance sector?**  
**A10.** There are a couple of positive changes for the IT sector:
  - **Lower tax withholding:** If you’re an IT or IT-enabled service provider (like software development, call center, etc.), the tax withheld on your payments/contracts is now reduced to **4%**【14†L5618-L5625】, whereas other services face up to 15% withholding. This means more cash in hand for you and potentially a lower final tax liability if your net profit margins are slim.
  - **Clarity on digital services:** The law explicitly includes digital and online services in the tax net, which means if you were operating under the radar, you should formalize your business. However, exports of IT services still enjoy tax exemptions or reduced rates under separate provisions (which remain intact). The Finance Act’s changes ensure domestic digital service revenues are reported and taxed fairly.
  
  Overall, the government is encouraging the tech industry with tax concessions (like the lower withholding), while also requiring **compliance** (registration and reporting). If you’re a freelancer or IT startup, it’s a good time to register as a taxpayer, keep proper accounts, and take advantage of any tax credits or lower rates available.

**Q11. What if I sell my personal house that I’ve lived in for many years? Is there any tax relief on that?**  
**A11.** Yes, the Act introduced a **one-time exemption for long-held personal homes**. Normally, when you sell property, the buyer has to collect advance tax on the sale (under section 236C) and you might owe capital gains tax if the property appreciated. Now, if the house was **your personal residence for at least 15 years**, and it was declared in your wealth statements throughout that period, you can apply for an **exemption certificate** so that **no advance tax is collected on its sale【9†L4504-L4512】【9†L4513-L4521】**. Essentially, a home you’ve owned and lived in for a long time can be sold without the usual property tax hassle, but this benefit can only be claimed **once in fifteen years**【9†L4527-L4534】. It recognizes that this is not speculative trading but a genuine change of home. You’d need to provide evidence of personal use and declaration in tax filings to get this exemption.

**Q12. What’s the overall goal of these changes – how will they impact taxpayers and the economy?**  
**A12.** The overarching goals are **documentation, fairness, and modernization**:
  - More people brought into the tax net (especially **wealthy non-filers and online businesses**), which should increase revenue and level the playing field for honest taxpayers.
  - Encouraging a **digital economy** but also ensuring it contributes taxes like the traditional economy. This includes taxing online sales slightly, forcing online sellers to register, and making digital payments preferable (via disallowing cash dealings).
  - Providing targeted **reliefs** – like for home loans, senior pensioners, IT services – to spur economic activity in those areas.
  - **Strengthening compliance** through data integration (with banks, etc.), stricter penalties, and quicker audits/appeals, which should reduce tax evasion.
  - For the broader economy, if these measures succeed, they could **widen the tax base**, increase government revenues without overburdening existing taxpayers, and formalize more of the economy. In the long run, that can lead to better public services or lower rates. In the short term, some individuals and businesses will need to adjust their practices (e.g., file returns, adopt digital payments, maintain documentation) to comply with the new rules.
  
Overall, taxpayers who are already compliant might not feel a big impact aside from a few new rates or procedures. Those who were operating informally or avoiding taxes will feel the pinch – but they also have now clear pathways to come into the system. The Finance Act 2025 sends a message: **Pakistan’s tax regime is getting stricter but also more attuned to the modern, digital economy and taxpayers’ needs**. By simplifying some rates and incentivizing good behavior while punishing evasion, the hope is for a more balanced and efficient tax system moving forward.

# Amendments to Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (via Sindh Finance Act 2025)

**Introduction:**  
The Sindh Finance Act 2025 has introduced significant changes to the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (SSTSA 2011). Effective July 1, 2025, these amendments overhaul how services are taxed in Sindh. The goal is to simplify the tax system by broadening the tax base, updating definitions, adjusting tax rates, and revising exemptions and penalties. In this blog post, we’ll break down the most important changes in a **conversational, easy-to-understand way**. Whether you’re a business owner, a service provider, or a consumer in Sindh, read on to learn what’s new and how it might affect you.

## **Overview of the 2025 Amendments**  
The Sindh Finance Act 2025 brings a **major structural shift** in Sindh’s sales tax on services framework. In simple terms, the law has moved from a “**positive list**” approach to a “**negative list**” approach. This means **all services are now considered taxable by default**, except those specifically listed as exempt【10†L34-L42】. Previously, only services that were listed in the law were taxable; now *everything is taxable unless it’s on the exempt list*. 

To support this broad approach, the definition of what counts as a **“service”** has been **greatly expanded**. The law now defines *service* in very broad terms to include **any activity, facility, utility, or advantage** provided – even the granting or surrendering of a right is considered a service【10†L49-L57】【26†L41-L45】. In essence, if you’re doing something for someone and getting paid, it’s likely a “service” under the tax law now. This wider definition closes loopholes and ensures new kinds of services (especially in our modern digital and services-driven economy) are covered.

Another key change is the **adoption of international classification codes**. Sindh has introduced the use of **United Nations Central Product Classification (CPC)** codes to categorize services【2†L163-L171】【22†L81-L89】. This sounds technical, but for the general public it means the tax authorities will use a standardized coding system to identify services. It helps align Sindh’s tax system with international standards and reduces confusion. In practice, businesses might see these codes on tax forms or schedules. The law also empowers the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) to resolve any disputes about how a service is classified under these codes【22†L95-L103】. Many of the old specific service definitions in the Act have been **removed** since the CPC codes will handle categorizing services【22†L90-L98】. So the law text is a bit leaner and less repetitive now.

Finally, the amendments aim to **“rationalize” tax rates and exemptions**. The standard tax rate has been adjusted, several new exemptions are introduced (especially to benefit small or specific businesses), and penalties for breaking the rules have been made stricter. We’ll explore each of these in the sections below.

## **Tax Rate Updates: Standard Rate and Special Rates**  
One of the first questions business owners ask is: *what’s the sales tax rate now?* The **standard Sindh sales tax rate on services is now 15%** of the service’s value【2†L249-L257】. This is referred to as the “standard rate” in the law. Previously, Sindh’s standard rate was 13% (it had remained 13% for several years) – so this change represents a 2% increase in the general rate【20†L553-L561】. The increase to 15% brings Sindh in line with some other provinces and was aimed at rationalizing tax rates【20†L553-L560】.

What about services that had **special rates** (either higher or lower than the standard)? The Sindh Finance Act 2025 has revamped the Second Schedule of the SSTSA 2011. Now the Second Schedule is split into two parts: 

- **Part I: Services Taxable at Higher than Standard Rate** – This part lists services that are taxed above 15%. For example, **telecommunications services** (like phone calls, internet, etc.) remain taxed at **19.5%**, as before【9†L1151-L1159】【9†L1162-L1170】. Telecom was already at 19.5% and continues at that rate (essentially as a special higher rate service). A few other related tech/communication services are also in this higher bracket at 19.5%【22†L139-L143】.

- **Part II: Services Taxable at Reduced (Lower) Rates** – This part lists various services that are now taxed at a rate **lower than 15%**, often to encourage certain industries or behaviors. Typically, when a service is taxed at a reduced rate, **no input tax credit** is allowed for that service (meaning if you opt for the lower rate, you cannot claim adjustments for tax you paid on your inputs)【9†L1179-L1188】【9†L1189-L1197】. Here are some notable examples of reduced rates:  
  - **Restaurants (Food & Beverage Services):** Restaurants that meet certain conditions (e.g. the bill is paid via credit/debit card, mobile wallet or QR scan) will charge a lower **8%** SST instead of 15%【9†L1273-L1281】. This is an incentive for digital payments and was in place earlier as well (with slight tweaks). If you walk into a restaurant and pay by card or digital means, the sales tax on your bill might be 8% in Sindh. (Do note, restaurants that *don’t* meet the conditions or choose not to opt for the reduced rate will charge the standard 15%, but then they can claim input tax credits on their expenses – it’s an optional thing for the business【9†L1181-L1189】【9†L1190-L1198】.)  
  - **Ride-Hailing and Taxi Services:** Services provided by ride-hailing app drivers or taxi operators are now taxed at **5%**【9†L1279-L1287】. So, using a cab or ride-share in Sindh carries a modest 5% SST (often this was already being charged in your app’s fare breakdown). The idea is to tax this emerging sector at a lower rate to keep it affordable and ensure compliance.  
  - **Construction Services (Government projects):** Construction services for **government-funded public works** are now taxed at a concessional rate of **5%**【9†L1228-L1236】. This reduced rate applies when a constructor is working on projects paid out of the federal, provincial or local government budget (like public infrastructure). It helps reduce the cost burden on public projects.  
  - **Commission Agents/Wholesale Dealers:** If you are an **auctioneer or a car dealer (acting as an agent)**, those fall under “wholesale trade service on a fee or contract basis” and are now taxed at **8%**【9†L1237-L1244】. This is a change from standard rate and is meant to support trading businesses. There’s even a further reduced **3%** rate for certain cases where services are provided by individuals receiving payments from abroad in foreign exchange【9†L1241-L1249】 – essentially to encourage export of services by individuals (for example, a freelancer in Sindh serving clients overseas could qualify for 3% SST on that income).  
  - **Travel & Transportation Services:** Some transport-related services have special rates. For instance, **rent-a-car services** and **vehicle rental with operator** services are at **8%**【9†L1291-L1299】【9†L1301-L1309】. On the other hand, services provided by **truck stands or bus terminals** (facilitating freight or bus operations) are now effectively at **0% (Nil)** rate【9†L1317-L1325】【9†L1319-L1326】 – which means those stand operators won’t charge SST, likely to avoid double-taxing the transport sector. (Petroleum transport via oil tankers is specifically excluded from this concession, so those remain taxable normally.)  

Overall, the **standard rate is 15%** for most services, but the Second Schedule’s new Parts I and II enumerate cases where the rate is either higher (like telecom at 19.5%) or lower (like the ones above). If you’re a service provider, it’s worth checking if your service falls in one of those special categories now. Otherwise, assume 15% is applicable if not exempt.

## **All Services Taxable Unless Exempt (The New “Negative List” Approach)**  
Perhaps the **biggest conceptual change** is how the law views taxable services. **Previously**, Sindh operated on a *positive list* – meaning only services listed in the law were subject to sales tax. If something wasn’t listed, it wasn’t taxed. This often led to ambiguity or new services falling through the cracks. **Now**, the law has flipped to a *negative list* approach: **everything is taxable unless the law says it’s exempt**【10†L34-L42】【22†L111-L119】. 

What does this mean for ordinary people and businesses? In practical terms: 

- **Many more services could come under the tax net.** If you were providing a service that wasn’t explicitly covered before, you should double-check if it’s exempt. If it’s not in the exemption list, it’s likely taxable now. For example, services like **consultancy, maintenance, training, etc.** – most of these were already being taxed under broad categories, but any that were missed before might now be captured. The idea is to avoid any service activity going untaxed just because it wasn’t named in old schedules.  

- **The law introduced a comprehensive First Schedule listing Exempt Services.** This First Schedule (substituted by the 2025 Act) is essentially the “negative list” – i.e. services that are *not* taxed (or taxed at 0%). Everything not on this list is taxable. We’ll cover the major exemptions in the next section. 

- **Constitutional limitations are respected:** Importantly, the amendments explicitly ensure that if a service falls under a domain **only the federal government can tax (per the Constitution)**, then Sindh will not treat it as a taxable service【2†L201-L207】【22†L123-L131】. For instance, “terminal taxes on goods or passengers carried by rail, sea or air” are a federal subject (Entry 53 of the Constitution’s Federal Legislative List). The new law clarifies that any service that essentially amounts to those federal-domain taxes will *not* be taxed by Sindh【22†L123-L131】. This clarification came due to past legal disputes – e.g. courts struck down SST on certain shipping agent services, saying it overlapped with federal taxes on freight【22†L133-L139】. So now the law explicitly carves those out as non-taxable by Sindh. (For a layperson: it means Sindh won’t tax things like airline tickets or railway fares, since those are a federal matter – which was already the case, but now it’s crystal clear in the law).

In summary, **if you’re providing any service in Sindh, assume it’s subject to SST at 15% unless you find a specific exemption for it.** The net has widened, which simplifies things (no more searching whether your service is listed – instead check if it’s exempt). This change aims to create a level playing field and future-proof the tax system for new types of services.

## **Updated Exemptions and Reliefs (First Schedule)**  
With everything taxable by default, the **list of exemptions becomes crucial**. The Sindh Finance Act 2025 introduced a brand-new **First Schedule** in the law, which enumerates services that are **exempt from sales tax** (or effectively taxed at 0% with conditions). The First Schedule is quite detailed, but here we’ll highlight the key exemptions and what they mean in simple terms:

- **Essential Sectors (Unchanged Exemptions):** Core services that were traditionally not taxed remain exempt. This includes most **education services** (schools, colleges, universities) and **healthcare services** (medical services by clinics, hospitals, doctors). For example, recognized educational institutions’ services are exempt【18†L13-L22】. Similarly, basic health and life insurance for individuals have exemptions up to certain limits (life insurance for small policy values, health insurance for individuals, etc., which we’ll mention shortly). **Public utilities** like **electricity, gas, and water** supply are also not subject to SST (they are handled by other taxes)【17†L615-L619】. So, consumers don’t see SST on their electricity bills – that remains the case.

- **Government and Public Services:** The law now explicitly exempts **services provided by courts, tribunals, Parliament, Provincial Assemblies, and local government members in performance of their official duties**【2†L233-L241】. In plain language, this means government and legislative functions aren’t treated as taxable services (which makes sense – you won’t charge sales tax on a court judgment or an MPA’s legislative role!). Additionally, **central banking and regulatory bodies** are exempt – services by the State Bank of Pakistan, Securities and Exchange Commission, Competition Commission, etc., are not taxed【17†L588-L596】. These were mostly not taxed before either, but it’s now clearly written.

- **Small Businesses (New Exemption!):** A *big relief* for small service providers: If your **annual turnover is under Rs. 4 million**, you are **exempt from SST**【12†L99-L107】. This is a general exemption aimed at small businesses and startups, sparing them from the burden of sales tax compliance until they grow bigger. However, there are **important caveats**: if you provide services to **withholding agents** (typically large companies or government bodies that are required to deduct SST), or to **registered businesses (like companies registered for sales tax or income tax)**, the exemption doesn’t apply【28†L423-L431】【28†L425-L433】. In other words, the Rs.4 million threshold is mainly to help small B2C service providers or those serving unregistered persons. The moment your client is a big registered entity that can claim withholding or input, the exemption is off the table for that service. Also, if a specific service category had its **own turnover-based exemption threshold** already defined (and some did), those specific rules prevail over the general 4 million rule【28†L431-L438】. Finally, any service that was **fully taxable before June 30, 2025, without a turnover exemption** will continue to be taxable now regardless of turnover【12†L101-L109】【28†L429-L438】. This prevents someone from claiming a new exemption on a service that was always taxed and had no threshold (for example, telecom services – a small ISP with under 4m sales is likely still taxed, since telecom sector didn’t have a threshold exemption). Despite the fine print, this is a welcome step for micro and small enterprises – a lot of very small service providers (think along the lines of a one-person consulting firm or a tiny home-based service business) get breathing room until they hit Rs 4 million in sales a year.

- **Construction and Housing:** Several exemptions target the construction sector, especially to promote certain types of development:
  - Construction services related to **Export Processing Zones (EPZs), Special Economic Zones (SEZs),** and diplomatic or consular buildings are exempt【3†L379-L387】【3†L391-L399】. These zones often have special tax incentives, and Sindh has aligned with that. 
  - The construction of a **single private residential house** (for personal use of the owner) is exempt provided the covered area is not more than 10,000 square feet【3†L391-L399】. So if you’re building your own modest home, the construction services aren’t taxed. 
  - **Low-cost housing projects** sponsored by the federal or Sindh government are exempt, subject to size limits (e.g. houses on plots up to 125 sq. yards or apartments up to 900 sq. ft. in those schemes)【17†L401-L410】【17†L413-L421】. This encourages affordable housing development by reducing tax costs.
  - Notably, **construction services by very small construction businesses** (annual turnover not exceeding Rs. 4 million) are also exempt【17†L417-L424】 – effectively the general small business exemption, but explicitly mentioned for construction too.
  - **Maintenance and repair related to agriculture, horticulture, animal husbandry, dairy farming** is exempt【17†L413-L421】. So, services like repairing farm equipment or maintaining a greenhouse, etc., are not taxed – a boon for the agriculture sector.

- **Restaurants and Catering (Small-scale):** While larger restaurants are taxed (and have the option of reduced 8% if they go cashless), **very small eateries are exempt**. The First Schedule exempts restaurants/caterers if their annual turnover is **≤ Rs. 5 million**, **provided they are not part of a larger franchise/chain or located in upscale premises**【17†L475-L483】【17†L477-L485】. The exemption is lost if the restaurant has any air-conditioning in use in the year or operates in an air-conditioned mall, or is inside a hotel/club, or is a franchise, or has more than one outlet, etc.【17†L479-L487】【17†L489-L497】. Essentially, this targets the tiny local dhabas and small canteens – if you’re a small eatery that is not fancy (no AC) and your sales are under 5 million, you don’t have to charge SST. This relief acknowledges the small roadside food stalls and local cafes, to keep their prices low for consumers.

- **Transportation and Storage:** **Passenger transport services** are generally exempt, which means things like tickets for local buses, vans, rail, etc., don’t have SST. The exemption, however, does *not* cover certain specific transport-related services like rent-a-car, vehicle rental, ride-hailing (cab aggregator) services, or chartered flights originating in Sindh – those remain taxable as we noted with reduced rates or standard rates【17†L525-L534】【17†L535-L543】. So your daily commute in a local bus is not taxed, but an Uber ride is (at 5%), and a private charter flight is taxed (likely at standard rate).  
  **Storage and warehousing services** are exempt *only* for storage of **agricultural produce and foods**【17†L543-L551】【17†L547-L555】. Storage of other goods (general warehousing) is taxable. So a cold storage holding vegetables isn’t charging SST, but a warehouse storing general merchandise would.

- **Property Rental:** The **renting of immovable property** (which is considered a service in sales tax laws) has targeted exemptions: renting for **religious purposes**, for **agricultural use**, or **purely residential use** is exempt【17†L571-L579】【17†L581-L589】. For instance, if a mosque (a religious body) rents a hall to another religious organization, that’s exempt. Leasing out land for farming is exempt. Renting houses or apartments for people to live (residential) is exempt. But renting out commercial buildings or renting for business purposes remains taxable.

- **Insurance Services:** Sindh has provided exemptions for certain **insurance services**, typically those that benefit individuals or key sectors. **Life insurance for individuals** is exempt up to a policy coverage of Rs. 500,000【17†L595-L603】 (so small life policies aren’t taxed; very high-value policies might be taxed or considered different). **Health insurance for individuals** (not group/corporate policies) is exempt【17†L601-L608】, so your personal health insurance premium isn’t subject to SST. **Crop insurance** for farmers is exempt【17†L599-L604】. And **marine insurance for export goods** is exempt【17†L609-L613】 (to support exporters). Other types of insurance (like car insurance, property insurance, large group policies, etc.) remain taxable as before.

- **Miscellaneous:** The First Schedule covers many other specific items. Some examples: **Funeral and burial services** are exempt (a humane consideration), services by **extraterritorial organizations** (like UN or other international bodies) are exempt, and interestingly, there’s an entry that effectively exempts **domestic household services** (perhaps covering servants, etc., though those typically weren’t taxed anyway since they aren’t formal “services sector” businesses). Also, **printing services for newspapers, journals, textbooks** are exempt【28†L435-L438】 – meaning if you’re printing or publishing recognized newspapers or educational texts, that’s not taxed.

In summary, the exemptions aim to protect basic services and small providers: education, health, public transport, essential food and agriculture, small businesses, and socially important sectors get relief. If you’re a **business owner**, you should review if any of these exemptions apply to your service – it could mean you don’t have to charge sales tax (or can zero-rate it). For **consumers**, these exemptions mean certain services (like schooling, medical treatment, utility bills, public transport, etc.) won’t have an extra 15% tax added, keeping them affordable.

## **Stricter Penalties and Compliance Measures**  
Alongside expanding the tax net, the amendments also **harden the penalties** for those who don’t comply. The idea is to encourage timely filing and payment by making the cost of default higher. Here are the key changes in penalties and enforcement:

- **Late Filing of Returns:** If a registered service provider files their monthly SST return late, the penalty is now **Rs. 100 for each day of delay**【3†L309-L318】. For example, if you file 10 days after the due date, that’s Rs. 1,000 fine. Earlier, there was a different fixed penalty or formula (previously it was Rs. 1,000 total or a smaller amount, which wasn’t a strong deterrent). Now it accrues daily, up to a certain maximum. This change makes it costly to procrastinate on filing returns【12†L89-L97】.

- **Late Payment or Non-Payment of Tax:** The penalty for not paying the tax due (or short paying) has been increased. Previously a **3%** of the tax amount per month penalty applied in some cases – it appears that has been raised to **5%** (and the “per month or part thereof” wording was removed)【3†L313-L321】. In simple terms, if you don’t pay your sales tax, you could face a straight 5% penalty on the amount owed (in addition to the tax and any default surcharge interest). So, for example, if Rs. 100,000 tax was due and you didn’t pay, a Rs. 5,000 penalty might apply (earlier it might have been calculated monthly at 3%). This change is meant to prod businesses to deposit taxes on time.

- **Penalty Cap Doubled:** Certain offenses had a maximum fixed penalty of Rs. 50,000 under the old law (for instance, obstructing tax officers or failing to allow inspection). The amendment has doubled some of these to **Rs. 100,000**. Notably, the penalty for **denying the authorized officer access to business premises or records** is now up to Rs. 100,000 (it was Rs. 50k before)【12†L91-L97】. So if the SRB officials come knocking for an audit or inspection, barring their entry can cost you a hefty sum.

- **Registration Obligations:** The law slightly tweaked wording in Section 24 to ensure **anyone providing taxable services must register**【3†L297-L305】. They broadened it by replacing “provide or render any taxable service” clearly as a trigger to register【3†L299-L307】. Failing to register when required is an offense that can also attract penalties (usually a fixed fine, which, as noted, might have increased). The exact penalty for not registering can be significant, so new service providers should register with SRB promptly if they cross the threshold or if their service is taxable.

- **Active Taxpayer Requirement:** A new condition has been introduced that certain things (like getting licenses or permissions from government) will require the applicant to be a **“registered and active taxpayer”** under SST law【26†L59-L66】. This means if you need a license in Sindh (say for a trade or operation), you might have to show you’re on the Active Taxpayers List of SRB (i.e., you are registered and have filed your returns). This change links compliance with other business privileges – an effort to increase the tax net compliance. It’s also mentioned that if a non-resident is providing services to Sindh residents, having any office or branch in Sindh will count (they changed “registered office” to just **“office”** in the law)【26†L51-L59】. For businesses, the takeaway is: keep your **tax registrations active and filings up-to-date** if you want smooth sailing in regulatory matters like license renewals.

- **Transitional Relief (No sudden tax on previously taxed services):** The amendments include a “no surprises” clause: any service that was already taxable as of June 30, 2025 will continue to be taxed at the same rate, unless specifically changed【3†L347-L354】. In other words, just because they re-wrote the schedules, you won’t find something that was taxed at (say) 13% suddenly taxed more without it being explicitly in the new schedule. This protects against any inadvertent changes and reassures businesses that there’s continuity. It’s a bit technical, but basically the law says the overhaul itself shouldn’t create an unintended tax holiday or hike for services unless stated. 

All these measures indicate that SRB is serious about enforcement. **For business owners**, it means you should be diligent: register if required, file returns on time, pay on time, and maintain proper compliance, because penalties for slipping up are heavier now. **For the general public**, stricter enforcement ideally means a more fair system where everyone who owes tax pays it (leveling the playing field) and hopefully better revenue for the province that can be spent on public services.

Before we conclude, let’s address some common questions in a straightforward FAQ format:

## **FAQ: Common Questions about the 2025 SST Amendments**

**Q1. Are all services really taxable now? What does “negative list” mean?**  
**A:** Yes – virtually **all services provided in Sindh are now subject to sales tax** by default. The “negative list” approach means the law doesn’t try to name every taxable service. Instead, it lists the services which are **not taxed (exempt)**, and everything *not* on that list is taxable【10†L34-L42】. So if you’re providing any kind of service (from consultancy to digital services to event management – anything), you should assume SST applies unless you find a clear exemption for it. This is a change from the old system where only specifically listed services were taxed and some unlisted services fell outside the net. The goal is to cast a wide net and reduce ambiguity.

**Q2. What is the sales tax rate on services in Sindh now?**  
**A:** The **standard SST rate is 15%** of the value of the service【2†L249-L257】. This is an increase from the previous 13%. So, for most taxable services, if you charge a customer Rs.100, the SST would be Rs.15 (making the total bill Rs.115, if you choose to pass it on). There are some exceptions: a few services have higher or lower rates. **Telecom services** (e.g., phone bills, internet) are taxed at **19.5%** (this hasn’t changed). A number of services have **reduced rates** (below 15%) – for instance, certain restaurant bills, ride-hailing, construction for government, etc., can be **5% or 8%** with conditions. But unless you know you fall in a special category, plan for 15%. Consumers will generally see 15% SST on their invoices for services (higher on telecom).

**Q3. Did the Finance Act 2025 raise the tax on any services or reduce any taxes?**  
**A:** It’s a mix of both:  
- The **general rate went up to 15%** (which effectively raised the tax on any service that was previously at 13%). If you were paying 13% SST on something in June 2025, you’ll pay 15% from July 2025 onward (unless it falls in a reduced rate now).  
- Some **services got reduced rates** or exemptions: for example, small restaurants under certain conditions now pay 0% (exempt) or can opt 8% instead of 15%; freelancers receiving payments from abroad might get a 3% rate, etc. And notably, **small businesses under Rs.4m turnover are now fully exempt** – which is a tax cut for them (previously they would have been taxed if their service was listed).  
- On the other hand, a few new services that weren’t taxed before might now become taxable because of the “everything is taxable” rule (for example, maybe certain professional services or new digital services that were arguable before are clearly taxable now). But the law also provided that anything previously taxable stays taxed at the same rate unless changed【3†L347-L354】, so there’s no sudden spike like taxing something at a higher rate without notice. 

**Q4. I run a small business. Do I need to register for Sindh sales tax and charge it to my customers?**  
**A:** It depends on your **annual revenue and customer type**. Under the new amendments, if your **annual turnover is less than Rs. 4 million**, your services are **exempt from SST**【12†L99-L107】. This means you **do not need to register or charge SST**, as long as you stay below that threshold. This is great news for many small startups, freelancers, and home businesses. *However, be careful:* if you provide services to large companies or government (who are *withholding agents* or registered entities), those particular services don’t enjoy the exemption【28†L425-L433】. For example, if you’re a small graphic designer making <4m a year, you normally wouldn’t charge SST to local small clients. But if you take a job from a big corporation, they might require you to be registered and charge SST so they can deduct it. Also, some specific service sectors might have different thresholds (the general Rs.4m won’t override an existing rule for that sector if any). If you cross Rs.4m in a year, you must register and start charging the tax thereafter. When in doubt, consult the SRB or a tax advisor, but the intent is to spare very small businesses from this compliance burden.

**Q5. Which services are exempt from SST now?**  
**A:** The list is pretty extensive (the First Schedule lists exempt services). Here are the major ones in plain language:  
  - **Education services** – Schools, colleges, universities, and related educational services (especially by recognized institutions) are exempt.  
  - **Health services** – Medical services by hospitals, clinics, doctors, etc., are exempt. Also certain health insurance policies for individuals are exempt.  
  - **Public transportation** – Passenger transport by buses, rail, etc., is exempt (excluding things like rented cars or ride-hailing). Goods transport by trucking is generally taxable, but services by truck/bus terminals (addas) are given a concession (0% in some cases).  
  - **Utilities** – Electricity, water supply, and natural gas distribution services are not taxed under SST (these are billed without SST as they fall under other tax regimes).  
  - **Financial services by government bodies** – State Bank and other regulators’ services are exempt. Interest/loan services are outside SST by nature as well.  
  - **Insurance** – Life insurance (for small policy values), health insurance (individual), crop insurance, and export-related marine insurance are exempt. Other insurance like general insurance is taxable at standard rate.  
  - **Real estate renting** – Purely residential rentals are exempt. Also renting for agriculture or by religious bodies to other religious bodies is exempt. Commercial property rent remains taxable.  
  - **Agriculture-related** – Services in agriculture, like livestock farming services, tilling, etc., are mostly exempt (to support farmers). Also storage of agricultural produce is exempt from warehousing tax.  
  - **Small enterprises** – Any service business with turnover < Rs.4 million/year (and fulfilling the conditions) is exempt. Also, independent small restaurants (turnover <5m, no AC, etc.) are exempt. Small construction projects by low-turnover persons are exempt.  
  - **Miscellaneous social services** – e.g. funeral and burial services, charitable organizations’ certain services, etc., are exempt.  
This is not the full list, but covers the big categories. Essentially, essential public services and small-scale providers get relief. If your service isn’t in one of these broad categories, it’s likely taxable.

**Q6. I provide IT/technical services to clients abroad from Sindh. Do I need to pay SST on that export income?**  
**A:** There is a favorable provision: if you’re an individual providing services and **receiving payment in foreign exchange** from outside Pakistan, there’s a special **3% reduced rate** under certain conditions【9†L1239-L1248】. In some cases, such export of services could even be considered outside scope or zero-rated, but Sindh hasn’t explicitly zero-rated exports across the board in the law (unlike the federal sales tax which zero-rates exports of goods). Instead, Sindh offers this 3% concession for certain foreign currency receipts for services. If you want to avail the **reduced 3%**, you likely need to opt in by filing an option with SRB (as per rules)【9†L1189-L1197】. If you don’t opt, technically the service is at 15% but then possibly you could argue it’s an export and maybe not taxable in province? This is a complex area. For a straightforward answer: **Yes, SST can apply to services exported**, but Sindh gives a **concessionary rate** to make it easier. Export-oriented IT companies often lobby for zero tax; for now, 3% is what the law provides for certain cases (like freelance individuals). It’s best to consult SRB if you are exporting services, to see if you qualify for the reduced rate or any exemption. Keep in mind, *if* your services are considered “export” and you don’t charge SST, you must comply with State Bank regulations (bring the money through proper banking channels etc., as the condition states).

**Q7. What happens if I file my SST return late or forget to pay the tax?**  
**A:** Under the new rules, the **penalties have increased**. If you file your tax return after the due date, you’ll incur a penalty of **Rs.100 per day** of delay【3†L309-L317】. So a one-month delay (about 30 days) means Rs. 3,000 fine, which can rack up quickly. If you **don’t pay the tax** (or underpay), the penalty can be around **5% of the tax amount** (subject to some minimum/maximum as prescribed) – higher than before【3†L313-L321】. Additionally, if you **don’t allow SRB officials to inspect or you fail to register when required**, those penalties can go up to **Rs.100,000** in some cases【12†L91-L97】. The bottom line: it’s important to file and pay on time. If you genuinely can’t file on time, it’s wise to inform SRB or seek an extension (though those are rare) to avoid penalties. The emphasis on timely compliance is much stronger now.

**Q8. I’m a consumer. Will I be paying more now when I use services in Sindh?**  
**A:** In general, you **might see a slight increase on some bills**. For example, previously you might have paid 13% SST on your salon/spa bill or your internet/cable bill – now it will be 15%. That’s a 2% increase in tax which businesses often pass on to consumers. On a Rs.1,000 service, that’s Rs.20 more. Not huge, but noticeable over time. On the other hand, some things might get cheaper or stay the same: if you dine at restaurants that adopt the 8% digital-payment SST, you effectively pay a lower tax than before. Ride-hailing apps were already charging 5% SST, and that stays 5%. Telecom bills remain at 19.5% (no change there). Many services that were not taxed before might now start having SST – for example, if some niche service wasn’t listed before and now it’s taxable under the new system, you could see a new tax line on those receipts. However, essential services (education, health, etc.) that you use have no SST, so no change there. Overall, for most common taxable services, expect the tax to be 15% instead of 13%. Businesses have to display SST on invoices, so you’ll know when you’re being charged SST. If you’re a final consumer, you cannot recover this tax (it’s a consumption tax). The positive spin is that this helps the province’s revenue which can fund public programs.

**Q9. What are CPC codes and do I need to worry about them as a business owner?**  
**A:** CPC codes are basically **classification numbers for types of services**. The Sindh Revenue Board has switched to using these internationally recognized codes to categorize services【2†L163-L171】【22†L83-L90】. For example, a particular code may represent “construction services” and another code for “software development services” and so on. As a business owner, you might see these codes in the updated law schedules or in the tax return forms. It helps to know which code applies to your service type for proper filing. **However, you don’t need to memorize them** – the SRB will provide guidance on which code corresponds to your activity. The main idea is to standardize definitions. So, when registering or filing, you might have to pick your service category by CPC code. If unsure, you can ask SRB or refer to their lists. The good news is this is more of a back-end/system change – it doesn’t change how you operate or tax rate by itself. It’s for classification consistency. If you’re a consumer, you likely won’t notice this at all (it might be printed on receipts or notices, but it doesn’t affect the amount you pay).

**Q10. When did these changes take effect?**  
**A:** All these amendments came into force on **July 1, 2025**【1†L63-L66】, which is the start of Sindh’s fiscal year 2025-26. So any services provided from that date onward are subject to the new rules. If you provided a service in June 2025, it was under the old regime; if you provide it in July 2025, the new rules apply. Businesses had to update their systems and billing by that date to the new rates and classifications. There was a transition clause that basically says whatever services were taxed as of June 30 will just continue at the same rate until changed【3†L347-L354】 – meaning no gap or confusion at the midnight of the switch-over.

We hope this explanation has made the 2025 changes clearer. The Sindh government’s overhaul is quite comprehensive, but it boils down to **broadening the tax base, updating laws to current needs, and making compliance more robust**. If you’re affected by these changes, it’s a good idea to consult with tax professionals or reach out to the Sindh Revenue Board for any specific guidance. For the general public, it’s useful to know why your bills might have changed and which services are taxed or not taxed. 

*By staying informed and compliant, businesses can avoid penalties and consumers can better understand their costs. The SST on services is a major revenue source for Sindh, and these reforms aim to make it more effective while balancing the burden through exemptions and lower rates for small players.* 

**Sources:** The information above is based on the Sindh Finance Act, 2025 as published (Amendments to SSTSA 2011) and analyses by tax experts. Key references include the text of the Finance Act【2†L249-L257】【3†L309-L318】, summaries by professional firms【10†L34-L42】【12†L89-L97】, and official explanations by SRB. These sources highlight the shift to a negative list, revised definitions, new rates, and penalties that we have conveyed in simpler terms.

Overview of the 2025 Amendments
The Sindh Finance Act 2025 brings a major structural shift in Sindh’s sales tax on services framework. In simple terms, the law has moved from a ‘positive list’ approach to a ‘negative list’ approach. This means all services are now considered taxable by default, except those specifically listed as exempt. Previously, only services that were listed in the law were taxable; now everything is taxable unless it’s on the exempt list.
To support this broad approach, the definition of what counts as a ‘service’ has been greatly expanded.
