# Amendments to Punjab Sales Tax on Services Act (2012) – Punjab Finance Act 2025 Explained

## Introduction

In **Punjab (Pakistan)**, the provincial government has introduced major changes to how services are taxed. These changes came through the **Punjab Finance Act 2025**, which amends the Punjab Sales Tax on Services Act, 2012. Effective **July 1, 2025**【1†L41-L48】【1†L63-L70】, the amendments aim to **simplify and broaden** the sales tax regime on services. In simple terms, the law now taxes **all services by default** (a shift to a “negative list” system) and provides a specific list of **“tax-free services”** that will not be taxed. It also revises certain tax rates and imposes new rules to encourage **digital payments** (with penalties for non-compliance). 

This blog post breaks down the key changes in plain language – covering new definitions, which services are tax-free, what the updated tax rates are, the digital payment requirements, and other important tweaks. We’ll also answer frequently asked questions to help you understand what the Punjab Sales Tax 2025 amendments mean for you.

## All Services Taxable by Default (New 'Negative List' System)

One of the biggest changes is a **shift from a “positive list” to a “negative list” taxation model**. Under the old system, only services specifically listed in the law were subject to sales tax (a positive list). Now, **all services are considered taxable** **unless** they are explicitly mentioned as not taxable. In legal terms, **“all services…will be treated as taxable services” except those categorized as tax-free or otherwise exempt【11†L81-L87】**. This effectively broadens the tax base – many services that were previously not taxed will now fall under the tax net unless they appear on the exempt list【8†L17-L24】. 

To enable this change, the definition of “service” in the law was updated (Section 2(38) of the 2012 Act) to include services covered in the new First and Second Schedules【11†L72-L79】【11†L83-L87】. The **charging section (Section 3)** was also amended to reflect that *all services provided in Punjab are taxable by default*【6†L91-L99】【6†L92-L100】. In short, Punjab has moved to a **universal taxation of services** with a specific exclusion list – a system similar to what other provinces like Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa have adopted【8†L19-L27】.

For consumers and businesses, this means you should **expect sales tax on any service** you purchase, **unless** it’s one of the specially exempted **tax-free services** described below. The idea is to make the system more **comprehensive and fair**, by not leaving out entire sectors from taxation, while still protecting certain essential services from tax.

## Introduction of Tax-Free Services in Punjab

With everything taxable by default, the government has created a new category of **“tax-free services”** – services that will **not** be charged any Punjab sales tax. A new Section 3A was inserted into the law to define *tax-free services*, and an entirely **new First Schedule** now lists all these exempt services【11†L89-L97】. If a service is listed in this First Schedule (and meets any condition specified), it is **not subject to Punjab sales tax**.

What services are tax-free? The list is quite comprehensive, covering many **essential and public-interest services**. Here are some of the key categories of services that **remain tax-free** in Punjab under the 2025 amendments:

- **Public Healthcare and Education**: Services in **government healthcare facilities** – for example, consultation or visit fees of doctors and specialists, hospital bed/room charges in public sector hospitals – are not taxed【18†L265-L273】. Similarly, **educational services** are exempt: this includes **general education** (schools, colleges, universities) and any education provided by public sector institutions【18†L281-L289】. (Private schools and colleges offering general education are also covered under “general education services,” so they remain tax-free as well.)

- **Public Transport and Government Services**: **Public transport** services provided by the government (such as government-run bus or train services) are tax-free【18†L289-L297】. In addition, certain fees and services provided by government departments are not taxed – for instance, **passport issuance, national ID card services, or other registration services by federal/provincial/local governments** have no sales tax【18†L302-L310】. Basic **postal and courier services by government** (e.g. Pakistan Post) are exempt when provided to government bodies【18†L295-L303】.

- **Charitable and Non-Profit Services**: Services provided by **charitable organizations** or **non-profits** are generally exempt. If a service is provided by a **registered charity or a religious institution for public benefit**, or by certain approved international NGOs or international agencies, it is tax-free (as long as any applicable federal tax exemptions also apply)【18†L336-L343】. This ensures genuine non-profit activities aren’t burdened by provincial tax.

- **Affordable Housing and Construction**: To promote housing development, services by **property developers and builders** can be tax-free, but only for **affordable housing projects**. For example, construction services under government-sponsored low-cost housing schemes (notified by the Punjab Housing & Town-Planning Agency) are exempt from tax【18†L325-L333】. Additionally, there are exemptions for certain **construction projects**: small residential construction (houses below a certain size), projects funded by foreign grants, or cases where a builder is already paying tax under another category – these specific scenarios are carved out as tax-free to avoid double taxation and encourage development.

- **Insurance and Financial Services**: Most **insurance services** are taxable (as we’ll note later), but the law continues to **exempt a couple of important insurance categories**: **marine insurance for export goods** and **crop insurance** for farmers are both tax-free【18†L345-L353】. These are crucial for exporters and the agriculture sector. Moreover, services by **foreign exchange dealers or money changers** are exempt from Punjab sales tax (financial exchange services are not taxed in the province)【26†L448-L456】【26†L450-L458】.

- **Personal Care & Others**: Small businesses providing personal care services get relief. **Small beauty parlors or salons without air-conditioning** are exempt from tax – they fall under tax-free services【26†L368-L372】. (By contrast, larger, air-conditioned salons have to charge tax, but at a low rate, which we’ll explain shortly.) Similarly, **photography services** by small independent photographers are exempt – for example, a lone photographer or a tiny photo studio (as declared by the authority) doesn’t charge sales tax【26†L396-L404】【26†L390-L398】. **Home rentals** are also protected: renting out a **personal dwelling for residential use** is tax-free, so if you rent a house/apartment to someone to live in, that rental income is not hit by sales tax【26†L400-L404】. 

- **Religious, Cultural, and Recreational Services**: Services related to the general public’s welfare provided by the government are exempt. This includes things like entry fees or services at **museums, libraries, parks, zoos, sports facilities, or cultural centers** run by government – no sales tax on those【18†L309-L317】. Also, services related to religion are exempt; for instance, charges for participation in religious events or facilities provided by the government or a religious institution for the public would be tax-free. Furthermore, **diplomatic missions’ services** (anything provided by foreign embassies/consulates) are exempt by nature【26†L398-L404】.

- **Hajj, Umrah, and Pilgrimage Services**: In recognition of religious travel, the law exempts certain travel services. **Tour operators and travel agents** do not charge sales tax on packages or services for **Hajj and Umrah pilgrims (and Ziyarat)**【2†L372-L380】. Likewise, any air travel services (like airline tickets) for Hajj or Umrah passengers are tax-free, as are services for diplomats and certain aviation crew【2†L386-L394】. This means pilgrims from Punjab heading for Hajj or Umrah will not pay provincial sales tax on those specific travel arrangements.

The above are highlights – the First Schedule (tax-free list) actually contains **over 25 categories** of services with various conditions. But the common thread is that these are either *essential services, public services, or socially important activities*. By keeping them tax-free, the government is ensuring it doesn’t make critical services more expensive for the public. If a service **isn’t** on this tax-free list, it’s generally taxable under the new rules.

*(Note: “Tax-free” services in Punjab function similarly to “exempt” services – no sales tax is charged. Businesses providing only tax-free services might not need to register for sales tax, although if they are mixed (taxable and tax-free), they must keep records for both【11†L111-L115】. Also, providers of tax-free services typically **cannot claim input tax credits** on their business purchases related to those services, since no output tax is charged – the law explicitly disallows input tax adjustment in such cases【11†L103-L110】.)*

## Revised Tax Rates and Schedules for Taxable Services

Alongside defining tax-free services, the Punjab Finance Act 2025 **revised the tax rate structure** for all the remaining **taxable services**. The Second Schedule of the law, which lists taxable services, has been completely substituted with a new schedule divided into parts (Part I for standard rates, Part II for fixed amounts, Part III for reduced rates)【8†L25-L32】. Here’s what you need to know about the **tax rates** under the new regime:

- **Standard Rate – 16%**: Punjab’s general sales tax rate on services remains **16% of the service value**. If a service doesn’t qualify for some special reduced rate or isn’t tax-free, it will be taxed at **16%** (this is the default rate). For example, many professional services, consultancy, and others not mentioned elsewhere will be at 16%. The law also ensures that if any service somehow gets charged above 16%, that excess isn’t claimable as input tax, effectively cementing 16% as the ceiling for normal services【6†L132-L139】. So, **16% is the standard Punjab Sales Tax rate** for most services (unchanged from before).

- **Higher Rate for Telecom – 19.5%**: **Telecommunication services** – such as mobile phone services, landlines, internet services, etc. – continue to be taxed at a higher rate of **19.5%**【6†L132-L139】. Punjab, like other provinces, traditionally taxes telecom at around 19.5%. So if you recharge your phone or pay a telecom bill, you’ll see around **19.5% Punjab sales tax** on it (same as prior years). This rate covers things like call charges, SMS, data packages, and so on. (The law notes that any tax beyond 19.5% on telecom is not admissible as input credit, reaffirming 19.5% as the set rate【6†L132-L139】.)

- **Reduced Rate for Goods Transport – 15%**: **Transportation of goods by rail or road** now enjoys a slightly **reduced tax rate of 15%** (down from the standard 16%)【6†L132-L139】. So trucking, logistics, or goods train services are taxed at 15% in Punjab. This reduction may help lower the cost of moving goods. For example, if a cargo company transports merchandise within Punjab, the service charge will carry 15% sales tax instead of 16%. (Again, any tax above 15% on such services cannot be claimed as input, to ensure the effective rate stays 15%【6†L134-L138】.)

- **Fixed Amount Taxes (Specific Charges)**: For some services, Punjab has moved to a **fixed-tax scheme** instead of a percentage of value. This is typically for sectors where valuing the service or profit margins is tricky. Two notable cases:
  - **Property Developers and Builders**: Instead of paying 16% on the full price of a construction project (which could be huge), builders/developers are charged a fixed tax based on the area of the project. The new rate is **Rs. 100 per square yard** of land development, and **Rs. 50 per square foot** of building construction【3†L625-L633】. This means if a developer is developing, say, 5000 square yards of land, the sales tax is 5000 × Rs100. This fixed levy simplifies things for the real estate sector and is aimed at standardizing the tax burden on construction.
  - **Freight Forwarders**: Freight forwarding agents (who handle logistics and shipments, often international freight) are now taxed at **Rs. 1,000 per bill of lading**【3†L635-L638】. A bill of lading is a shipping document for a cargo shipment. So regardless of the shipment’s value, each shipment document is taxed a flat 1000 rupees. This is another simplification, likely replacing an ad-valorem (percentage) tax with a fixed fee.

  These fixed rates (in **Part II of Second Schedule**) provide certainty – businesses know exactly how much tax in rupees to pay per unit of activity. It can especially benefit sectors where invoiced values are high but margins vary. Keep in mind, if you’re a consumer, you usually won’t directly see these fixed taxes (they are between the business and government), but they could indirectly factor into prices.

- **Reduced Rates for Certain Services**: The Punjab government has also set **lower tax rates** for some services to encourage particular industries or behaviors. These are in **Part III of the Second Schedule**. Some examples that affect the general public:

  - **Restaurants & Food Outlets**: There is a big incentive for digital payments here. Restaurants, cafés, and other eateries in Punjab will charge only **5% sales tax** (instead of 16%) **if the customer pays through digital means** (credit/debit card, mobile wallet, or QR code)【20†L748-L757】. This is **5% without input tax adjustment** for the restaurant, which essentially means the restaurant can’t claim input credits but gets to charge a low rate. If you pay in **cash**, however, the restaurant is supposed to charge the full **16%** tax. So, next time you dine out, using a card or digital payment could save you – effectively, the bill will have lower tax. This dual rate is designed to push both businesses and consumers toward cashless transactions. *(Note: Many restaurants may choose to advertise prices as “tax included”, but the point-of-sale systems will account for the difference behind the scenes. As a consumer, just know that paying by card in Punjab eateries is rewarded with lower tax on the bill.)*

  - **Hotels and Guest Houses**: To support small hospitality businesses, **small hotels** are taxed at a **reduced rate**. If a hotel, motel, or guest house has **fewer than 20 rooms and is not part of a franchise/chain**, it charges only **5% sales tax (without input credits)** on room rentals【20†L659-L667】【20†L669-L673】. Bigger hotels (20 or more rooms, or those run by companies or chains) continue to charge the standard 16%. So, a small independent guest house gets a tax advantage it can pass on to customers via lower room rates.

  - **Marriage Halls & Catering Services**: Wedding and event services often had special treatment before, and that continues. **Banquet halls, marquees, “pandal and shamiana” (tent services), and catering services** are subject to a **lower tax rate**, generally around **5% without input adjustment** (conditions apply). This means if you rent a marriage hall or hire a caterer in Punjab, the sales tax charged could be only 5% (making your event a bit less expensive tax-wise than it would be at 16%). The exact conditions (such as non-corporate ownership, etc.) are specified in the schedule, but the headline is a reduced rate for these event services.

  - **Personal Care / Salons**: We noted that **very small salons (no air-conditioning)** are completely tax-free. For the rest of the beauty industry (salons, spas, beauty clinics that **do** have air-conditioning and thus aren’t exempt), Punjab now imposes a **low 5% sales tax** (with no input credit) on their services【26†L368-L372】【20†L868-L876】. This is a significant reduction from 16%. For example, a larger salon or spa will add 5% sales tax to your bill for a haircut, makeup, or spa service. This concession aims to support these businesses and perhaps encourage them to register and comply (since 5% is not too burdensome). So consumers might not feel much difference in price, and small roadside barbers or parlors remain completely untaxed.

  - **Insurance Services**: Insurance was touched on in the tax-free list for certain types. For all other insurance, the Second Schedule Part III sets *differentiated rates*. Notably, **health insurance for individuals is 0% (zero-rated)** – meaning if you buy a personal health insurance policy, there’s no sales tax on the premium【20†L706-L714】. **Life insurance** is typically exempt by federal law already, but Punjab is aligning with that by not taxing life or health premiums for individuals. **Insurance agents and brokers** (the people or firms who sell insurance) are taxed at **5%** for their services【20†L711-L719】. Meanwhile, other kinds of insurance (like fire, property, auto insurance, etc., and any insurance services not specifically reduced) are charged at the **standard 16%** of the premium【20†L715-L723】. In short, *individual-centric insurance is favored with low/no tax*, while general insurance services see standard taxation. This is meant to encourage people to get health insurance without an extra tax burden, and to keep the insurance sector broadly taxed fairly.

These are just a few examples; the Second Schedule’s reduced rate section covers other services too (like **franchise fees, information technology services, government construction contracts** at special rates, etc.). But for the general public, the key takeaway is that **some services will now be cheaper tax-wise** – especially if you use digital payments or are dealing with small service providers – and most other taxable services remain at 16%. 

The government can also more easily update these **First or Second Schedules by notification** now【11†L95-L103】 (previously it was only the Second Schedule). So, we might see further tweaks or additions to the tax-free or reduced-rate lists over time, without needing a new Act each time.

## Push for Digital Payments (and Penalties for Non-Compliance)

Another notable aspect of the 2025 amendments is the strong push towards a **digital payment culture**. The government not only offered incentives (like the restaurant tax discount) but also introduced a **strict penalty for businesses that refuse to accept digital payments**.

- **Mandatory Acceptance of Digital Payments**: If you’re a business providing taxable services in Punjab, you are now expected to **offer customers the option to pay via digital means** – whether it’s a debit/credit card, a mobile wallet, or QR code payment. This doesn’t mean you can’t accept cash, but it **does** mean you **cannot refuse** a customer who wants to pay digitally. The law has added a specific penal provision for anyone **“who refuses to accept payments through digital means (debit/credit cards, mobile wallets or QR scanning)”**【18†L201-L209】【18†L217-L225】.

- **Heavy Penalties for Refusal**: The penalty for not complying with the above is quite steep. A business that **refuses to take a digital payment** can face a fine of **up to Rs. 1,000,000 (1 million)**【18†L217-L225】. Furthermore, the law sets minimum fines: **at least Rs. 400,000 for the first offense**, and **Rs. 300,000 for each subsequent offense**【18†L219-L227】. These are very large penalties, underscoring how serious the government is about this. And it doesn’t stop at fines – if a business is caught **three times** refusing digital payments, the authorities can even **seal the business premises for up to one month**【18†L229-L237】【18†L233-L241】. This could mean a temporary shutdown of the shop/office, which is a strong deterrent.

- **Why such strict measures?** The goal is to encourage a **shift to digital transactions**, which are more transparent and easier to track for tax purposes. When customers pay by card or mobile app, the sales record is digitized, making it harder for businesses to hide or under-report sales. It also provides convenience and security for consumers. The Punjab government has been promoting digitization of the economy, and these measures support that policy by effectively mandating modern payment methods.

For consumers, this means you have a right to expect that shops, restaurants, and service providers will accept your card or online payment. If someone insists on “cash only” and has no facility for digital payment, they’re actually violating the Punjab sales tax rules now. Over time, this should lead to more Point-of-Sale machines in stores and more QR codes at small businesses, making payments easier and reducing the need to carry cash.

- **Digital Incentives Recap**: Don’t forget the flip side – the law isn’t just using a stick; it’s also offering carrots. The **5% tax rate for digitally-paid restaurant bills**【20†L748-L757】 is effectively a customer incentive (and a business incentive) to go cashless. Some other service providers (like certain contractors or professionals) also have lower rates if payments are digital (as seen in Part III of the schedule). So, by paying with your card or phone, you might be indirectly contributing to a lower tax scenario for that service, which could translate into future discounts or simply a more compliant economy.

In summary, Punjab’s tax amendments strongly encourage businesses to **“go digital or face penalties.”** This modernizes the tax collection process and aligns with broader trends to document the economy. As a consumer, embracing digital payments not only offers convenience but also supports a system that could reduce costs (via tax incentives) and improve governance.

## FAQ: Punjab Sales Tax 2025 Amendments

**Q1. What is the Punjab Finance Act 2025 and why is it important?**  
**A:** The Punjab Finance Act 2025 is a law passed in June 2025 that brings a number of changes to the Punjab Sales Tax on Services Act, 2012. It’s important because it **overhauls the way services are taxed in Punjab**. Previously, only certain services were taxed; now **almost all services are taxable** unless specifically exempt. It introduces the concept of **“tax-free services”** (a list of services on which no sales tax will be charged)【11†L89-L97】, revises tax rates for various services (some taxes went down, e.g. goods transport to 15%, some stayed the same, e.g. telecom at 19.5%), and it includes measures to promote **digital payments** (including fines for businesses that don’t accept cards or digital payments). These amendments are aimed at increasing the tax net in a fair way and making it easier for the government to collect taxes in a digital economy. For the general public, it means you might see **sales tax being charged on more services** than before, but essential services like healthcare and education remain untaxed.

**Q2. What are “tax-free services” under the new amendments?**  
**A:** *Tax-free services* are the services that the Punjab government has decided **should not have sales tax** on them (to benefit the public or certain sectors). They are listed in the **First Schedule** of the Punjab Sales Tax law【11†L89-L97】. This list includes:
  - **Health services by government institutions** (e.g. treatments in public hospitals, consultation fees of doctors in government hospitals are tax-free).
  - **Educational services** – general education (schools, colleges, universities) and any education in public sector institutions are not taxed.
  - **Public transport** provided by government (like government bus or train services).
  - **Services by charities and non-profits** (registered charitable organizations, certain NGOs and UN agencies) for public benefit.
  - **Certain insurance services** like crop insurance and export-related marine insurance (no sales tax on those premiums).
  - **Affordable housing construction** – services of developers/builders in approved low-cost housing schemes.
  - **Small personal care services** – e.g. a small beauty parlor *without air-conditioning* does not have to charge tax【26†L368-L372】.
  - **Photography by small shops**, **home residential rents**, **religious and cultural services by government**, **Hajj/Umrah travel services**, etc., are also tax-free.
  
  In essence, tax-free services cover essential public services, welfare activities, and small-scale providers. If a service is “tax-free,” you **won’t see Punjab sales tax on its bill**, and the provider doesn’t need to deposit sales tax for it.

**Q3. I run a small salon. Do I need to charge sales tax now?**  
**A:** It depends on the setup of your salon. Under the new rules, **small beauty parlors or salons *without air-conditioning*** are treated as **tax-free services**【26†L368-L372】. That means if your salon **does not have an AC unit installed** (and you don’t use AC at all), you **do not charge any Punjab sales tax** to your customers. This is intended to spare very small businesses from the tax burden. **However, if your salon is air-conditioned**, then it is considered a taxable service – but with a **reduced tax rate of 5%** (with no input tax credit)【20†L868-L876】. So, an AC-equipped salon in Punjab must **register and charge a 5% sales tax** on services (like haircuts, make-up, etc.). This is still a low rate compared to the standard 16%. 

To summarize: if you’re a tiny beauty parlor with no AC, you remain **tax-exempt**. If you have AC (even if you’re a small business), you need to start charging 5% sales tax on your services and comply with filing requirements.

**Q4. Have the sales tax rates on services changed? Will I pay more tax now?**  
**A:** The **standard sales tax rate** on services in Punjab is still **16%**, so for many common services you won’t see a change – you were likely paying 16% before and that continues. However, there are **some changes in specific areas**:
  - **Telecom services** (phone calls, mobile internet, etc.) remain at **19.5%**【6†L132-L139】, so no change on your mobile bills from these amendments.
  - **Goods transport services** are now **15%** (slightly lower than the standard)【6†L132-L139】, which could marginally reduce costs for logistics and might eventually reflect in slightly lower shipping costs for goods.
  - **Restaurants** and certain eateries: If you pay by card or digital means, the tax charged is only **5%** now (previously it was effectively 16% regardless). So dining out *could* become cheaper tax-wise if you use digital payment – a clear change consumers might notice. Cash payments would still be taxed at 16%, so it incentivizes paying by card【20†L748-L757】.
  - **Sectors with fixed taxes**: If you’re engaging services of a property builder or freight forwarder, the way they tax is different now (fixed rupee amounts rather than a percentage). As a consumer, you might not directly see this, but it could lead to more stable pricing. For example, the cost of a construction project might be quoted with a fixed tax amount included, rather than 16% of the unpredictable total cost【3†L625-L633】.
  - **Reduced-rate sectors**: Some services have *lower* tax rates than before. For instance, **wedding halls, catering, gyms, tour operators for pilgrims, certain insurance premiums, small hotels, and salons** have reduced rates (ranging from 0% to 5%). If you use these services, you may notice you’re charged a smaller tax or none at all, compared to 16% in the past. 

Overall, the intention was not to hike rates but to **streamline them**. Many people will see **no change** for things like banking services (still 16%), telecom (19.5%), etc. But **some previously untaxed services might now have a 16% tax**, *and* some previously taxed at 16% might be lower. If you were buying a service that wasn’t in the old taxable list (say, certain consultancy or digital services), that **might now become taxable at 16%** – so in that sense, yes, you *could* pay more on those because earlier you paid 0%. The net effect for the average consumer will vary depending on what services you use. The government has balanced this by exempting basics (so you’re not paying tax on, say, hospital visits or school fees) and reducing rates for some everyday things (like restaurants with digital pay). 

**Q5. What does it mean that “all services are taxable unless exempt”? Can you give examples of services that weren’t taxed before but are now taxed?**  
**A:** This means Punjab’s sales tax is now like a blanket – it covers every service by default, *except* those specifically listed as tax-free. Before 2025, Punjab had a list of taxable services, and if something wasn’t on that list, no sales tax applied. Now, the approach flipped. 

Examples of services that previously might not have been taxed but now would be:
  - **Professional services** like **lawyers, accountants, consultants** (if not already taxed earlier) could now fall under the tax net at 16%. Previously, some of these were not explicitly listed and thus not taxed. Now, unless exempted, they’re taxable.
  - **Private healthcare services**: Visits to private clinics or hospitals were generally not subject to provincial sales tax before. Under the new regime, a **private hospital or clinic** providing, say, general medical services *could now be required to charge 16% sales tax* on its services, because only public sector healthcare was put on the tax-free list. (There may be some nuance here – for instance, lab test services are exempt【3†L431-L439】, and certain medical-related services might still remain untaxed – but broadly, private healthcare isn’t explicitly tax-free now.)
  - **Private education/tuitions**: General education services are tax-free (covering most schooling), but let’s say **specialized training or courses** not under “general education” – those might now be taxable. For example, a private computer training institute or a professional development course might start charging sales tax if it doesn’t qualify under the exempt education category.
  - **Digital and IT services**: Punjab may now tax a range of digital services (unless they come under a reduced rate or federal exemption). For instance, an online advertising service, software development service, ride-hailing service fees, etc., could be taxed. (Punjab had some provisions for IT services at reduced rates in the schedule, but generally the ambiguity of “not listed, not taxed” is gone – if it’s a service and not exempted, it’s taxable).
  - **Personal services** like **fitness training** (gym memberships run by private entities, personal trainers) or **entertainment services** (like private museums, amusement parks) – previously these might not have been clearly taxed. Now, unless they are government-run (government parks, etc., are exempt), private ones would be taxable.

In essence, if you can name a service and it’s not clearly on the tax-free list, assume it’s now subject to Punjab Sales Tax. The government has pretty much closed the gaps so that the tax system is more uniform.

**Q6. I’m a service business owner – what do I need to do to comply with these new rules?**  
**A:** If you’re providing services in Punjab, here are the key things to check post-2025 amendments:
  1. **Determine if your service is tax-free or taxable.** Go through the new First Schedule (tax-free list) and see if your service (or your category) is mentioned there. If it is, and you meet the conditions, you **do not charge Punjab sales tax** to customers. (You should still keep records of those services because the law now explicitly requires maintaining records of tax-free services too【11†L111-L115】.)
  2. **If taxable, note the applicable rate.** Check the Second Schedule to find your service category. Many services are at 16%, but some have a special rate. For example, **a catering business** should note it’s 5% without input tax. **A software/IT service provider** might have a special reduced rate (some IT services have 5% or even 0% for certain sub-categories). **Restaurants** should implement the dual-rate: 5% for digital payments, 16% for cash. **Builders/freight forwarders** need to apply fixed charges, etc. It’s crucial to apply the correct rate – the Punjab Revenue Authority (PRA) might issue guidance on categories. 
  3. **Registration and Invoicing**: If you weren’t registered for sales tax before but now your service is taxable, you must register with PRA and start issuing sales tax invoices charging the appropriate Punjab Sales Tax. The threshold for registration might still apply (small businesses under a certain turnover might be spared), but generally, new categories coming into tax will need to comply.
  4. **Input Tax Credits**: Be aware of the new input tax disallowances. If you’re in a business now charging 5% without input (like a salon or catering service under reduced rate), you **cannot claim input tax credits** on your purchases – your output tax is low, but you bear the input cost. Also, if you somehow paid higher tax on a service you consumed (like you paid 18% on something but Punjab only allows 16%), that extra bit is not claimable【11†L103-L110】. This is technical, but your accountant should know – essentially, don’t claim more input credit than the standard percentages allow.
  5. **Digital Payments Compliance**: Very importantly, **set up a means to accept digital payments**. If you don’t have a card machine or QR code, get one. It’s not just good for business – it’s now legally risky to refuse. Train your staff that they must never say “we don’t take cards” to a customer. The fines are massive【18†L217-L225】. Even if you prefer cash, you should technically have the option available for those who want it.
  6. **Stay Updated**: The PRA and Punjab government may issue detailed rules, especially for how to transition to this new system. Keep an eye on official notifications or reach out to a tax advisor. The law also allows the government to amend schedules easily, so new exemptions or changes might come – for example, they could later add an exemption or change a rate by notification. Being in the loop will help you remain compliant.

In summary, **figure out your category**, **charge the correct tax if applicable**, **update your billing systems**, and **embrace digital payments**. If in doubt, consult PRA’s helpdesk or a professional – the initial period of such sweeping change is when mistakes can happen, but also when authorities might be slightly lenient if you show you’re trying to comply.

**Q7. What if a shop or service provider refuses to accept card payments from me?**  
**A:** The new amendments give you, as a customer, some leverage. If a business in Punjab refuses your credit/debit card or digital payment and insists on cash only (despite you wanting to pay digitally), they are violating the Punjab Sales Tax law. The government can fine them heavily – up to Rs. 1 million, as mentioned earlier – and even shut down their business temporarily after repeated offenses【18†L217-L225】【18†L233-L241】. 

Practically, as a consumer, you could inform the business about the new rule (they might not know yet). If they still refuse, you can report them to the Punjab Revenue Authority. The PRA has helplines and offices; you’d ideally need to provide evidence (e.g., a complaint noting the time and place, maybe a receipt or witness). While minor reporting from one customer might not trigger action immediately, if the PRA finds a pattern or does spot checks and finds no card machine, the business is in trouble. 

The goal, of course, is not to punish businesses for no reason – it’s to encourage them to offer digital payment options. Over time, you should see fewer “Cash Only” signs. If you do run into one, know that the law is on your side. In the meantime, you could choose to carry cash as a backup (some very small vendors might still be catching up with compliance), but the direction is clear: **Punjab wants digital payments to be universally accepted**.

**Q8. When did these changes take effect and are they permanent?**  
**A:** The changes took effect from **July 1, 2025**【1†L41-L48】【1†L63-L70】. That means any services provided **on or after that date** fall under the new rules. The changes are part of an Act, so they are **permanent** unless amended by another Act or an official notification. The government has empowered itself to tweak the schedules (list of taxable/tax-free services) through notifications, so minor adjustments could happen without needing to go back to the Assembly. For instance, if they want to add a service to the tax-free list or change a tax rate, they can likely do that via a notification now. 

Every year during the budget (June), provincial governments often make some tax changes. So, while the broad framework is likely to stay (negative list system, digital payment push, etc.), specific rates or exemptions could evolve. It’s a good idea to stay informed each fiscal year if you’re a business. For the public, any major changes (like if a currently tax-free service becomes taxable or vice versa) would be publicized in the news around budget time. But as of July 2025, the described system is in place going forward.

**Q9. Is there any difference between “exempt services” and these new “tax-free services”?**  
**A:** In everyday language, **“exempt” and “tax-free”** mean the same thing – you don’t pay tax on them. The distinction is mostly legal/technical. Before 2025, the law used the term “exempt services” for services not charged to tax (they were often listed in the Second Schedule as exempt). The new law introduced the term “tax-free services” for the First Schedule entries【6†L151-L160】. Practically, you can consider **exempt services = tax-free services**. 

One possible reason for the new term is that now *all services are taxable unless they are made “tax-free”*. The law even updated Section 31 to mention “exempt or tax free services” together【6†L153-L160】. So you might see both terms. There is no difference to the consumer – if a service is called *tax-free* or *exempt*, no sales tax will be charged on it. To a business, it means that output tax is not charged, and typically input tax cannot be claimed for that service.

Think of “tax-free” as the province’s own list of exemptions. There might still be something considered “exempt” by federal law (for example, the federal government traditionally exempts certain services like life insurance or educational services countrywide). Those would continue to be non-taxable as well. But now Punjab’s law formally categorizes its exemptions as “tax-free services” in the First Schedule. Bottom line: For users of services, you don’t need to worry about the semantic difference – just know whether a service you’re dealing with is subject to tax or not.

**Q10. Why is Punjab doing this – making all these changes in 2025?**  
**A:** The Punjab government’s stated intent is to **“rationalize the structure of sales tax on services”**【1†L41-L48】. In simpler terms, they want to modernize and streamline the tax system for services in a way that’s fair, broad-based, and easier to administer. Here are a few likely reasons:
  - **Broadening the Tax Base**: Punjab (and Pakistan in general) wants to increase its tax revenues without overburdening the existing taxpayers. By moving to a system where all services are taxed by default, the province brings many previously untaxed services into the net【8†L17-L24】. This can increase revenue which can be spent on public services for citizens.
  - **Alignment with Other Regions**: Other provinces like Sindh and KPK have been considering or moving towards this negative list approach【8†L21-L28】. It creates consistency – businesses operating in multiple provinces can follow similar principles. It’s also how many countries tax services (tax everything unless exempt).
  - **Removing Anomalies and Loopholes**: Under the old system, if a service wasn’t listed, it wasn’t taxed – this created opportunities where new services (think of the digital economy, new types of consultancy, etc.) weren’t caught by law and thus paid no tax. It also could lead to misclassification to avoid tax. The new system closes that loophole – if it’s a service and you charge for it, assume it’s taxed unless clearly carved out as free.
  - **Encouraging Digital Economy**: The emphasis on digital payments (with both carrots and sticks) shows the government’s intent to document the economy. Digital payments leave a trail, making it harder to under-report sales, thus improving tax compliance. It also aligns with a broader strategy of modernizing the economy (which has benefits like reducing theft, enhancing convenience, etc.).
  - **Targeted Relief**: The government did **not** simply tax everything at one high rate. They carefully exempted things like health, education, and charitable services – this keeps essential services affordable and supports social causes. They also gave reduced rates to sectors like tourism (hotels, travel agents for pilgrims), food (restaurants), etc., which can stimulate those sectors or at least not hurt them. This targeted approach indicates they’re trying to balance revenue needs with economic growth and public welfare.
  - **Simplification and Clarity**: Having all exemptions in one schedule and taxable services in another, with clear parts for rates, can simplify understanding of the law for businesses. It’s more black-and-white: either your service is in Schedule I (no tax) or Schedule II (taxable, at X rate). This was likely done to make compliance and enforcement easier.

In summary, the Punjab Finance Act 2025’s changes aim to **make the tax system more efficient, fair, and in tune with current economic realities**. It’s a significant reform for Pakistan’s largest province and is generally seen as a move to improve tax collection without imposing “new taxes” in the traditional sense (the provincial finance minister even highlighted that no *new* taxes were introduced in Budget 2025-26, rather the system was revamped). For the public, if this results in better public services funded by a broader tax base – while protecting everyday essentials from tax – then it’s a win-win in the long run.

## Conclusion

The Punjab Finance Act 2025 has brought a **major shake-up** to the sales tax on services landscape in Punjab. To recap the key points in plain terms:
- **All services are now taxable** by default, *except* a well-defined list of **tax-free (exempt) services**. This means the tax net is wider, but it also means a more straightforward system (everything is taxed unless it’s on the “no tax” list)【11†L81-L87】.
- The **tax-free services** include critical areas like public health and education, charity, basic transportation, and other socially important services, so that the general public isn’t taxed on essentials.
- **Most taxable services remain at the standard 16% rate**, with some special cases: telecom at 19.5%, goods transport at 15%, and several reduced or fixed rates for particular sectors. If you’re a consumer, you’ll mostly see the same taxes on common services, but you might notice lower taxes on things like dining out (with digital payments) or hotel stays at small guest houses, etc. Conversely, some services you never paid tax on before might now come with a 16% charge – because the law now covers them.
- The government is **serious about digital payments** – encouraging them through lower tax rates in some cases, and effectively mandating them by penalizing businesses that refuse. This digital push is a step towards a modern, documented economy, and it can benefit consumers with more payment options and possibly better record-keeping (like getting proper receipts everywhere).
- For businesses and service providers, there’s an adjustment period: they need to update billing systems, possibly register for sales tax if they were previously out of scope, adhere to the new rate structure, and ensure compliance with the digital payment acceptance rule. The PRA will likely be active in auditing and guiding during this transition.

Overall, these amendments strive to make the tax system more **transparent, equitable, and efficient**. Punjab is moving with the times – broadening the tax base but not arbitrarily; the changes are calibrated to protect the common citizen’s wallet on necessities while asking for contribution from sectors that can afford it. If implemented well, this could mean a larger revenue pool for the province to spend on development and public services, **without** disproportionately hurting the average person【8†L17-L24】【11†L81-L87】. As with any policy shift, the real impacts will be seen over time, but understanding these changes is the first step for citizens and businesses to adapt and benefit where possible (like availing digital-payment discounts) or comply where required.

Dear Sir, this is the standard message received from FBR, whenever the taxpayer file income tax return. It's just like acknowledgement for filing of income tax return for tax year 2025.

Here’s a more refined version of your text:  

---

Dear Sir, this is the standard acknowledgment message issued by FBR whenever a taxpayer files their income tax return. It simply serves as confirmation that the return for Tax Year 2025 has been successfully filed.  

---  

Would you like me to make it even more formal, suitable for inclusion in correspondence with clients?

Respected Sir/Madam,  

**Subject:** Clarification on advance tax notice (S.236K) for Plot No. 107/1/1, Phase‑VI, DHA, Karachi  

This is with reference to the advance tax collection notice dated April 1, 2024 (under Section 236K of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001) concerning **Plot No. 107/1/1, 4th Street, Phase‑VI, DHA, Karachi**. The notice suggests that a new property was purchased, warranting advance tax of Rs. 1,518,750. We wish to clarify that *no new acquisition* occurred in Tax Year 2024. Mr. Moid Khaliq Malik (CNIC: 42301-5163415-3) has owned the aforesaid property since 1999, and the 2024 transaction was merely the formal **lease registration (Form “B” lease)** after construction completion – not a sale or new purchase of property. We provide the following points with documentary references for your kind consideration:

- **Form “B” Lease is a post-construction requirement, not a sale:** Under the Pakistan Defence Officers’ Housing Authority Order, 1980 (PDHO Order), Article 21(1) mandates that upon completing construction on an allotment, the lessee must obtain a formal “Lease in Form B” from the Authority. The attached *Form B Lease Deed* (dated 2-Apr-2024) is explicitly labeled **“FORM ‘B’ LEASE”**【18†L432-L439】. It identifies “**Mr. MOID KHALIQ MALIK S/O MALIK ABDUL KHALIQ**” as the Lessee of *“House/Plot No. 107/1/1, 4th Street, Phase‑VI, DHA, Karachi”*【18†L450-L454】. The deed records separate Stamp Duty (Rs.365,625) and Advance Tax (Rs.1,518,750) payments【18†L413-L420】, confirming that taxes were assessed on lease registration. In short, this document is a lease instrument – **not a sale deed** – and it reflects only the continuation of Mr. Malik’s existing interest in the property.  

- **Continuity of ownership since 1999 (Form “A” and Form “B”):** The 2024 Form B Lease itself recites that the same plot was initially allotted to Mr. Malik under a *Form “A” Sub-Lease* in 1999. Specifically, it states that by a deed dated 22‑08‑1999 (Form A), the sub-lessee (Mr. Malik) was granted the right to enter upon “Plot of land bearing No. 107/1/1, 4th Street, Phase‑VI (500 sq. yds)” for constructing a building【18†L486-L495】. Thus, the 1999 Form A shows Mr. Malik (S/O Malik Abdul Khaliq) as the sub-lessee of the same plot. The 2024 Form B lease simply implements the agreed Clause 14(1) of the Form A arrangement (i.e. granting a final lease after construction). Both documents refer to **the same Plot 107/1/1** and name Mr. Malik, evidencing that ownership/leasehold has been continuous. In no way did the 2024 transaction create a new asset; it formalized the title on a property he already owned.  

- **Completion Certificate confirms built property:** Enclosed is the official *Completion Certificate* issued by the Clifton Cantonment Board for the bungalow on Plot No. 107/1/1, dated 14‑12‑2005. This certificate certifies that the bungalow on **Plot No. 107/1/1, 4th Street, Phase‑VI, Clifton Cantonment** “has been completed” as of that date【11†L75-L83】. The sanction and completion (2005) of the building are documented, which is precisely why the Form B lease was executed later. This certificate underscores that a fully constructed house existed on the plot (and was legally approved) well before 2024. The issuance of the completion certificate triggered the statutory requirement for the Form B lease, and **does not imply any sale**. In essence, the property was already developed and owned; the formality in 2024 was only to register the completed house.  

- **Declaration in Wealth Statement (Section 116 filing):** Mr. Malik has consistently declared this asset in his tax filings. In his voluntarily-filed *Statement of Assets & Liabilities* under **Section 116** (Income Tax Ordinance, 2001) for Tax Year 2014, he listed “**House No. 107/1/1, 4th Street, Phase‑VI, DHA, Karachi**” under Personal Assets with a value of **Rs. 14,000,000**【12†L108-L112】. The statement (dated 05-Dec-2014) – when he was a resident taxpayer – explicitly includes this property on the ‘Personal Assets/Liabilities’ page at the declared amount【12†L108-L112】. This long-standing declaration confirms that the asset was fully owned and accounted for years prior to 2024. There was no undisclosed addition or purchase in 2024; the property was already on record.  

- **Advance tax relates to lease, not purchase (no Section 111(1) implication):** The advance tax of Rs. 1,518,750 collected under Section 236K was computed on the basis of the lease registration (as per the Form B deed) and not on a sale. As the Form B deed clearly itemizes, this tax is on a lease transaction【18†L413-L420】. Since Mr. Malik did not buy a new property, Section 111(1) (which deals with unexplained assets/income or short‑term capital gains on disposals) is not applicable. No capital gains or unexplained investment has occurred in this case, because the transaction did not constitute disposal of the asset. Therefore, the advance tax paid should be accepted as payment on account of lease formalization, and the notice under S.111(1) should be withdrawn with respect to this matter.  

**Conclusion:** In summary, all documents show *continuity of title* and clarify that the 2024 transaction was a lease formalization only. The *Form A* (1999) and *Form B* (2024) deeds together confirm Mr. Malik as the long-standing lessee of the same plot【18†L486-L495】【18†L450-L454】. The Completion Certificate proves the building was long completed【11†L75-L83】. The wealth statement confirms the property was already declared and valued at Rs. 14,000,000【12†L108-L112】. We therefore request that FBR treat the advance tax as correctly paid for lease registration, and clarify that Section 111(1) is not triggered in this case. We trust this explanation and the enclosed evidence will resolve any misunderstanding. 

We remain at your disposal for any further clarification.  

Yours faithfully,  

**Moid Khaliq Malik**  
CNIC: 42301-5163415-3  
House No. 107/1/1, 4th Street, Phase‑VI, DHA, Karachi  
(Date)  

**Enclosures:** Form A Sub-Lease (22‑08‑1999); Form B Lease Deed (02‑04‑2024); Completion Certificate (Clifton Cantt, 14‑12‑2005); Wealth Statement (S.116, Tax Year 2014)【11†L75-L83】【12†L108-L112】.

Amendments to Punjab Sales Tax on Services Act (2012) – Punjab Finance Act 2025 
Introduction
In Punjab (Pakistan), the provincial government has introduced major changes to how services are taxed. These changes came through the Punjab Finance Act 2025, which amends the Punjab Sales Tax on Services Act, 2012. Effective July 1, 2025, the amendments aim to simplify and broaden the sales tax regime on services. In simple terms, the law now taxes all services by default (a shift to a ‘negative list’ system) and provides a specific list of ‘tax-free services’ that will not be taxed. It also revises certain tax rates and imposes new rules to encourage digital payments (with penalties for non-compliance).
This blog post breaks down the key changes in simple language, covering new definitions, which services are tax-free, what the updated tax rates are, the digital payment requirements, and other important tweaks. We’ll also answer frequently asked questions to help you understand what the Punjab Sales Tax 2025 amendments mean for you.
All Services Taxable by Default (New 'Negative List' System)
One of the biggest changes is a shift from a ‘positive list’ to a ‘negative list’ taxation model. Under the old system, only services specifically listed in the law were subject to sales tax (a positive list). Now, all services are considered taxable unless they are explicitly mentioned as not taxable. In legal terms, ‘all services…will be treated as taxable services’ except those categorized as tax-free or otherwise exempt. This effectively broadens the tax base, many services that were previously not taxed will now fall under the tax net unless they appear on the exempt list.
To enable this change, the definition of ‘service’ in the law was updated (Section 2(38) of the 2012 Act) to include services covered in the new First and Second Schedules. The charging section (Section 3) was also amended to reflect that all services provided in Punjab are taxable by default. In short, Punjab has moved to a universal taxation of services with a specific exclusion list, a system similar to what other provinces like Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa have adopted.
For consumers and businesses, this means you should expect sales tax on any service you purchase, unless it’s one of the specially exempted tax-free services described below. The idea is to make the system more comprehensive and fair, by not leaving out entire sectors from taxation, while still protecting certain essential services from tax.
Introduction of Tax-Free Services in Punjab
With everything taxable by default, the government has created a new category of ‘tax-free services’ services that will not be charged any Punjab sales tax. A new Section 3A was inserted into the law to define tax-free services, and an entirely new First Schedule now lists all these exempt services. If a service is listed in this First Schedule (and meets any condition specified), it is not subject to Punjab sales tax.
What services are tax-free? The list is quite comprehensive, covering many essential and public-interest services. Here are some of the key categories of services that remain tax-free in Punjab under the 2025 amendments:
•	Public Healthcare and Education: Services in government healthcare facilities for example, consultation or visit fees of doctors and specialists, hospital bed/room charges in public sector hospitals are not taxed. Similarly, educational services are exempt: this includes general education (schools, colleges, universities) and any education provided by public sector institutions. (Private schools and colleges offering general education are also covered under ‘general education services,’ so they remain tax-free as well.)

•	Public Transport and Government Services: Public transport services provided by the government (such as government-run bus or train services) are tax-free. In addition, certain fees and services provided by government departments are not taxed, for instance, passport issuance, national ID card services, or other registration services by federal/provincial/local governments have no sales tax. Basic postal and courier services by government (e.g. Pakistan Post) are exempt when provided to government bodies.

•	Charitable and Non-Profit Services: Services provided by charitable organizations or non-profits are generally exempt. If a service is provided by a registered charity or a religious institution for public benefit, or by certain approved international NGOs or international agencies, it is tax-free (as long as any applicable federal tax exemptions also apply). This ensures genuine non-profit activities aren’t burdened by provincial tax.

•	Affordable Housing and Construction: To promote housing development, services by property developers and builders can be tax-free, but only for affordable housing projects. For example, construction services under government-sponsored low-cost housing schemes (notified by the Punjab Housing & Town-Planning Agency) are exempt from tax. Additionally, there are exemptions for certain construction projects: small residential construction (houses below a certain size), projects funded by foreign grants, or cases where a builder is already paying tax under another category, these specific scenarios are carved out as tax-free to avoid double taxation and encourage development.

•	Insurance and Financial Services: Most insurance services are taxable (as we’ll note later), but the law continues to exempt a couple of important insurance categories: marine insurance for export goods and crop insurance for farmers are both tax-free. These are crucial for exporters and the agriculture sector. Moreover, services by foreign exchange dealers or money changers are exempt from Punjab sales tax (financial exchange services are not taxed in the province).

•	Personal Care & Others: Small businesses providing personal care services get relief. Small beauty parlors or salons without air-conditioning are exempt from tax – they fall under tax-free services. (By contrast, larger, air-conditioned salons have to charge tax, but at a low rate, which we’ll explain shortly.) Similarly, photography services by small independent photographers are exempt – for example, a lone photographer or a tiny photo studio (as declared by the authority) doesn’t charge sales tax. Home rentals are also protected: renting out a personal dwelling for residential use is tax-free, so if you rent a house/apartment to someone to live in, that rental income is not hit by sales tax.

•	Religious, Cultural, and Recreational Services: Services related to the general public’s welfare provided by the government are exempt. This includes things like entry fees or services at museums, libraries, parks, zoos, sports facilities, or cultural centers run by government, no sales tax on those. Also, services related to religion are exempt; for instance, charges for participation in religious events or facilities provided by the government or a religious institution for the public would be tax-free. Furthermore, diplomatic missions’ services (anything provided by foreign embassies/consulates) are exempt by nature.

•	Hajj, Umrah, and Pilgrimage Services: In recognition of religious travel, the law exempts certain travel services. Tour operators and travel agents do not charge sales tax on packages or services for Hajj and Umrah pilgrims (and Ziyarat). Likewise, any air travel services (like airline tickets) for Hajj or Umrah passengers are tax-free, as are services for diplomats and certain aviation crew. This means pilgrims from Punjab heading for Hajj or Umrah will not pay provincial sales tax on those specific travel arrangements.
The above are highlights the First Schedule (tax-free list) actually contains over 25 categories of services with various conditions. But the common thread is that these are either essential services, public services, or socially important activities. By keeping them tax-free, the government is ensuring it doesn’t make critical services more expensive for the public. If a service isn’t on this tax-free list, it’s generally taxable under the new rules.
Revised Tax Rates and Schedules for Taxable Services
Alongside defining tax-free services, the Punjab Finance Act 2025 revised the tax rate structure for all the remaining taxable services. The Second Schedule of the law, which lists taxable services, has been completely substituted with a new schedule divided into parts (Part I for standard rates, Part II for fixed amounts, Part III for reduced rates). Here’s what you need to know about the tax rates under the new regime:
•	Standard Rate – 16%: Punjab’s general sales tax rate on services remains 16% of the service value. If a service doesn’t qualify for some special reduced rate or isn’t tax-free, it will be taxed at 16% (this is the default rate). For example, many professional services, consultancy, and others not mentioned elsewhere will be at 16%. The law also ensures that if any service somehow gets charged above 16%, that excess isn’t claimable as input tax, effectively cementing 16% as the ceiling for normal services. So, 16% is the standard Punjab Sales Tax rate for most services (unchanged from before).

•	Higher Rate for Telecom – 19.5%: Telecommunication services, such as mobile phone services, landlines, internet services, etc. continue to be taxed at a higher rate of 19.5%. Punjab, like other provinces, traditionally taxes telecom at around 19.5%. So if you recharge your phone or pay a telecom bill, you’ll see around 19.5% Punjab sales tax on it (same as prior years). This rate covers things like call charges, SMS, data packages, and so on. (The law notes that any tax beyond 19.5% on telecom is not admissible as input credit, reaffirming 19.5% as the set rate.)

•	Reduced Rate for Goods Transport – 15%: Transportation of goods by rail or road now enjoys a slightly reduced tax rate of 15% (down from the standard 16%). So trucking, logistics, or goods train services are taxed at 15% in Punjab. This reduction may help lower the cost of moving goods. For example, if a cargo company transports merchandise within Punjab, the service charge will carry 15% sales tax instead of 16%. (Again, any tax above 15% on such services cannot be claimed as input, to ensure the effective rate stays 15%.)

•	Fixed Amount Taxes (Specific Charges): For some services, Punjab has moved to a fixed-tax scheme instead of a percentage of value. This is typically for sectors where valuing the service or profit margins is tricky. Two notable cases:

•	Property Developers and Builders: Instead of paying 16% on the full price of a construction project (which could be huge), builders/developers are charged a fixed tax based on the area of the project. The new rate is Rs. 100 per square yard of land development, and Rs. 50 per square foot of building construction. This means if a developer is developing, say, 5000 square yards of land, the sales tax is 5000 × Rs100. This fixed levy simplifies things for the real estate sector and is aimed at standardizing the tax burden on construction.

•	Freight Forwarders: Freight forwarding agents (who handle logistics and shipments, often international freight) are now taxed at Rs. 1,000 per bill of lading. A bill of lading is a shipping document for a cargo shipment. So regardless of the shipment’s value, each shipment document is taxed a flat 1000 rupees. This is another simplification, likely replacing an ad-valorem (percentage) tax with a fixed fee.

We refer to your query regarding whether interest is required to be charged on every temporary withdrawal made by an employee from an approved provident fund.  

Under the Income Tax Rules, 2002:  

- **Rule 103** provides the framework for approved provident funds, including the conditions under which temporary withdrawals or advances may be granted to employees. The trustees are under a statutory obligation to charge interest at the minimum rate prescribed, and failure to comply could jeopardize the approved status of the provident fund under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

**Subject:** Clarification on Interest Requirement for Temporary Withdrawals from Provident Fund  

Dear [Client’s Name],  

We refer to your query regarding whether interest is required to be collected on every temporary withdrawal made by employees from a recognized provident fund.  

For clarity, under the **Income Tax Rules, 2002**:  

- **Rule 103 (Permitted Withdrawals)** specifies the circumstances under which employees may withdraw from their accumulated balance in a recognized provident fund. These include medical treatment, education, marriage, purchase or repair of a house, life insurance premiums, purchase of shares, repayment of loans, or other specified needs. Certain withdrawals—such as those for house purchase, life insurance, or leave preparatory to retirement—are expressly permitted without the need to be repaid.  

- **Rule 106 (Repayment of Amounts Withdrawn)** draws a distinction between withdrawals that are non-repayable and those that are repayable with profit. Specifically:  
  - Withdrawals allowed under Rule 103(1)(aa), (f), (h), (i), (j), or (k) **need not be repaid**.  
  - Withdrawals allowed for **any other purposes** (such as illness, marriage, funeral expenses, overseas passage, or purchase of a motorcycle/scooter) are **treated as loans**. These must be repaid in up to 48 monthly installments and carry profit (interest) at the rate prescribed under the Rules. The interest is calculated either as additional installments or, at the trustees’ discretion, at a rate 1% above the profit credited to fund balances.  

In summary, **not all withdrawals require collection of interest**. Only those temporary withdrawals categorized as repayable under Rule 106(2) (i.e., purposes other than those listed as non-repayable) must bear interest. Withdrawals under the specific exempt categories in Rule 106(1) are not subject to repayment or interest.  

Accordingly, your provident fund trustees should carefully classify each withdrawal request under Rule 103 and then apply Rule 106 to determine whether repayment with interest is mandatory.

**Subject:** Clarification on Interest for Temporary Withdrawals from Provident Fund  

Dear [Client’s Name],  

We refer to your query regarding whether interest must be charged on all temporary withdrawals made by employees from a recognized provident fund.  

Under the **Income Tax Rules, 2002**, Rule 103 allows employees to withdraw from their provident fund balance in certain circumstances, such as illness, education, marriage, Haj, purchase or construction of a house, life insurance premiums, or retirement-related needs. Rule 106 then sets out whether these withdrawals must be repaid and whether they attract interest (profit). In essence, the law draws a distinction between two categories: (i) withdrawals that are repayable loans and must carry interest, and (ii) withdrawals that are not repayable and do not require interest.  

To make this distinction clearer, please see the following guide:  

---

### **Reference Guide: Provident Fund Withdrawals & Interest Requirement**

| **Purpose of Withdrawal (Rule 103)** | **Repayment Required?** | **Interest/Profit Required?** |
|--------------------------------------|-------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Illness of employee or family | Yes | Yes – repayable with profit in installments |
| Transfer to approved pension fund | No | No |
| Purchase of motorcycle/scooter | Yes | Yes – repayable with profit in installments |
| Overseas passage (health/education) | Yes | Yes – repayable with profit in installments |
| Marriage/funeral/ceremonies | Yes | Yes – repayable with profit in installments |
| Haj expenses | Yes | Yes – repayable with profit in installments |
| Purchase/building of house or site | No | No |
| Repairs/renovation of house | No | No |
| Life insurance premium | No | No |
| Purchase of public company shares | No | No |
| Age 50+ withdrawals (house/agri land/loan repayment/other) | No | No |
| Leave preparatory to retirement | No | No |

---

On the other hand, withdrawals made for house purchase or repairs, life insurance, purchase of shares, benefits available after the age of fifty, or leave preparatory to retirement **do not require repayment or interest**.  

Accordingly, not all withdrawals require interest—only those classified as repayable loans under Rule 106 fall within this requirement. This distinction should be carefully observed by the trustees of the provident fund to ensure compliance.

Here’s a formal draft response for you, grounded in the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** and FBR’s framework on Active/Inactive taxpayers:  

---

**Subject:** Opinion on Withholding of Income Tax on Rental Payments to Inactive Landlord  

Dear Mr. Ahmed,  

Thank you for your email. We have reviewed the matter in light of the provisions of the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** and the notifications issued thereunder regarding withholding tax compliance in respect of payments to persons appearing as *Inactive* on the Active Taxpayers’ List (ATL).  

### Legal Position  
1. **Deduction of Tax at Source**  
   - Under **section 155 of the Ordinance**, rental income is subject to deduction of income tax at source by the tenant.  
   - The rate of deduction is prescribed under **Division V of Part III of the First Schedule**.  

2. **Inactive Persons – Double Rate**  
   - Pursuant to **section 100BA read with Tenth Schedule to the Ordinance**, where the payee is not appearing on the ATL and remains classified as *Inactive* on the FBR portal, the rate of tax deduction is required to be **increased by 100% (i.e., doubled)**.  
   - This requirement is automatic, statutory, and binding on the withholding agent; it applies for as long as the payee’s name is not on the ATL.  

3. **No Refund or Reimbursement by Withholding Agent**  
   - Once deducted and deposited into the Government Treasury, the tax so withheld constitutes payment on behalf of the landlord (the recipient of rental income).  
   - The withholding agent (your company) has no legal authority under the Ordinance to reimburse or adjust such amount to the landlord.  
   - Any claim for refund or adjustment can only be made by the landlord through their income tax return filed under **section 114 read with section 170 of the Ordinance**.  

4. **Change of Status from Inactive to Active**

Based on the **Sales Tax Act, 1990** and the **Sales Tax Rules, 2006**, here’s the position for a pharmaceutical retailer:

---

### 1. General Registration Requirement under Section 14
Section 14 of the Sales Tax Act requires every person engaged in making **taxable supplies in Pakistan** to be registered if they fall into specific categories. This includes:
- **Retailers who are liable to pay sales tax under the Act or rules** (excluding those covered by electricity bill–based collection under section 3(9))【15:0†Sales Tax Act,1990 updated by Finance Act, 2024 upto 30.06.2024.pdf†L11-L19】.

So, if a pharmaceutical retailer is making taxable supplies and not paying through the electricity-bill mechanism, registration is mandatory.

---

### 2. Taxability of Pharmaceutical Products
Pharmaceutical products (drugs/medicaments) fall under Chapter 30 of the Customs Tariff.  
- Certain **raw materials for pharmaceuticals** are taxable at reduced or special rates (e.g., 1%) and **zero-rating provisions** exist for some medicines【15:5†Sales Tax Act,1990 updated by Finance Act, 2024 upto 30.06.2024.pdf†L1-L12】.  
- However, **zero-rating does not eliminate the requirement of registration**; it only affects the output tax. Registered persons still must file returns to claim input adjustment or refunds.

---

### 3. Special Provisions for Pharmaceutical Sector
The **Sales Tax Rules (Chapter V-B)** specifically address the **refund mechanism for the pharmaceutical sector**. These apply to registered persons engaged in import or supply of zero-rated drugs/medicaments【15:8†Sales Tax Rules 2006 Updated upto 31-10-2023.pdf†L48-L57】.  
This indicates that FBR expects pharmaceutical suppliers/retailers dealing in zero-rated goods to be registered in order to process refunds or input tax adjustments.

---

### 4. Compulsory Registration Rules
Rule 6 of the Sales Tax Rules empowers the Commissioner to compulsorily register any person who is liable but has not applied voluntarily【15:2†Sales Tax Rules 2006 Updated upto 31-10-2023.pdf†L41-L61】.  
That means if a pharmaceutical retailer is liable under section 14 but unregistered, the department can enforce registration.

---

### **Conclusion**
A **pharmaceutical retailer must obtain sales tax registration** if:
- They are making **taxable supplies** (not just exempt ones),  
- They do not fall under the electricity-bill-based collection regime, and  
- They wish to avail **input tax credits or refunds** under the pharmaceutical refund mechanism.

Relevant provisions:
- **Section 14(1)(b) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990** – mandatory registration of retailers.  
- **Chapter V-B of Sales Tax Rules, 2006** – refund regime for registered pharmaceutical suppliers.  
- **Rule 6 of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006** – compulsory registration powers.

---

This creates a clear compliance obligation: even if many medicines are zero-rated or exempt, pharmaceutical retailers generally must **register under sales tax** to comply with law and secure input/refund benefits.

I’ve gone through the relevant part of **SRO 144(I)/2025**. The clause you highlighted is in paragraph **(q)**, which reads:

> “the value of commercial built up excluding ground floor shall be reduced by 25%”【9†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.

### What this means
When valuing **commercial built-up property** (for example, shops, offices, plazas), the **ground floor** is considered the most valuable portion because it has direct access, visibility, and higher commercial utility. Upper floors usually have less commercial demand.  

So, under this clause:
- The **ground floor** of a commercial building is valued at the full prescribed rate.
- The **floors above the ground floor** (first floor, second floor, and so on) are each given a **25% reduction** in the valuation compared to the ground floor rate.

### Example
Suppose the notified valuation rate is **Rs. 10,000 per sq. ft** for commercial built-up property in a given area:
- Ground floor: Rs. 10,000 per sq. ft (no reduction).
- First floor (and above): Rs. 7,500 per sq. ft (25% reduction).

### Practical implication
This reduction affects:
1. **Computation of fair market value** under section 68 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.
2. Consequently, it impacts **capital gains tax, withholding taxes on property transfers, and stamp duty valuation** where FBR’s valuation tables are applied.

This clause basically acknowledges the economic reality that upper floors in commercial property don’t fetch the same value as the ground floor.

### Explanation in overall context  
This SRO was issued under section 68 of the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, which empowers FBR to notify **fair market values of immovable properties** for tax purposes (e.g., capital gains tax, advance tax on purchase/sale, withholding, etc.).  

The notification provides **valuation rules and adjustments** for different types of property—residential, commercial, industrial, flats, plots, high-rises, basements, etc. These adjustments reflect market realities: for instance, older buildings are given depreciation-based reductions, basements are valued lower, and DHA commercial plots facing main roads are valued higher.  

Within this framework, **Clause (q)** recognizes that **upper floors in commercial buildings (above the ground floor)** generally have **less commercial value** than the ground floor, due to reduced visibility, footfall, and accessibility.  

- **Ground floor** → valued at full notified rate.  
- **Upper floors** → valued at 25% less than the ground floor rate.  

### Overall takeaway  
Clause (q) is part of a set of valuation adjustments meant to bring FBR’s property valuation tables closer to **actual market practices**, ensuring fairer tax computations for different types and portions of property.

### Explanation in context  
This SRO was issued by FBR under **section 68 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** to notify property valuation rates for tax purposes. These notified rates are used to determine the “fair market value” of immovable property, which directly affects calculation of **capital gains tax**, **advance tax on purchase/sale of property**, and **stamp duty assessments**.  

Clause (q) specifically deals with **commercial built-up properties** (like shops, offices, plazas). It recognizes that **upper floors** of such properties usually have less commercial value compared to the **ground floor**, which enjoys premium location and accessibility. Therefore:  
- Ground floor: valued at **100% of notified rate**.  
- All upper floors: valued at **25% lower** than ground floor rate (i.e. taken at 75% of the notified rate).  

### Overall purpose  
This adjustment ensures a **more realistic valuation** of commercial buildings for taxation, preventing overvaluation of upper floors that typically sell or rent for less than the ground floor.
