# Understanding Your New 2025 Tax Rules (Individuals)

**Pakistan’s Federal Finance Act, 2025** (enacted June 2025, effective July 1, 2025) introduced **major changes for individual taxpayers** (salaried and non‑salaried). The headline: **lower rates** for most salaried earners, new tax credits, and tighter compliance. In plain English, here’s what changed and how it affects you. 

- **New Tax Slabs for Salaried Individuals:** The income thresholds (brackets) remain the same (Rs. 600,000 tax-free, then 6 segments up to Rs. 4.1 million+), but the **rates have dropped sharply** in the lower and middle brackets. For example, previously a person earning Rs. 1.2 million paid 5% on income above Rs. 600k (about Rs. 30,000 tax); now they pay just **1% on income above Rs. 600k** (only Rs. 6,000)【20†L1078-L1085】. Similarly, the next slabs (Rs. 1.2m–2.2m and Rs. 2.2m–3.2m) saw their base tax and rates fall (see **Table below**). In practical terms, a mid‑level salaried earner can now save **tens of thousands of rupees** in tax each year. (A graphic example: someone on Rs. 4 million annual salary paid ~Rs. 670k tax before; under the new rules they pay ~Rs. 586k【20†L1078-L1085】 – saving ~Rs. 84k.) These new rates are summarized from official tax schedules【20†L1078-L1085】.  

- **Tax Slabs for Non‑Salaried Individuals (Business/Other Income):** If **≤75%** of your income is salary, you fall under the “non‑salaried” (business/AOP) rates. The **basic brackets remain unchanged** (0% up to Rs. 600k, then 15%, 20%, 30%, 40%, 45% in higher brackets)【34†L1825-L1833】【34†L1843-L1852】. The key change is the **surcharge**: high‑income non‑salaried taxpayers now pay a 9% surcharge on their income tax if total income exceeds Rs. 10 million (down from 10% before)【34†L1854-L1858】【27†L386-L388】. (Professional “AOP” firms still have 40% top rate instead of 45% in the highest bracket.) 

- **Salaried vs. Non‑Salaried Test:** It often confuses taxpayers: if **more than 75%** of your income is from salary, you use the *salaried* slabs; otherwise use the *non-salaried/AOP* slabs. In either case, consult your tax adviser to pick the correct table.

**Before vs. After:** The table below illustrates the drop in **annual tax liability** under the new 2025‑26 slabs for some common salary levels:

| Annual Salary (Rs.)  | Old Tax (2024‑25) | New Tax (2025‑26) | Saving |
|----------------------|-------------------|-------------------|--------|
| 600,000 (exempt)     | 0                 | 0                 | –      |
| 1,200,000           | 30,000            | 6,000             | –24,000 (80% reduction) |
| 2,000,000           | 150,000           | 94,000            | –56,000 (37%) |
| 3,000,000           | 380,000           | 300,000           | –80,000 (21%) |
| 4,000,000           | 670,000           | 586,000           | –84,000 (13%) |
| 6,000,000           | 1,365,000         | 1,281,000         | –84,000 (6%) |

*(Tax figures from official sources【20†L1078-L1085】.)* These illustrate **progressive relief** – the largest *percentage* cuts are for low‑middle incomes.

## Key Changes in Brief

- **Basic Exemption Unchanged:** The first Rs. 600,000 of annual income is still tax‑free. 
- **Lower Rates:** For salaries above Rs. 600k, the rates were slashed. E.g., 600k–1.2m is now 1% (was 5%), and 1.2m–2.2m slab is 11% after a small base (was 15% after a bigger base)【20†L1078-L1085】. 
- **Top Tax Rate:** The top rate (35% above Rs. 4.1m) remains the same for salaried incomes. 
- **Surcharge for High Earners:** If your income exceeds Rs. 10m, you pay an extra **9% surcharge** on your income tax【27†L386-L388】【34†L1854-L1858】 (down from 10% before). For example, someone with Rs. 20m salary will pay 9% of their tax bill as surcharge. 
- **Non-Salaried Surcharge:** All individuals and AOPs (business owners) also face 9% surcharge on income tax above 10m【34†L1854-L1858】 (again, from 10%).
- **Advance and Withholding Taxes:** **Advance tax on buying property** has been **cut**, benefiting real‑estate buyers【27†L392-L394】. By contrast, **withholding tax on bank interest** has increased from 15% to **20%**【27†L394-L396】 (to boost revenue on passive income). Also, **cash withdrawals over Rs. 50,000** by non‑filers now carry 0.8% tax (up from 0.6%)【27†L406-L408】.
- **Definitions of Filers:** The Finance Act drops the old “filer/non-filer” language. Now FBR calls people **“eligible”** or **“ineligible”** taxpayers. If you’re not on the Active Taxpayers List (ATL) by June 30, 2025, you become an *ineligible person*. Ineligibility means **severe restrictions** on major transactions – you cannot buy property or vehicles, open business bank accounts, register companies, or bid on government contracts unless you file your return【16†L69-L77】【27†L396-L399】. In short: **file on time** to stay “eligible.”

## New Deductions and Credits

Several **tax breaks** have been introduced or restored:

- **Home Loan Interest Credit:** A long‑awaited **credit for housing loan interest** is back. If you take a loan from a bank (or specified financial institution) to *buy or build* your first home (land up to 2,500 sq. ft. or a flat up to 2,000 sq. ft.), you can claim a credit on the interest (“profit”) you pay. The credit is capped at the lesser of actual interest paid or **30% of your taxable income**【45†L606-L614】. This effectively reduces your tax if you service a home loan for modest housing. (Each person can use this credit only once in a lifetime, and not again for 15 years.) 

- **Teachers and Researchers:** The **25% tax rebate** for full-time teachers and researchers was reinstated retroactively (for July 2022–June 2025)【45†L623-L627】. In practice, qualified teachers must claim this rebate in their returns to reduce their tax by a quarter (subject to rules). 

- **Senior Citizens and Pensioners:** Under the new law, **pension income** is taxed specially【54†L19-L23】. Pension from a former employer is **0%** (tax‑free) up to Rs. 10 million per year; above that, only **5%** is charged on the excess【54†L19-L23】【59†L119-L126】. (In other words, lump-sum or large pension payouts are lightly taxed.)  Notably, **pensioners aged 70+ are fully exempt**: they owe *no income tax* on pension income, even above Rs.10m【59†L119-L126】.  (One should still report it, but the tax is nil.) Note: If you continue working for the same employer, your pension payments are treated as regular salary and taxed normally. Also, any *commuted pension* (lump-sum retirement payment) and other pension fund income remain exempt as before【54†L19-L23】.

- **Other Rebates:** The old 50% tax reduction for citizens over 60 (on income up to a ceiling) remains intact. And the special relief on dividend income (from mutual funds/REITs) under clause 37A continues for FY2025.  

## Illustrative Example

Consider **Ahmed**, a schoolteacher earning Rs. 1,800,000 per year (Rs. 150,000 per month). Under FY2024-25 rules he would pay:  
- 0% on the first 600k  
- 5% on the next 600k = 30,000  
- 15% on the next 600k = 90,000  
**Total tax:** ~Rs. 120,000.  

Under FY2025-26 rates:  
- 0% on first 600k,  
- 1% on next 600k = Rs. 6,000,  
- 11% on remaining 600k = Rs. 66,000 (plus base 6,000).  
**Total tax:** ~Rs. 72,000.  

Ahmed saves **Rs. 48,000** in tax – a 40% cut. (We cite the official rate formulas from KPMG: 1% and 11%【20†L1078-L1085】.)  

## Filing and Compliance Tips

- **File on Time (June 30 Deadline):** To benefit from these changes and avoid penalties, file your tax return by **June 30, 2026** (for tax year 2025). Even if your tax burden is lower, filing is mandatory if you have taxable income.  
- **Stay on the ATL:** Ensure your NTN is on the FBR’s Active Taxpayers List. Falling off (i.e. becoming “ineligible”) brings **problems**: banks will be notified to flag your large transactions, you may face higher withholding taxes on banking, utilities, and property deals, and you could be blocked from buying vehicles or registering businesses【16†L69-L77】【27†L396-L399】. Simply filing by June 30 each year preserves your “eligible” status.  
- **Check Payroll Withholding:** Employers will adjust your salary withholding to the new slabs. It’s wise to check your payslip: for example, if you earn between Rs. 600k and 1.2m annually, your monthly withholding rate should be very low (1% of income above Rs. 50k, not the old 5%). If in doubt, use a salary tax calculator or ask HR to ensure they apply the new table.  
- **Claim New Credits:** If you took a home loan, gather your bank interest statements and claim the home‑loan credit. Similarly, if you qualify as a full-time teacher/researcher, claim your 25% rebate on the tax return (even though it’s retrospective through June 2025)【45†L623-L627】.  
- **Recordkeeping:** Keep careful records (bank statements, rent receipts, etc.) as usual. The government is integrating CNIC/NTN data, so ensure all major transactions (car purchase, property sale, high-value bank payments) are documented with tax IDs. 

## Common Concerns

- **“My income is X, how will this affect me?”** In general, **low‑ and middle-income salaried taxpayers get big breaks**. Salaries up to ~Rs. 4.1m see substantially lower tax than before. High earners still pay more tax overall, but only moderately more than last year (and now face 9% surcharge instead of 10%). Non‑salaried taxpayers see little change in base rates, except the slight surcharge cut. Use the new rate tables【20†L1078-L1085】【34†L1825-L1833】 to recalc your tax or consult a tax professional for your exact situation.

- **“Do I still need to file if my tax dropped?”** **Yes.** Even if your computed tax is now small, filing is mandatory for all earning above the exemption threshold. The only exceptions are incomes fully covered by final taxes (like certain capital gains or interest already taxed at source). Filing also keeps you on the good side of FBR and qualified for ATL benefits.

- **“What about allowances and deductions?”** Basic allowances (like zakat-deductible income, charitable donations, etc.) generally follow the old rules. The Finance Act did **not** cap or remove common deductions for individuals. Just apply the usual deductions first, then calculate tax on the remainder using the new slabs.

- **“Will my tax refund/change?”** If you have tax deducted at source (e.g. via your salary), the lower rates may mean you overpaid under old tables. When you file, you might get a refund. Conversely, if you were under-deducted, you’ll owe the new (lower) tax.

## Sources and Further Reading

All figures above come from official Finance Act 2025 summaries and reputable tax analyses. For details, see the FBR and professional tax firm releases: KPMG’s Finance Act brief shows the new salary tax table【20†L1078-L1085】, and PwC explains major points for individuals【27†L386-L394】【27†L400-L404】. FBR’s circular (Aug 2025) and income‑tax ordinances list the exact wording. Our summary simplifies these changes; always refer to official tables or a tax advisor for precise calculations. 

Overall, **the 2025 budget is designed to give relief to the salaried class** while broadening compliance. By understanding the new brackets and credits (and filing dutifully), individual taxpayers can take advantage of these changes and avoid pitfalls. 

**Citations:** Official rate comparisons and notes from Finance Act 2025 reviews【20†L1078-L1085】【34†L1825-L1833】【27†L386-L394】【45†L606-L614】【54†L19-L23】【16†L69-L77】 (see sources for full context).

# Tax Changes for Individuals in Pakistan’s Finance Act 2025

The Federal Finance Act 2025 (enacted June 2025) brought several important amendments to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – especially for **individual taxpayers** (both salaried and non-salaried). Key changes include **revised tax slabs and rates**, updated **surcharges**, new **tax credits**, and taxes on **digital/e-commerce transactions**. This blog explains these changes in plain English, with examples and tables to help individuals understand their 2025–26 tax obligations. It also offers practical tips on tax planning, filing advice, and answers common FAQs for salaried and non-salaried filers.

## Income Tax Rates & Slabs (FY 2025–26)

The **tax brackets for salaried individuals** have been adjusted to reduce the tax burden on middle-income earners. Under the new law, **income up to Rs. 600,000 per year remains tax-free** (0%), and the remaining slabs are lower than before. The updated tax schedule (for income `> 75%` from salary) is:

- **Up to Rs. 600,000**: **0%** tax (no tax).  
- **Rs. 600,001 – 1,200,000**: **1%** of the amount exceeding Rs. 600,000.  
- **Rs. 1,200,001 – 2,200,000**: **Rs. 6,000** plus **11%** of the amount above Rs. 1,200,000.  
- **Rs. 2,200,001 – 3,200,000**: **Rs. 116,000** plus **23%** of the amount above Rs. 2,200,000.  
- **Rs. 3,200,001 – 4,100,000**: **Rs. 346,000** plus **30%** of the amount above Rs. 3,200,000.  
- **Above Rs. 4,100,000**: **Rs. 616,000** plus **35%** of the amount above Rs. 4,100,000.

These new rates (effective 1 July 2025) replace last year’s table. For comparison, the old 2024–25 rates were higher in each bracket (for example, 5% instead of 1% in the 600k–1.2M range). The table below summarizes the change:

| Taxable Income (PKR)           | Rate FY2025–26       | Rate FY2024–25       |
|:------------------------------:|:---------------------|:---------------------|
| **0 – 600,000**                | 0%                   | 0%                   |
| 600,001 – 1,200,000            | 1% of excess         | 5% of excess         |
| 1,200,001 – 2,200,000          | Rs. 6,000 + 11%      | Rs. 30,000 + 15%     |
| 2,200,001 – 3,200,000          | Rs. 116,000 + 23%    | Rs. 180,000 + 25%    |
| 3,200,001 – 4,100,000          | Rs. 346,000 + 30%    | Rs. 430,000 + 30%    |
| **4,100,001 and above**        | Rs. 616,000 + 35%    | Rs. 700,000 + 35%    |

【41†embed_image】 *Visual example: A typical taxpayer calculating income tax.  Under the new Finance Act, those earning Rs. 1.5 million yearly would pay **Rs. 39,000** in tax, versus **Rs. 75,000** under the old rates (a saving of Rs. 36,000). Similarly, a person earning Rs. 10 million would pay Rs. 2.681 million instead of Rs. 2.765 million, saving about Rs. 84,000.【65†L305-L314】*

In short, the 2025–26 slabs **lower the tax rates** for most brackets, reducing taxes due for middle-income groups【65†L305-L314】. In particular, only 1% tax applies on income over 600,000 (down from 5%), and other brackets saw similar cuts. **Salaried taxpayers** now benefit from substantially lower tax in each income group【65†L305-L314】. Importantly, the **tax-free threshold remains Rs. 600,000** per year, so up to that amount no tax is owed【65†L305-L314】.

For **non-salaried individuals (including self-employed and AOPs)**, the tax rates are unchanged by this Act and remain higher. Their schedule still starts at 0% for up to Rs. 600,000, but the next slab jumps to 15% (up from 11%), etc. **Additionally, non-salaried taxpayers** with income over Rs. 10 million face a **10% surcharge** on their tax【16†L412-L413】 (unchanged). By contrast, as explained below, **salaried taxpayers’ surcharge is now 9%**.

## Surcharges on High Incomes

The **surcharge** is an extra tax on top of the normal tax for very high incomes (above Rs. 10 million). Under Finance Act 2024, both salaried and other individuals had a 10% surcharge on tax if their income exceeded Rs. 10 million. In FY2025–26, the government **reduced the surcharge for salaried individuals**:

- **Salaried persons (income > Rs. 10M)**: **9%** surcharge on the calculated tax【3†L3420-L3428】 (down from 10%).  
- **Non-salaried persons/AOPs (income > Rs. 10M)**: **10%** surcharge (unchanged)【16†L412-L413】.

For example, a salaried taxpayer with a Rs. 15M income, whose normal tax (from the slabs above) is Rs. 4 million, would pay an additional 9% of Rs. 4M = Rs. 360,000. In contrast, a businessperson with the same income still pays a 10% surcharge (Rs. 400,000).  

In summary: **Only salaried individuals get a slight break (9% rate) on surcharge**, while other individuals remain at 10%【3†L3420-L3428】【16†L412-L413】. The threshold (Rs. 10 million) has not changed. 

## Pension Income Rules

One notable change affects pension income from a former employer. Under previous law, a citizen’s pension from a Pakistani employer was completely exempt. The Finance Act 2025 **removes that full exemption** but still gives favorable treatment for most pensioners:

- **Pension up to Rs. 10,000,000 per year**: **0% tax**. In other words, pensions **≤10M are tax-free** (0%).  
- **Pension above Rs. 10,000,000**: **5% tax on the excess** (only on amount over 10M)【7†L5089-L5098】.  
- **Senior exemption**: A person aged **70 years or above pays no tax on pension at all**, regardless of amount【3†L3488-L3490】.  
- **Working retirees**: If an employee continues to work for the pension-paying organization, pension is taxed as normal salary (not at the special rates).

These rules mean that most pension income is still tax-free or lightly taxed. For example, a 68-year-old receiving Rs. 12M pension yearly would pay 5% on Rs. 2M (Rs. 100,000 tax)【7†L5089-L5098】. A 72-year-old in the same situation would owe **zero tax** on that pension【3†L3488-L3490】. 

The law codifies these rates under a proviso to the First Schedule and a new sub-section in the Ordinance【7†L5089-L5098】【3†L3488-L3490】. In practice, pensioners should ensure their payroll or tax withholding reflects these new thresholds. 

## New Tax Credits & Deductions

**1. Housing Loan Interest Credit:** A brand-new tax credit (Section 63A) is available for home-loan interest paid by individuals. If you take a loan to build or buy a **“low-cost” house**, you can offset your tax by the interest paid. Key points【4†L3631-L3639】【4†L3675-L3683】:

- Applies only to loans for a **house (land ≤ 2,500 sq. ft.) or apartment (≤ 2,000 sq. ft.)**. 
- You claim a credit each year equal to **(Interest Paid ÷ 12) × (Taxable Income ÷ Taxable Income)**, effectively **up to 30% of your taxable income**. 
- You can get this credit **only once per family** (spouse or owner is family head), and **cannot claim again for 15 years** after first use【4†L3689-L3692】. 
- You **cannot double-dip**: if you already deducted that interest elsewhere (e.g. under Section 15A), you cannot claim it again as this credit【4†L3685-L3692】.

This is a generous credit – for example, if your taxable income is Rs. 1,000,000 and you paid Rs. 200,000 interest on a qualifying house loan, your credit would be up to Rs. 300,000 (30% of 1,000,000). In most cases the credit is capped by the actual interest amount, effectively **covering all or most of the interest**. To claim it, keep records of loan payments and ensure your tax return includes the new credit form. 

Aside from this, **most existing deductions (e.g. donations, medical, education, etc.) remain the same** as before. No major new exemptions were introduced for ordinary individuals. As always, be sure to claim any deductible expenses and charitable donations that you are eligible for under the law.

## Digital Economy & Final Taxes

The Finance Act 2025 targets the **digital economy** by introducing final taxes on e-commerce transactions delivered from Pakistan. A new section (6A) sets a final tax on payments received through online marketplaces or platforms. The rates【11†L156-L163】 are:

- **1%** of gross receipts for payments made via digital/banking channels (e.g. credit cards, online wallets) on e-commerce sales.  
- **2%** of gross receipts for sales on a “cash on delivery” basis via courier.  

This means if you sell goods online from within Pakistan (even as an individual), the platform or payment intermediary will withhold 1% of each digital payment (2% for COD orders) as a final tax【11†L156-L163】. These taxes **do not apply to exports** (payments treated as export of goods/services under Sections 154/154A are exempt)【11†L160-L164】. Banks and courier companies have been authorized to withhold these amounts at source.

In practice, individual sellers on local online marketplaces or those offering digital services will see a small 1–2% tax withheld on their sales. This is separate from income tax – it’s a final tax, meaning it satisfies your tax liability on that sale. Keep records of these withholdings (a withholding certificate) to avoid double taxation when you file your return.

## Advance Tax and Compliance

Beyond rates, a few compliance-related changes affect individuals:

- **Higher Tax on Cash Withdrawals:** Non-filers (inactive taxpayers) now face an **advance tax of 0.8%** on any bank cash withdrawal exceeding Rs. 50,000 per day (previously 0.6%)【67†L7-L14】. In other words, if you are not in the tax net and withdraw large cash amounts, a higher advance tax will be deducted. Filers are not subject to this.  
- **Exemption Certificate (Property Sales):** A new provision allows exemption certificates for advance tax on sale of *long-held* residential property. (If your home has been for personal use 15+ years, you may apply to avoid upfront tax collection.) Check FBR rules on Section 236C for details.
- **Mutuality and Clubs:** The Act clarifies that income of clubs/associations from members is now taxable (closing a loophole). Relevant only if you run such an organization.

## Tax Planning Tips & Filing Advice

**Plan early:** With the new slabs and credits in place, individuals should update their withholding and estimates. For salaried workers, the low tax rates mean **monthly tax deductions (FBR’s PAYE)** should be recalculated from July 1, 2025. Use updated tables or an online calculator to avoid shortfall or excess.

**Claim credits:** If you have a home loan on a qualifying property, **claim the housing interest credit**. Provide bank loan statements when filing. Also continue to claim any existing rebates (e.g. for life insurance, pension fund contributions, disabled persons, etc.) that apply.

**Maintain records:** Keep evidence of all deductions, salary slips, banking transactions, and receipts. This will make filing easier and justify claims if FBR questions them.

**File on time:** The deadline for filing returns (typically September 30) and paying any balance tax should be noted. Late filers may face penalties. Even if tax is withheld at source, still file an annual return to be compliant and, if applicable, to get a refund of overpaid tax.

**Digital transactions:** If you earn by selling online, expect a 1–2% withholding. Report that income in your return but deduct it as final tax (no additional tax on that portion). For any large cash transactions (withdrawals, real estate deals, vehicle purchases), ensure you are a tax filer to avoid extra advance taxes under rules like Section 114C and 231AB.

**Stay informed:** Follow FBR updates (they often issue circulars) and consult a tax professional if unsure. Changes like the ones above can interact in complex ways (e.g. splitting income between salary and business, or eligible vs. ineligible transactions). 

【53†embed_image】 *Filing tip: Use online e-filing portals or official FBR forms to file your return before the deadline. Consult official sources or tax advisors for the latest forms and procedures. The image above illustrates the concept of preparing your tax return documentation.*

By staying organized and aware of the new rules, most individual taxpayers can take advantage of lower rates and credits, while avoiding pitfalls like under-withholding or missing deductions.

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

**Q: What are the new income tax slabs for salaried individuals?**  
A: The Finance Act 2025 restructured the brackets. Income up to **Rs. 600,000** is tax-free (0%). Then 600,001–1,200,000 is taxed at **1%** of the excess; 1,200,001–2,200,000 at 11% (plus Rs. 6,000); 2,200,001–3,200,000 at 23% (plus Rs. 116,000); 3,200,001–4,100,000 at 30% (plus Rs. 346,000); and above 4,100,000 at 35% (plus Rs. 616,000)【65†L305-L314】. These rates are significantly lower than last year’s in each bracket.

**Q: How does this compare to last year?**  
A: For example, last year’s rates on 600,001–1.2M were 5% (now 1%), and on 1.2–2.2M were 15% (now 11%)【65†L305-L314】. In every bracket the new tax is lower. Salaried taxpayers will therefore see a reduction in tax due for any given income. 

**Q: Is the tax-free threshold still Rs. 600,000?**  
A: Yes. The **income up to Rs. 600,000 per year remains completely exempt**【65†L305-L314】. In monthly terms, about Rs. 50,000 per month is tax-free.

**Q: What about non-salaried taxpayers?**  
A: The new slabs above apply only to income which is predominantly from salary. Non-salaried individuals (business/profession/AOP incomes) still use the previous schedule: after 0–600k at 0%, the next slab was 15% for 600k–1.2M, etc. Importantly, **non-salaried taxpayers with income over Rs. 10 million still pay a 10% surcharge on their tax**【16†L412-L413】 (unchanged). 

**Q: How has the surcharge changed?**  
A: Previously there was a 10% surcharge on tax for incomes above Rs. 10 million (for both salaried and others). Now, **salaried individuals pay 9%** surcharge (down from 10%) on their tax if income exceeds Rs. 10M【3†L3420-L3428】. Non-salaried persons remain at **10%** surcharge for income above Rs. 10M【16†L412-L413】. So high-earning professionals and businesses see no change, but high-earning employees get a slightly lower surcharge rate.

**Q: How is pension income taxed now?**  
A: Pension from a former employer is mostly tax-free. **Up to Rs. 10 million of pension income is taxed at 0%**. Above Rs. 10 million, only **5%** is charged on the excess【7†L5089-L5098】. Additionally, if you are **age 70 or above**, you pay **no tax on pension at all**【3†L3488-L3490】. For example, a 75-year-old getting Rs. 15M pension would owe **zero tax** (vs. 5% on Rs. 5M if under 70). 

**Q: What new credits or deductions can I use?**  
A: The big new benefit is a **housing loan interest credit (Section 63A)**. If you have taken a loan to buy or build a house (house land ≤2,500 sq ft or flat ≤2,000 sq ft), you get a tax credit for the interest paid. The credit works out to up to 30% of your taxable income【4†L3631-L3639】【4†L3675-L3683】. In practice it often covers all the interest. You can claim this once per family (spouse) and not again for 15 years【4†L3689-L3692】. Other usual deductions (charity, medical, education, etc.) remain the same as before.

**Q: How are online/e-commerce earnings taxed?**  
A: New final taxes apply to goods/services sold online through Pakistani platforms. If you receive payment digitally (bank transfer, credit card, etc.), **1%** of the gross amount is deducted as tax【11†L156-L163】. If you sell on COD (cash on delivery), **2%** is deducted【11†L156-L163】. This tax is final (you don’t owe additional tax on that sale). Export sales are excluded from this 1–2% levy【11†L160-L164】. 

**Q: What about advance taxes or other collection issues?**  
A: A few points: Non-filers now face an **0.8% advance tax on large cash withdrawals** (above Rs. 50,000/day)【67†L7-L14】 (up from 0.6%). Also, for very long-held residential property, you can apply for an exemption certificate to avoid upfront tax on sale (if you’ve lived there 15+ years). In general, ensure your employer and banks have your correct tax status to avoid over-withholding.

**Q: Any tips for filing my return?**  
A: Yes – **file online** via FBR’s portal or authorized e-return systems before the deadline. Use the new tax tables when filling salary details so the computation is correct. Claim all eligible credits (especially the new home loan credit if applicable). Keep receipts and bank statements handy. If you took a home loan or had any final taxes withheld (e.g. on e-commerce sales), upload those as proof. If uncertain, consult FBR’s circulars or a tax advisor. Being proactive will help you get any refund due or avoid penalties for underpayment.

**Q: Where can I learn more?**  
A: Refer to the FBR’s official Income Tax Circulars and the amended **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** (First Schedule tables) for full details. Reliable guides include tax firms’ briefs (like KPMG or PwC tax summaries) and government notifications. The key is to match your income sources to the right section of the law – “salary” vs. “other” – and apply the correct rates and credits we’ve summarized above.

By understanding these changes and planning accordingly, individual taxpayers can meet their obligations and even save tax where possible under the Finance Act 2025.

# Finance Act 2025 – Key Income Tax Changes for Individuals

The Federal Finance Act, 2025 has introduced significant amendments to the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**. These changes are particularly important for **salaried persons, non-salaried individuals, business owners, and non-resident Pakistanis**. Below is a breakdown of the most relevant updates.

---

## 1. Tax Brackets for Salaried and Non-Salaried Persons
The **basic income tax brackets for individuals** remain broadly unchanged:
- **0%** on annual income up to Rs. 600,000  
- Progressive rates of **15%, 20%, 30%, 40%, and 45%** apply to higher income slabs.  

However, a new **income-based surcharge** has been introduced for **non-salaried individuals** (business/AOP category).  
- If **75% or less** of your total income is salary, you fall under non-salaried rates.  
- High-income individuals in this category will now face a **9% surcharge** on the calculated income tax.  

This move is intended to bridge the gap between salaried and non-salaried tax burdens, as businesses are often perceived to have more flexibility in tax planning.

---

## 2. Advance Tax on Cash Transactions
To discourage cash dealings and encourage digital payments:
- **Section 21(s)** has been tightened further. Any expenditure paid in cash exceeding **Rs. 200,000** will be **disallowed as a deductible expense**.  
- Individuals running businesses must ensure payments are made through banking channels to claim them for tax purposes.  

For salaried persons, this doesn’t directly affect salary income, but it impacts those engaged in side businesses or partnerships.

---

## 3. Digital Economy and E-Commerce Tax
A brand-new **Section 6A** has been inserted to tax the digital economy:
- Income earned from **digital platforms, e-commerce, online marketplaces, and digital services** is now explicitly brought into the tax net.  
- Pakistani residents earning from platforms like YouTube, freelance sites, or app-based income will be liable to tax.  
- For non-resident digital service providers, withholding obligations are placed on Pakistani payment intermediaries and couriers.  

This ensures that the **rapidly growing online economy** contributes fairly to the tax base.

---

## 4. Surcharge on High-Income Individuals
The **income-based surcharge under Section 4AB** has been rationalized:
- For **Tax Year 2026**, the surcharge has been **reduced to 9%** (previously higher in earlier proposals).  
- It applies only on income exceeding the notified high-income thresholds.  

This amendment is expected to relieve some pressure on professionals and business owners who were heavily burdened in prior years.

---

## 5. Housing Loan Tax Credit
A **new tax credit under Section 63A** has been introduced:
- Individuals availing **housing finance loans** can now claim a **credit against tax payable**.  
- This is designed to encourage home ownership by lowering effective tax burdens for those repaying mortgage installments.  
- Conditions and maximum limits of the credit will be notified by FBR.  

This is a welcome relief for middle-income salaried individuals.

---

## 6. Eligible vs. Ineligible Persons for Filing Returns
The Act has further defined **Section 114C**:
- Certain individuals (termed **ineligible persons**) may be **restricted from filing simplified returns** and must instead file complete tax returns with full documentation.  
- This is aimed at enhancing compliance from persons earning from multiple sources.  

---

## 7. Withholding Tax Changes Relevant to Individuals
Several adjustments have been made in withholding tax provisions:
- **Imports (Section 148):** Updated classifications mean individuals importing goods for personal/business use may face different withholding rates.  
- **Property Transactions (Section 236C):** Rules for non-resident Pakistanis using **Foreign Currency Value Accounts (FCVA) or NRVA accounts** have been clarified to ensure final tax treatment applies only where conditions are fully met.  
- **Profit on Debt & Dividends (Sections 151 & 150):** Rates have been slightly revised upward for higher slabs of investment income.  

---

## 8. Section 7E – Tax on Immovable Property
The **controversial deemed income tax on immovable property (Section 7E)** remains intact but with **further clarifications**:  
- Certain exemptions have been extended (e.g., agricultural land, self-occupied residential property).  
- Compliance is expected to be stricter with enhanced property data integration.  

---

# Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

**Q1: Do salaried individuals face any increase in basic tax rates?**  
No. The basic salaried tax slabs remain unchanged. The main change is the continuation of surcharge on higher-income non-salaried individuals.

**Q2: What is the difference between salaried and non-salaried classification?**  
If more than **75% of your income comes from salary**, you are treated as salaried. Otherwise, you are classified under non-salaried (business/AOP) rates, which may attract the new surcharge.

**Q3: Does the new housing loan credit apply to existing mortgages?**  
Yes, individuals already paying housing loans through recognized banks can claim the credit from Tax Year 2026, subject to limits.

**Q4: How does Section 21(s) affect individuals?**  
Business individuals cannot claim deductions for cash expenses exceeding Rs. 200,000. For salaried persons with no business income, this does not apply.

**Q5: Are freelancers and YouTubers required to file tax returns now?**  
Yes. Under **Section 6A**, digital and e-commerce income is taxable in Pakistan. Residents must declare such income in their returns.

**Q6: What about property tax under Section 7E?**  
Individuals owning immovable property above thresholds may still face deemed income tax, unless exempt (e.g., self-residence, agriculture land).

**Q7: What is the new surcharge rate?**  
The surcharge under **Section 4AB** has been rationalized to **9%** for high-income individuals.

---

# Conclusion
The **Finance Act 2025** reflects the government’s push toward **broadening the tax base, discouraging cash dealings, and formalizing the digital economy**. For individuals, the key takeaways are:  
- **No change in basic slabs** for salary income.  
- **9% surcharge** for high-income non-salaried taxpayers.  
- **New housing loan credit** under Section 63A.  
- **Stricter rules** on property income and cash transactions.  
- **Digital economy income (Section 6A)** now fully taxable.  

Staying compliant under these changes will not only avoid penalties but also help in making informed financial decisions for Tax Year 2026 and beyond.

# Federal Finance Act 2025: Income Tax Changes for Individuals

The 2025 Finance Act made several changes to Pakistan’s Income Tax Ordinance (2001) that affect individual taxpayers.  In plain language, here’s what you need to know about new tax rates and key rule changes for salaried persons, business individuals, and associations of persons (AOPs) not registered as firms.

## New Income Tax Rates for Individuals

- **Salaried individuals:** The tax slabs for salary earners have been revised slightly upward in the middle and upper ranges.  The **basic exemption remains Rs.600,000**, but the rates above that are lower than before.  Under the new schedule (for tax year 2025–26): 0% up to Rs.600k; 1% on income over Rs.600k up to 1.2m; Rs.6,000 + 11% on income over 1.2m up to 2.2m; Rs.116,000 + 23% on income over 2.2m up to 3.2m; Rs.346,000 + 30% on income over 3.2m up to 4.1m; and Rs.616,000 + 35% on income over Rs.4.1m【20†L1074-L1082】【22†L1101-L1108】.  For example, someone earning Rs.3.2m now pays Rs.346,000 in tax instead of Rs.430,000 – a reduction of Rs.84,000【22†L1114-L1118】. 

- **Non-salaried individuals and AOPs:** Business income (and income of any AOP such as a partnership) follows a different schedule.  The new rates for **all other individuals/AOPs** are: 0% up to Rs.600k; 15% on income over Rs.600k up to 1.2m; Rs.90,000 + 20% on income over 1.2m up to 1.6m; Rs.170,000 + 30% on income over 1.6m up to 3.2m; Rs.650,000 + 40% on income over 3.2m up to 5.6m; and Rs.1,610,000 + 45% on income over Rs.5.6m【25†L1824-L1832】【25†L1843-L1851】.  (Certain professional AOPs pay 40% instead of 45% on the top bracket.) 

- **Reduced Surcharge for high-income salaried people:**  Previously a 10% surcharge applied to *all* taxpayers (including salaried) with taxable income over Rs.10 million.  The Finance Act 2025 **cuts this to 9% for salaried persons** (others still pay 9% as before)【24†L132-L140】.  In effect, the maximum marginal rate for a high-earning salaried person is now slightly lower (38.15% instead of 38.5%)【35†L98-L104】.

- **Pensioners:**  A new provision taxes pension income from a former employer at 0% if the *annual pension* is up to Rs.10 million, and 5% on the amount above Rs.10m【22†L1118-L1124】【64†L165-L170】.  (This applies for pension payments made in 2025–26 to retirees under age 70. Deductions for already withheld tax and certain credits can be adjusted as well.)

- **Cash withdrawal tax:**  Banks now withhold **0.8%** (up from 0.6%) on cash withdrawals over Rs.50,000 in a single day【20†L1070-L1073】.  This applies at the banking level on large withdrawals.

## Other Tax Changes Affecting Individuals

- **Bank interest and investment income:**  The tax on “profit on debt” (bank deposit interest, etc.) is now **20% for interest from banks/financial institutions** and 15% for other cases【64†L134-L142】.  For non-corporate taxpayers (individuals, partnerships, etc.), this is a final tax on interest up to Rs.5m per year.  (E.g. interest on your savings account is now taxed at 20% at source.) 

- **Dividend income from mutual funds:**  Dividend rates are adjusted: tax is 15% if the fund’s income is mostly equity, or 25% if it is mostly debt【64†L147-L154】.  (This aligns the tax with the underlying fund income mix.)

- **Housing loan tax credit (new Section 63A):**  Individuals taking a loan for a *first home* can get a new tax credit on the interest (profit on debt) they pay.  The home must be a *single* house (≤ 2,500 sq ft) or flat (≤ 2,000 sq ft), financed by a bank or approved institution.  You can claim a credit equal to your average tax rate on the interest paid (up to 30% of your taxable income)【41†L294-L303】【41†L308-L313】.  (This credit cannot be reused on another house for 15 years.) This encourages buying homes and effectively lowers the cost of mortgage interest for qualifying loans.

- **Wealth statements and declarations:**  If you plan large purchases or investments, the new rules emphasize declaring the source of funds.  Taxpayers should file annual wealth statements or a “Sources of Investment and Expenditure” statement on the FBR portal to validate big transactions【65†L167-L175】【65†L182-L189】.  Having **“sufficient resources”** declared (130% of the transaction value, in cash and equivalents) is key to being considered an *eligible person* for big deals【65†L167-L175】【65†L182-L189】.

## New Rules for Big Transactions (Eligible vs. Ineligible Persons)

A major change is **Section 114C**, which creates *eligible* and *ineligible* persons.  Only eligible persons can carry out certain large financial transactions without extra hurdles【65†L185-L189】【64†L242-L259】. In simple terms:

- An **eligible person** (including immediate family members of an individual) is someone who *filed a tax return for the last year and has 130%+ of the transaction’s value in declared assets* (cash, gold, stocks, etc.)【65†L167-L175】【65†L182-L189】.  Alternatively, one who filed the online sources statement showing sufficient funds also qualifies.
- An **ineligible person** is anyone not meeting these criteria【65†L185-L189】.

**Restrictions on ineligible persons:** If you are ineligible, you **cannot**:
  - Buy or register a motor vehicle costing over **Rs.7 million**【65†L185-L189】.
  - Buy or transfer immovable property with market value over **Rs.100 million**【65†L185-L189】.
  - Invest in securities/mutual funds costing over **Rs.50 million** in a year (with conditions)【65†L185-L189】.
  - Withdraw cash above **Rs.100 million** per year from your bank accounts【65†L194-L198】.

*(For example, a person without filed returns would be blocked from registering a car over Rs.7m or buying a house above Rs.100m until they become eligible.)* These provisions are intended to expand the tax net and reward those who file returns.  (Transactions by public companies or non-residents are exempt from most of these limits, except cash withdrawals.) 

## Other Notable Procedural Changes

- **Active Taxpayer List (ATL) concept:**  The old “filer vs non-filer” labels have been replaced. Now taxpayers are either *eligible* or *ineligible*, as above.  Remaining on the ATL by timely filing each year means you stay eligible and avoid higher withholdings【65†L182-L189】【64†L242-L259】.
- **Withholding on property transactions:**  Advance tax on property sale/purchase varies by ATL/eligible status.  For **eligible/ATL taxpayers**, tax on buying property is 1.5–2.5% (depending on price) and on selling is 4.5–5.5%【58†L5256-L5264】【62†L5037-L5044】.  For **ineligible/non-ATL persons**, purchase tax jumps to 10.5–18.5% and sale tax is 11.5% flat (for any price)【58†L5260-L5269】【62†L5037-L5044】.  (Late filers pay intermediate rates.)  Thus, if you stop filing, buying/selling real estate becomes much more expensive【58†L5260-L5269】【62†L5037-L5044】.
- **Extended audit timelines:**  The time for the tax authorities to complete amended assessments after issuing a show-cause notice has been extended from 180 days to **1 year**【1†L453-L463】, giving taxpayers a bit more breathing room in disputes.
- **E-notices:**  The law clarifies that service of notices/orders by electronic means counts as valid for *all taxpayers (persons)* except resident individuals【29†L42-L45】.  (So check your online accounts!)
- **Digital transactions:**  A final withholding tax of 1% is imposed on payments via digital channels (e.g. e-commerce) and 2% on cash-on-delivery sales【24†L147-L154】.  This mainly affects online sellers and platform users, but salaried individuals won’t see this unless they sell goods online.
- **Biometric verification (sales tax filers):**  Although not an Income Tax change, note that sales-tax filers must verify their biometrics by July 31 each year or face complications【13†L125-L133】.  

## FAQ: What Does This Mean for You? 

**Q1: How much will my salary tax go up?**  If you earn above Rs.600,000, your tax will generally *decrease*, because the new middle rates are lower. For example, a Rs.3m salary taxpayer now pays Rs.346,000 instead of Rs.430,000【22†L1114-L1118】. Check with a calculator or your payroll department to update monthly deductions to the new slabs.  

**Q2: I’m self-employed/business individual – what changed?**  The tax on non-salary income is unchanged in structure (0–45% rates) but you pay a **9% surcharge** if income >Rs.10m【24†L132-L140】.  Surcharge for business/AOP remains 9%. Make sure to file your returns on time to stay “eligible” and avoid higher withholding rates on your expenses and transactions.

**Q3: What is this “eligible person” rule, and how could it affect me?**  It means if you want to, say, register a car over Rs.7m or buy a house over Rs.100m, you must be an *eligible person* – i.e. have filed last year’s tax return and have ample declared resources.  Otherwise, your application will be blocked【65†L185-L189】.  **Tax planning tip:** Stay eligible by filing timely and honestly declaring your income or sources; this keeps your ATL status and avoids new curbs on big purchases.

**Q4: Are there new ways to save on tax?**  Yes.  Most notably, the new Section 63A lets you **claim credit for home loan interest** on one personal residence【41†L294-L303】. If you take a mortgage or loan (from a bank/approved source) for a qualifying house/flat, you get a credit on the interest up to 30% of your income.  Also, keep filing returns to benefit from lower withholding rates and avoid the “late filer” surcharge on transactions.

**Q5: How are pensions taxed now?**  Pension income up to Rs.10 million per year remains **tax-free**.  If you get more than Rs.10m in a year, tax is 5% on the excess【22†L1118-L1124】.  The payer (NIT or bank) will deduct this at source when you receive your pension.

**Q6: What about interest on my savings?**  Interest (profit on debt) from banks is now taxed at 20%, and other interest at 15%【64†L134-L142】.  This is usually final tax, so plan your deposits accordingly. (If you also have business income, remember these taxes and any credit from Section 63A when filing.)

**Q7: I haven’t been filing returns. What will happen?**  If you skipped filing, you will now be treated as “ineligible.” That means *very high* withholding on things like property, vehicles, etc. For instance, a non-filer pays 10.5–18.5% tax when buying property and 11.5% when selling, versus only ~2–5.5% if you had filed【58†L5260-L5269】【62†L5037-L5044】. To avoid this, it’s best to file your past returns, get on the ATL, and declare your assets.

**Q8: Any general tips under the new law?**  Yes – **file on time and keep records**.  Because so many benefits hinge on being an “eligible” filer, make sure to submit your tax return by the deadline.  Keep copies of wealth statements or bank statements for large transactions.  If you earn dividends or rental income, consider paying any due tax voluntarily to stay compliant.  And if you’re planning a big purchase (house, car, securities), check that you meet the asset thresholds or plan the timing (e.g. save/invest extra to bolster your declared wealth) before you buy.

**Sources:**  The above is based on the Income Tax Ordinance as amended by Finance Act 2025, FBR circulars, and expert tax analyses【20†L1074-L1082】【22†L1118-L1124】【25†L1824-L1832】【65†L185-L192】【64†L134-L142】, which explain the new rates and rules. (All figures and citations are to official/reputable tax commentary on the 2025 amendments.)

# Personal Income Tax Changes in Finance Act 2025

The Federal Finance Act 2025 (effective July 1, 2025) made several direct changes affecting individual taxpayers (salaried and non-salaried) under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.  This post highlights those changes – **tax slabs, surcharges, exemptions, deductions, and procedural rules** – comparing each to last year’s rules.  Citations to official summaries and analyses are provided for every change so readers can verify details【42†L1074-L1083】【30†L1097-L1105】.

## Revised Tax Rates for Salaried Individuals

The **annual income tax slabs for salaried persons** have been reduced in most brackets (the exempt limit of PKR600,000 remains unchanged).  Under the new law, the first PKR600,000 of taxable salary is still tax-free, but rates above that have been cut.  For example, the second bracket was lowered from 5% to 1%, and the third bracket from 15% to 11%【42†L1074-L1083】【30†L1097-L1105】.  In effect, a taxpayer with PKR1,200,000 taxable income pays only PKR6,000 (new law) instead of PKR30,000 (old law), an 80% reduction【30†L1113-L1117】.  Even at higher incomes the savings are notable: someone with PKR3,200,000 tax base now pays PKR346,000 vs PKR430,000 previously (20% less)【30†L1113-L1117】.  (The full comparison table appears in official analyses【42†L1074-L1083】【30†L1097-L1105】.)

> **Q:** *How does my tax change for a given salary?*  
> **A:** Under the new slabs, income up to Rs.600,000 remains untaxed【42†L1078-L1081】.  For example, a taxable salary of Rs.1,200,000 now incurs Rs.6,000 tax (at 1%), whereas last year it was Rs.30,000 (at 5%)【42†L1078-L1083】【30†L1113-L1117】. Similarly, income between Rs.2.2m–3.2m is taxed at 23% (plus a fixed Rs.116,000), down from 25% (with Rs.180,000).  In short, most middle-income brackets see lighter rates and lower tax bills.

### Surcharge for High Incomes

Finance Act 2024 had introduced a **10% surcharge** on income tax for salaried individuals with taxable income above Rs.10 million.  Finance Act 2025 reduces this surcharge to **9%** for such taxpayers【11†L132-L142】.  In other words, if you earned over Rs.10m last year you paid tax plus a 10% extra; now that extra is 9%.  (For comparison, no change was made to surcharge on non-salaried income this year.)

> **Q:** *I earn over Rs.10 million. What surcharge do I pay?*  
> **A:** Under the new law, only a 9% surcharge applies on top of your normal tax (for salaried income)【11†L132-L142】.  Last year it was 10%.  For example, if your calculated tax was Rs.1,000,000, the surcharge is now Rs.90,000 instead of Rs.100,000.

## Pension and Retirement Income

**Pensions from Former Employers** are now partially taxable.  Previously most old-age pensions were exempt; Finance Act 2025 makes them subject to a “final tax” at low rates【13†L27-L36】.  Specifically, the pension income up to Rs.10 million is taxed at **0%**, and only the excess is taxed at **5%**【30†L1120-L1128】.  (Importantly, **commuted pension** – the one-time lump sum – remains fully exempt【13†L29-L36】.)  

> **Q:** *If I receive an annual pension of Rs.12 million, how is it taxed?*  
> **A:** The first Rs.10m of your pension is tax-free; the extra Rs.2m is taxed at 5%, i.e. Rs.100,000 final tax.  If your pension were Rs.8m, you’d pay zero tax.  This change (introduced in Finance Act 2025) contrasts with 2024 when pension from a former employer was essentially untaxed【13†L29-L36】【30†L1120-L1128】.

## Rebates and Other Exemptions

- **Teachers and Researchers – 25% Rebate Restored:**  A 25% income tax credit for full-time teachers and researchers has been reinstated retroactively for tax years 2023–25【41†L1515-L1522】.  In effect, eligible teachers get a one-time 25% tax refund (or reduction) of their tax liability for each of those years.  (This benefit had been in limbo since 2022, but the Finance Act now explicitly restores it until June 2025【41†L1515-L1522】, after which it lapses.)  

  > **Q:** *I’m a school teacher. Do I still get the 25% tax rebate?*  
  > **A:** Yes. The 2025 law *reinstates* the 25% rebate for full-time teachers/researchers (for FY2023–25)【41†L1515-L1522】.  That means 25% of your calculated tax is credited back. For example, a Rs.100,000 tax bill would be reduced by Rs.25,000 under this scheme.

- **Pension Fund Withdrawals:**  A proposal to remove exemptions on withdrawals from approved pension funds was *dropped*.  In other words, withdrawals from qualifying pension funds remain exempt as before【13†L27-L29】. 

- **Personal Deductions:**  The basic exemption (Rs.600,000 for salaried people) and standard allowances (for children’s education, housing, etc.) were not changed.  Only the rates/slabs above Rs.600k were adjusted as described.

## Filers vs Non-Filers (Eligible vs Ineligible) and Withholding Taxes

Finance Act 2025 formally replaces the old “non-filer” category with **“Ineligible Persons”** and “Eligible Persons,” defined by a new Fifteenth Schedule of conditions【18†L42-L50】.  In simple terms, you must file your tax return by June 30 each year to be an *eligible* (ATL) taxpayer. Those who fail to file (now “ineligible” persons) face penalties and restrictions on many transactions【18†L42-L50】.

A major effect for individuals is on withholding taxes: **ineligible persons pay much higher rates**.  The law explicitly notes that any person *not on the Active Taxpayers List* pays **100% higher withholding rates** (i.e. double) on most payments【57†L13-L17】.  For example:

- **Cash withdrawals:** Previously, a non-ATL person faced 0.6% tax on any single-day withdrawal over Rs.50,000.  Now that rate is **0.8%**【42†L1068-L1072】. (ATL filers still pay the lower rate – effectively 0.4% – which is unchanged.)  
- **Vehicle and property transactions, utility bills, etc.:**  All standard withholding taxes remain in place for filers, but ineligible persons see them doubled (e.g. car tax, property sale/purchase tax, utility payments, etc.). The Finance Act’s new schedule confirms that non-ATL rates are 100% higher across the board【57†L13-L17】.  

> **Q:** *I haven’t filed taxes yet. How does that affect me?*  
> **A:** If you’re not on the ATL (ineligible), banks and other payers will withhold taxes at double the normal rates【57†L13-L17】. For instance, on large cash withdrawals the bank now deducts 0.8% instead of 0.4%【42†L1068-L1072】. Similarly, advance tax on vehicle purchase or property will be higher. Filing your return and staying “eligible” avoids these surcharges.

- **E-Commerce Sales:** A new final tax regime applies to all payments for goods or services ordered online via local platforms.  Under FA2025, the *seller* (and payment intermediaries or couriers) must withhold: **1%** on digital/electronic receipts, and **2%** on cash-on-delivery (CoD) receipts【18†L73-L76】.  This tax is collected at source on gross sales, and it is final.  

  > **Q:** *I sell products on an online marketplace. How is my income taxed?*  
  > **A:** Any sale through a Pakistani e-platform is subject to 1% tax if paid electronically, or 2% if paid by COD【18†L73-L76】. For example, on a Rs.100,000 sale, Rs.1,000 would be collected by the platform/bank as tax (electronic) or Rs.2,000 if COD. This replaces any prior income tax on that sale.

## Real Estate and Capital Gains

Several changes touch on property transactions:

- **Personal Home Sale Exemption:**  Finance Act 2025 grants a *one-time benefit* for individual sellers of their long-held personal residence.  If you sell a house that you’ve lived in for at least 15 years (and declared in your wealth statements for that period), the Commissioner of Income Tax *may exempt you from advance tax on the sale*【18†L58-L66】.  Moreover, that sale’s gain is **excluded from the “Super Tax” (Section 4C) altogether**【18†L62-L66】【41†L1547-L1553】.  In practice, once every 15 years you can sell your principal home tax-free (on these two counts).  

  > **Q:** *My family home (owned 20 years) qualifies. What taxes do I pay on selling it?*  
  > **A:** Under the new rules, you can apply for a certificate to avoid the usual 2% withholding tax on the sale【18†L58-L66】. Also, any capital gain on that sale is exempt from the 4C super-tax (4% above normal tax)【41†L1547-L1553】.  So you would pay only the standard capital gains tax (if any), not the extra taxes. 

- **Advance Tax on Property:**  The Act tweaks rates for filers vs non-filers on property transactions.  Notably, it *reduces* the advance tax rates on purchasing property for non-ATL persons, while *raising* the rates on selling property for non-ATL persons【51†L130-L134】.  (Filers generally pay lower “filer” rates; non-filers used to pay double. The Act narrows that gap for buyers and widens it for sellers【51†L130-L134】.)  For example, a non-filer buying property may now pay a slightly lower rate than before, whereas a non-filer selling pays a bit more.  Eligible filers continue to enjoy the standard (lower) rates.

## Key Points to Remember (FAQs)

- **Basic Exemption Remains Rs.600,000:** The zero-tax threshold is unchanged, but rates above it have been reduced【42†L1078-L1081】.  
- **ATL Status Is Crucial:** File your return by June 30 to be “eligible.” Non-filers lose many tax benefits and face doubled withholding rates【57†L13-L17】.  
- **Teacher Rebate Is Time-Limited:** The 25% rebate for educators only applies through tax year 2025【41†L1515-L1522】 (after that it ends unless extended).  
- **Pension Commutation Still Exempt:** If you take a lump-sum payout from your pension fund, that amount remains tax-free despite the other pension changes【13†L29-L36】.  
- **Digital Sales Tax:** Online sellers must ensure the 1%/2% tax is collected – this replaces part of normal income tax on those transactions【18†L73-L76】.  

By comparing each change to last year’s rules, we see that **most individual taxpayers will benefit from lower effective tax rates and preserved exemptions, provided they stay compliant**.  The biggest new costs fall on non-filers or on special cases (very high salaries, certain large transactions).  For further detail on any item above, please consult the cited sources and FBR’s official tax circulars.

I’ve structured it in a way that’s accessible for general readers but still detailed enough for professionals, and included FAQs at the end for clarity.

# Finance Act 2025 – Key Income Tax Amendments for Businesses and Corporates

The Federal Finance Act, 2025 has introduced several important changes to the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** that directly impact companies, associations of persons (AOPs), and business individuals. These amendments aim to broaden the tax base, tighten compliance, and address loopholes in digital and cross-border transactions. Below is a breakdown of the most significant changes.

---

## 1. Corporate Tax Rates
The corporate tax rate remains **unchanged at 29%** for tax year 2026. However, businesses in banking and specific regulated sectors continue to face higher rates. No new reduced rate schemes have been introduced for companies.

---

## 2. Minimum Tax on Turnover (Section 113)
- **Rate maintained at 1.25%** of turnover for most companies.
- Certain sectors (oil, gas, power generation, exploration and production) continue to enjoy reduced rates.  
- Clarifications were added to reduce disputes in apportionment for exempt and taxable income.

---

## 3. Super Tax / Surcharge (Section 4B & Section 4AB)
- The **super tax** continues for high-earning companies (income above Rs. 150 million) on progressive slabs.  
- For tax year 2026, the **surcharge under section 4AB** has been **reduced to 9%** (down from 10%) on the payable income tax. This applies across businesses, easing overall burden but still targeting high-profit entities.

---

## 4. Tax on Cash Transactions (Section 21(s))
- Disallowance of business expenses paid in cash above **Rs. 200,000** per transaction has been reinforced.  
- Companies must ensure digital banking channels are used to avoid disallowance.

---

## 5. Withholding on Imports (Section 148)
- The **withholding tax regime** on imports has been further clarified:  
  - **Industrial undertakings** continue to be taxed at lower adjustable rates.  
  - **Commercial importers** remain subject to final tax.  
  - New CPC (Customs Procedure Codes) introduced for classification to reduce misuse.

---

## 6. Controlled Foreign Companies (Section 109A)
- The scope of **Controlled Foreign Company (CFC) rules** has been widened.  
- Now applies where a resident Pakistani company (or group) has **more than 40% ownership** in an offshore entity and the foreign tax paid is less than **60% of local corporate tax**.  
- This prevents shifting profits to low-tax jurisdictions.

---

## 7. Group Taxation (Section 59AA, 59B, 59C)
- Adjustments made to **group relief provisions** to ensure losses are only set off where **active business** exists.  
- Stricter rules for unbundling/restructuring groups, particularly in energy and infrastructure sectors.

---

## 8. Depreciation and Amortization
- Amendments now require clearer reconciliation between **accounting depreciation (IFRS)** and **tax depreciation**.  
- Disputes over deferred revenue and consumer-funded assets (e.g., power companies) have been addressed by inserting clarifying provisions.

---

## 9. Digital Economy and E-Commerce
- Section **6A (Digital Services Tax)** has been reinforced:  
  - **Non-resident digital platforms** (advertising, streaming, marketplaces) are taxed at **10%** of gross Pakistan-sourced receipts.  
  - Companies making payments must withhold at source.  
- Section **152** has been amended to expand withholding obligations for payments to non-residents providing cloud, hosting, and e-commerce support.

---

## 10. Penalties and Compliance
- Higher penalties for **non-integration with FBR’s digital invoicing system** (SRO 709/2025).  
- Companies failing to e-report invoices may face **disallowance of input tax credit and monetary fines**.  
- **Stricter record-keeping** obligations have been imposed for businesses engaged in cross-border or digital sales.

---

# FAQs on Business / Corporate Amendments

**Q1: Has the corporate tax rate changed for tax year 2026?**  
No, it remains at **29%**. Only specific sectors like banking face higher rates.

**Q2: What is the minimum tax if my company reports a loss?**  
The minimum tax is **1.25% of turnover**, unless you fall under reduced-rate sectors such as oil marketing or power generation.

**Q3: Does the 9% surcharge apply to all companies?**  
Yes, the surcharge under **section 4AB** applies on payable income tax for corporates with high income, but it has been reduced from 10% to 9%.

**Q4: Can I still pay suppliers in cash?**  
Yes, but any payment **over Rs. 200,000 in cash** will not be allowed as a deductible business expense under **section 21(s)**.

**Q5: How do the new rules affect imports?**  
Industrial undertakings continue to enjoy **lower adjustable rates**, but commercial importers remain under **final tax**. Correct CPC codes must be used at customs.

**Q6: My company owns a subsidiary abroad. Do CFC rules apply?**  
If you hold **40% or more** in a foreign company and it pays less than **60% of Pakistan’s corporate tax**, its income may be taxed in Pakistan under **section 109A**.

**Q7: What about digital payments to Google, Facebook, or AWS?**  
Payments to non-resident digital platforms are subject to **10% withholding tax** under section 6A, unless covered by a Double Taxation Treaty.

**Q8: What are the risks of non-compliance with digital invoicing?**  
Companies not integrated with FBR’s digital invoicing may face **loss of input tax credit**, penalties, and inclusion in the **non-compliant list**.

---

### Conclusion
The **Finance Act 2025** pushes businesses toward **greater documentation, digital compliance, and transparency in cross-border dealings**. While corporate tax rates remain stable, companies must pay close attention to **minimum tax, surcharge, cash disallowance, CFC rules, and digital economy obligations**.  

For corporates, the key takeaway is simple: **move fully digital, strengthen compliance systems, and review group structures** to stay ahead of FBR’s tightening net.

# Key Corporate Tax Amendments (Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – through Finance Act 2025)

The Federal Finance Act, 2025 introduced numerous amendments to Pakistan’s Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 that affect resident companies and foreign/controlled foreign companies.  These include changes in tax rates and surcharges, deductions, withholding taxes, incentives, and compliance rules.  Below is a detailed overview of each relevant amendment, with concise summaries and comparative tables of old vs new provisions where applicable.

## Corporate Tax Rates and Surcharges  
- **Corporate tax rate:** The basic corporate tax rate remains unchanged (29% for most companies, 39% for banking companies).  
- **Super tax:** First introduced for high earners in 2022, the *Finance Act 2025* slightly reduced super-tax slabs.  Under the new slabs, incomes above Rs 250 million up to Rs 500 million are taxed 0.5% lower than before【42†L380-L387】【51†L426-L428】.  For example, a company with Rs 300m income now pays 3.5% super tax (down from 4%).  (Incomes above Rs 500m remain at 10%.)  A summary of the final super-tax rates (Tax Year 2025) is shown below.  

| **Taxable Income (Rs)** | **Super-tax Rate (New 2025)** | **Super-tax Rate (Pre-2025)** |
|-----------------------:|:-----------------------------:|:-----------------------------:|
| 150m – 200m            | 1.0%                          | 1.0%                          |
| 200m – 250m            | 1.5%                          | 1.5%                          |
| 250m – 300m            | 2.5%                          | 3.0%                          |
| 300m – 350m            | 3.5%                          | 4.0%                          |
| 350m – 400m            | 5.5%                          | 6.0%                          |
| 400m – 500m            | 7.5%                          | 8.0%                          |
| Over 500m             | 10.0%                         | 10.0%                         |

*Table 1: Super-tax slab rates, showing the 0.5% reduction in rates above Rs 250m【51†L426-L428】【42†L380-L387】.*

- **Minimum (turnover) tax credits:** The carry-forward period for turnover-tax (minimum tax) credits has been shortened from **3 years** to **2 years**【42†L389-L392】.  Companies should adjust their tax planning accordingly.

- **SME taxation:** The special tax regime for manufacturing SMEs (sales up to Rs 250m) remains in place.  SMEs continue to pay 7.5–15% on profits (depending on turnover), or may opt into a final (turnover-based) regime.  The *Finance Act 2025* did not change SME rates but requires registration on FBR/SMEDA portals【17†L443-L452】【51†L430-L438】.

## Deductions and Allowances  
- **Disallowance of cash sales:**  A major new restriction disallows **50% of expenses** attributable to any **cash sale above Rs 200,000**【42†L382-L384】.  This means if a company sells goods/services for cash over Rs 200k, half of related cost-of-sales or similar expenses cannot be deducted.  
- **Purchases from non-NTN sellers:**  The Finance Act 2025 introduced a flat **10% disallowance** on expenses for purchases made from vendors who do not hold a National Tax Number (NTN)【42†L385-L387】.  (As amended, this 10% penalty applies generally; for agricultural goods the disallowance is triggered only if purchased via middlemen rather than directly from growers.)  
- **Intangible assets amortization:**  The amortization period for *indefinitely-lived intangibles* (like brand names, goodwill, licenses) has been shortened from **25 years to 15 years**【42†L387-L388】.  This accelerates cost recovery for such assets.  

| **Feature**                                 | **Old Provision**   | **New Provision (FA 2025)**       |
|--------------------------------------------|---------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Useful life of indefinite-lived intangibles | 25 years (for tax)  | **15 years**【42†L387-L388】        |
| Carry-forward for turnover tax credits      | 3 years             | **2 years**【42†L389-L392】         |

*Table 2: Key changes in amortization and tax credit rules.*

- **Group relief (loss set-off):**  Existing group-loss relief rules continue (allowing loss transfer among a 100%-owned group).  However, losses of a subsidiary whose income is taxed at a special rate **cannot** be surrendered to a holding company【37†L397-L401】.  Moreover, *Finance Act 2025* explicitly forbids using business losses to offset *rental income*, closing a loophole where firms previously shifted losses to passive rents【42†L399-L402】.

- **Transfer pricing disallowances:**  The Act made no new TP rate changes, but amended documentation rules and disallows 10% of certain “advertising, promotion and royalty” expenses if no arm’s-length evidence is provided (new authority added in FA 2024).

## Withholding Tax Updates  
- **Profit on debt (interest):** Under *Section 7B*, companies receiving interest income saw the tax rate rise.  Profit-on-debt paid by a banking company or financial institution – and by extension interest on government bonds – was taxed at 15% (FY2024); **now it is 20%**【42†L392-L394】.  

| **Interest Income Source**           | **Old WHT Rate** | **New WHT Rate (FA 2025)**【42†L392-L394】 |
|------------------------------------|------------------|------------------------------------|
| Interest from banks/financial inst. | 15%              | **20%**                             |
| Interest on government securities    | 15%              | **20%**                             |

*Table 3: Withholding tax on profit on debt, increased to 20% for company recipients【42†L392-L394】.*

- **Mutual fund dividends:** Previously, dividends from mutual funds were taxed differently by source: 25% on the debt-income portion and 15% on the equity-portion (for FY2024)【4†L1213-L1220】. The new law aligns this by taxing each portion at the same rates (25% and 15%, respectively) and adds a proviso: **corporate recipients will pay 29% tax on the debt-income portion of such dividends**【4†L1213-L1221】【42†L395-L397】. In practice, companies investing in debt-heavy mutual funds will now have 29% tax on that income component.  

- **Digital/e-commerce transactions:** A new *final-tax regime* was introduced for online platforms and digital payments.  Effective July 2025, any person receiving payments for digitally-ordered goods/services delivered in Pakistan is subject to 1% withholding (if paid digitally or through banks) or 2% (for Cash-on-Delivery)【42†L403-L406】【33†L73-L77】.  (This regime is separate from exporters’ final tax, which remains 0–1%.)  

| **Transaction Type**                    | **Old Tax Rate** | **New Final Tax Rate (FA 2025)**【42†L403-L406】 |
|---------------------------------------|------------------|------------------------------------------|
| E-commerce sales (digital/banking)     | N/A              | **1%** (final tax)                       |
| E-commerce sales (cash on delivery)    | N/A              | **2%** (final tax)                       |

*Table 4: Withholding/final tax on online/digital sales via e-commerce platforms【42†L403-L406】.*

- **Other withholding changes:** The tax on cash withdrawals remains 0.8% (raised earlier).  No change to standard 15%/20% withholding on dividends (companies still pay 15%).  However, **branch profits** now fall under the definition of “dividend”: FA2025 explicitly added “[remittance of] after tax profit of a branch of a foreign company operating in Pakistan” to the dividend definition【48†L525-L530】.  In effect, when a foreign company remits branch profits, Pakistan will treat it like a dividend payment (subject to standard WHT).

## Incentives and Exemptions  
- **Tax holidays (SEZ/STZ):** The preferential tax holiday for approved **Special Economic Zone (SEZ)** and **Special Technology Zone (STZ)** enterprises was capped.  These entities can no longer extend holidays beyond June 30, 2035【42†L398-L400】.  (Any holiday previously granted still runs to 2035 at most.)  
- **Other incentives:**  Most other incentive regimes (e.g. R&D, investment tax credits) remain intact unless separately amended.  
- **Exemption certificates:**  Withholding agents can still apply for reduced-rate/exemption certificates.  Notably, **the FBR is now empowered to issue full (100%) exemption certificates to public limited companies**【33†L37-L41】, instead of only reduced rates.  This simplifies planning for large corporations that qualify.  

## Foreign Companies and CFC Rules  
- **Tax on foreign companies:** A foreign company (without permanent establishment) is taxed only on Pakistan-source income via WHT or separate charges.  Branches of foreign companies, however, now face special tax treatment: as noted, **branch profit remittances count as dividends**【48†L525-L530】, so 15% WHT will generally apply (subject to treaty relief).  
- **Thin capitalization:**  New thin-capitalization rules limit deductions for foreign debt.  If a foreign-controlled company or foreign branch has foreign debt exceeding 3:1 (debt:equity) during the year, the excess interest expense is disallowed【37†L481-L491】.  A carry-forward mechanism was introduced for disallowed interest (up to 3 years).  
- **Controlled Foreign Companies (CFCs):** Pakistan’s CFC regime (inserted in 2019) remains in force.  Income of a non-resident company is treated as “CFC income” for a Pakistani resident if the resident holds *more than 50%* of capital or voting power (or >40% individually) and the foreign tax paid is below 60% of Pakistan’s tax on that income【44†L510-L518】.  Undistributed CFC income (above a Rs 10m de minimis) is included in the Pakistani taxpayer’s income and taxed at **15% (dividend rate)**【44†L510-L518】.  Importantly, any CFC income already taxed in Pakistan will not be taxed again on repatriation【44†L526-L529】.  These rules ensure that passive foreign income of Pakistani owners is taxed, with relief for taxes paid abroad.  

## Tables of Major Changes  

Several key amendments are highlighted in the tables below, showing old vs. new provisions:

| **Item**                                | **Old Provision**               | **New Provision (FA 2025)**             |
|---------------------------------------|---------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| **Interest WHT (bank bonds)**          | 15%                             | **20%** (on profit from bank/fin. co.)【42†L392-L394】 |
| **Intangible assets (indefinite)**     | Amortized over 25 years        | **15-year amortization**【42†L387-L388】 |
| **NTN non-compliance disallowance**    | No general disallowance        | **10% disallowed** on purchases from non-NTN persons【42†L385-L387】 |
| **Cash sales disallowance**            | No such rule                  | **50%** of costs disallowed if sale > Rs 200k【42†L382-L384】 |
| **Turnover-tax credit carryforward**   | 3 years                        | **2 years**【42†L389-L392】              |
| **E-commerce payment tax (digital)**   | N/A                            | **1%** final tax (digital/banking)【42†L403-L406】 |
| **E-commerce payment tax (COD)**       | N/A                            | **2%** final tax (cash-on-delivery)【42†L403-L406】 |
| **SEZ/STZ tax holiday expiry**         | No explicit cap               | End date **June 30, 2035**【42†L398-L400】  |

*Table 5: Summary of select amendments (FA 2025) affecting companies, contrasted with prior rules.*  

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

- **Q: Did the corporate tax rate change?**  
  **A:** No. The standard corporate income tax rate remains 29% (with banking companies at 39%), and sales/turnover tax surcharges (super tax) were slightly reduced (by 0.5% for incomes between Rs 250–500m)【51†L426-L428】【42†L380-L387】.  

- **Q: What new withholding taxes should companies expect?**  
  **A:** The main changes are: (1) Profit-on-debt (interest) income from banks/financial institutions and government debt is now taxed at 20% (up from 15%)【42†L392-L394】; (2) Payments for e-commerce transactions incur a new final withholding (1% digital, 2% COD)【42†L403-L406】; (3) Branch profits remitted by foreign companies are treated as dividends (15% WHT)【48†L525-L530】; (4) Dividends from mutual funds’ debt-income portion paid to companies are taxed at the corporate rate (29%)【4†L1213-L1221】【42†L395-L397】.  

- **Q: How are deductions restricted?**  
  **A:** Major new limits include: 50% disallowance of expenses on any cash sale over Rs 200k【42†L382-L384】; 10% disallowance on purchases from vendors without an NTN【42†L385-L387】; and accelerated amortization (15-year life) for indefinite intangibles【42†L387-L388】.  Loss offset rules were tightened so that business losses cannot be used against rental income【42†L399-L402】.  

- **Q: What changes affect foreign or controlled foreign companies?**  
  **A:** The Act broadened taxation of foreign entities: after-tax branch profits are now taxed as dividends【48†L525-L530】.  Pakistan’s existing CFC rules remain in force: undistributed income of a majority-owned foreign company is included in the Pakistani owner’s taxable income (taxed at dividend rate)【44†L510-L518】.  Additionally, new thin-capitalization rules disallow excess interest if foreign debt exceeds 3:1【37†L481-L491】.  

- **Q: Have any tax holidays or incentives been altered?**  
  **A:** Yes. The tax holiday for companies in Special Economic Zones and Special Technology Zones is now limited to run only until June 30, 2035【42†L398-L400】.  All other incentives (e.g. for renewable energy, R&D) remain as before unless separately modified.  Also, new powers allow the tax authorities to issue full (100%) withholding-tax exemption certificates to public companies【33†L37-L41】 (previously only reduced rates).  

- **Q: What should companies do to comply?**  
  **A:** Companies should update their accounting and tax systems to incorporate the new rates and disallowances.  For example, identify all purchases from non-NTN suppliers and apply the 10% penalty, track any digital sales for the new withholding, and adjust intangibles amortization schedules to 15 years.  Foreign-invested companies must review ownership thresholds to determine if CFC rules apply.  It is advisable to consult with tax advisors to ensure all procedural updates (appeals, reporting requirements, etc.) are followed.  

**Sources:** The above summaries are based on the Finance Act 2025 and official commentary【42†L380-L387】【42†L392-L400】【44†L510-L518】【48†L525-L530】, which detail all amendments to the Income Tax Ordinance affecting companies. These include provisions for both resident corporations and foreign-controlled entities. Further details can be found in the cited sources and the official ordinance text.
