**To**  
The Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue  
Unit-4, Zone-II, Large Taxpayers’ Office  
Karachi  

**Subject:** Response to Show Cause Notice No. SCN/Dig.Inv./Unit-4/Zone-II/LTO/KHI/25-26 dated September 15, 2025  

**Respected Sir,**  

We write on behalf of our client, M/s. Fauji Oil Terminal & Distribution Company Limited (FOTCO), in connection with the Show Cause Notice issued under Section 33(25A) read with Section 11E of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, alleging non-implementation of digital invoicing under Rule 150Q of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006. At the outset, we submit that the impugned notice is misconceived both in law and on facts. FOTCO is exclusively engaged in rendering terminal operator services at Port Qasim and is duly registered with the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) under the category of “Terminal Operator Services.” The company has been consistently discharging its provincial sales tax obligations under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011, which governs the taxation of services after the 18th Constitutional Amendment.  

It is pertinent to highlight that FOTCO does not supply any taxable goods within the meaning of Section 2(41) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990. The Act primarily governs sales tax on goods, whereas FOTCO’s operations pertain entirely to the provision of services, which fall exclusively within the domain of provincial sales tax legislation. Consequently, the mandatory digital invoicing regime prescribed under SRO 1413(I)/2025 dated August 1, 2025, and Chapter XIV, Rule 150Q of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006, is not applicable to our client. The invocation of penal provisions under Section 33(25A) and Section 11E of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, therefore, does not have lawful basis in the present case, as FOTCO cannot be penalized for non-compliance with a statutory obligation that does not extend to its business activities.  

In view of the above submissions, it is most respectfully requested that the subject Show Cause Notice may kindly be withdrawn, as the same has been issued without lawful authority and is not tenable against our client. FOTCO remains fully compliant with all applicable tax laws within its jurisdiction and continues to discharge its obligations under the Sindh Sales Tax regime.  

With highest regards,  
**For and on behalf of**  
*M/s. Fauji Oil Terminal & Distribution Company Limited*  

---

Fauji Oil Terminal & Distribution Company Limited (FOTCO), in connection with the Show Cause Notice issued under Section 33(25A) read with Section 11E of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, alleging non-implementation of digital invoicing under Rule 150Q of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006. At the outset, we submit that the impugned notice is misconceived both in law and on facts. FOTCO is exclusively engaged in rendering terminal operator services at Port Qasim and is duly registered with the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) under the category of “Terminal Operator Services.” The company has been consistently discharging its provincial sales tax obligations under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011, which governs the taxation of services after the 18th Constitutional Amendment.

---

**To**  
The Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue  
Unit-4, Zone-II, Large Taxpayers’ Office  
Karachi  

**Subject:** Response to Show Cause Notice No. SCN/Dig.Inv./Unit-4/Zone-II/LTO/KHI/25-26 dated September 15, 2025  

**Respected Sir,**

We write on behalf of our client, **M/s. Fauji Oil Terminal & Distribution Company Limited (FOTCO)**, in connection with the above-captioned Show Cause Notice issued under Section 33(25A) read with Section 11E of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, alleging non-implementation of digital invoicing under Rule 150Q of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.  

At the outset, we respectfully submit that the impugned notice is misconceived in law and on facts due to the following:  

1. **Nature of Business and Registration with SRB**  
   Our client is exclusively engaged in rendering terminal operator services at Port Qasim. In line with this business activity, FOTCO is duly registered with the **Sindh Revenue Board (SRB)** under the head *“Terminal Operator Services”* and has been discharging its provincial sales tax obligations regularly under the **Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011**.  

2. **No Taxable Supply under the Sales Tax Act, 1990**  
   The services rendered by our client do not constitute a *“taxable supply”* within the meaning of Section 2(41) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990. The Act governs sales tax on goods, whereas FOTCO’s entire business model pertains exclusively to the provision of services, which fall under the provincial domain post-18th Constitutional Amendment. Consequently, our client does not fall within the purview of mandatory digital invoicing envisaged for suppliers of goods under Chapter XIV, Rule 150Q of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.  

3. **Erroneous Invocation of Penal Provisions**  
   Since our client neither supplies taxable goods nor falls within the category of registered persons required to implement digital invoicing under SRO 1413(I)/2025 dated August 1, 2025, the invocation of Section 33(25A) and Section 11E of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 is misplaced. The imposition of penalty of Rs. 500,000/- in such circumstances would amount to penalizing a taxpayer for a statutory obligation that is not legally applicable to it.  

4. **Request for Withdrawal of Notice**  
   In view of the above submissions, it is most respectfully requested that the subject Show Cause Notice may kindly be **withdrawn/dropped** in the interest of justice, as the same has been issued without lawful authority and is not tenable against FOTCO.  

We trust that the above clarifies our client’s legal and factual position. Our client remains committed to full compliance with all applicable tax laws and continues to discharge its obligations under the Sindh Sales Tax regime.  

With highest regards,  
**For and on behalf of**  
*M/s. Fauji Oil Terminal & Distribution Company Limited*  

---

**To**  
The Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue  
Unit-4, Zone-II, Large Taxpayers’ Office  
Karachi  

**Subject:** Response to Show Cause Notice No. SCN/Dig.Inv./Unit-4/Zone-II/LTO/KHI/25-26/12221 dated September 15, 2025  

**Respected Sir,**  

We refer to your Show Cause Notice No. SCN/Dig.Inv./Unit-4/Zone-II/LTO/KHI/25-26/12221 dated September 15, 2025, issued to our client, through which it has been alleged that the Company has failed to implement the mandatory digital invoicing process as required under the provisions of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 (the “Act”), specifically referencing Chapter XIV, Rule 150Q of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006 (the “Rules”). You have therefore called upon our client to explain as to why a penalty of Rs. 500,000 may not be imposed under Section 11E of the Act read with Section 33(25A).  

In this regard, it is respectfully submitted that our client fully acknowledges the statutory requirement of implementing digital invoicing and has been making genuine and consistent efforts to comply in good faith. Initially, our client duly registered for digital invoicing and selected Pakistan Refinery Limited (PARL) as the licensed integrator. However, despite repeated follow-ups, PRAL did not issue the essential token number required for further processing. This token is a prerequisite for carrying out sandbox testing and finalizing the implementation of digital invoicing. The delay, therefore, was not attributable to any inaction or omission on the part of our client but stemmed from PRAL’s non-responsiveness in facilitating the mandatory step.  

Recognizing the urgency of compliance, our client has since engaged WebDNA Works Private Limited, a licensed integrator duly approved by FBR. Necessary approvals have already been obtained, and the process of final integration is underway. Our client remains fully committed to completing this exercise at the earliest possible time.  

It is pertinent to emphasize that there is no element of willful default, mala fide intention, or deliberate non-compliance. On the contrary, the Company has consistently acted in good faith, taken proactive measures, and diligently pursued resolution of technical and administrative hurdles beyond its control. As a matter of settled law, the imposition of penalties under tax statutes requires proof of mens rea — a deliberate and blameworthy default. In the present case, the delay was entirely dependent upon PRAL and the initial integrator, coupled with our client’s bona fide efforts to transition to an alternate authorized integrator.  

In view of these facts, imposition of penalty in the given circumstances would be inconsistent with the spirit and intent of Rule 150Q, Rule 150V, and the scheme of the Sales Tax Act, 1990. We therefore respectfully request that the subject Show Cause Notice be withdrawn, recognizing our client’s bona fide efforts and ongoing compliance process.  

With highest regards,  
**For and on behalf of**  
*M/s. Fauji Oil Terminal & Distribution Company Limited*  

---

**Dear Sir/Madam,**

We refer to your query regarding the attached agreement and confirm that it clearly qualifies as a **service agreement**, not a commission agreement.  Indeed, the document is titled *“Service Agreement”*【32†L1003-L1007】, and it consistently uses service‑related language.  For example, in the definitions it specifies **“Services”** (as detailed in Annexure I)【32†L1089-L1091】, and payment is expressly called a **“Service Fee”** rather than a commission.  In particular: 

- **Agreement Title:** The very title on page 1 is “*SERVICE AGREEMENT*”【32†L1003-L1007】, and the introductory clause begins “*THIS SERVICES AGREEMENT…*”. This unmistakably frames the contract as one for services.  
- **Terminology:** Throughout the document, the second party is referred to as the *“Service Provider”*, and the scope of work is defined in terms of **services** to be performed (see “Services means the details as set out in Annexure I”【32†L1089-L1091】). There is no reference to a commission, brokerage, agency or intermediary; the word “commission” does not appear in the operative clauses.  
- **Obligations:** The agreement imposes ongoing obligations on the Service Provider to perform specified tasks (as per the Annexure/Scope of Services) and even includes penalty provisions tied to service performance (e.g. failure to meet agreed standards). These obligations are typical of a services arrangement. The structure is focused on the *delivery of services*, not on achieving sales or collection targets in a way an agent or introducer would be bound.  
- **Payment Mechanism:**  The compensation is structured as a periodic fee for services, not a lump-sum on sales.  For instance, the Payment Terms (Appendix) state: *“Service Fee to the Service Provider will be based on recovered amount on monthly basis”*【8†L2370-L2371】. This shows a **monthly service fee**, not a one-time percentage commission. (In contrast, a commission agreement would typically tie payment to individual sales or introductions, without such a set periodic fee.)  
- **Absence of Commission Language:** Nowhere does the agreement call the payment a commission or fee for introduction. There are no references to “introducer,” “brokerage,” or similar terms. The rights and remedies clauses also emphasize breach of *service obligations*, reinforcing that the contract is governed by service-delivery standards, not by contingent commission formulas.

Given these features, the arrangement falls squarely within the definition of a service contract.  Finally, please note that as this is a service arrangement, each fee payment is subject to income tax withholding under **Section 153(1)(b)** of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (since payments “for services” are covered by that provision). In practical terms, K‑Electric (as the payer) will need to deduct the applicable withholding tax on each service fee (for example, the standard 5% rate on individual service fees) and deposit it with the tax authorities.  

We trust this clarifies your query.  Please let us know if you require any further explanation. 

**Yours faithfully,**

[Your Name]

I’ve gone through the agreement you shared. Here’s my analysis:

---

### Nature of the Agreement
This is a **Service Agreement**, not a commission agreement.

---

### Reasons for Qualification as a Service Agreement  

1. **Express Title & Language**  
   The document itself is repeatedly titled *“Service Agreement”*【9†source】. Throughout the clauses, terms like *“Services,” “Service Provider,” “Service Fee,”* and *“obligations”* are used. Nowhere does it use the legal or commercial terminology of “commission” (which would normally reference brokerage, agency, or intermediary arrangements).

2. **Scope of Work**  
   The agreement sets out specific obligations the Service Provider must perform for K-Electric (e.g., consumer recovery, disconnection, technical support, maintaining records, compliance with KE standards, health and safety requirements, etc.)【9†source】. These are operational functions, not merely referrals or introductions that would attract a commission.

3. **Remuneration Basis**  
   Payment is structured as a **Service Fee**, not a percentage-based commission. While some amounts may be linked to recovery targets or performance, they are still described as “fees for services rendered,” payable monthly or quarterly【9†source】. Commission arrangements typically say “X% of sales/proceeds generated,” but this agreement carefully avoids that language.

4. **Relationship of Parties**  
   The agreement clarifies that the Service Provider and its personnel are not employees of KE, but independent contractors performing defined services【9†source】. In commission arrangements, the relationship is usually principal–agent, where the agent earns a commission for facilitating contracts or sales. Here, it is framed strictly as provision of services.

5. **Obligations & Liabilities**  
   The Service Provider is required to maintain staff, equipment, insurance, safety standards, and is subject to penalties for non-performance【9†source】. These are typical of service contracts, not commission agreements.

---

### Conclusion
The agreement is clearly a **Service Agreement** because it involves the provision of defined services with payment structured as a service fee, along with detailed operational obligations, performance standards, and liabilities. It is not a commission arrangement, which would be characterized by an agency relationship and remuneration linked directly to a percentage of transactions facilitated.

2. Are payments to the second party based on specific commissions from amounts recovered, or is it a fixed fee or service-based compensation?

Thank you. I’ll review the agreement to determine whether it constitutes a services contract or a commission agent relationship. I’ll assess the legal substance of the transaction and explain the reasons for the classification, considering factors like compensation structure, degree of supervision, and legal responsibilities.

I'll get back to you shortly with a detailed assessment.

# Classification of the Arrangement

The contract in question is titled a **“Service Agreement”** between KE and Muhammad Salman.  It provides that the Service Provider will recover certain debts for KE and be paid on a *commission* basis (a percentage of amounts recovered).  At first glance, a commission-style payment might suggest an agency/commission-agent relationship.  However, the legal substance must govern.  Applying general agency principles and contractor tests shows this looks more like a *contract for services* rather than a true commission‐agent arrangement.

- **Payment Model:** The contract pays Salman a **commission on amounts recovered**, not a fixed salary.  Commission payment is indeed common in agency contracts (an agent often earns a percentage on sales).  For example, one treatise notes that a “commission contract” is typically one where an intermediary undertakes to carry out a sale or services “in his own name, but on behalf of another (the principal),” with compensation usually a percentage of the deal【75†L122-L126】.  However, a service contract (independent contractor arrangement) can also tie fees to performance.  The mere fact of commission-based pay does *not* automatically create an agency relationship.  What matters is *how* the work is performed and what authority the person has.  In this case, although compensation is commission-based, the balance of factors points to a service arrangement. (For comparison, a true commission agent in commercial law acts independently to sell goods for a principal and “assumes the risk” of the transactions【75†L122-L126】.  Here Salman is simply collecting KE’s own receivables under KE’s direction.) 

- **Control and Supervision:** A key factor is the **degree of control** KE exercises.  The context states Salman is working under KE’s *direct supervision and control*.  By contrast, an independent commission agent normally works with autonomy.  For example, British tax guidance notes that a genuinely self‑employed contractor (“service provider”) is typically *not* under direct supervision by the hiring party【42†L163-L172】.  One official source states that a person is likely self-employed if “they’re not under direct supervision when working”【42†L163-L172】.  In other words, *direct supervision suggests an employment/contract-for-services model, not an independent agent.*  Because KE controls how Salman carries out the collections, this factor points toward a **service contract**.  It is inconsistent with the freedom expected of an independent commission agent.  

- **Autonomy in Performing Tasks:** Commission agents generally have significant freedom in how they do the job.  Britannica explains that a commission agent is *“independent of his principal”* and may carry on transactions “as he sees fit”【24†L231-L239】.  In a true agency, the agent acts in his own name for the principal’s account, subject only to the principal’s overall instructions.  By contrast, a service provider/contractor typically follows the client’s detailed directions.  The facts suggest Salman has little autonomy and must follow KE’s processes.  This lack of independence – coupled with KE’s close direction – is **not consistent** with a commission‐agent role, and instead aligns with a services/contractor relationship.  

- **Authority and Representation:** In an agency (commission agent) relationship, the agent often deals with third parties (e.g. selling products) either in his own name or explicitly on the principal’s behalf【75†L122-L126】.  Crucially, a commission agent usually holds authority to negotiate or conclude transactions for the principal.  Here, Salman’s task is debt recovery: he collects KE’s money from debtors.  The agreement does not appear to give him the power to bind KE to new contracts or to assume KE’s rights beyond collection.  He acts as a *debt collector*, not as an agent negotiating deals.  Commission agents normally have a fiduciary agency role: they “act on behalf of the principal” in transactions【55†L259-L267】.  No such principal-agent authority is evident here.  This suggests Salman is an *independent service provider* performing a specified task for KE, rather than an agent contracting with debtors in his own name or directly representing KE beyond collecting owed funds. 

- **Risk and Liability:** Another difference is who bears risk and liability.  A commission agent typically “assumes the risk” of the operations (for example, if he carries inventory or advances funds)【75†L122-L126】.  In this agreement, the Service Provider is explicitly **required to assume his own liabilities and insurance costs**.  The contract mandates that Salman “provide [his] own medical insurance at [his] own expense” and that KE “shall not be responsible” for his injuries or liabilities【62†L1246-L1254】.  This is characteristic of an independent contractor: he bears the risk (e.g. of accidents or lawsuits arising from his work) and must carry his own insurance.  A true commission agent (like an employee) would not normally bear such obligations.  The fact KE disclaims liability and shifts all risk/costs onto Salman again indicates a service contract status, not an employer-agent one.  

- **Legal Definitions – Agency vs Services:** Under general contract law, an **agency (principal-agent) relationship** is a fiduciary arrangement where one party (agent) is empowered to act on behalf of another (principal)【55†L259-L267】.  A *commission agent* is a special kind of commercial agent who acts in his own name for the principal and earns a commission【24†L231-L239】【75†L122-L126】.  By contrast, a *service contract* (contract for services) is simply an agreement for one party to perform tasks for another, with no fiduciary agency implied.  The evidence here (formal title “Service Agreement,” detailed instructions by KE, lack of agent-like authority, and explicit non-agent terms) all point to a contract for services.  The provider is treated as an independent contractor under KE’s direction, not as an agent of KE. 

**Conclusion:**  Weighing the factors, this arrangement functions as a **services contract (independent contractor agreement)** rather than a true commission‐agent relationship.  Although pay is commission-based, Salman is clearly bound by KE’s instructions and control, with no genuine agency authority. Commission agents are normally independent actors trading for a principal【24†L231-L239】【75†L122-L126】; here, Salman operates under KE’s supervision and bears his own business risks, fitting a service agreement.  Therefore the contract should be classified as a **contract for services (service agreement)**, not an agency/commission-agent contract.

Landmark Win for Taxpayers: Tribunal Reverses Overreach of Tax Authority Regarding Refunds!
Regarding Sprint Oil and Gas Services FZC v Commissioner Inland Revenue, Islamabad’s Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (ATIR) has rendered a historic ruling in a strong and precedent-setting manner. This decision unequivocally narrows the extent of refund procedures under section 170 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, and makes clear: administrative excess cannot compromise taxpayers’ rights. For all complying taxpayers, the ruling is a great triumph and a big step toward Pakistani tax system integrity restoration.

Background What Set off the Conflict?
Operating in Pakistan since 2004, Sprint Oil and Gas Services—a UAE-based company—filed income tax returns and sought reimbursements for extra withholding taxes (WHT) deducted on imports and services. Tax officials started refund procedures and shockingly categorized the withheld taxes as “final tax liability,” a move meant to withhold the refund even if legally approved returns were accepted and considered assessment orders. They also tried to ignore binding precedents, notably the Supreme Court’s decision in the Honda Atlas case, on grounds of time-barred.

The Key Legal Issues and Conventions the Tribunal responded to basic concerns:
Can Section 170 reclassify the kind of tax deducted in refund procedures?
Can completed or changed assessment orders cause disruptions during refund handling? 
Does the three-year reimbursement time restriction absolutely rule against legitimate claims? 
Is contempt of court what results from disobeying legally binding precedents?
The Tribunal decided in the taxpayer’s favour on all these grounds. It maintained that authorities cannot review or categorize taxes during refund determination and that refund procedures are just confined to proving the proof of tax paid. Once an assessment ruling has reached finality, the Tribunal underlined, it cannot be challenged or changed under the cover of refund adjudication.

The Tribunal further underlined that public agencies have to act with justice and honesty and that technical restrictions cannot be utilized arbitrarily to refuse appropriate reimbursements.

Landmark Win for Taxpayers: Tribunal Reverses Overreach of Tax Authority Regarding Refunds
A strong message here: Safeguarding Taxpayers' Rights:
Described as “patently illegal, arbitrary,” “a gross abuse of authority,” the ATIR sharply attacked the behavior of tax officers. The ruling underlined unequivocally that tax officials have constitutional obligations to behave ethically, honestly, and legally within their context. As this case shows, maladministration, prejudice, and deliberate contempt of final court decisions compromise not only taxpayers’ rights but also confidence in Pakistan’s revenue collection. Significantly, the Tribunal stressed that reimbursement claims connected to completed evaluations ought to be respected right once without re-litigation of resolved matters.

Important Notes from the Tribunal's Decision:
Technical grounds must not defeat legitimate claims; limited defenses must not be used unfairly; refund procedures under Section 170 are limited to verification only; once concluded, they cannot be reopened; binding court decisions must be respected. Ignoring Supreme Court rulings constitutes serious contempt. This ruling essentially supports the rule of law and increases taxpayer defenses against administrative abuses.

An Appeal for Systematic Changes in Institutions:
Apart from the specific matter, the Tribunal has advised the Chairman FBR to provide explicit directions to tax officials thereby guaranteeing adherence to constitutional values and court decisions. The Tribunal also underlined the need of creating a tax culture anchored in justice, honesty, and professionalism whereby quick refund issuing is seen as a characteristic of excellent government, not a compromise. The ruling makes it abundantly evident that tax officials have to respect taxpayer rights, build public trust, and help Pakistan’s tax system to regain credibility.

Closing Notes:
This decision not only marks a triumph for Sprint Oil and Gas but also offers optimism for every Pakistani tax payer. It underlines that justice ought to be done not only but also clearly perceived to be done. It reminds public servants that their job is to enforce the law with openness and justice rather than to profit from technicalities. The Tribunal has strengthened a basic fact by making the tax authorities answerable: taxpayers’ money is a trust rather than a goal.

WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala called it a “pivotal moment” toward fairer global trade. While China insists it remains a “responsible developing country,” the decision addresses long-standing concerns from wealthier nations that Beijing’s economic clout is inconsistent with developing-nation privileges. # Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 – Amendments under the Sindh Finance Act, 2025

The Sindh Finance Act, 2025 introduced extensive changes to the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011. These affect definitions, tax rates, exemptions and administrative procedures. Below is a section‐wise summary of the key amendments, aimed at business owners and the general public.

## Amended Definitions and Scope  
- **New “CPC Code” definition:** The Act adds clause (19A) defining “CPC Code” as the United Nations’ Central Product Classification code adapted by the Board for this Act【6†L146-L148】.  
- **Omitted clauses:** Dozens of outdated definitions were removed.  For example, clauses (1)–(3), (5)–(7), (15)–(16), ..., (100)–(101) of section 2 have been omitted【6†L149-L156】.  This streamlines terminology, removing obsolete or redundant definitions.  
- **“Service” definition updated:** The definition of “service” (clause 79) was rewritten for clarity.  It now covers any activity, facility or advantage and expressly states that even if a service involves goods, it remains a service【6†L159-L168】.  
- **Taxable service clarified:** The phrase “A taxable service is a service listed in the Second Schedule” was changed to simply “Taxable service means a service”【7†L170-L177】.  An important new “Explanation II” clarifies that any service on which tax can be imposed under entry 53 of the Federal Legislative List is *not* a Sindh taxable service【7†L175-L179】.  In other words, services under federal jurisdiction (e.g. certain air or sea transport) will not be taxed by Sindh【7†L175-L179】.  
- **Other tweaks:** The terms “registered office” were changed to “office” in a couple of places【7†L186-L194】, but these are largely drafting clean-ups. 

## Revised Tax Rates  
- **Standard rate at 15%:** The general (“standard”) sales tax rate on services remains 15%【7†L208-L214】 (it had been raised from 13% to 15% in the prior year).  
- **Higher rate (19.5%):** The Second Schedule Part I now imposes a higher 19.5% rate on certain specialized services【10†L777-L785】. For example, telephony and internet communications services and certain IT “collocation” services are taxed at 19.5%【10†L777-L785】.  
- **Reduced rates for many services:** Part II of the Second Schedule lists numerous services at lower rates (ranging from 2% up to 8%, or fixed amounts), often with conditions. Some highlights include:  
  - **Construction, trade and transport:** Many construction and trade services are taxed at 5%–8% instead of 15%. For instance, government-funded construction work is 5%, and wholesale/retail (auctioneering, vehicle dealerships, etc.) is generally 8%【11†L948-L956】【10†L881-L889】. Local bus transport and parking are 5%【10†L881-L889】.  
  - **Hospitality and rentals:** Taxi and rent-a-car services (via apps) are 5%【10†L881-L889】. Hospitality services (hotels, restaurants) can be 5% or 8% under certain conditions (e.g. payments by digital card may qualify for 8%).  
  - **Professional/IT services:** Research & development, legal and accounting services are generally 8%【11†L948-L956】. Some IT and software licensing services (especially if exported) can be as low as 3%【11†L923-L931】【11†L948-L956】.  
  - **Finance and insurance:** Motor third-party insurance is 5%【10†L881-L889】, while foreign exchange services (“spread” on forex trades) are 3%【11†L898-L903】. Other financial services are mostly at the standard rate.  
  - **Export services:** Several categories of services exported outside Pakistan are taxed at reduced rates to promote exports (e.g. call-center services at 3%, certain IT exports at 3%).  
- **Input tax conditions:** The bill also notes that when a reduced rate applies, input tax credits may be restricted unless the provider opts into the reduced rate option as prescribed (mirroring conditions under federal law)【23†L275-L284】.  

## Newly Exempt Services (First Schedule)  
The First Schedule of the Act (list of exempt services) has been overhauled. Key exempt categories include (with major conditions or exceptions noted):

- **Construction (CPC 54):** Exempt services include construction of Export Processing Zones, Special Economic Zones and official buildings, construction of small private houses (≤10,000 sq ft for owner use), low-cost government housing (plots ≤125 sq yd or houses ≤900 sq ft)【8†L339-L347】. Farm maintenance/repair is also exempt.  
- **Trade (CPC 611, 62):** Wholesale (611) and retail (62) trade services are generally exempt.  **Exceptions:** Services on a fee/contract basis or by ship-chandlers are *not* exempt【8†L374-L382】.  
- **Accommodation and food (CPC 63):** Many small-scale hospitality services are exempt – e.g. private clubs with low fees, student hostel accommodations, in-flight catering on foreign-bound flights, and restaurants/caterers with annual turnover ≤Rs.5 million.  **Exceptions:** Exemption does *not* apply to air-conditioned venues, franchises, outlets with multiple branches, high-bill establishments, or banquet services in hotels/clubs【8†L374-L382】.  
- **Passenger transport (CPC 64):** Most public passenger transport is exempt, *except* rent-a-car/vehicle rental and cab-aggregator services, and charter flights within Sindh【8†L426-L433】.  
- **Agriculture and storage:** Farm-related support (e.g. fumigation, cleaning for horticulture) is exempt【9†L542-L548】. Warehousing/storage of food/agricultural commodities (CPC 672) is exempt【8†L440-L448】.  
- **Utilities (CPC 69):** Electricity, gas and water distribution are exempt on own account (except certain generation services under CPC 69111)【8†L444-L449】.  
- **Central banking (CPC 71110):** Exempt (nil conditions)【8†L449-L450】.  
- **Insurance (CPC 713):** Exempt except for commercial non-life insurance. Specifically, individual life insurance (non-group) up to PKR 500,000 cover, crop insurance, individual health insurance, and marine export insurance are exempt【8†L451-L460】. Other insurance services (e.g. general insurance, large corporate) are taxable.  
- **Financial regulators (CPC 71552):** Services by the State Bank, Competition Commission, and SECP are exempt【8†L467-L471】.  
- **Real estate leasing (CPC 7211):** Exempt when leasing immovable property for agriculture, by religious bodies between religions, or residential/hostel buildings used by educational institutions【8†L472-L480】. Commercial or mixed-use leases remain taxable.  
- **IT and software exports (CPC 7331, 8313–8316):** Licensing rights to use computer software and related services are exempt if the service is exported (deliverable outside Pakistan) and the value is received in foreign exchange through banking channels【8†L492-L501】. This also applies to IT consulting, development, hosting, and network services exported from Sindh.  
- **Research & development (CPC 81):** Exempt when provided by HEC-recognized educational institutions【8†L506-L510】.  
- **Professional exports (CPC 822):** Accounting, auditing, bookkeeping services are exempt if exported (with foreign exchange receipt)【8†L512-L520】.  
- **Veterinary (CPC 835):** All veterinary services exempt (nil conditions)【9†L522-L526】.  
- **Advertising (CPC 8363):** Exempt for government‐funded ads, UNICEF public service ads, and print media ad space (except commission-based)【9†L522-L531】.  
- **News (CPC 844) & Library/Archives (845):** Exempt (nil conditions)【9†L538-L542】.  
- **Cleaning services (CPC 853):** Exempt when related to agriculture, horticulture, animal husbandry or dairy farming【9†L542-L548】.  
- **Travel/tour operators (CPC 855):** Exempt for Hajj/Umrah services and educational trips organized by bona fide schools (non-commercial)【9†L548-L556】.  
- **Call centers (CPC 85931) and support services (85999):** Exempt if services are exported, with value received in foreign exchange and reported to SBP【9†L560-L569】.  
- **Event services (CPC 85961):** Convention/wedding hall services are exempt for small halls (plot ≤800 sq yards) that are not air-conditioned, not in hotels/clubs, not franchise, and not multi-branch【9†L572-L580】.  
- **Agriculture support (CPC 861):** All support services to agriculture and fishing are exempt, *except* “support & operation services to hunting”【9†L591-L595】.  
- **Maintenance/repair (CPC 871):** Exempt when related to agricultural machinery or small workshops (turnover ≤Rs.4m) for auto/electronics repair and car washing【9†L596-L604】.  
- **Toll manufacturing (CPC 892–893):** Manufacturing on physical inputs owned by others (on a toll basis) is exempt, analogous to federal toll processing exemption【9†L621-L629】.  
- **Printing services (CPC 8912):** Exempt for printing newspapers, periodicals, journals and textbooks on contract【9†L638-L642】.  
- **Public administration (CPC 91):** Services rendered by federal, provincial or local governments “to the community as a whole” are exempt【9†L642-L646】.  
- **Education (CPC 92):** Exempt generally, but **not** if fees per student exceed Rs.500,000 per year, or for sport schools (CPC 92912) operated commercially【9†L648-L656】.  
- **Healthcare (CPC 931):** Exempt generally, but **not** for cosmetic/plastic surgery (aesthetic purposes), high-priced doctor consults (>Rs.3,000), or private hospital rooms/ward charges above Rs.25,000/day【9†L656-L664】.  
- **Beauty salons (CPC 972):** Exempt if annual turnover ≤Rs.2.5m.  Exemptions do **not** apply to salon services in hotels/clubs, franchises, multi-branch outlets, or those with high utility bills【9†L672-L680】.  
- **Social/environmental services (CPC 933–944, 964):** Many community and environmental services are exempt.  For example, residential care and social services for the elderly/disabled are exempt; government remediation/environmental services exempt; museums, athlete services, sports facilities, etc. have broad exemptions【9†L669-L677】【10†L712-L720】.  
- **Membership organizations (CPC 95):** Exempt if service is against a fixed membership fee (non-professional services)【9†L704-L707】.  
- **Entertainment (CPC 96150, 963, 964):** Film projection (96150) and museum services (964) are exempt.  Certain performing arts (963) have exemptions; e.g. stage designers are taxed.  
- **Laundry (CPC 971):** Exempt for laundries/dry cleaners with turnover ≤Rs.2.5m, unless they are located in hotels, are franchises/multi-branch, etc.【10†L712-L720】.  
- **Funeral (CPC 973), domestic (CPC 98), extraterritorial (CPC 99):** These services are exempt (nil conditions).  
- **Small-turnover threshold:**  A new **general exemption** is provided: *all* services provided by a person whose total turnover does not exceed Rs.4 million in a year are exempt【10†L742-L750】, subject to some exclusions (e.g. services to withholding agents, registered businesses, etc. are not covered by this threshold exemption).  

These changes greatly expand the scope of exempt services.  Businesses should review the First Schedule to see if their services now qualify as exempt (often subject to the conditions above).

## Procedural and Administrative Updates  

- **Expanded exemption powers (Sec.10):** The Board may now exempt services or classes of persons with government approval.  New sub-clauses allow, for example, the SRB to exempt specific taxpayers, recipients or classes of taxpayers wholly or partly from tax【7†L239-L247】.  Exemptions can be back-dated if announced later. This formalizes and broadens the Board’s notification powers.  
- **Filing penalties revised (Sec.43):** Penalties for non-compliance have been updated for simplicity and higher deterrence.  For instance, the late-return penalty is now **Rs.100 per day** of delay (instead of Rs.10,000 per month)【23†L300-L304】.  Failure to pay tax due carries a penalty of Rs.10,000 or 5% of tax (whichever is higher) if not paid within 5 days【23†L305-L314】.  The obstruction-of-officer penalty is doubled to **Rs.100,000** or 100% of due tax【23†L344-L348】.  (In all cases the option of prosecution still exists.) These changes align Sindh penalties more closely with the federal sales tax system.  
- **Professional member of Tax Tribunal (Sec.60):**  The eligibility for appointment as the technical member of the SRB Appellate Tribunal is made stricter.  Now a candidate must have been Commissioner SRB for at least **8 years** (with 3 years as Commissioner Appeals)【7†L281-L289】, instead of the previous 5 years.  
- **Active‐taxpayer requirement (Sec.72A):**  The amendment inserts a requirement that anyone applying for a license or permission to provide a service must also be an “active taxpayer” under clause 2(1A). In practice, this means SRB (with government approval) can prevent regulators from issuing/renewing trade licenses unless the business is registered and current in its sales-tax filing【7†L287-L289】【24†L1-L4】.  
- **Classification code (Sec.72B):**  A new section allows the SRB to notify a classification code (based on CPC) for services【7†L293-L302】. Importantly, however, the code itself does *not* determine whether a service is taxable or not – it is merely for administrative classification.  Any dispute over classification is to be resolved by the SRB (whose decision is final)【7†L293-L302】.  
- **Jurisdiction clarification:** By expressly excluding services under federal legislative power (see Definitions above), the law avoids overlap with federal taxes. This ensures Sindh does not tax services reserved for Islamabad’s jurisdiction【7†L175-L179】.  
- **Transitional provisions:** A new Section 72C clarifies that *all* services that were subject to Sindh tax on June 30, 2025 continue to be taxed at the same rates after the amendments, unless they are expressly exempted or re-rated【7†L306-L312】. This provides certainty that existing taxpayers aren’t inadvertently deregistered.  
- **“Removal of difficulties” (Sec.74):** The SRB (with government approval) is empowered to issue orders adapting or modifying provisions of the Act for up to three years after commencement【20†L1256-L1263】. This allows practical tweaks (e.g. through notifications) to ensure the amendments work smoothly, but only for a limited transitional period.

Each of these procedural changes has been carefully enacted to refine the tax law’s application and enforcement. Business owners should note, for example, that their eligibility for exemptions or licenses may depend on these new rules. 

**Sources:** Official finance act amendments【6†L146-L148】【7†L207-L214】【7†L239-L247】【8†L339-L347】【9†L656-L664】【10†L742-L750】 and authoritative commentaries【23†L300-L304】【20†L1256-L1263】 have been used to prepare this summary. Each cited excerpt is from the Sindh Finance Act 2025 or its published analyses.

### **Online Application System for Change of Tax Jurisdiction Launched**  
The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has rolled out an online facility allowing taxpayers to apply for a change of jurisdiction without visiting tax offices. This digital process aims to streamline requests, reduce delays, and improve transparency in how cases are transferred between field formations.

### **Supreme Court Clarifies Section 66 of the Sales Tax Act**  
In a significant ruling, the Supreme Court has provided clarity on how Section 66 of the Sales Tax Act applies to refund claims. The decision narrows disputes over the time limitation and procedural hurdles for refunds, setting a precedent for both taxpayers and the FBR to follow in future cases.

### **Advance Tax Obligations Under Section 147 Highlighted**  
Tax authorities have reiterated that advance tax under Section 147 of the Income Tax Ordinance must be paid based on the prescribed timelines, regardless of seasonal or structural business changes. Companies are urged to correctly compute and deposit advance tax to avoid penalties and interest.

### **Government Employees in Advocacy Roles Questioned**  
A recent review has flagged concerns about government employees appearing as advocates or tax consultants for private parties, which raises conflict-of-interest and ethics issues. Regulatory bodies are examining measures to restrict such practices and enforce compliance with service rules.

### **FTO Reports on Performance and Maladministration Cases**  
The Federal Tax Ombudsman (FTO) has published new performance figures, showing a sharp rise in complaints against tax authorities and an increasing number of suo motu interventions. The FTO continues to push for timely disposal of complaints and systemic reforms in tax administration.

### **Income Tax Return Filing Trends and Compliance Drive**  
The FBR is intensifying efforts to increase the number of income tax return filers ahead of the September 30 deadline. Tax bars and associations are urging extensions, while the FBR emphasizes that timely, accurate filing is essential for avoiding notices and for self-assessment under Section 120.

---

### **Pakistan Signals IMF It Will Miss Quarterly Tax Target**  
Islamabad has formally told the IMF it will fall short of the Rs 3.1 trillion July–September tax goal. Officials are banking on inflation, stronger economic activity, and higher solar panel imports to close a Rs 190 billion gap later in the year. The FBR also walked back a controversial “fair market value” data-gathering column in tax returns after political pushback【9†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  

### **Solar Imports and Circular Debt: The Twin Pillars of Revenue Strategy**  
Tax authorities highlighted two pillars to reassure the IMF: boosting revenue through a 10% levy on solar imports (already yielding Rs 6 billion in two months) and tackling the Rs 1.25 trillion power-sector circular debt. A syndicated Islamic-finance package with 18 banks will retire this debt within six years, backed by a Rs 3.23/unit surcharge to guarantee repayment and pass Rs 350 billion savings to consumers【9†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  

### **Petroleum Division Pushes for GST Waiver Resolution to Unlock $6 Billion Refinery Upgrades**  
The petroleum ministry will use the IMF review mission to press for a clear framework on GST for petroleum products. The current tax holiday has cost refiners Rs 40 billion and discouraged new investment—including from Chinese partners—jeopardising planned upgrades under the Pakistan Brownfield Oil Refining Policy 2023【9†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  

### **Super Tax Challenge in the Supreme Court: Banks vs. Section 4B**  
A five-member bench is hearing constitutional challenges to the super tax regime. Banks argue they face a punitive 39% rate compared to 29% for other corporates and warn of double taxation. The case tests how far Parliament can go in amending income-tax law without violating constitutional protections【9†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  

### **FTO Directs FBR to Operationalise ‘Significant Economic Presence’ Rules**  
In a rare own-motion investigation, the Federal Tax Ombudsman has faulted the FBR for “neglect, inattention, delay and ineptitude” in implementing Section 101(3A) and (3B), which were designed to tax non-resident digital and educational businesses extracting revenue from Pakistan. Without prescribed thresholds, huge outflows remain untaxed despite tripling of the offshore digital-services rate to 15% in 2025【9†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  

### **Export Facilitation Schemes Cost Exchequer Rs 44 Billion in FY 2023-24**  
The FBR’s new Tax Expenditure Report shows nine schemes—including DTRE, EPZs, manufacturing bonds, export-oriented units, and temporary import concessions—eroded nearly Rs 44 billion in revenue last year. Chapter 99 of the Customs Tariff also recorded exemptions on inputs, packing material and machinery for re-export【9†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  

### **FBR Drops ‘Estimated Market Value’ Column to Ease Compliance**  
Following a committee headed by the law minister and approved by the prime minister, the FBR has removed the controversial column requiring filers to declare estimated fair market value of assets in their tax returns. The step aims to simplify filing ahead of the 30 September deadline after severe criticism from tax bar associations that warned it would depress filer numbers【9†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  

### **Jewellers Put on Notice: Compliance Grading System Rolled Out**  
In a high-profile meeting with the Sarafa Gems and Jewellers Association, the FBR revealed that 14,000 jewellers had not filed any return and 15,000 had under-reported income. Raids are suspended until 30 September while a four-category grading system is launched, requiring shops to display compliance plates—green for top-tier taxpayers and yellow for mid-tier—with stricter action promised thereafter【9†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  

### **Karachi Port ‘Customs Breach’ Disputed: Terminal Operator Cites Tribunal Orders**  
V.N. Lakhani & Co. has issued a detailed rebuttal to reports of a “major customs breach” involving restricted steel consignments. The firm says the clearance was executed under Customs Appellate Tribunal instructions and Pakistan Single Window controls, disputing claims of illegal release or system holds and reserving its right to pursue legal action for alleged defamatory reporting【9†files_uploaded_in_conversation】.  

---

---

## ⏳ Need More Time to File Your Tax Return?  
**Here’s how to request an extension legally and on time!**  

### 1️⃣ Understand the Rule  
Under Section 119 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, a taxpayer may apply to the Commissioner Inland Revenue for an extension of time to file an income tax return or statement. This must be done **before the due date** of filing.  

### 2️⃣ Prepare Your Application  
Your application should:  
- Clearly state the **reason(s)** for the delay (e.g., awaiting certificates, illness, system issues).  
- Specify the **additional time** you’re requesting.  
- Include your **NTN/FTN**, tax year, and contact details.  

### 3️⃣ File Electronically via IRIS  
Log in to the FBR IRIS portal and select **“Extension of Time for Filing Return”** under the e-services menu.  
Fill out the online form, attach supporting documents (if any), and submit.  

### 4️⃣ Await Approval  
The Commissioner may:  
- Grant extension up to **15 days** (or longer in exceptional circumstances).  
- Reject your application if reasons are insufficient.  

You will receive confirmation or rejection through your IRIS account.  

### 5️⃣ File Within the Extended Date  
If approved, file your return **within the granted time** to avoid penalties under Section 182 of the Ordinance.  

---

### ⚠️ Quick Tips for Success  
- Apply as early as possible; don’t wait until the last day.  
- Keep evidence supporting your reason for delay.  
- Check your IRIS notifications regularly for updates on your application.  

---

**Subject:** Response to Notice Regarding Sindh Workers’ Profits Participation Fund (SWPPF) – Tax Year 2024  

**Dear Sir,**  

We acknowledge receipt of your notice requiring deposit of the Sindh Workers’ Profits Participation Fund (“SWPPF”) for the year ended June 30, 2024. The audited financial statements for the said year were duly reviewed and approved by the Company’s Board of Directors on September 23, 2025. However, in accordance with Section 233 of the Companies Ordinance, 1984, audited accounts must be laid before the shareholders at the Annual General Meeting for adoption. The Company has therefore scheduled its Annual General Meeting/Annual Review for November 11, 2025 to seek the shareholders’ formal approval of the audited accounts.  

The approval of the shareholders is a statutory prerequisite before any final appropriation of profits or allocation of funds can be made. Only after this approval can the Company lawfully proceed with the obligations set out in the Sindh Companies Profits (Workers’ Participation) Act, 2015 (“the Act”), including transferring the prescribed percentage of profits to the SWPPF Fund, calculating each eligible worker’s share, disbursing such shares, and reconciling any unclaimed or leftover balance to be deposited with the Sindh Revenue Board in terms of Section 6 of the Act.  

These steps are not mere formalities but involve detailed computations, verification of eligible workers, disbursement of amounts and reconciliation with statutory returns. Experience shows that this process requires at least three months after the Annual General Meeting to complete transparently and in full compliance with the Act. It is therefore premature at this stage to determine or deposit any “leftover balance” of SWPPF with SRB for the year ended June 30, 2024.  

We assure you that once the shareholders’ approval has been obtained and the statutory process completed, any balance determined to be payable under the Act will be deposited promptly with SRB. This approach ensures strict compliance with both the Companies Ordinance, 1984 and the Sindh Companies Profits (Workers’ Participation) Act, 2015, and safeguards the rights of eligible workers while also meeting SRB’s regulatory requirements.  

Yours faithfully,  
For and on behalf of  
[Client Name]  

---

### Introduction of Final Tax Regime on Digitally Ordered Goods and Services  

A new final tax regime under **Section 6A** of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 has been introduced to levy tax on persons receiving payments for **digitally ordered goods and services**. This regime applies to goods and services delivered from within Pakistan through locally operated online platforms—including online marketplaces and websites—at the following rates:

| Sr. No. | Collection Agent | Final Tax Rate for Seller (Section 6A) | Withholding Tax Rate (Section 153(2A)) |  
|---------|------------------|----------------------------------------|---------------------------------------|  
| (i) | Payment Intermediary | Filer: 1% / Non-Filer: 1% | 2% |  
| (ii) | Courier Business | Filer: 2% / Non-Filer: 2% | 4% |  

Export proceeds already subject to withholding tax under **Sections 154 and 154A** are excluded from Section 6A. Moreover, where tax is collected under Section 6A by the designated withholding agents, no deduction of withholding tax under **Section 153(1)** will apply.

---

### Filing Requirements  

**(i) Payment Intermediaries & Courier Services**  
Every payment intermediary and courier service responsible for collecting tax under Section 6A must file a **quarterly withholding statement** in the prescribed form setting out:  

- Seller’s name, NTN/CNIC and address;  
- Transaction date, invoice number/unique identifier, and total transaction value;  
- Amount of tax deducted at the time of payment to the seller; and  
- Any other particulars as prescribed.  

**(ii) Online Marketplaces**  
Every online marketplace operating in Pakistan is required to submit a **monthly statement** containing the following details for each vendor registered on its platform:  

- Name, address, Sales Tax and Income Tax registration numbers;  
- Transactional and aggregated monthly turnover of the seller; and  
- Amount deposited into the seller’s bank account against such transactions.  

Other provisions of **Section 165**—such as timing of filing, revision of statements, extension of time and reconciliation—also apply to these statements.

---

### Registration Requirements  

- Any person selling digitally ordered goods or services from within Pakistan through an online marketplace or courier service must **obtain income tax registration (NTN)**.  
- Online marketplaces and courier services must **not allow unregistered vendors** to use their platforms for e-commerce transactions unless the vendor holds a valid NTN.  

---

### Penalties  

To ensure compliance, the following penalties have been prescribed:  

| Sr. No. | Offence | Penalty |  
|---------|---------|---------|  
| 1 | Failure to furnish statements within the due date (including online marketplaces, payment intermediaries, and courier services). | Rs. 50,000 if the tax collected/withheld has been paid within due date and the statement is filed within 90 days; otherwise Rs. 2,500 per day of default (minimum Rs. 10,000). Where no tax was required to be deducted/collected during the period, minimum penalty remains Rs. 10,000. |  
| 2 | Failure of a banking company, payment gateway or courier service to deduct or deposit tax under **Section 160** on payments for digitally ordered goods or digitally delivered services via an e-commerce platform. | 100% of the amount of tax involved. |  
| 3 | Failure by a seller of digitally ordered goods or digitally delivered services through an online marketplace to obtain mandatory registration under the Ordinance. | Rs. 500,000 for the first default; Rs. 1,000,000 for every subsequent default. |  

---

### Key Definitions  

- **Courier Service:** Any specialized entity providing fast, secure, often tracked transportation of documents, packages and small freight—typically door-to-door—with delivery of digitally ordered goods, including collection of cash (CoD) on behalf of sellers. This includes (but is not limited to):  
  - Logistic services  
  - Ride-hailing services  
  - Food delivery platforms  
  - E-commerce services  

- **Payment Intermediary:** Any third-party entity—including banking companies, financial institutions, licensed foreign exchange companies or payment gateways—that facilitates transfer of funds or payment instructions between two or more parties to enable, process, route or settle payments without being the ultimate source or recipient.  

- **Digitally Delivered Services:** Any service delivered over the internet or electronic networks where delivery is automated and requires minimal or no human intervention. Examples include music/audio/video streaming, cloud services, online software, telemedicine, e-learning, online banking, architectural design, consultancy reports, accounting files or any other online facility.  

- **E-Commerce:** Sale or purchase of goods and services conducted over computer networks through methods specially designed for receiving or placing orders—via websites, mobile applications or online marketplaces—using digital ordering features such as mobile phones, tablets or automated computer-to-computer systems.  

- **Online Marketplace:** Expanded to include online interfaces facilitating, for a fee, direct interaction between multiple buyers and multiple sellers via digital orders for supply of goods and services, regardless of whether the platform takes ownership of goods or provides/render the services being sold.  

---

## **Super Tax on High-Earning Persons in Pakistan**  
**[Division IIB of Part I of the First Schedule]**

The **Finance Act 2025 (FA 2025)** revises the **super tax rates on high earners under Section 4C**. From tax year 2025 onward, individuals, AOPs and companies with high income brackets face the following rates:

| Income under Section 4C | Tax Year 2025 | Tax Year 2026 & onwards |
|-------------------------|--------------|------------------------|
| Up to Rs.150 million | 0% | 0% |
| Rs.150–200 million | 1% | 1% |
| Rs.200–250 million | 2% | 1.5% |
| Rs.250–300 million | 3% | 2.5% |
| Rs.300–350 million | 4% | 3.5% |
| Rs.350–400 million | 6% | 5.5% |
| Rs.400–500 million | 8% | 7.5% |
| Exceeding Rs.500 million | 10% | 10% |

This change is designed to enhance **progressive taxation in Pakistan** and increase revenue from high-income segments.

---

## **Tax on Dividends from Mutual Funds**  
**[Division III of Part I and Division I of Part III of the First Schedule]**

Previously, **dividends from mutual funds** were taxed at 15%, except for funds deriving 50% or more income from profit on debt (taxed at 25%). FA 2025 refines this:

- **Dividends from mixed investments** (equity + debt) will be taxed at **15% and 25% respectively**, based on proportionate income derived from average annual investment in equity and debt securities.  
- For **corporate recipients**, the component derived from **debt securities** is now taxed at **29% instead of 25%**.  

Corresponding amendments have been made to **withholding tax provisions on such dividends** to ensure alignment with these revised rates.

---

## **Profit on Debt – Revised Tax Rates**  
**[Division IIIA of Part I, Division IA of Part III of the First Schedule]**

The **profit on debt tax regime** has been overhauled. Below are the new withholding tax rates (percentages in brackets represent rates for those **not on the Active Taxpayers’ List (ATL)**):

| Recipient | National Savings Schemes etc. | Govt. Securities | Bank Deposits |
|-----------|------------------------------|-----------------|---------------|
| **Individuals** | 15% (30%) | 15% (40%) | 20% (40%) |
| **AOPs** | 15% (30%) | 20% (40%) | 20% (40%) |
| **Companies** | 15% (30%) | 20% (40%) | 20% (40%) |

For **individuals and AOPs**, where profit on debt does not exceed **Rs.5 million**, the withholding tax will constitute **final tax**. This change incentivises digital and documented savings.

---

## **Fee for Offshore Digital Services**  
**[Section 152(1C) read with Division IV of Part I of the First Schedule]**

The **tax rate on fees for offshore digital services** has increased from **10% to 15%**. However, **banking companies and financial institutions** will not deduct tax where the recipient is already liable to **Digital Presence Proceeds Levy** and the same has been collected, preventing double taxation in Pakistan’s **digital economy**.

---

## **Enhanced Withholding Tax Rates for Services and Contracts**  
**[Division II and Division III of Part III of the First Schedule]**

Withholding tax rates under **Sections 152(2A) and 153(1)** have been enhanced:

- **PE of Non-Resident Person**: 8% on listed services such as transport, freight forwarding, courier, manpower outsourcing, hotel, security, software development, engineering, car rental, inspection, certification, training, oilfield services, and other specified services.  
- **Resident Person**: 6% on the above services.  
- **IT services and IT-enabled services** remain at 4%.  
- **Other services**: Companies 15%, Others 15%.  
- **Execution of contract by sportspersons**: increased from 10% to 15%.
